docs.title: Development guide
docs.text:
Thanks for helping improve ddi-l! Two documents cover contributing:

  • CONTRIBUTING.md on GitHub is the short version: set up, run the checks, open a pull request. Start there.
  • This guide is the in-depth reference behind it: the architecture, the XSD-driven code generator, adding a DDI version, the XML backends, the documentation toolchain, and the release process.

docs.title: Set up your environment
docs.text:
Python 3.11 or newer is required. The project is managed with uv, and uv.lock is the single source of truth for dependency versions; CI installs from it with --locked.

uv sync --group dev              # Runtime + development dependencies
uv sync --group dev --extra full # ...plus the optional lxml backend
uv sync --group docs             # Documentation toolchain

uv.lock installs ddi-l-native as its pure-Python stand-in (native/fallback/), so none of these needs Rust, and tests run on lxml or the standard library. The XML backends says how to build and test the native core.

Prefix commands with uv run (uv run pytest), or activate the environment with source .venv/bin/activate.

full is an extra, not a dependency group

The optional lxml backend is declared under [project.optional-dependencies], so it installs with --extra full. Asking for it as a group (--group full) fails.

If you prefer plain pip:

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e '.[full]' ./native/fallback --group dev   # pip 25.1+ reads groups

docs.title: Quality gates
docs.text:
Run these before opening a pull request:

uv run ruff format --check .   # Formatting
uv run ruff check .            # Linting (includes Google-style docstrings)
uv run mypy src tests          # Type checking (blocking in CI)
uv run pytest                  # Tests (target: 90% coverage)
uvx pip-audit --strict         # Dependency vulnerability scan
git diff --exit-code           # A test run must not modify tracked files

pytest runs on every core (-n auto, pytest-xdist); pass -n 0 to run in one process, as --pdb needs.

ruff and mypy are pinned to exact versions in the dev group. A new release of either can change what counts as a violation, so the pin is what keeps CI reproducible, so bump it deliberately, in its own commit.

The Makefile also provides:

make release-check             # Build distributions and verify packaging
make docs-build                # Build docs with strict mode
make docs-serve                # Live preview server

make release-check is the gate that matters before a release. It builds both distributions, asserts the bundled XSDs and example files are present, asserts that ddi_l is the only top-level package in the wheel, then installs the wheel into a clean virtualenv and validates a document with it.

docs.title: Mutation testing
docs.text:
Coverage says a line ran. It does not say a test would notice if the line were wrong. mutmut checks that: it makes small changes to the code ("mutants"), runs the tests, and reports each change no test noticed (a "survivor").

make mutation                           # mutmut run, then the baseline check
uv run mutmut results                   # what survived
uv run mutmut show <mutant-name>        # the diff for one survivor
uv run mutmut run <mutant-name>         # re-check one after adding a test

Scope. [tool.mutmut] in pyproject.toml lists seventeen modules with real branching: lint, the fact base its rules share and what incremental lint keeps, the Colectica rules, the condition reader and editor, the spec language with its evaluator and solver encoding, conformance with its instrument index, the reachability of a flow, validation, I/O and conversion. Not the generated models, whose mutants are almost all equivalent.

The gate. tests/mutation_baseline.txt lists the known survivors. scripts/check_mutation.py fails when a mutant survives that the list does not name, and when a listed one no longer survives, so the list only shrinks. .github/workflows/mutation.yml runs both monthly (on the 1st) and on demand; a full run takes hours, so it is not run on every PR.

Examples. Under mutmut, each property test draws at most 30 examples, the same ones on every run (tests/helpers/examples.py): it runs once for each mutant it covers, and a mutant must be caught on every run or on none. The suite itself draws 300.

When the check fails on a new survivor, run mutmut show <name> and decide:

  • A real gap: a test would catch a bug like this one. Write that test.
  • Equivalent: no test can tell the mutant from the original, such as getattr(node, "nsmap", ) in place of getattr(node, "nsmap", None). Add the name to the baseline with # equivalent: and the reason.
  • Stdlib backend only: the run uses lxml, so a change to code only the standard-library backend runs survives. Add # stdlib backend only: and why.
  • Native backend only: likewise for code only the native backend runs, such as what incremental lint keeps (ddi_l/_incremental.py); its tests run on the native backend. Add # native backend only: and why.

Changing a function renumbers its mutants. After such a change, run uv run python scripts/check_mutation.py --update, which keeps the reasons of the entries still there, and read the diff of the baseline.

docs.title: Coding standards
docs.text:
• Line length: 88 characters.
  • Linting: ruff with E, F, W, I, N, UP, B, SIM, RUF, and D (Google docstrings) rule sets.
  • Type hints: mypy on src/ and tests/, blocking in CI.
  • Docstrings: Google style with Args:, Returns:, Raises: sections.
  • Tests: pytest with pytest-cov. Coverage target is 90%.
  • Imports: Ruff's isort integration handles ordering.

docs.title: XSD-driven codegen pipeline
docs.text: All model classes are generated from the DDI 3.3 XSD files. The XSD is the single source of truth for fields, element ordering, namespaces, and documentation text.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. codegen/xsd_introspect.py extracts the complete content model from the XSD (the ordered particle tree, cardinality, namespaces, attributes, mixed flag, and xs:documentation text.
  2. codegen/generate_model_bases.py emits field-only base dataclasses under src/ddi_l/models/_generated/. Each carries its XSD-derived fields plus three class-level tables: _FIELD_XML_MAP (field name to element tag and type), _ATTR_XML_MAP (field name to XML attribute), and _ELEMENT_ORDER (the XSD-declared child order). It also emits _generated/label_slots.py, a schema-wide table of which elements may carry an r:Label, used by the ddi.maintainable.labels lint rule to avoid asking for labels the schema does not allow) and by ALLOW_LABELS, which is derived from it at class creation rather than kept by hand. A second schema-wide table, _generated/fixed_attributes.py, records the attributes the XSD pins to a fixed value; the JSON-to-XML conversion drops them, since an attribute the schema pins carries no information and writing it back would make the round-trip return more than it was given. Three more serve round-trip fidelity: _generated/child_order.py gives each content model's children in rank groups (members of a repeating choice share one, so their interleaving survives), which the models use to put content they keep without mapping back in schema order at any depth; _generated/element_layout.py records which empty elements hold text, attribute declaration order and substitution-group heads, for the Colectica writer (ddi_l.colectica); and _generated/fragment_items.py lists every item type a ddi:Fragment can carry, from which ddi_l.models.items registers a model for each type without a hand-written one.
  3. The generic XML engine in MaintainableBase.from_xml() / .to_xml() (src/ddi_l/models/base.py) drives serialization off those tables, emitting children in XSD-declared order. Anything the tables do not name is preserved verbatim through the other_elements / other_attributes passthrough, so round-tripping never drops content.
  4. Hand-written classes in src/ddi_l/models/*.py inherit the generated bases and add only helpers, validation, and convenience constructors.

docs.title: Regenerating models
docs.text:
uv run python -m codegen.generate_model_bases

CI includes a drift check that fails if generated code differs from what the XSD would produce:

uv run python -m codegen.generate_model_bases
git diff --exit-code src/ddi_l/models/_generated/

Never edit files under _generated/ by hand.

docs.title: Coverage audit
docs.text: uv run python -m codegen.coverage_audit regenerates codegen/COVERAGE_AUDIT.md, which measures how much of the XSD the generated layer exposes as named fields versus preserves through passthrough.

docs.title: Supporting a new DDI version
docs.text: This section exists so the next person does not have to reverse-engineer what is tied to a DDI version. It is deliberately a decision framework rather than a migration script: DDI 4.0 is not fully released, and a step-by-step plan written against a specification that has not landed would be fiction.

docs.title: What is actually version-coupled
docs.text:
The single most misunderstood thing about this package:

Validation is multi-version. The model layer is 3.3-only.

doc.validate(version="3.1") genuinely works. ddi_l.models.* is a DDI 3.3 model that happens to also validate 3.1 and 3.2 documents. Adding "3.4" to SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS would buy you validation and nothing else.

Coupling point Where Notes Bundled XSDs src/ddi_l/schemas/ddi/v3_1/, v3_2/, v3_3/ Shipped in the wheel; resolve via importlib.resources Supported versions _schema_versions.SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS Drives normalize_version() and the CLI's --version Namespace templates _schema_versions._SCHEMA_NAMESPACE_TEMPLATES Assumes every namespace is ddi:{module}:{suffix} Archive checksums _schema_versions.SCHEMA_ARCHIVE_CHECKSUMS SHA-256 per release; verified on download Schema refresh schema_sync.update_schema_package() Downloads and rewrites a v3_x/ tree Version detection schema_loader/_versions.py Infers the version from a document's namespace or schemaLocation Codegen entry point codegen/xsd_introspect.py Hardcoded to 3.3: SCHEMA_DIR = .../v3_3, ENTRY_SCHEMA = instance_3_3.xsd, and a literal namespace map

docs.title: Path A: a new DDI 3.x minor release
docs.text:
This path is well-trodden; 3.1 and 3.2 were both added this way.

  1. Record the release archive's SHA-256 in SCHEMA_ARCHIVE_CHECKSUMS.
  2. Run update_schema_package("3.x") to populate src/ddi_l/schemas/ddi/v3_x/.
  3. Add the version to SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS.
  4. Confirm the ddi:{module}:{suffix} convention still holds. If the release adds a namespace, tests/test_schema_versions.py will fail: it derives the expected set from the shipped XSDs rather than trusting the hand-written list.
  5. Decide explicitly whether the generated model layer moves to the new version. It is not automatic and it is not free: regenerating against a new XSD changes _FIELD_XML_MAP, _ATTR_XML_MAP and _ELEMENT_ORDER, which changes serialized output, which invalidates every golden fixture under tests/fixtures/. Treat it as a breaking change.

docs.title: Path B: DDI 4.0
docs.text:
Do not assume this is Path A with a bigger number. This section records what the DDI Lifecycle 4.0 beta 4 model says, read from tag v4.0-beta.4 (January 2026) of ddialliance/ddimodel, the release the DDI Alliance put forward as the last beta before public review. These are facts about a beta: recheck each one against the final release before building on it.

Generate from the model, not the XSD. 4.0 is model-first. Its source is a set of CSV files maintained with COGS (the DDI Alliance's Convention-based Ontology Generation System), and XML Schema is one of about a dozen formats COGS generates from them, alongside JSON Schema, OWL, SHACL, ShEx, UML XMI, LinkML and a C# library. codegen/xsd_introspect.py could introspect the published XSD, but the CSVs carry more:

Source What it holds ItemTypes/<Name>/<Name>.csv 172 item types (the identifiable objects), one row per property with its type and cardinality CompositeTypes/<Name>/<Name>.csv 320 structured value types ItemTypes/<Name>/Extends.<Base> Inheritance: 72 item types extend Versionable, 42 Maintainable, the rest one of nine other abstract bases DeprecatedNamespace, DeprecatedElementOrAttribute columns For 2,325 of the 2,631 properties, the 3.3 namespace each came from and whether it was an element or an attribute; the other 306 are new in 4.0 Topics/ Eight groupings: Agent, Classification, Data Capture, Data Description, Foundational and Study, plus the catch-alls "All Content Items" and "Non-Packaging Items"

The Deprecated* columns matter most to this package: the 3.3 to 4.0 mapping is part of the model, not something to reverse-engineer.

The namespace convention does not survive. The official build publishes the XSD into one namespace, ddi:instance:4_0 (cogs publish-xsd ... --namespace "ddi:instance:4_0" in build/build-windows.bat), where 3.3 has seventeen. _build_release() formats every namespace from a single ddi:{module}:{suffix} template, and the generator writes one Python module per namespace, so neither carries over. 4.0 needs its own release description, and the generated modules need another grouping key: the model's topics, or each type's majority 3.3 namespace from the Deprecated* columns, which would keep today's module names.

Containment becomes reference. A property whose type is an item type is a reference, and 635 properties are. A 4.0 VariableScheme lists VariableReferences instead of containing Variable elements, so items stand alone and schemes point at them. The hand-written models assume 3.3 nesting (a Document walks StudyUnit → LogicalProduct → VariableScheme → Variable), which makes this the change with the widest reach, well beyond any rename.

Identification. Every 4.0 item has a required URN as well as Agency, ID and Version (Settings/Identification.csv and Identification.Mixin.csv). The 3.3 reference machinery maps onto this, but the URN is no longer optional.

A successor, with a long overlap. The DDI Alliance describes 4.0 as the 3.3 content in a structure that supports several syntaxes, so it succeeds 3.3 rather than sitting beside it the way DDI-CDI does. 3.3 files will be in use for years, so the conclusion is unchanged: add a second model package next to the existing one rather than migrating ddi_l.models, which would break every consumer for no benefit to people who still have 3.3 data.

Round-trip fidelity is still open. The other_elements / other_attributes passthrough and the golden fixtures are the guarantees this package is built on. The model says nothing about how they carry over; answer that before prototyping.

docs.title: Suggested order of work
docs.text:
1. Wait for the final release. Beta properties and types can still change.
  2. Validation only. Bundle the 4.0 XSD, add a release entry that bypasses the 3.x namespace template, teach schema_loader/_versions.py the ddi:instance:4_0 namespace, and add "4.0" to SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS. This is Path A plus that one exception, and it gives users validate(version="4.0") without touching the models. Take the file names and entry schema from the published package; they are not in the model repository.
  3. Models. Add a second front end to codegen/ that reads the COGS CSVs at a pinned ddimodel tag and writes generated bases into a separate package (for example ddi_l.models_v4), reusing the type mapping in generate_model_bases.py. Leave the 3.3 pipeline untouched.
  4. Conversion. Build a 3.3 ↔ 4.0 property map from the Deprecated* columns and base conversion on it. The 306 new properties need decisions by hand.

docs.title: Invariants to defend, whichever path is taken
docs.text:
These are what keep a future migration contained instead of a rewrite:

  • Everything generated stays behind src/ddi_l/models/_generated/ and is consumed only as base classes. Hand-written code must never import generator internals. This seam is why swapping the generator is a contained project.
  • The codegen drift check stays green. Regenerating on a clean tree must be a no-op, so a schema refresh and a generator change are distinguishable in review.
  • SCHEMA_ARCHIVE_CHECKSUMS stays populated, for the same reason.
  • One namespace list. codegen/xsd_introspect.py and _schema_versions.py both enumerate the DDI namespaces; tests/test_schema_versions.py checks them against the bundled schemas. Run it if you touch either.

docs.title: Synthetic namespaces, and the rule that governs them
docs.text:
_schema_versions._SYNTHETIC_NAMESPACE_TEMPLATES declares urn:ddi-l:extension:process:1 and urn:ddi-l:extension:methodology:1. No DDI Lifecycle release declares either. They hold model types DDI 3.3 does not define: Process, ProcessStep, ProcessControl, ProcessMethod, their schemes, plus MethodologyItem, MethodologyScheme and ReviewEvent. DDI's own process vocabulary (ProcessingEvent, ProcessingInstruction, ControlConstruct) lives in ddi:datacollection:3_3 and is modelled separately.

The rule: a type that has a home in the schema must use it. Synthetic namespaces are only for content DDI does not define. Methodology, for example, is a DDI 3.3 element and is written in ddi:datacollection:3_3.

tests/test_namespace_provenance.py enforces both halves: no model may emit a ddi:-shaped namespace that is neither schema-declared nor registered synthetic, and no type in a synthetic namespace may have a real element of that name in the XSDs. Adding a new synthetic type requires listing it explicitly, so it is a decision rather than an accident.

The synthetic namespaces are deliberately not ddi:-shaped, so nobody mistakes them for DDI Alliance namespaces, and they carry no DDI version: every release maps to the same URI. Version detection uses only the instance namespace and the schema filename.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
src/ddi_l/
  __init__.py                # Public API: new_study, open_ddi, Document
  document.py                # Document, DDIDocument, DDIFragment, StudyCursor
  _document_maintainables.py # Maintainable lookup / attachment helpers
  _document_namespaces.py    # Namespace handling for Document
  models/
    base.py                  # InternationalString, Reference, MaintainableBase
                             # and the generic from_xml / to_xml engine
    _generated/              # Generated field-only bases (do not edit)
    datacollection/          # DataCollection types (the one model subpackage)
    logicalproduct.py        # Variables, code lists, categories, NCubes
    conceptualcomponent.py   # Concepts, universes, conceptual variables
    reusable.py, study.py, archive.py, group.py, physical.py, process.py,
    quality.py, comparison.py, methodology.py, classification.py, ...
  schema_loader/             # Schema resolution, validation, JSON conversion
  schemas/                   # Bundled DDI 3.1 / 3.2 / 3.3 XSDs (CC-BY-4.0)
  examples/                  # Packaged sample instances and fixtures
  validation.py              # High-level validation
  lint.py                    # Lint engine and rules
  cli.py                     # CLI entry point (`ddi`)
  io.py                      # Low-level read/write and streaming helpers
  index.py                   # Identifier index for find() / reference checks
  registry/                  # Maintainable type registry
  schema_sync.py             # Refresh the bundled schema bundle

Supporting directories outside the package: codegen/ (build-time generators), tests/, benchmarks/, demo/, and docs/. None of these are packaged, so nothing in them may back a console script or be imported at runtime.

docs.title: The XML backends
docs.text:
lxml is an optional accelerator installed with ddi-l[full], and the native core (native/, the ddi-l-native wheel ddi-l depends on) another. Whether either is present must not change what ddi-l means by a document. DDI_L_XML_BACKEND=native|lxml|stdlib picks the backend for a test run.

ddi-l-native is published twice at each version: compiled wheels for the platforms in .github/workflows/publish.yml, and a pure-Python stand-in (native/fallback/) that pip takes anywhere else. Importing the stand-in raises ModuleNotFoundError, so ddi-l falls back to lxml or the standard library and installing it never compiles Rust. uv.lock installs the stand-in; build the real core over it (Rust, and on Windows Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload), then run with --no-sync, since uv sync and uv run put the stand-in back:

DDI_L_XML_BACKEND=lxml uv run pytest
uv pip install --reinstall-package ddi-l-native ./native
DDI_L_XML_BACKEND=native uv run --no-sync pytest --no-cov

Native elements behave like the standard library's, so the native backend shares the stdlib backend's helpers in ddi_l/_etree.py and only parses differently. The pure-Python code is the reference: tests/test_native.py checks the parser against the standard library's (and fuzzes it), and the native digests and source index against ddi_l/_lossless.py.

The Rust code lives in native/. After changing it, rebuild the extension and run its checks:

uv pip install --reinstall-package ddi-l-native ./native
cd native && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings

On the native backend, what lint and revise read from an element is kept under its content digest (ddi_l/_incremental.py), so a later call reads again only what changed. A reader passed to per_element or per_chunk must depend on the element alone. A rule in _PER_ITEM (ddi_l/colectica_lint.py) must report about an item from that item alone, through _Context.finding. tests/test_incremental.py checks, after random edits, that each run reports what a run that reads everything reports.

There is a real difference in how stdlib and lxml resolve prefixes that is worth understanding before touching serialization:

  • stdlib ElementTree resolves prefixes at serialization time, from a registry. ddi-l keeps that registry itself, per thread or task (it never writes ElementTree's process-wide one), so a prefix registered while building one document affects every later one in the same thread.
  • lxml resolves from each element's nsmap, which is fixed when the element is created. It cannot be rebound in place, which is why apply_namespace_map() returns a root rather than mutating one.

This asymmetry is the most common source of backend-specific behaviour, so run the suite on every backend when changing serialization.

docs.title: What is guaranteed
docs.text:
• Documents ddi-l authors serialize byte-identically on both backends. Every DDI namespace resolves to its canonical prefix, and declarations are hoisted onto the root. tests/test_backend_parity.py pins this.
  • Round-tripping never changes content, on either backend: same elements, same qualified names, same attributes, same text.

docs.title: What is not guaranteed
docs.text:
Round-tripping a third-party file whose namespaces are laid out differently from ours (a prefixed root plus per-element xmlns= redeclarations, as in the bundled Quality_of_Life.xml) can differ in prefix spelling between the backends. lxml echoes the source layout; the stdlib canonicalises it onto the root. The documents are semantically identical.

Matching byte-for-byte would mean rebuilding every subtree that carries its own nsmap inside write(), a real cost on the hottest path for prefix cosmetics. Any change here must keep the stdlib backend on the canonical c:/d:/l: prefixes; measure both backends on Quality_of_Life.xml and example_instance.xml.

docs.title: Bundled schemas
docs.text:
The DDI XSDs ship inside the package at src/ddi_l/schemas/ so that validation works offline from a plain pip install ddi-l. Always resolve them through importlib.resources (resources.files("ddi_l.schemas")), never through a path relative to the repository root. A repo-relative path works in a clone and breaks in an installed wheel.

The schemas are licensed CC-BY-4.0 by the DDI Alliance. license.txt and readme.txt are redistributed alongside them to satisfy attribution and must stay in the distribution.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation site uses MkDocs with the Material theme and bilingual (EN/FR) support. Pages come in .en.md / .fr.md pairs: update both when you change user-facing content.

make docs-serve    # Live preview
make docs-build    # Build and validate

Prefer the make targets over calling mkdocs directly: they set NO_MKDOCS_2_WARNING, without which every invocation prints a multi-line advisory from the Material for MkDocs authors about MkDocs 2.0.

The logo, favicon and their usage rules are described in branding assets.

The curriculum's answer keys page is generated by hooks/answer_keys.py from the ??? success answers in each module. Add or change an answer in the module, never on the answer-key page.

docs.title: Documentation toolchain versions
docs.text: uv.lock fixes the exact versions; CI and the deploy both install with uv sync --locked --group docs. mkdocs and mkdocs-material are capped below their next major in pyproject.toml so a new major is adopted deliberately; Dependabot opens that update as a CI-tested pull request. tests/test_docs_site_config.py checks that every plugin mkdocs.yml activates has a requirement in the docs group.

docs.title: The version selector only appears under mike
docs.text:
extra.version.provider: mike makes the theme fetch versions.json, resolving it as ../versions.json relative to the site base, because mike publishes each version under <site_url>/<version>/ and keeps the manifest beside them.

That is right in production and wrong locally. A plain mkdocs serve builds no version, so the base stays /ddi-l/ and ../versions.json overshoots to /versions.json, which nothing serves: a 404 on every page load, for a selector that could not work locally anyway.

hooks/version_selector.py drops extra.version unless MIKE_DOCS_VERSION is set (the variable mike exports when it drives a build. If you need to preview the selector itself, run uv run mike serve, or set the variable by hand.

docs.title: Why the build log is short
docs.text:
mkdocs-static-i18n logs, at INFO, the entire value it overrides each config key with, once per language, on every rebuild. For nav that is the whole navigation tree, so a build printed several thousand characters of echoed configuration around the five lines that matter.

hooks/quiet_i18n_logs.py filters exactly those Overriding/Updating … config … records. Building '<lang>' documentation to directory: … is kept, and nothing at WARNING or above is touched; a genuine Unknown '<lang>' config override still surfaces. Run mkdocs serve --verbose to see everything again.

The filter is attached to the handler on the mkdocs logger, not to the plugin's logger. Python consults an ancestor logger's handlers when a record propagates but not its filters, and the plugin logs from submodules, so a filter on mkdocs.plugins.mkdocs_static_i18n silently does nothing.

docs.title: VIRTUAL_ENV does not match the project environment path
docs.text: A uv warning, not a project setting: nothing in this repository chooses an environment path. It means your shell has one virtualenv active while uv resolves the project's to somewhere else, usually because UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT is set in your profile. Either unset it, point it at this repository's .venv, or pass --active to make uv use whatever is currently activated.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: Releases are published to PyPI by .github/workflows/publish.yml using trusted publishing (OIDC, no API token), with PEP 740 attestations.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. On PyPI and TestPyPI, add a pending trusted publisher for each of the projects ddi-l and ddi-l-native: owner pbisson44, repository ddi, workflow publish.yml, environment pypi (TestPyPI: testpypi).
  2. In the GitHub repository settings, create the pypi and testpypi environments. Protect pypi with required reviewers.

docs.title: Each release
docs.text:
1. Set the version and the release date with one command:

    uv run python scripts/set_version.py 0.3.0 --date 2027-01-15
# or: patch, minor, major instead of the version; --date defaults to today

    ddi-l and ddi-l-native share one version. The script writes it in pyproject.toml (with the ddi-l-native==X.Y.Z dependency), native/pyproject.toml, native/Cargo.toml, native/Cargo.lock, native/fallback/pyproject.toml, CITATION.cff, the citations in the README and on the home page, and the "(unreleased)" heading of the release notes; it sets date-released and the citations' year, then runs uv lock. It writes nothing unless every file matches. When it starts a new series, add it to the table in SECURITY.md; the script says so. tests/test_release_metadata.py and the publish workflow refuse a release where the versions differ, and tests/test_set_version.py fails when another file starts stating the version. 2. Date the heading in docs/release-notes.en.md and docs/release-notes.fr.md. 3. Run the local gate: uv run make release-check and the full test suite. 4. Dry run: trigger Publish to PyPI from the Actions tab with target testpypi, then install from TestPyPI in a clean environment:

    pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ \
    --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ ddi-l

  2. Publish a GitHub Release with tag vX.Y.Z. The workflow builds, checks that the tag matches the packaged version, and uploads to PyPI; the docs workflow publishes the versioned documentation.

docs.title: Submitting changes
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository and create a feature branch.
  2. Write or update tests alongside code changes.
  3. Update both the English and French pages for user-facing changes.
  4. Run the quality gates listed above.
  5. Commit with clear messages describing the intent.
  6. Open a pull request with a summary and related issue references.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Generated from the docstrings in the source.

This page covers the public API: what import ddi_l exposes and what semantic versioning applies to. For the wider model layer, see Models reference for the guided tour and Schema coverage for what is supported at which level.

Where to start

new_study() and open_ddi() return a Document, which is the front door. DDIDocument, DDIFragment and StudyCursor are the advanced layer underneath it. Reach for them when you need to work with raw elements, partial instances, or a specific study in a multi-study file.

docs.title: Creating and opening documents
docs.text:
Create a new DDI document with a StudyUnit.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default title str

Human-readable title for the study.

required agency str

Maintenance agency responsible for the study.

Optional identifier; auto-generated if omitted.

docs.title: revise
docs.text:
revise(
    *items: str | MaintainableBase | Element,
    cascade: bool = True,
    dry_run: bool = False,
    responsibility: str | None = None,
    version_date: str | None = None,
    rationale: str | Mapping[str, str] | None = None,
) -> RevisionPlan

Give items a new version and, with cascade, every item pinning them.

Each item gets the next major version ("6" becomes "7"), and so does every identifiable it declares (its parameters, its codes), as Colectica numbers them. Every item revised in one call gets the same versionDate (if it has one), as when Colectica saves several items at once, and responsibility (default: the one set with ddi_l.configure). With cascade, every item referring to an old version without lateBound (of a revised item or of what it declares) gets its reference re-pointed and is revised in turn, up to the top of the instrument; the TopLevelReference follows. Late-bound references already mean "the latest version" and are left alone. Each item is revised once, however many paths lead to it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *items str | MaintainableBase | Element

The changed items, by r:ID, typed model or element.

() cascade bool

Also revise the items pinning them.

True dry_run bool

Return the plan without changing the fragment.

False responsibility str | None

Recorded as r:VersionResponsibility.

None version_date str | None

The versionDate of every item revised (default: now, in Colectica's format), so that items made in the same change can share it.

None rationale str | Mapping[str, str] | None

Why the items changed, recorded as each revised item's r:VersionRationale, as Colectica records the message of a save on every item it saves: a string, or {language: text}. Each revised item's previous rationale is dropped either way: it explained the previous version.

None

docs.title: colectica
docs.text:
Write a FragmentInstance exactly as Colectica Designer writes one.

Colectica exports items as a DDI FragmentInstance: one <Fragment> per item, each item declaring its module's namespace as the default, the reusable namespace bound to r:, and two-space indentation. Most exports start with a UTF-8 byte-order mark, but not all: some exports from Colectica's server-side tools have none, so the writer keeps whichever the source had. A general-purpose serializer produces the same information laid out differently -- prefixes on every element, namespaces hoisted to the root, attributes in parse order -- so a file read from Colectica and saved back is a different file, and a diff against the original is all noise.

to_colectica_bytes writes the layout byte for byte. Reading a Colectica export and writing it back yields the identical file; items built or edited with the typed models come out as Colectica would have written them.

The conventions, all taken from Colectica's output:

  • <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>, preceded by a byte-order mark when the source had one (or, for a new document, by default), then \n line ends and no newline after the closing root tag.
  • <ddi:FragmentInstance xmlns:r=... xmlns:ddi=...> and <ddi:TopLevelReference> use the ddi: prefix; each <Fragment> sits at column 0 and declares xmlns:r and the instance namespace as default.
  • An element outside the namespace in force declares its own as the default, written after its other attributes.
  • Attributes in schema declaration order, base type first.
  • An empty element is <a></a> when its type holds text and <a ... /> otherwise.
  • Text escapes &, < and >; attribute values also escape " and write tab, newline and carriage return as character references.

docs.title: apply_colectica_conventions
docs.text:
apply_colectica_conventions(
    items: Iterable[Element],
    *,
    reusable_ns: str,
    version_date: str | None = None,
) -> None

Give items built in code what Colectica writes on every item.

Only what is missing is added; an item read from a Colectica export already has all of it and comes through unchanged.

  • isUniversallyUnique="true" and a versionDate (version_date, or now) on the item.
  • An r:URN built from its Agency, ID and Version, as its first child.
  • The r:VersionResponsibility set with ddi_l.configure, if any.
  • Each identifiable the item declares (a parameter, a code) gets isUniversallyUnique="true", the item's version if it has none, and an r:URN.
  • References lose an r:URN that only restates their Agency, ID and Version: Colectica identifies a reference by those three alone.

docs.title: Spreadsheets
docs.text: Load a study's metadata (concepts, questions and the questionnaire flow, code lists, variables, data files and more) from CSV files or an Excel workbook. See Load DDI from spreadsheets.

docs.title: tables
docs.text:
Bulk-load DDI items from spreadsheets: a folder of CSV files or one workbook.

Each table (studies, concepts, questions, flow, variables, datasets and the others in TABLES, plus settings) is one CSV file, or one sheet of an .xlsx workbook. Rows point at each other by id: a variable's question column holds a question's id. Text in several languages goes in one column per language (label@en, label@fr); properties of your own go in custom:<name> columns.

::

from ddi_l.tables import load_tables, write_table_templates

write_table_templates("my-survey", example=True)   # start from the example
tables = load_tables("my-survey")
tables.to_fragment().save("my-survey.xml")         # for Colectica

The guide, with every column, is the "Load DDI from spreadsheets" page of the documentation; the templates are on the "Spreadsheet templates" page.

The functions behind DDIFragment.revise, move_construct, wrap_in_condition, duplicate and repair_shared_identifiables. They edit the fragment's XML directly (an item's typed model is a copy), and work on DDI 3.3 fragments only.

docs.title: Colectica conditions
docs.text:
Read, edit and explain the conditions Colectica stores in r:Command.

Colectica keeps the logic of an IfThenElse (in d:IfCondition, and in the d:IfCondition of each d:ElseIf) and of a ComputationItem (in r:CommandCode) as an r:Command whose r:ProgramLanguage says how to read its r:CommandContent. DDI keeps a loop's condition the same way: a Loop's in d:LoopWhile (with d:InitialValue and d:StepValue), a RepeatUntil's in d:UntilCondition and a RepeatWhile's in d:WhileCondition.

The content can be:

Neutral JSON built by Colectica's condition editor::

    {"LogicGroups":[{"GroupBooleanType":0,"Statements":[
        {"StatementBooleanType":0,
         "Subject":"urn:ddi:example.org:<in-parameter id>:1",
         "Operator":7,
         "Value":{"ValueNotNeeded":true,"SelectedCodes":[]}}]}],
     "Synopsis":"Q1 Empty","Version":1}

Parsed into a `Condition`.

Blaise5DataLookup JSON listing the fields a data lookup reads ({"DataLookupFields":[{"Name":..,"Type":..,"IsAssigned":.., "Identifier":..}]}). Parsed into a DataLookup. anything else (Blaise, ...) Native code, kept as text in a NativeCondition.

A statement's Subject names an r:InParameter of the item holding the command, by URN; a parent sequence binds that parameter to a question's r:OutParameter. SelectedCodes name l:Code items by URN.

The integer codes are Colectica's: Operator for a statement's comparison, GroupBool and StmtBool for how groups and statements join. A value the enum does not list is kept as-is (Operator(99).name == "UNKNOWN_99") and written back unchanged.

Only the codes' names are known: not how a statement treats a question with no answer, nor in what order And and Or mixed in one group are evaluated.

Writing a condition back reproduces the original text byte for byte when nothing was changed; an edited one is re-encoded the way Colectica writes JSON (compact separators, keys in their original order, non-ASCII written as is unless the source escaped it).

docs.title: Questionnaire specs
docs.text:
Specs, the expression language of their gates and edits, its compilers to Colectica conditions, and the comparison of an instrument with a spec; see Check a questionnaire against a spec. Reading a spec needs the spec extra; decide, which tells whether two expressions hold for the same respondents, needs the logic extra.

Check a questionnaire against a spec of what it should contain.

A spec lists a survey's modules, questions, response domains, gates and edit checks in YAML or JSON (load_spec); conform compares an instrument with it. The expression language of gates and edits (ddi_l.spec.expression) and its compilers to Colectica's condition JSON and to Blaise (ddi_l.spec.compile) need nothing beyond the standard library; reading a spec file needs the spec extra (pip install "ddi-l[spec]"). Deciding whether two expressions hold for the same respondents (decide) needs the logic extra (pip install "ddi-l[logic]").

docs.title: normalise
docs.text:
normalise(node: Expression) -> Expression

Rewrite node into the canonical form equivalent compares.

  • missing(x) becomes empty(x) or refused(x), and answered(x) becomes not empty(x) and not refused(x);
  • a literal compared with something else goes on the right (3 < x becomes x > 3), and two other operands are put in a fixed order;
  • not is pushed inward over and and or, and not not x becomes x; a comparison under not is kept as it is, since not (x > 3) holds when x has no answer and x <= 3 does not;
  • in an and, not empty(x) and not refused(x) go when another part compares x, since a comparison is false without an answer (answered(x) and x > 3 is x > 3);
  • nested and (or) are flattened, repeats dropped and the operands sorted;
  • numbers compare by value (3.0 is 3).

Arithmetic is left as written: nothing is calculated.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Standardized exception hierarchy for DDI operations.

All DDI-specific exceptions inherit from DDIError and provide rich context including source location, XPath, and original cause.

Exception Hierarchy

DDIError (base) ├── DDIReadError - File/stream reading failures │ └── DDIParseError - Malformed XML or unexpected elements ├── DDIWriteError - Serialization failures ├── DDIValidationError - Schema validation failures ├── DDIModelError - Model constraint violations │ ├── ModelValidationError - Validation check failures │ ├── ModelBuildError - Builder/construction failures │ └── DuplicateIdentifierError - Identifier already in use (ValueError) └── DDIReferenceError - Reference resolution failures (LookupError)

Warning hierarchy

UserWarning └── DDIReferenceWarning - References to items missing from a saved study

docs.title: CLI recipes
docs.text:
The ddi console entry point bundles commands for validating and transforming instance documents. This page collects the most common tasks as commands you can copy and adapt.

Bundled sample paths

When ddi-l is installed from a wheel, sample XML lives alongside the package. Export a helper variable before running the commands below so the paths resolve correctly on any platform:

export DDI_L_FIXTURES=$(python -c "from pathlib import Path; import ddi_l; print(Path(ddi_l.__file__).resolve().parent / 'examples' / 'tests' / 'fixtures')")

Replace src/ddi_l/examples/tests/fixtures/... in the examples with $DDI_L_FIXTURES/... if you are not working from a cloned repository.

docs.title: Validate instances with ddi validate
docs.text:
Use the validator as a pre-flight check before committing XML changes or shipping a new extract. The command exits with status code 0 for valid payloads and 1 when schema or lint issues are detected.

CommandExpected output 
ddi validate src/ddi_l/examples/tests/fixtures/minimal_instance.xml

Document is valid.

Pass - to read from standard input when piping content from another tool. Successful runs print exactly Document is valid. (no emoji or prefix), while failing runs emit structured JSON so automated pipelines can react programmatically.

Protect validation artefacts

Scrub personal or confidential details from the JSON output (or restrict distribution entirely) before sharing it outside the immediate team. Pass --redact-context to skip the contextual snippet in the CLI output, and use the flag alongside --validate for to-json and roundtrip when pipelines echo the diagnostic JSON. When calling the Python helpers directly, validation.validate_document(..., include_context=False) offers the same protection. For redaction workflows, revisit the automation playbook's cautionary guidance.

Failing runJSON issuesRedacted JSON 
cat src/ddi_l/examples/tests/fixtures/invalid_instance_missing_id.xml | ddi validate

error: Missing required identification element(s): ID (line 3)
    at /DDIInstance
    context: <DDIInstance>
1 issue found.

ddi validate --format json src/ddi_l/examples/tests/fixtures/invalid_instance_missing_id.xml

[
  {
    "message": "Missing required identification element(s): ID",
    "xpath": "/DDIInstance",
    "severity": "error",
    "line": 3,
    "column": null,
    "context": "<DDIInstance>"
  }
]

ddi validate --format json --redact-context src/ddi_l/examples/tests/fixtures/invalid_instance_missing_id.xml

[
  {
    "message": "Missing required identification element(s): ID",
    "xpath": "/DDIInstance",
    "severity": "error",
    "line": 3,
    "column": null
  }
]

Continue with the Validate and lint DDI content guide for a deep dive into available lint rules, custom profiles, and advanced configuration options.

docs.title: Tune lint checks with ddi lint
docs.text:
Run lint rules directly and customise the built-in checks without writing Python code. Combine agency overrides, citation toggles, and language requirements to mirror your organisation's policy.

Use ddi lint --list-rules or ddi lint --list-profiles to inspect the available checks before running them. Pair --list-format table with either flag for a compact columnar view instead of newline-delimited JSON.

CommandWhat it does 
ddi lint src/ddi_l/examples/tests/fixtures/minimal_instance.xml \
  --allowed-agency org.example --required-citation-language en \
  --no-require-citation-title --skip-rule ddi.agency.allowed
  • Turns on the agency check and restricts it to org.example. The check is off by default: ddi-l has no basis to decide which organisation identifiers are legitimate, so it only runs once you supply the set your organisation accepts.
  • Enforces citation titles in English while letting the citation title rule be optional.
  • Ignores the agency allow-list lint finding when computing the exit code and in the output payload.
  • Returns exit code 0 unless a finding at or above the default error severity is emitted. Pass --fail-severity warning to fail on warnings too, which is what you want once a corpus is clean.

Pair the lint flags with --profile to run a custom profile or --validate to include schema issues alongside lint findings in the output JSON.

docs.title: Smoke-test edits with ddi roundtrip
docs.text:
ddi roundtrip re-serialises a document after parsing it with the internal model. Use it to catch formatting problems, missing namespaces, or invalid content introduced during manual edits.

CommandExpected output 
ddi roundtrip src/ddi_l/examples/tests/fixtures/minimal_instance.xml --validate

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<DDIInstance xmlns="ddi:instance:3_3" xmlns:r="ddi:reusable:3_3" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance">
  <r:Agency>example.agency</r:Agency>
  <r:ID>minimal-instance</r:ID>
  <r:Version>1.0</r:Version>
  <r:Citation>
    <r:Title>
      <r:String xml:lang="en">Minimal Instance</r:String>
    </r:Title>
  </r:Citation>
</DDIInstance>

Add --no-pretty-print or --no-declaration when you are diffing files that should retain their original formatting. When you want to write to disk, pass a destination path instead of -. With --validate, the command mirrors ddi validate by returning exit code 1 and streaming JSON issues if the source is invalid.

The command-line automation playbook shows how to integrate round-tripping with conversion and packaging steps for a larger publishing pipeline.

docs.title: Check a questionnaire with ddi conform
docs.text:
ddi conform compares an instrument with a questionnaire spec, a YAML or JSON file listing its modules, questions, domains, gates and edits. It needs the spec extra (pip install 'ddi-l[spec]').

ddi spec example > pet-survey.spec.yaml       # start from the example
ddi spec validate pet-survey.spec.yaml
ddi conform export.xml --spec pet-survey.spec.yaml --format table
ddi conform export.xml --spec pet-survey.spec.yaml --module pets --fail-severity warning

It exits with 0 when no finding reaches --fail-severity (error by default), 1 when one does, and 2 when it cannot run (a spec that does not pass its checks, an unknown module). See Check a questionnaire against a spec for the spec format and every rule.

docs.title: Export snapshots with ddi to-json
docs.text:
Transform XML into a normalised JSON structure for integration tests, content mirrors, or downstream APIs. The converter reuses DDIDocument.to_dict() so the shape matches the Python model.

CommandExpected output 
ddi to-json src/ddi_l/examples/tests/fixtures/minimal_instance.xml --validate --indent 2

{
  "@isMaintainable": true,
  "{ddi:reusable:3_3}Agency": "example.agency",
  "{ddi:reusable:3_3}ID": {
    "@type": "ID",
    "#text": "minimal-instance"
  },
  "{ddi:reusable:3_3}Version": "1.0",
  "{ddi:reusable:3_3}Citation": {
    "{ddi:reusable:3_3}Title": {
      "{ddi:reusable:3_3}String": {
        "@{http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace}lang": "en",
        "#text": "Minimal Instance"
      }
    }
  }
}

The converter streams only JSON to standard output so you can redirect it to a file (> build/artifacts/minimal.json) or pipe it into other programs. Combine the converter with jq or similar tools to extract specific sections when preparing review packages.

docs.title: Wire the CLI into CI pipelines
docs.text:
Treat validation and conversion as regression tests by running them in your continuous integration workflows. The snippet below illustrates a GitHub Actions job that validates every XML file under metadata/ (change the path to wherever your DDI files live) and keeps round-tripped output up to date.

name: Validate DDI payloads

on:
  push:
    paths:
      - "**/*.xml"
  pull_request:

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - name: Install ddi-l
        run: |
          pip install 'ddi-l[full]'
      - name: Validate DDI files
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          find metadata -name "*.xml" -print0 \
            | xargs -0 -n1 -P4 ddi validate
      - name: Rebuild round-trip artefacts
        run: |
          mkdir -p build/roundtrip
          for input in metadata/*.xml; do
            output="build/roundtrip/$(basename "$input")"
            ddi roundtrip "$input" --output "$output" --validate
          done

Augment the workflow with ddi to-json to publish machine-readable snapshots alongside XML outputs or hand control to a custom script as described in the command-line automation playbook.

docs.title: Work with Colectica exports
docs.text:
Not affiliated with Colectica

ddi-l is an independent project. It names Colectica to say which files it reads and writes; the Colectica-specific formats described here are inferred, not taken from a Colectica specification.

Colectica Designer and Colectica Repository exchange DDI 3.3 as a FragmentInstance: one item per <Fragment>, references between items by Agency, ID and Version, and a TopLevelReference naming the item the export was made for. ddi-l reads these files, gives you each item as a typed model, and writes them back the way Colectica does, so a file you open and save without editing comes back byte for byte.

docs.title: Open an export
docs.text:
ddi.open_fragment() opens a FragmentInstance. (ddi.open_ddi() is for a DDIInstance document and points you here when given a fragment.) So that this page runs on its own, the first block builds a small export and saves it; with a real one, start at open_fragment.

import ddi_l as ddi

age = ddi.Variable(
    agency="example.org",
    identifier="5f0e3c1a-0b8e-4d3e-9a5e-6a1b2c3d4e5f",
    version="1",
    labels=[
        ddi.InternationalString("Age", lang="en"),
        ddi.InternationalString("Âge", lang="fr"),
    ],
)
ddi.DDIFragment.from_items([age]).save("export.xml")

fragment = ddi.open_fragment("export.xml")
for item in fragment.items():
    print(type(item).__name__, item.identifier, item.version)

items() parses every item into its model; pass a model class to keep one type, as in fragment.items(ddi.Variable). Every item type a DDI 3.3 fragment can carry has a model (161 of them), including the schemes, groups, managed representations, geographic types and record layouts that have no hand-written class: those come from ddi_l.models.items.

docs.title: Look up, edit and put back
docs.text:
get() finds an item by ID. A Colectica export can hold several versions of one item; without a version= you get the highest. The models are copies, so write an edited item back with put():

variable = fragment.get("5f0e3c1a-0b8e-4d3e-9a5e-6a1b2c3d4e5f")
variable.labels.append(ddi.InternationalString("Age (years)", lang="en-CA"))
variable.increment_major_version()
fragment.put(variable)
fragment.save("export.xml")

put() replaces the item with the same Agency, ID and Version; failing that, the single item with the same Agency and ID (the version you just bumped); and otherwise adds the item in a new <Fragment>. remove() deletes items, and top_level_item() returns the item the TopLevelReference names.

Everything you did not touch is written back exactly as read. That includes versionDate, r:VersionResponsibility, r:BasedOnObject lineage, user attribute pairs (on items and inside references), multilingual names and labels kept in one element, audienceLanguage on question text, controlled-vocabulary attributes, the original spelling of values ("1" for true, "01"), and references that carry no r:URN.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Colectica numbers versions with whole numbers (1, 2, ... 78) and stamps each version with a versionDate. ddi-l keeps both conventions when you bump an item:

  • increment_major_version() turns "2" into "3". On an item that has a versionDate, it also sets it to now, in Colectica's format (2026-07-16T15:15:11.7905158Z). An item without one is left without; pass touch=False to keep the old date.
  • increment_minor_version() and increment_subversion() refuse a whole-number version, because Colectica numbers versions with whole numbers and a dotted one such as "3.1" may not read back. Pass allow_dotted=True if you do want one. A version that is already dotted ("1.0") bumps as before.
  • responsibility="..." records who made the change as r:VersionResponsibility. To record the same name on every bump, set it once with ddi.configure(version_responsibility="..."); responsibility=None records none on one bump, whatever is configured. ddi-l never invents one.
variable = fragment.get("5f0e3c1a-0b8e-4d3e-9a5e-6a1b2c3d4e5f")
variable.increment_major_version(responsibility="Questionnaire team")
print(variable.version, variable.version_date, variable.version_responsibility)

try:
    variable.increment_minor_version()
except ddi.DDIModelError as error:
    print(error)

with ddi.configured(version_responsibility="Questionnaire team"):
    variable.increment_major_version()
fragment.put(variable)

ddi.configured(...) applies a setting inside a with block, in the current thread or task only, and restores the previous one afterwards. ddi.reset_configuration() restores the defaults.

docs.title: Lint an export
docs.text:
ddi lint --profile colectica-questionnaire runs the checks written for Colectica content:

ddi lint export.xml --profile colectica-questionnaire
  • colectica.maintainable.labels accepts any of r:Label, r:Name or an item's own name element (ConstructName, QuestionItemName, ...), provided it holds text. Colectica items usually carry a name rather than a label, so the default profile's ddi.maintainable.labels reports nearly all of them.
  • References resolve the way Colectica means them. A reference marked lateBound="true" means "the latest version". Colectica writes late-bound parameter references at version 1 while the parameter itself is at, say, 4, so any version present resolves one (lateBound="1" counts too). With a lateBoundRestriction such as 4, only versions within major version 4 do. A late-bound reference naming a version newer than any present, or whose restriction matches no version present, is reported by ddi.reference.version.
  • ddi.reference.version (warning) reports an exact reference whose item is in the file, but at other versions only, and lists the versions that are there.
  • ddi.reference.provenance-external (info) reports a r:BasedOnReference, or a reference inside an r:UserAttributePair, whose item is not in the file. These record where an item was copied from, and the source usually lives elsewhere.
  • ddi.reference.integrity keeps everything else that does not resolve. It is a warning in a fragment, which may be partial, and an error in a DDIInstance.

info findings never fail ddi lint. Use --fail-severity warning or --fail-severity info for a stricter gate.

The profile also checks a questionnaire's own design for common problems, each named after the item it is found in (type, short ID and name):

  • Identifiers and bindings: a parameter or code declared in two items (a copy that kept its source's IDs), a binding to a parameter the file does not declare.
  • Conditions: malformed or empty conditions (with the description that probably holds the intended logic), groups that can never be true, native code that is not one expression, inputs a condition never uses, a stored synopsis that names another variable, and a gate that wraps only the first construct of a page.
  • Domains: a code domain without a code list, a domain label naming another variable, a question whose wording does not fit its answer type.
  • Text: missing translations, unresolved template placeholders, user-interface words pasted from mock-ups, malformed or undeclared #{name} pipes, and statements that are design notes.
  • Lookups and aliases: duplicate or suspicious data lookup fields, and parameter aliases whose escaping compounded (_x005F_) or that hold question text.

Several rules depend on your organisation's conventions: required languages, the names the run-time system supplies, a variable naming scheme. They do nothing until configured:

ddi lint export.xml --profile colectica-questionnaire --format table \
  --required-language en-CA --required-language fr-CA \
  --known-names runtime-names.txt --lint-config lint.json

The lint rule reference lists every rule with an example finding, and every option.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
DDI defines where an IfThenElse or a ComputationItem keeps its logic, an r:Command, but not what goes inside it: r:ProgramLanguage names the language and r:CommandContent holds the code as text. Colectica writes three kinds of content, which ddi_l.colectica_logic reads:

r:ProgramLanguage Content Parsed into Neutral JSON from Colectica's condition editor: groups of statements Condition Blaise5DataLookup JSON listing the fields a data lookup reads DataLookup anything else (Blaise, ...) native code NativeCondition (the text, unchanged)

A Neutral statement compares a subject, the URN of one of the item's r:InParameters, with a value or a set of codes. A parent sequence binds that parameter to a question's answer.

from ddi_l.colectica_logic import Operator, parse_command, serialize_condition

text = (
    '{"LogicGroups":[{"GroupBooleanType":0,"Statements":[{"StatementBooleanType":0,'
    '"Subject":"urn:ddi:example.org:q1-in:1","Operator":3,"Value":{"Value":"2",'
    '"ValueNotNeeded":false,"SelectedCodes":[]}}]}],"Synopsis":"Q1 Greater than 2",'
    '"Version":1}'
)
condition = parse_command("Neutral", text)
statement = condition.logic_groups[0].statements[0]
print(statement.operator is Operator.GREATER_THAN, statement.value)
assert serialize_condition(condition) == text  # unchanged: written back as read

statement.value = "3"
print(serialize_condition(condition))

parse_condition(item) does the same from an IfThenElse or ComputationItem (an element or a typed model), and write_condition(item, condition) writes an edited condition back into it. An unchanged condition is written back byte for byte. An edited one is written the way Colectica writes JSON: no spaces, keys in the order read, and non-ASCII characters escaped only if the source escaped them.

Loops keep their condition the same way: a Loop in d:LoopWhile, a RepeatUntil in d:UntilCondition and a RepeatWhile in d:WhileCondition, which parse_condition() and write_condition() read and write. A Loop's d:InitialValue and d:StepValue hold assignments rather than a condition; which="InitialValue" or which="StepValue" reaches them. Each d:ElseIf of an IfThenElse has a condition of its own: pass the ElseIf element. The lint rules check every branch, and an input that only an ElseIf tests counts as used, there and in ddi explain-condition.

docs.title: The codes are Colectica's
docs.text:
The integers in the JSON are Colectica's codes: Operator for a statement's operator, GroupBool and StmtBool for how groups and statements join. A value not listed is kept unchanged, so a condition using it still parses and writes back as read (Operator(99).name == "UNKNOWN_99").

Enum Values GroupBool (how a group joins the groups before it) 0 None (FIRST, the first group), 1 And, 2 Or StmtBool (how a statement joins the statements before it) 0 None (FIRST, the first statement), 1 And, 2 Or Operator 0 None, 1 Equal (EQUAL_TO), 2 NotEqual, 3 GreaterThan, 4 GreaterThanOrEqual, 5 LessThan, 6 LessThanOrEqual, 7 Empty, 8 NotEmpty, 9 Contains, 10 DoesNotContain, 11 ContainsAny, 12 ContainsAll, 13 ContainsNone, 14 Refused, 15 NotRefused, 16 DontKnow, 17 NotDontKnow

Only the codes' names are known: not how a statement treats a question with no answer, nor in what order And and Or mixed in one group are evaluated; Check a questionnaire against a spec says how ddi-l reads them.

docs.title: Check a stored synopsis
docs.text:
Colectica stores a Synopsis next to the logic: the text its editor last showed. It can be stale, and it numbers codes by their position in the list rather than their value. render_synopsis(condition, fragment) writes one from the logic itself, naming each subject after the question bound to it and each code by its value and label. From the command line, ddi explain-condition shows both, the condition's description, and which of the item's inputs the condition uses:

ddi explain-condition export.xml 22222222-2222-4222-8222-000000000030

Item              IfThenElse 22222222-2222-4222-8222-000000000030 (version 1)
Language          Neutral
Stored synopsis   (PetName Contains All 2 Cat) And ((PetCount Greater than 2) Or (PetCount Refused))
Rendered          (PetKind contains all of 3 "Cat") and (PetCount > 2 or PetCount is refused)
Synopsis mismatch the stored synopsis does not name PetKind
Description en-CA Show when a cat lives here and there are more than two pets.
Inputs used       PetKind, PetCount
Inputs unused     PetAge

--format json prints the same as JSON, and explain_condition(fragment, id) returns it as a ConditionExplanation.

docs.title: Repair a template
docs.text:
Colectica references an item at a fixed version. Change a sequence, give it a new version, and every item pointing at the old version is out of date: its reference needs the new version, which changes that item in turn, up to the instrument. DDIFragment does that walk, and edits a fragment's sequences without leaving its references behind.

  • revise(*items, cascade=True, dry_run=False, responsibility=None, version_date=None, rationale=None) gives each item the next major version, and gives it to every identifiable the item declares too (its parameters, its codes), as Colectica numbers them. Every item revised in one call gets the same versionDate (version_date, or now), as when Colectica saves several items at once, and responsibility (or the one set with ddi.configure()). With cascade, every item referring to an old version, of an item or of what it declares, is re-pointed and revised too, each once, up to the top; the TopLevelReference follows. Late-bound references already mean "the latest version" and are left alone. rationale (a string, or {language: text}) is recorded as the r:VersionRationale of every item revised, as Colectica records the message of a save on every item it saves; the rationale an item carried is dropped either way, since it explained the previous version. dry_run=True returns the plan and changes nothing.
  • move_construct(construct, from_sequence, to_sequence, index=None) moves a construct between sequences.
  • insert_construct(sequence, construct, index=None, before=None, after=None) places a construct in a sequence: one already in the fragment, or a new typed item, which is added with what Colectica writes on every item: the configured responsibility among it, and an r:URN and the item's version on each identifiable it declares.
  • wrap_in_condition(sequence, constructs, condition) puts constructs under a new IfThenElse, in a Then sequence of type ConditionalChildContainer. The two new items share one versionDate and record the configured responsibility.
  • duplicate(item) copies an item with new IDs for it and everything it declares, and records the source in r:BasedOnObject. The copy and what it declares start at version 1. A copy made this way shares no parameter ID with its source; place it with insert_construct().
  • repair_shared_identifiables(dry_run=True) gives each copy of a shared identifiable (what colectica.identifiable.shared-id reports) an ID of its own, keeping the original's: the earliest versionDate, else the item with no r:BasedOnObject. The bindings in the copy's own question constructs follow; any other reference to the shared ID is listed as ambiguous rather than guessed.

The editing helpers change no version: they return the items they touched, for revise(). A page whose gate wraps only its first statement, fixed:

fragment = ddi.open_fragment("template.xml")

touched = set()
for statement in statements_after_the_gate:
    result = fragment.move_construct(statement, entry_page, gate_then_sequence)
    touched.update(result.touched)

plan = fragment.revise(*touched, dry_run=True)
for step in plan:
    print(step.item_type, step.identifier, step.old_version, "->", step.new_version)

fragment.revise(*touched, responsibility="Questionnaire team")
fragment.save("template.xml")

Only the items on the path from the change to the instrument get a new version: the two sequences touched, the IfThenElse pinning the Then sequence, and the section, root and instrument above them.

A new statement after a page's last question, the same way:

from ddi_l.models import InternationalString, StatementItem

thanks = StatementItem(
    agency="example.org",
    identifier=new_statement_id,
    version="1",
    construct_names=[InternationalString("Thanks", lang="en")],
)
result = fragment.insert_construct(page, thanks, after=last_question)
fragment.revise(*result.touched)

Re-import not verified

Whether Colectica accepts items whose identifiables were given new IDs by repair_shared_identifiables() on re-import has not been verified. Try it on a copy of the repository first.

docs.title: Build a fragment from scratch
docs.text:
DDIFragment.from_items() writes one item per <Fragment>, names the first in the TopLevelReference, and gives each item what Colectica writes on every item: isUniversallyUnique="true", a versionDate (now, in Colectica's seven-digit UTC format, unless you pass one) and an r:URN. References are identified by Agency, ID and Version alone, as Colectica writes them.

question = ddi.QuestionItem(
    agency="example.org",
    identifier="c2b1a9e4-7d3f-4b8a-9e21-0f6d5c4b3a29",
    version="1",
    question_texts=[ddi.InternationalString("What is your age?", lang="en")],
)
package = ddi.DDIFragment.from_items([question, age])
print(package.validate())
package.save("package.xml")

To build many items at once from metadata kept in spreadsheets (a study, its questionnaire, variables, data files and more), see Load DDI from spreadsheets: load_tables(...).to_fragment() gives the same kind of fragment.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
A file you read is written back with its unchanged parts as they were read, byte for byte, whatever tool wrote it: save(), to_xml(), ddi.write_ddi(), ddi roundtrip and the HTTP API. Only what you add or change is laid out, in Colectica's layout for a FragmentInstance. Any other FragmentInstance (built in code, or by ddi from-json) is written all in Colectica's layout. That is UTF-8, the ddi: prefix on the root and TopLevelReference, each <Fragment> at the left margin declaring the reusable namespace as r:, each item declaring its module's namespace as the default, attributes in schema order, two-space indentation. layout="colectica" (--layout colectica, ?layout=colectica) writes the whole file in Colectica's layout, and layout="default" in this library's usual pretty-printed layout, as do pretty_print=False, xml_declaration=False or an encoding other than UTF-8, which only that layout has. A DDIInstance read from a file keeps its own layout the same way, when it uses the canonical prefixes (r, s, d...); one built in code is written in this library's layout.

From the command line:

ddi validate export.xml
ddi lint export.xml
ddi roundtrip export.xml -o copy.xml

ddi roundtrip on an unedited export writes an identical file.

Inline XHTML keeps its spaces. In <r:Content><b>Kind</b> <i>of pet</i></r:Content> the space between the two elements is text: the label reads "Kind of pet" on both backends, and the file is written back as read. Whitespace between XHTML blocks (<p>, <ul>...) is layout. lxml drops blank text as it reads, so a file where inline XHTML has no text before it in its element is parsed a second time, keeping every blank and then removing the indentation: reading such a file takes up to twice as long, and other files are read as before.

docs.title: Byte-order mark
docs.text: Most Colectica exports start with a UTF-8 byte-order mark; some exports from Colectica's server-side tools have none. ddi-l records which one it read (fragment.source_bom) and writes the same, so both kinds round-trip byte for byte. Pass bom=True or bom=False to save(), to_colectica_bytes() or ddi.write_ddi() to choose. A fragment built in code gets a mark.

docs.title: Related Python packages
docs.text: Packages that are useful next to ddi-l when you read, validate or transform DDI Lifecycle (DDI-L) content. Apart from the dependencies ddi-l already installs, none of them is required.

docs.title: XML parsing and validation
docs.text:
• xmlschema: validates documents against the bundled DDI schemas. It is a dependency of ddi-l, so it is always installed.
  • lxml: a faster XML parser and serializer. Install it with pip install 'ddi-l[full]'; ddi-l uses it automatically when it is present and falls back to the standard library otherwise.

docs.title: Data processing
docs.text:
• pandas: turn variables, questions or code lists into tables for reports and checks.
  • polars: a faster alternative to pandas for large documents or many files.
  • pyarrow: write Parquet or Feather files, or move data frames between pandas and polars.

docs.title: Files, HTTP and command-line tools
docs.text:
• requests or httpx: download DDI instances, schemas or controlled vocabularies before you validate them.
  • typer or click: build your own command-line tools on top of ddi-l.
  • fsspec: read and write files on local disk, S3-compatible storage or other remote file systems with the same code.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• pytest: the test runner this repository uses.
  • hypothesis: property-based tests for validation rules or conversion code.
  • ruff: linting and formatting.

docs.title: Dependency management
docs.text: • uv: this repository uses uv and its uv.lock file. Run uv sync --group dev to get the same development tools as CI.

docs.title: Choosing packages
docs.text:
• Pin optional dependencies in a lock file, and use the same lock file in deployment, so a pipeline behaves the same everywhere.
  • Validate at the boundaries of each pipeline step (doc.validate(), or ddi validate on the command line) so a malformed file is caught where it enters, not several steps later.

docs.title: ddi-l
docs.text:
DDI (Data Documentation Initiative) is the international standard that statistical agencies, data archives and researchers use to describe surveys and datasets: what was asked, what each variable means, and who was surveyed. ddi-l lets you write and check that documentation in Python instead of editing XML by hand.

You work with studies, questions and variables as Python objects, and ddi-l writes the XML. It reads, validates and lints DDI Lifecycle 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, so archives can check older holdings with the same tool, and it authors new documents in DDI 3.3.

Install ddi-l Start the training curriculum

docs.title: How a study fits together
docs.text:
A DDI study (a StudyUnit) keeps its metadata in modules, the boxes below: concepts and universes in a ConceptualComponent, the questionnaire and its questions in a DataCollection, variables, code lists and categories in a LogicalProduct, record layouts in a PhysicalDataProduct, each data file in a PhysicalInstance, and organizations and people in an Archive. Items refer to each other across modules (dashed arrows): a variable to the question that collected it, the concept it measures, its universe and its code list; a data file to the record layout and the logical record that list its variables.

flowchart TB
    accTitle: How a DDI study fits together
    accDescr: A StudyUnit holds its metadata in modules: concepts and universes in a ConceptualComponent; the instrument, its control constructs and the questions in a DataCollection; variables, code lists, categories and data relationships in a LogicalProduct; record layouts in a PhysicalDataProduct; each data file in a PhysicalInstance; organizations and individuals in an Archive. Dashed arrows are references: a variable refers to its question, concept, universe and code list; a data file refers to its record layout and data relationship, which list its variables.
    subgraph SU["StudyUnit"]
        direction TB
        subgraph CC["ConceptualComponent"]
            CON[Concept]
            UNI[Universe]
        end
        subgraph DC["DataCollection"]
            INS[Instrument]
            CTL["Sequence, IfThenElse,\nQuestionConstruct..."]
            QI[QuestionItem]
        end
        subgraph LP["LogicalProduct"]
            VAR[Variable]
            CL[CodeList]
            CAT[Category]
            DR["DataRelationship\n(LogicalRecord)"]
        end
        subgraph PDP["PhysicalDataProduct"]
            RL[RecordLayout]
        end
        subgraph PI["PhysicalInstance"]
            DF["DataFileIdentification\n(the data file)"]
        end
        subgraph AR["Archive"]
            ORG["Organization,\nIndividual"]
        end
    end
    INS -.->|ControlConstructReference| CTL
    CTL -.->|QuestionReference| QI
    QI -.->|ConceptReference| CON
    QI -.->|"CodeDomain:\nCodeListReference"| CL
    VAR -.->|QuestionReference| QI
    VAR -.->|ConceptReference| CON
    VAR -.->|UniverseReference| UNI
    VAR -.->|"CodeRepresentation:\nCodeListReference"| CL
    CL -.->|"Code:\nCategoryReference"| CAT
    DR -.->|VariableUsedReference| VAR
    RL -.->|"DataItem:\nVariableReference"| VAR
    PI -.->|RecordLayoutReference| RL
    PI -.->|DataRelationshipReference| DR

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import ddi_l as ddi

# Create a new study
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="example.org")

# Add a question and the variable that records its answer. `label=` is
# optional, but `ddi lint` warns about every item without one.
q_age = doc.add_question(text="How old are you?", label="Age question")
doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q_age, label="Age in years")

# Save to XML
doc.save("household-survey.xml")

# Open an existing study
doc = ddi.open_ddi("household-survey.xml")

for v in doc.variables:
    print(v.identifier)

Check the file from the command line. Both commands exit with status 0 when the file is clean, so you can use them in scripts and CI:

ddi validate household-survey.xml
ddi lint household-survey.xml

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install ddi-l from PyPI. The full extra adds the faster lxml backend (see Installation).

pipuvPoetry 
pip install ddi-l

uv add ddi-l
uv run ddi --help

poetry add ddi-l
poetry run ddi --help

For a one-page tour of the Document API, see the user guide. The API reference and the models reference cover every class. To contribute, start with the contributor guide; the development guide covers the architecture, code generation and release process in depth.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: ddi-l requires Python 3.11 or newer and is available on PyPI.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
Use this unless you want to change ddi-l itself.

pipuvPoetry 
pip install ddi-l
ddi --help

uv add ddi-l
uv run ddi --help

poetry add ddi-l
poetry run ddi --help

Verify the installation

  • ddi --help confirms the CLI entry point is on your PATH.
  • python -c "import ddi_l; print(ddi_l.__version__)" prints the installed version.

docs.title: What pip install ddi-l gives you
docs.text: pip install ddi-l reads, writes, validates and lints DDI documents with nothing else installed. It brings the native XML core, the ddi-l-native package at the same version, wherever a compiled wheel exists: Linux (x86_64 and aarch64), macOS and Windows (x64), on CPython 3.11 and later. Anywhere else pip installs a pure-Python stand-in with the same name, and ddi-l works the same, more slowly. pip never compiles anything.

docs.title: Extras: when you need one
docs.text:
An extra adds a feature or a backend most people do not need. Install one when your work matches its "Install it when" column; combine them as pip install 'ddi-l[spec,logic]'.

Extra Install it when What it adds spec You check questionnaires against a spec: ddi spec, ddi conform, or a YAML or JSON spec read in Python. PyYAML and jsonschema; see Check a questionnaire against a spec. Without it, ddi spec and ddi conform say what to install. logic You want gates compared exactly: equivalent() and ddi conform then decide whether two gates hold for the same respondents and name a respondent who tells them apart, and lint reports constructs no respondent reaches. The Z3 solver (MIT, about 57 MB installed); see Check a questionnaire against a spec. Without it, gates are compared as written. server You run the HTTP API, ddi serve. Litestar and uvicorn; see HTTP API. Without it, ddi serve says what to install. full Your platform has no compiled native core (Alpine Linux, Windows on ARM, PyPy, free-threaded Python), or you mostly write new documents laid out from scratch (layout="default"), which lxml writes faster. lxml, used when the native core is not there; set DDI_L_XML_BACKEND=lxml to use it anyway.

docs.title: XML backends
docs.text:
ddi-l reads and writes XML with the first of these that is installed:

  1. native, from ddi-l-native where a compiled wheel exists;
  2. lxml, from the full extra;
  3. the standard library, always there.

Each gives the same documents, the same validation issues and the same lint findings. Set the DDI_L_XML_BACKEND environment variable to native, lxml or stdlib to choose one; it is read once, when ddi_l is imported. ddi_l._etree.BACKEND names the backend in use.

The native backend also validates against the schema in one pass; see how schema validation runs. A document laid out afresh (a new document, or layout="default") is written by Python code on the native and standard library backends, and is slower to write there than with lxml.

Schemas are already included

The DDI 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3 XML Schemas ship inside the package, so doc.validate() and ddi validate work offline with no extra download and no network access.

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text:
Developers contributing to ddi-l should install from a local checkout:

git clone https://github.com/pbisson44/ddi-l.git
cd ddi-l
pip install -e . ./native/fallback

./native/fallback is ddi-l-native's pure-Python stand-in. pip does not read uv.lock, and a version of ddi-l not released yet has no ddi-l-native on PyPI to install.
