Install the development toolchain. The project is managed with uv, and uv.lock pins every dependency version:

uv sync --group dev              # Runtime + development dependencies
uv sync --group dev --extra full # ...plus the optional lxml backend

Note that full is an extra, not a dependency group: --group full fails. In a checkout, ddi-l-native is its pure-Python stand-in (native/fallback/), so no one needs Rust. To use the native core, build it over the stand-in; this needs a Rust toolchain (rustup) and, on Windows, Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload. uv sync and uv run put the stand-in back, so run commands with uv run --no-sync:

uv pip install --reinstall-package ddi-l-native ./native
uv run --no-sync python -c "import ddi_l._etree as e; print(e.BACKEND)"  # native

With plain pip instead (pip 25.1 or later reads dependency groups):

pip install -e '.[full]' ./native/fallback --group dev

For documentation work (docs is a dependency group, not an extra):

uv sync --group docs
# or
pip install -e . ./native/fallback --group docs

docs.title: Verify with a quick smoke test
docs.text:
import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Test", agency="example.org")
doc.add_question(text="Does it work?")
print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> 1

For more details, see the user guide or the development guide.

docs.title: Work with other tools
docs.text: ddi-l reads DDI Lifecycle 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, and writes standard DDI Lifecycle 3.3 XML that validates against the DDI Alliance's schemas. Most tools that work with DDI can therefore share files with it. This page shows how, tool by tool, with examples you can run. Every example uses a small fictional pet survey.

docs.title: What ddi-l exchanges
docs.text: Format ddi-l reads ddi-l writes Use it with DDI Lifecycle 3.3 XML (DDIInstance, FragmentInstance) yes, and edits it yes DDI 3.3 tools, any XML tool DDI Lifecycle 3.1 and 3.2 XML yes: validate, lint, element access no DDI 3.1 and 3.2 tools JSON (ddi to-json, ddi from-json) yes yes web apps, document stores, any language JSON-LD (DDI-RDF Discovery vocabulary) no yes, a summary triple stores, SPARQL, data catalogues CSV files or an Excel workbook yes blank templates spreadsheets, pandas, R HTTP (ddi serve) yes yes any language that can send a request DDI Codebook 2.x no no convert it, as shown below

docs.title: Any XML tool
docs.text:
A file written by ddi-l is plain DDI XML. Build the survey once; the sections below reuse it:

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Pet survey", agency="example.org")
question = doc.add_question(
    text="How many pets live in your home?", label="Pet count question"
)
doc.add_variable(name="PetCount", question=question, label="Number of pets")
doc.save("pets.xml")

Any XML library can read it. This uses only Python's standard library, not ddi-l:

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

NS = {"l": "ddi:logicalproduct:3_3", "r": "ddi:reusable:3_3"}
for variable in ET.parse("pets.xml").iter("{ddi:logicalproduct:3_3}Variable"):
    print(variable.findtext("l:VariableName/r:String", namespaces=NS))
# -> PetCount

Any schema validator can check it. ddi-l ships the DDI Alliance's schemas, so xmllint (part of the open-source libxml2) can use them directly:

SCHEMA=$(python -c "from importlib.resources import files; print(files('ddi_l.schemas') / 'ddi' / 'v3_3' / 'instance_3_3.xsd')")
xmllint --noout --schema "$SCHEMA" pets.xml
# -> pets.xml validates

The same goes for XSLT processors, XQuery databases and XML editors.

docs.title: Linked data: RDF and SPARQL
docs.text:
ddi-l writes a study as JSON-LD with the DDI Alliance's DDI-RDF Discovery vocabulary: studies, variables, questions, concepts and universes. Any RDF tool can load it. With the open-source rdflib (pip install rdflib), a SPARQL query lists each variable and its question:

import json

from ddi_l.jsonld import to_jsonld
from rdflib import Graph

graph = Graph().parse(data=json.dumps(to_jsonld(doc)), format="json-ld")
rows = graph.query("""
    PREFIX disco: <http://rdf-vocabulary.ddialliance.org/discovery#>
    PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
    SELECT ?name ?text WHERE {
        ?variable a disco:Variable ;
                  skos:prefLabel ?name ;
                  disco:question ?question .
        ?question disco:questionText ?text .
    }
""")
for name, text in rows:
    print(f"{name}: {text}")
# -> PetCount: How many pets live in your home?

From the command line, ddi to-jsonld pets.xml --output pets.jsonld writes the same file, ready for a triple store that loads JSON-LD, such as Apache Jena.

The vocabulary describes a study for discovery, so the JSON-LD is a summary: questionnaire flow, record layouts and the rest are left out, and it does not convert back to DDI XML. For a full copy, use JSON.

docs.title: JSON, for web apps and other languages
docs.text:
ddi to-json writes the whole document as JSON, and ddi from-json turns it back into XML:

ddi to-json pets.xml --output pets.json
ddi from-json pets.json --output pets-again.xml

The JSON keeps the XML's structure, with namespaced names as keys, so any language can read and edit it. See Use the command line for more options.

docs.title: Spreadsheets and data frames
docs.text: Many teams keep metadata in spreadsheets. ddi-l loads a folder of CSV files or an Excel workbook as DDI, so anything that writes CSV can feed it: LibreOffice, Excel, pandas, R or a database export. See Load DDI from spreadsheets for the layout and the templates to start from. The DDI Codebook example below writes such tables from another tool's output.

docs.title: R
docs.text: R can call ddi-l through the open-source reticulate package: build a study from a data frame, read variables back into one, validate and lint. See Using ddi-l from R.

docs.title: Any language, over HTTP
docs.text:
ddi serve runs an HTTP API (install the server extra) that validates, lints and converts, so a tool in any language can use it without Python:

ddi serve --port 8080
curl --data-binary @pets.xml http://localhost:8080/v1/validate

The API describes itself at /schema/openapi.json, so client generators such as the open-source OpenAPI Generator can build a client for your language. See HTTP API.

docs.title: DDI Codebook files
docs.text:
DDI Codebook (versions 2.x) is the DDI standard many data archives use to document studies and their variables. For example, the open-source data repository Dataverse exports DDI Codebook 2.5. ddi-l does not read DDI Codebook, but its variables, questions and categories map onto the spreadsheet tables, which ddi-l does read. This converts a small DDI Codebook file:

import csv
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from pathlib import Path

from ddi_l.tables import load_tables

Path("codebook.xml").write_text(
    """<codeBook xmlns="ddi:codebook:2_5" version="2.5">
  <dataDscr>
    <var name="PetCount">
      <labl>Number of pets</labl>
      <qstn><qstnLit>How many pets live in your home?</qstnLit></qstn>
    </var>
    <var name="PetKind">
      <labl>Kind of pet</labl>
      <qstn><qstnLit>What kind of pet do you have?</qstnLit></qstn>
      <catgry><catValu>1</catValu><labl>Dog</labl></catgry>
      <catgry><catValu>2</catValu><labl>Cat</labl></catgry>
    </var>
  </dataDscr>
</codeBook>
""",
    encoding="utf-8",
)

C = {"c": "ddi:codebook:2_5"}
tables = {"questions": [], "code_lists": [], "codes": [], "variables": []}
for var in ET.parse("codebook.xml").iterfind(".//c:var", C):
    name = var.get("name")
    label = var.findtext("c:labl", namespaces=C)
    categories = var.findall("c:catgry", C)
    code_list = f"{name}_codes" if categories else ""
    # Without categories, this sketch reads a variable as a whole number.
    kind = {"code_list": code_list, "numeric_type": "" if categories else "Integer"}
    tables["questions"].append(
        {
            "id": f"{name}_q",
            "name": name,
            "text@en": var.findtext("c:qstn/c:qstnLit", namespaces=C),
            "response": "code" if categories else "numeric",
            **kind,
        }
    )
    tables["variables"].append(
        {
            "id": name,
            "name": name,
            "label@en": label,
            "question": f"{name}_q",
            "representation": "code" if categories else "numeric",
            **kind,
        }
    )
    if categories:
        tables["code_lists"].append({"id": code_list, "label@en": label})
        for category in categories:
            tables["codes"].append(
                {
                    "code_list": code_list,
                    "value": category.findtext("c:catValu", namespaces=C),
                    "label@en": category.findtext("c:labl", namespaces=C),
                }
            )

folder = Path("from-codebook")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(folder / "settings.csv").write_text(
    "setting,value\nagency,example.org\n", encoding="utf-8"
)
for table, rows in tables.items():
    with open(folder / f"{table}.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)

study = load_tables(folder).to_study("Pet survey")
print(study.validate())  # -> []
study.save("pets-lifecycle.xml")

The sketch covers names, labels, question text and categories. Codebook files vary from tool to tool: check what yours writes (missing values, value types, several languages) and add the matching columns, which Load DDI from spreadsheets lists.

docs.title: DDI 3.1 and 3.2 tools
docs.text:
Some tools write DDI 3.2. For example, CLOSER's open-source questionnaire editor Archivist documents questionnaires in DDI Lifecycle 3.2, according to CLOSER. ddi-l validates and lints such files: ddi validate reads the version from the file.

ddi validate archivist-export.xml

In Python, read_ddi() opens any of the three versions and gives element access to the XML. open_ddi(), with its typed models, is for DDI 3.3 and says so when given an earlier version.

legacy = ddi.read_ddi("archivist-export.xml")
print(legacy.validate())  # -> []

docs.title: Questionnaire generators
docs.text: Some open-source tools turn a questionnaire's DDI description into the questionnaires that interviewers and respondents use. For example, Insee's Eno produces web, telephone, face-to-face and paper questionnaires from DDI, and its designer Pogues works with it. Before handing a questionnaire to such a tool, check it with ddi-l: ddi validate, ddi lint, and ddi conform to compare it with a spec (see Check a questionnaire against a spec). Check which DDI version the tool expects first.

docs.title: Colectica
docs.text: Colectica's tools are commercial. ddi-l reads and writes the FragmentInstance files Colectica Designer exports; see Work with Colectica exports. ddi-l is not affiliated with or endorsed by Colectica.

docs.title: Find more tools
docs.text: The DDI Alliance keeps a catalogue of DDI tools, which you can filter by licence, at ddialliance.org/resources/tools. Before exchanging files with a tool, check which DDI it uses: Codebook, Lifecycle 3.x, or the newer Cross-Domain Integration (DDI-CDI), which ddi-l does not read.

docs.title: Before you exchange a file
docs.text:
• Validate and lint it. ddi validate and ddi lint catch most problems before the other tool does. See Validate and lint.
  • Use one DDI version on both sides. ddi-l writes 3.3.
  • Use a registered agency. Agency IDs come from the DDI Alliance's agency registry, so items from different organisations do not share a URN.
  • Keep identifiers and versions stable. Bump an item's version when you change it, rather than giving it a new ID, so other tools see the same item.
  • Try a round trip. Send a file through the other tool and back, and compare. ddi-l keeps what it does not model (user attribute pairs, custom namespaces); another tool may drop it.

docs.title: Lint rule reference
docs.text:
ddi lint and ddi_l.lint.run_lint() check a document against lint rules, grouped in profiles. This page is generated from the rule registry, so it lists every rule the installed version has, with an example of what each one reports.

Run the default profile, a named profile, or chosen rules:

ddi lint study.xml
ddi lint export.xml --profile colectica-questionnaire --format table
ddi lint export.xml --rules colectica.condition.empty,text.pipe-malformed
ddi lint --list-rules --list-format table

A finding is an error, a warning or info. Only errors make ddi lint exit non-zero, unless --fail-severity warning or --fail-severity info asks for a stricter gate. Skip a rule with --skip-rule RULE.

docs.title: Configure the rules
docs.text:
Rules marked heuristic guess at intent from wording or layout, and report a warning at most. Some rules depend on conventions that vary from one organisation to the next; their options start empty, so the rule does nothing until you configure it.

Option Used by Default required_languages i18n.missing-language none: the rule is off placeholder_patterns text.placeholder-unresolved ‹‹…››, <<…>>, «insert…», [insert …], "insert survey-specific" ui_chrome_tokens text.ui-chrome none: the rule is off logic_note_patterns colectica.statement.logic-note "Flow condition", "Display condition", "Logic:" and their French equivalents gate_description_patterns colectica.ifthenelse.partial-gate "go to … page", "aller à la page", "passer à la page" known_names text.pipe-undeclared none variable_code_pattern colectica.domain.label-mismatch none: the rule is off pipe_prefixes text.pipe-malformed none pipe_suffixes text.pipe-undeclared none

From the command line, --required-language (repeated) and --known-names FILE (one name per line) set the first two that most projects need, and --lint-config FILE sets any option from a JSON object:

{
  "required_languages": ["en-CA", "fr-CA"],
  "ui_chrome_tokens": ["Previous", "Next", "Save and finish later"],
  "variable_code_pattern": "Q\\d{3}",
  "pipe_suffixes": ["_E", "_F"]
}

In Python, lint_configuration() takes the same options and gives a configuration for one call, leaving every other call as it was:

from ddi_l import read_ddi
from ddi_l.lint import lint_configuration, run_lint

document = read_ddi("my-study.xml")
bilingual = lint_configuration(required_languages=["en-CA", "fr-CA"])
findings = run_lint(document, configuration=bilingual)

run_profile(), document.lint() and the validate_*() functions take it too. configure_lint() sets the same options as the default for every call in the process that is not given one.

docs.title: Default profile
docs.text: Rule Severity ddi.agency.allowed error ddi.citation.present error ddi.citation.title.present error ddi.citation.title.languages warning ddi.maintainable.labels warning ddi.reference.integrity error (warning in a fragment) ddi.reference.version warning ddi.reference.provenance-external info

docs.title: ddi.agency.allowed
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: default

Validate that the document agency identifier is present and allowed.

Example finding:

Agency 'example.com' is not an allowed value.

docs.title: ddi.citation.present
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: default

Ensure the root document contains a citation element when required.

Example finding:

DDIInstance is missing a <Citation> element.

docs.title: ddi.citation.title.present
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: default

Validate that a citation includes a human-readable title when required.

Example finding:

Citation is missing a <Title> element.

docs.title: ddi.citation.title.languages
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: default

Ensure citation titles cover the configured set of languages.

Example finding:

Citation title is missing required language 'fr'.

docs.title: ddi.maintainable.labels
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: default

Ensure maintainable elements include human-readable labels.

Example finding:

Maintainable element is missing a label.

docs.title: ddi.reference.integrity
docs.text:
Severity: error (warning in a fragment) · Profiles: default, colectica-questionnaire

Validate that all Reference elements resolve to items present in the document.

Iterates every element whose tag ends with Reference and whose payload includes a TypeOfObject child (the DDI convention for typed references). Each reference is checked against the identifiable items found by walking the raw XML tree, ensuring coverage of elements not yet natively modelled by the library (e.g. Category inside CategoryScheme).

A lateBound="true" reference resolves to any version of its item. A reference whose item is present at other versions only is reported by ddi.reference.version, and one recording provenance (inside r:BasedOnObject or r:UserAttributePair) by ddi.reference.provenance-external.

Example finding:

Reference to OutParameter '99999999-9999-4999-8999-999999999999' cannot be resolved to an item in this fragment.

docs.title: ddi.reference.version
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: default, colectica-questionnaire

Report references whose item is present, but not at the version named.

An exact reference to a version the document does not hold; a late-bound one naming a version newer than any it holds; or a late-bound one whose lateBoundRestriction (latest within major version 4, say) matches no version it holds.

Example finding:

Reference to QuestionItem '11111111-1111-4111-8111-000000000001' resolves to its ID, but version 3 is not present; available: 4.

docs.title: ddi.reference.provenance-external
docs.text:
Severity: info · Profiles: default, colectica-questionnaire

Note provenance references whose item is not in the document.

r:BasedOnReference and references inside r:UserAttributePair record where an item came from; the source usually lives elsewhere.

Example finding:

Provenance reference to QuestionItem '11111111-1111-4111-8111-0000000000ff' points outside this file.

docs.title: Profile colectica-questionnaire
docs.text: Rule Severity colectica.maintainable.labels warning colectica.identifiable.shared-id error colectica.binding.dangling error colectica.condition.malformed error colectica.condition.empty error colectica.condition.unsatisfiable error colectica.condition.native-invalid error colectica.condition.unused-inputs warning colectica.condition.synopsis-stale info colectica.ifthenelse.partial-gate warning colectica.codedomain.no-codelist error colectica.domain.label-mismatch warning colectica.domain.type-mismatch warning i18n.missing-language error (info for descriptions) text.placeholder-unresolved warning text.ui-chrome warning text.pipe-malformed error text.pipe-undeclared warning colectica.lookup.duplicate-field error colectica.lookup.unlisted-output error colectica.lookup.suspicious-field warning colectica.alias.escape-compounded error colectica.alias.malformed warning colectica.statement.logic-note warning colectica.flow.read-before-computed warning/info colectica.flow.unreachable warning/info colectica.condition.multi-answer-question warning

docs.title: colectica.maintainable.labels
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Ensure items carry a label or a name, as Colectica content does.

Colectica items routinely carry a ConstructName, QuestionItemName or r:Name instead of an r:Label. Any of them satisfies the rule, provided it holds text. Used by the colectica-questionnaire profile in place of ddi.maintainable.labels.

Example finding:

QuestionConstruct 11111111 has no label or name with text.

docs.title: colectica.identifiable.shared-id
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report an identifiable declared inside two or more different items.

Colectica's copy of a question can keep the source's OutParameter IDs, so two items declare the same parameter; a binding to it is ambiguous. Versions of one item sharing their children is expected and not reported.

Example finding:

OutParameter 33333333 is declared in 2 items: QuestionItem 11111111 (PetKind), QuestionItem 22222222 (PetKind).

docs.title: colectica.binding.dangling
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a binding whose source or target parameter is not in the file.

Late-bound references resolve to any version, so only a parameter missing at every version is reported.

Example finding:

A binding in Sequence 77777777 (Pet survey) has a source OutParameter 99999999 that is not declared in this file.

docs.title: colectica.condition.malformed
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a JSON condition that does not parse.

Neutral and Blaise5DataLookup commands must hold valid JSON.

Example finding:

IfThenElse 33333333 (Cat owners): Neutral command is not valid JSON: Expecting value (line 1, column 1).

docs.title: colectica.condition.empty
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a Neutral condition with no statement at all.

An empty condition is always true, so the branch always shows. A loop's empty condition tests nothing either, so whether the loop repeats no longer depends on the answers. The intended logic is often in the condition's description, quoted in the message.

Example finding:

IfThenElse 33333333 (Cat owners) has an empty condition; its description reads "Show when a cat lives here.".

docs.title: colectica.condition.unsatisfiable
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a logic group whose And-joined statements contradict each other.

On one subject: a value and Empty, Empty and Refused, a value and Refused, or two different EqualTo values. Such a group can never be true.

Example finding:

IfThenElse 33333333 (No pets) can never be true in group 1 (PetCount): the statements joined by And contradict each other on one subject.

docs.title: colectica.condition.native-invalid
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report native Blaise content that is not a valid condition or program.

A condition (an IfThenElse's, a loop's, or that of a ComputationItem with no output parameters, such as an edit check) should be one expression over the item's inputs: not statements (goto, set, several lines). A ComputationItem with output parameters holds a program, which may span lines and assign its outputs. Neither should use typographic quotes outside a string or a { comment }, nor name in {{name}} anything but the item's parameters.

Example finding:

ComputationItem 66666666 (Many pets) has Blaise code that is not a single valid expression: it uses typographic quotes.

docs.title: colectica.condition.unused-inputs
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report input parameters of an IfThenElse its conditions never use.

The inputs are the IfThenElse's, and its ElseIf branches test them too: an input only a branch uses is used, and so is one the item binds onward, to what its branches hold. An item with an empty, unreadable or data-lookup condition in any branch is left alone.

Example finding:

IfThenElse 33333333 (Cat owners) has 1 input(s) its condition never uses: PetAge.

docs.title: colectica.condition.synopsis-stale
docs.text:
Severity: info · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a stored synopsis that does not name a subject the logic tests.

Colectica stores the synopsis its editor last showed; a synopsis naming another variable, or missing while the condition has statements, no longer describes the logic. The message gives the synopsis rendered from the logic (see ddi_l.colectica_logic.render_synopsis).

Example finding:

IfThenElse 33333333 (Cat owners): the stored synopsis does not name PetKind; the logic reads "(PetKind contains all of 3 "Cat") and (PetCount > 2)".

docs.title: colectica.ifthenelse.partial-gate
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a gate that wraps only the first construct of a page.

Heuristic.

The IfThenElse holds a single construct in its Then branch, more constructs follow it unconditionally in the same sequence, it has no Else branch, and its description says it routes to a page (see gate_description_patterns): the gate probably should wrap the whole page.

Example finding:

IfThenElse 33333333 (Owner gate) gates only StatementItem 44444444 (Welcome), while the 2 construct(s) after it in Sequence 55555555 (Owner page) show unconditionally; its description reads "If an owner, go to the owner page". The gate probably should wrap the whole page.

docs.title: colectica.codedomain.no-codelist
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a CodeDomain without an r:CodeListReference.

Grid cell domains included.

Example finding:

QuestionGrid 11111111 (PetHours) has a code domain with no code list.

docs.title: colectica.domain.label-mismatch
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a domain label or item name naming another variable code.

Heuristic.

With variable_code_pattern set, the codes it matches in the item's output parameter alias are compared with those in its response domain labels and its names: a label naming only other codes was probably copied from another question.

Example finding:

QuestionItem 11111111 (P0012): "P0016" names P0016, but its output is P0012.

docs.title: colectica.domain.type-mismatch
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a question whose wording does not fit its domain type.

Heuristic.

A question opening with Why (Pourquoi), or What/Which (Quel...) without a date word, whose answer is a date; or one opening with When (Quand) whose answer is a code or text.

Example finding:

QuestionItem 11111111 (PetLeft) asks "Why did the pet leave?" but its answer is a date.

docs.title: i18n.missing-language
docs.text:
Severity: error (info for descriptions) · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report text missing a language listed in required_languages.

Question texts, statement display texts, category labels and numeric or text domain labels are errors; a condition's description is info. Nothing runs until required_languages is configured.

Example finding:

Category 22222222 (Bird): the label has no fr-CA.

docs.title: text.placeholder-unresolved
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report template placeholders left in text (placeholder_patterns).

Example finding:

StatementItem 44444444 (Welcome): unresolved placeholder "<<insert pet name>>" in en-CA text.

docs.title: text.ui-chrome
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report user-interface words pasted into content (ui_chrome_tokens).

Tokens match whole, case-insensitively. The default list is empty: the words depend on the application the mock-ups came from.

Example finding:

StatementItem 44444444 (Goodbye): user-interface text 'Previous', 'Next' in en-CA content.

docs.title: text.pipe-malformed
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a #{...} pipe that is empty, holds white space, or is a prefix.

Example finding:

StatementItem 44444444 (Welcome): the pipe '#{Owner Name}' contains white space.

docs.title: text.pipe-undeclared
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a piped #{name} that nothing in the file declares.

A name is declared by a data lookup field, a parameter alias, or known_names (what the run-time system supplies; --known-names FILE). pipe_suffixes are stripped first.

Example finding:

StatementItem 44444444 (Welcome) pipes #{VetName}, which no lookup field, parameter or known name declares.

docs.title: colectica.lookup.duplicate-field
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a name listed twice in one data lookup's fields.

Example finding:

ComputationItem 55555555 (Owner lookup) lists the lookup field 'OwnerName' 2 times.

docs.title: colectica.lookup.unlisted-output
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a data lookup output its field list does not hold.

Colectica gives a data lookup one r:OutParameter per field, whose ID is the field's Identifier and whose alias is the field's Name. An output no field lists carries no value, and one named otherwise hands its field on under another name, so whatever binds it reads the wrong thing. A field written without an Identifier is matched by its name.

Example finding:

ComputationItem 55555555 (Owner lookup): the output 'OwnerPhone' is not one of its lookup fields.

docs.title: colectica.lookup.suspicious-field
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a lookup field never assigned, or named like a value.

Heuristic.

A field whose name starts with a digit is more likely a value typed into the wrong place than a field.

Example finding:

ComputationItem 55555555 (Owner lookup): the lookup field '01' is named like a value.

docs.title: colectica.alias.escape-compounded
docs.text:
Severity: error · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report an alias whose XML escape was escaped again (_x005F_).

Escaping a name that already holds an escape turns its underscore into _x005F_, and each further pass doubles it: the alias grows on every propagation and becomes an unusable variable name.

Example finding:

OutParameter 88888888 of Sequence 77777777 (Pet survey) has an alias escaped 3 times over (44 characters): 'Pets_x005F_x005F_x002F_Count'.

docs.title: colectica.alias.malformed
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report an alias with an XML escape, too long, or made of text.

Heuristic.

Compounded escapes are reported by colectica.alias.escape-compounded.

Example finding:

OutParameter 88888888 of Sequence 77777777 (Pet survey): the alias 'Pets_x002F_Count' holds an XML escape.

docs.title: colectica.statement.logic-note
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a statement that is a design note shown as content.

Heuristic.

Its name or display text matches logic_note_patterns ("Flow condition: ...", "Display condition", ...). A statement Colectica types as a Note (extension:TypeOfStatement = Note) is not shown, so it is where such a note belongs and is not reported.

Example finding:

StatementItem 44444444 (Flow condition) reads "Flow condition: owners only": a design note shown to respondents as content.

docs.title: colectica.flow.read-before-computed
docs.text:
Severity: warning/info · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report an item that reads a value asked or computed later in the flow.

A condition, a fill or a computation can only read what an earlier question or computation produced: Colectica Designer's routing view reports a later source as broken. The flow is walked in document order, an item reached by several paths (a page reused by several exits, say) once on each, and each input is followed through the bindings of the containers on that path to the question construct or computation that produces it. An input with no binding is left to other rules.

With the logic extra, the solver also asks whether a respondent can reach the item before the question or computation: if so, the finding gives one; if not, it is info, since only the routing view is affected.

Example finding:

IfThenElse 44444444 (Vet gate), reached through IfThenElse 55555555 (Early exit), reads PetAge before QuestionConstruct 66666666 (PetAge) asks it. For example, when PetCount is 2.

docs.title: colectica.flow.unreachable
docs.text:
Severity: warning/info · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a construct no respondent reaches.

The gates on every way to it cannot all hold, for any answers: its ask-condition, the disjunction over the ways to it of the gates' conjunction, is unsatisfiable. Only the first construct on a way is reported, not those below it. A condition this rule cannot read (a data lookup, code in another language) may hold or not, and a loop's body counts as reached. Needs the logic extra: without it, a flow with a gate gets one info finding that it was not checked.

Example finding:

QuestionConstruct 77777777 (PetFood) is never reached: no answers meet the gates on every way to it.

docs.title: colectica.condition.multi-answer-question
docs.text:
Severity: warning · Profiles: colectica-questionnaire

Report a gate whose condition tests one answer of a multi-answer question.

Colectica Designer's routing view reports a condition on one answer of a question with several (a StructuredMixedResponseDomain) as broken, even when the answer's output is restated in its domain; a condition on a question with one answer resolves. Ask that answer as a question of its own.

Example finding:

IfThenElse 44444444 (Food gate) tests FoodGrams, answer 2 of 2 of QuestionItem 66666666 (PetFood): Designer's routing view reports a condition on one answer of a question with several as broken. Ask it as a question of its own.

docs.title: Models reference (advanced layer)
docs.text:
The ddi_l.models package provides generated dataclass wrappers for DDI 3.3 types. These are the advanced layer. Most users should start with the simple CRUD API instead.

When to use the model layer

Use the model classes directly when you need fine-grained control over DDI structures that the simple API does not expose, such as custom representations, classification hierarchies, or physical data products.

docs.title: Key model packages
docs.text: Package DDI module Example types ddi_l.models.base Reusable InternationalString, Reference, MaintainableBase ddi_l.models.logicalproduct LogicalProduct Variable, CodeList, Category, RepresentedVariable ddi_l.models.datacollection DataCollection QuestionItem, Instrument, CollectionEvent ddi_l.models.conceptualcomponent ConceptualComponent Concept, Universe, ConceptualVariable, UnitType ddi_l.models.study StudyUnit StudyUnit ddi_l.models.archive Archive Archive, Organization ddi_l.models.physical PhysicalDataProduct PhysicalStructure, PhysicalInstance ddi_l.models.methodology Methodology Methodology, MethodologyItem, MethodologyScheme

docs.title: Creating model objects
docs.text:
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Variable

var = Variable(
    agency="example.org",
    identifier="var-age",
    version="1.0",
    names=[InternationalString(text="Age", lang="en")],
    labels=[InternationalString(text="Age of respondent", lang="en")],
)

docs.title: XML round-tripping
docs.text:
Every model class supports from_xml() and to_xml():

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Variable

study = ddi.new_study(title="Demo", agency="example.org")
study.add_variable(name="age")
study.save("study.xml")

# ddi.read_ddi() works on either XML backend, so this snippet does not depend on
# lxml being installed.
doc = ddi.read_ddi("study.xml")
xml_element = doc.root.find(".//{ddi:logicalproduct:3_3}Variable")
var = Variable.from_xml(xml_element)

new_element = var.to_xml()

Unknown XML content is preserved in the other_elements list so that round-tripping does not lose information.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Use Reference to link model objects:

from ddi_l.models.base import Reference

ref = Reference(
    agency="example.org",
    identifier="var-age",
    version="1.0",
    type_of_object="Variable",
)

docs.title: Parameters and bindings
docs.text:
A construct passes values through parameters: a question construct's OutParameter carries its answer, and a condition (an IfThenElse, a Loop) tests its InParameters. A Binding on the sequence holding both feeds one into the other.

from ddi_l.models import Binding, InParameter, OutParameter

answer = OutParameter(
    agency="example.org", identifier="q1-out", version="1", alias="Q1"
)
gate_input = InParameter(
    agency="example.org", identifier="gate-in", version="1", alias="Q1"
)
binding = Binding.between(answer, gate_input, late_bound=True)

reference = binding.target_parameter_reference
print(reference.type_of_object, reference.identifier)

IfThenElse, Loop, StatementItem and Sequence hold theirs in in_parameters, out_parameters and bindings, read from a file as these types. So do the generated models that have them (ComputationItem, QuestionConstruct, Split, RepeatUntil, ..., and an Instruction's in_parameters). These lists also take a raw element, written as it is. A parameter's to_reference() and the references Binding.between() builds carry no r:URN, as Colectica writes them; late_bound=True marks them lateBound="true", so they follow the parameter's latest version.

docs.title: Generated models
docs.text:
Model classes under ddi_l.models._generated/ are auto-generated from the DDI 3.3 XSD files. Do not edit them by hand. To regenerate:

python -m codegen.generate_model_bases

See the development guide for details on the codegen pipeline.

docs.title: Namespace profiles and bindings
docs.text: The ddi_l.namespaces module centralizes the namespace bindings that appear throughout DDI 3.x instance documents. Profiles expose curated collections of prefix/URI pairs for common maintainable modules so downstream tooling can apply consistent bindings regardless of whether they rely on the stdlib or lxml XML backends. The default bindings target the bundled 3.3 release, while helpers in ddi_l.schema_loader expose namespace maps for 3.1 and 3.2 when legacy content needs to be processed.

docs.title: Built-in profiles
docs.text:
Profile constant Included prefixes DDI_DEFAULT_PROFILE Default namespace (ddi:instance:3_3), reusable (r), XML Schema Instance (xsi) DDI_REUSABLE_PROFILE Reusable (r) DDI_STUDY_UNIT_PROFILE Study Unit (s) and Conceptual Component (c) DDI_DATA_COLLECTION_PROFILE Data Collection (d) DDI_LOGICAL_PRODUCT_PROFILE Logical Product (l) DDI_PHYSICAL_DATA_PROFILE Physical Data Product (p) DDI_ARCHIVE_PROFILE Archive (a) DDI_CONCEPTUAL_COMPONENT_PROFILE Conceptual Component (cc) DDI_COMPARATIVE_PROFILE Comparative (cmp) DDI_PROFILE_PROFILE Profile metadata (pr)

Profiles live in the NAMESPACE_PROFILES mapping and can be retrieved with get_namespace_profile(name) when you need to inspect the raw bindings.

docs.title: Merging profiles
docs.text:
Use merge_namespace_profiles to combine named profiles with ad-hoc overrides. Conflicting bindings raise a ValueError by default so accidental rebinding is caught early. Pass allow_override=True or supply the overrides mapping when you intentionally want later values to replace earlier ones.

from ddi_l.namespaces import (
    DDI_DEFAULT_PROFILE,
    DDI_STUDY_UNIT_PROFILE,
    merge_namespace_profiles,
)

bindings = merge_namespace_profiles(
    DDI_DEFAULT_PROFILE,
    DDI_STUDY_UNIT_PROFILE,
    overrides={"custom": "http://example.com/ns"},
)

The returned dictionary can be supplied directly to XML builders or registered with global namespace registries when using the stdlib backend.

docs.title: Applying profiles to documents
docs.text:
DDIDocument.ensure_namespace_prefixes takes a single profile (or a prefix-to-URI mapping) plus optional ad-hoc bindings passed as the keyword-only extra_namespaces. The method normalizes the namespace declarations so the resulting XML contains consistent prefixes whether lxml is installed or not.

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.namespaces import DDI_STUDY_UNIT_PROFILE

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Demo", agency="example.agency")
doc.inner.ensure_namespace_prefixes(
    DDI_STUDY_UNIT_PROFILE,
    extra_namespaces={"custom": "http://example.com/ns"},
)

To apply more than one profile, merge them first. merge_namespace_profiles returns a mapping, which is one of the things the method accepts:

from ddi_l.namespaces import (
    DDI_PROFILE_PROFILE,
    DDI_STUDY_UNIT_PROFILE,
    merge_namespace_profiles,
)

doc.inner.ensure_namespace_prefixes(
    merge_namespace_profiles(DDI_PROFILE_PROFILE, DDI_STUDY_UNIT_PROFILE),
    extra_namespaces={"custom": "http://example.com/ns"},
)

extra_namespaces is applied last, so callers can override the profile's bindings deliberately. The conflict-detection controls (allow_override, overrides) belong to merge_namespace_profiles, not to this method. Do the merge, and its ValueError fires before the document is touched.

docs.title: Working with lxml and stdlib
docs.text: The namespace helpers hide the small differences between the stdlib and lxml backends. When lxml is available, the profiles are merged into the element nsmap and round-tripped through cleanup_namespaces. When only the stdlib is present the same bindings are registered with xml.etree.ElementTree so the serialized document still includes the requested declarations. The new helper module therefore ensures consistent output across environments.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: What costs time and memory in ddi-l, with measured numbers and the settings that change them.

docs.title: Indicative timings
docs.text:
A study with 5,000 variables (1.4 MiB of XML), Python 3.11 on a single core, median of several runs. Treat the numbers as proportions, not guarantees.

Operation lxml backend stdlib backend read_ddi(data) 0.02 s 0.18 s write_ddi(document) 0.06 s 0.35 s Document.to_xml() 0.6 s 0.3 s lint_source(data) 0.4 s 0.2 s validate_source(data) (schema only) 0.05 s 1.4 s Document.validate() 0.6 s 3.5 s import ddi_l 0.03 s 0.03 s ddi --help 0.08 s 0.08 s

With lxml installed, a document is first checked by libxml2's C validator, which confirms a valid document in milliseconds. Only when that check fails does xmlschema run, to produce the detailed issues, so the reported errors are the same on both backends. Without lxml every validation runs on xmlschema, which is pure Python and dominates the timings above. schema_loader.validate(..., backend="python") turns the libxml2 check off for one call, and schema_loader.set_validation_backend("python") for the whole application.

docs.title: The XML backends on a large export
docs.text:
A 9 MB Colectica export (112,000 elements), Python 3.13, best of five runs on one machine. benchmarks/backends_bench.py measures the same steps on any file, on the backend DDI_L_XML_BACKEND names.

Step native lxml stdlib Parse 0.05 s (185 MB/s) 0.07 s (124 MB/s) 0.22 s (41 MB/s) read_ddi 0.13 s 0.33 s 0.29 s First write_ddi (builds the source index) 0.23 s 1.4 s 1.7 s write_ddi again, unchanged 0.01 s 0.28 s 0.23 s write_ddi after changing one attribute 0.04 s 0.31 s 0.28 s write_ddi(layout="default") 0.80 s 0.26 s 0.76 s colectica-questionnaire profile 0.67 s 1.74 s 0.62 s
  • Parsing is not bound by memory bandwidth. Copying the same bytes takes 1 ms (6.5 GB/s); most of the native parse is making the tree's 112,000 nodes. Text that needed no decoding stays a range of the source bytes.
  • Writing back costs what changed. The native tree keeps each element's digest and clears it only on the path from a change to the root, so an unchanged document is written as its bytes, and an edited one hashes only that path.
  • A full layout is Python code on the native and standard library backends (the indentation, the namespace clean-up and ElementTree's writer), so a new document, or one written with an explicit layout, is written about three times faster by lxml.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
• Schemas load once per version. libxml2 compiles a version's XSDs in about 0.1 s. xmlschema takes about 2 s and 20–25 MiB, and is loaded only when it is needed; later validations in the same process reuse both. ddi serve loads the default version at startup.
  • Reading is cheap; the model index is lazy. read_ddi parses the XML and stops. The resolver index is built the first time DDIDocument.resolver is used, or up front with build_index=True.
  • Document serializes on demand. to_xml(), save() and validate() write the model back into XML each time they are called. Batch your edits and serialize once.
  • Reference checks run on save() only. Dangling references are reported as a single DDIReferenceWarning when saving.

docs.title: Large documents
docs.text:
Stream instead of loading the whole tree:

import ddi_l as ddi

for variable in ddi.iter_variables("large-study.xml"):
    print(variable.identifier)

iter_variables and iter_questions clear each element once it has been turned into an object, so memory stays close to the size of one item (about 190 KiB peak for the 5,000-variable study above). iterparse_ddi streams any maintainable type; request only the types you need, because an element is kept until the outermost requested element around it has been built.

docs.title: Lint and conformance
docs.text:
• One run builds each index once. The rules of one run_lint or run_profile call, and the checks of one conform call, share what they build from the document: its items and their versions, the reference resolutions, the bindings and the parsed conditions. The colectica-questionnaire profile on a 9 MB Colectica export (4,478 items) takes 2.0 s; it took 6.1 s when each rule built its own.
  • A later run reads only what changed (native backend). Each item's facts and per-item findings are kept under its content digest, so linting the same document again after an edit reads only the edited items. On that export the profile takes 0.8 s on a first run and 0.13 s after an edit. The rules that follow the whole flow still walk it, which is most of what is left.
  • Paths are counted, not walked. A flow whose pages rejoin after each of n gates has 2^n paths from the instrument. colectica.flow.read-before-computed and conform reach each construct once per state that can change what they report, so 20 chained gates (a million paths) take milliseconds; 16 took 9.1 s in conform. A flow that loops back on itself is still walked path by path.
  • Which constructs a respondent reaches is solved once per flow. colectica.flow.unreachable gives the solver one variable per construct, however many paths lead to it, settles what it can without it, and marks every construct each respondent it finds reaches. 40 chained gates (2^40 paths) take 0.16 s; a random flow of 300 constructs, 0.17 s.
  • Exact gate comparison costs about 5 ms a pair. With the logic extra, conform decides a pair of gates only when their normal forms differ, and each pair once, so the Pet fixture compares in about 8 ms with the solver or without it. Twenty chained gates take 33 ms with it and 16 ms without.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text: ddi serve processes at most --max-jobs documents at once (default: the number of CPUs) and answers 503 with Retry-After beyond that. Validation holds the GIL, so more concurrent jobs than cores adds memory, not throughput. Scale out with more processes behind a load balancer.

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text:
The benchmarks/ directory in the repository contains reproducible scripts:

uv run python -m benchmarks.iterparse_bench
uv run python -m benchmarks.validation_report_bench
uv run python benchmarks/colectica_profile_bench.py EXPORT.xml
DDI_L_XML_BACKEND=native uv run python benchmarks/backends_bench.py EXPORT.xml
  • Schema conversion benchmark

docs.title: Using ddi-l from R
docs.text:
R users can call ddi-l directly through reticulate, the standard R interface to Python. reticulate runs Python inside your R session and converts values in both directions, so there is no separate R package to install and every feature of ddi-l is available.

This page shows the R equivalents of the common tasks. The Python User guide covers each feature in more depth; the calls are the same, with $ in place of ..

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Install reticulate once, then create a Python environment for ddi-l:

install.packages("reticulate")

library(reticulate)
virtualenv_create("ddi-l")
py_install("ddi-l", envname = "ddi-l")   # or "ddi-l[full]" for faster parsing

In each session, select that environment before using Python:

library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv("ddi-l", required = TRUE)

reticulate 1.41 and later

reticulate::py_require("ddi-l") declares the dependency and lets reticulate provision a suitable Python environment automatically, in place of the two steps above.

Import the package. The object ddi is the Python module ddi_l:

library(reticulate)
ddi <- import("ddi_l")
ddi$`__version__`

docs.title: Create a study
docs.text:
doc <- ddi$new_study(title = "Household Survey", agency = "example.org")

q_age <- doc$add_question(text = "How old are you?", label = "Age question")
age <- doc$add_variable(name = "age", question = q_age, label = "Age in years")
age <- age$set_numeric("Integer", low = 0L, high = 120L)

doc$save("household.xml")
print(doc)
# -> Document(title='Household Survey', agency='example.org', questions=1, variables=1)

Model objects stay attached to the document: you can keep editing age after save(), and the next save includes the change.

docs.title: Build a study from a data frame
docs.text:
Loop over the columns of a data frame and describe each one. The example reads the curriculum's sample file; save it in your working directory first:

Download survey_sample.csv

survey <- read.csv("survey_sample.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

doc <- ddi$new_study(title = "Survey sample", agency = "example.org")
for (column in names(survey)) {
  values <- survey[[column]]
  variable <- doc$add_variable(name = column, label = column)
  if (is.numeric(values)) {
    type <- if (all(values == round(values))) "Integer" else "Decimal"
    variable <- variable$set_numeric(
      type,
      low = as.character(min(values)),
      high = as.character(max(values))
    )
  } else {
    variable <- variable$set_text()
  }
}
doc$save("survey.xml")
length(doc$variables)
# -> 5

docs.title: Read a study into a data frame
docs.text:
Python lists arrive in R as lists, so vapply() turns them into columns:

opened <- ddi$open_ddi("survey.xml")
variables <- opened$variables

catalogue <- data.frame(
  name = vapply(variables, function(v) v$names[[1]]$text, character(1)),
  label = vapply(variables, function(v) v$labels[[1]]$text, character(1)),
  identifier = vapply(variables, function(v) v$identifier, character(1))
)
catalogue[, c("name", "label")]

docs.title: Validate and lint
docs.text:
validate() returns schema issues and lint() returns quality findings; both are empty for a clean document:

issues <- opened$validate()
length(issues)
# -> 0

findings <- opened$lint()
lint_table <- data.frame(
  rule = vapply(findings, function(f) f$rule_id, character(1)),
  severity = vapply(findings, function(f) f$severity, character(1))
)
nrow(lint_table)
# -> 0

docs.title: Custom properties and lookups
docs.text:
age <- opened$find(catalogue$identifier[2])
age$set_property("myorg:source_system", "CRM-2024")
age$get_property("myorg:source_system")
# -> "CRM-2024"
opened$save("survey.xml")

docs.title: Handle errors
docs.text:
A Python exception becomes an R error, so tryCatch() works as usual. py_last_error() tells you which ddi-l exception it was:

message <- tryCatch(
  ddi$read_ddi("<DDIInstance><Broken></DDIInstance>"),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
py_last_error()$type
# -> "DDIParseError"

See Validation for the full list of exception types.

docs.title: JSON and linked data
docs.text:
ddi_l.jsonld renders a study as JSON-LD. The result arrives as a named R list, ready for jsonlite:

jsonld <- import("ddi_l.jsonld")
graph <- jsonld$to_jsonld(opened)
names(graph)
json_text <- jsonlite::toJSON(graph, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)

docs.title: The command line from R
docs.text:
The ddi command is the module ddi_l.cli, so it can be run with the same Python that reticulate uses:

output <- system2(
  py_exe(),
  c("-m", "ddi_l.cli", "validate", "survey.xml"),
  stdout = TRUE
)
output
# -> "Document is valid."

docs.title: Tips for reticulate
docs.text:
• Methods and attributes use $: doc$add_variable(...), variable$identifier.
  • Keyword arguments are named R arguments: label = "Age".
  • Integers: R numbers are doubles. Write 120L where Python expects an int, or pass a string where ddi-l accepts one (low = "0").
  • NULL is converted to Python None.
  • Lists returned by ddi-l are ordinary R lists, indexed from 1: doc$variables[[1]].
  • Chained calls such as set_numeric() return the object; assign the result (age <- age$set_numeric(...)) so R does not print it.
  • Special names need backticks: ddi$`__version__`.

docs.title: Behaviour changes
docs.text:
• The native XML core comes with ddi-l. pip install ddi-l also installs ddi-l-native, and ddi-l reads and writes XML with it before lxml, so an installation with the full extra now uses the native core. The results are the same; set DDI_L_XML_BACKEND=lxml to keep lxml. On a platform with no compiled wheel, pip installs a pure-Python stand-in and nothing changes; see which extras you need.
  • A file read is written back as read. write_ddi(), save(), to_xml(), ddi roundtrip and POST /v1/roundtrip write a document read from a file or bytes with every unchanged element as it was read, byte for byte: its quotes, character references, CDATA, comments, prefixes and indentation. Only new or changed elements are laid out, like the file around them (Colectica's layout in a FragmentInstance, the file's own indentation otherwise). Elements are matched by content, so an item moved, copied or rebuilt from its model unchanged keeps its bytes. Before, only a FragmentInstance already in Colectica's layout came back unchanged, and a DDIInstance came back in this library's layout. A DDIInstance whose file binds a DDI namespace to another prefix (p0, ns1) is still laid out afresh by save() and to_xml(), with the canonical prefixes (c, s...). Pass layout="colectica" or layout="default" (--layout, ?layout=) to lay the whole file out as before; DDIFragment.save() now defaults to layout=None for the same reason. A document keeps the bytes it was read from, so it holds the file's size in memory as well.
  • Schema validation reports every error. validate() and everything built on it (ddi validate, Document.validate(), POST /v1/validate) reported the first schema error and stopped. They now report each one, then the warnings. An error found before the schema is read, such as a missing identification, is still reported alone. validate(max_issues=) stops after that many errors with a warning saying so; the HTTP API stops at ServerConfig.max_schema_issues (100 by default).
  • conform decides gates and edits exactly when the logic extra is installed. A gate written differently that always agrees with the spec's (PetCount > 0 and PetCount >= 1, for a question whose domain has no decimals) is no longer spec.gate.different, and a page gate is found the same way. A spec.gate.different or spec.edit.different finding names a respondent the two disagree on, in its message ("(they differ when PetCount is 1)") and in a new example field, which JSON output has only when it is set. The spec's response domains and variable types say what each name is. ddi conform --semantics syntactic (conform(semantics= "syntactic")) compares normal forms, as before; --semantics smt needs the extra.
  • equivalent() calculates when the logic extra is installed. Gates written differently that always agree are equivalent: x + 1 > 3 and x > 2. equivalent(exact=False) compares normal forms only, as before; without the extra nothing changes.
  • Lint configuration is per call. run_lint(), run_profile(), document.lint() and the validate_*() functions take a configuration from the new lint_configuration(), for that call alone; configure_lint() still sets the default for calls given none. ddi lint no longer changes the process default, so calling cli.main() twice in one process no longer carries the first call's options into the second.
  • Scoped settings stay in their thread or task. ddi.configured() changed the process-wide default for the length of its with block, so other threads saw it. It now applies to its own thread or task only; ddi.configure() still sets the default for every thread.
  • ddi-l no longer writes ElementTree's namespace registry. On the standard library backend, the prefixes a document registered went to ElementTree.register_namespace, which the whole process shares: other code using ElementTree saw them, and so did other threads. They are now kept for the current thread or task, and the writer names namespaces from them. Output in one thread is unchanged; a document built in one thread and written with a layout in another writes ns0, ns1... for prefixes registered only in the first.
  • The validation backend is chosen per call. schema_loader.validate() takes backend="python" or "lxml", and the new schema_loader.validation_backend() scopes one to a with block, in its own thread or task. set_validation_backend() still sets the application default, which the new get_validation_backend() returns. VALIDATION_IMPLEMENTATION now names the best backend available, fixed at import; it no longer follows set_validation_backend().
  • lint.ALLOWED_AGENCIES and namespaces.NAMESPACE_PROFILES are read-only. ALLOWED_AGENCIES was a set an application could change in place, which the agency rule read when the default configuration had no list. It is now a frozen view of the default configuration: set the list with configure_lint(allowed_agencies=[...]).
  • A fragment is linted as a fragment over HTTP too. POST /v1/lint and POST /v1/validate linted a FragmentInstance inside a made-up DDIInstance, so a dangling reference was an error there and a warning in ddi lint, and an allowed-agency list checked the made-up container's agency. Both now lint the fragment itself, as ddi lint does: a fragment whose only problem is a dangling reference is now valid.
  • Of two copies of one version, the first counts everywhere. An export that holds an item twice at the same version (a shared ID) named the second copy in condition explanations, synopses and ddi conform, and the first everywhere else; it is now the first throughout.
  • Reference findings are split three ways. ddi.reference.integrity matched (agency, id, version) exactly, so on Colectica exports it reported every late-bound parameter reference (written at version 1 while the parameter is at, say, 4) and every BasedOn link to the item a copy came from. On the bundled Colectica sample it reported 116 references, of which 2 were really unresolved. Now:
  • a lateBound="true" reference resolves to any version of its item;
  • ddi.reference.version (warning) reports a reference whose item is present, but not at the version named, and lists the versions that are;
  • ddi.reference.provenance-external (info) reports a BasedOn or user-attribute reference to an item outside the file;
  • ddi.reference.integrity keeps the rest, at the same severity as before.
  • A new info severity. info findings never fail ddi lint unless you pass --fail-severity info, which is now accepted. ddi lint used to treat any severity other than warning as an error. A finding with a severity other than error, warning or info now raises ValueError.
  • run_lint() without rules= runs the default profile rather than every registered rule, so rules meant for a named profile (such as the new colectica-questionnaire) stay out of ddi lint. A rule added with register_rule() still joins the default profile unless you pass default=False.
  • A minor or subversion increment refuses a whole-number version. increment_minor_version() turned "6" into "6.1", a version tools that number versions with integers, Colectica among them, may not read. It now raises DDIModelError; increment_major_version() gives "7", and allow_dotted=True keeps the old behaviour. New items start at "1", so a minor bump on one now needs allow_dotted=True or a three-part version set first. increment_all_versions() checks every item before changing any.
  • Parameters and bindings of control constructs are typed. On IfThenElse, Loop and StatementItem, r:InParameter, r:OutParameter and r:Binding were kept in other_elements, as was r:InParameter on Sequence; they are now in in_parameters, out_parameters and bindings. Sequence.bindings holds Binding objects rather than elements, and OutParameter.representation holds any representation (it took only a code or numeric one; the others were in other_elements). The lists are typed list[InParameter | Element] and so on, Sequence's out_parameters included (it was list[OutParameter]), and still accept raw elements; code checked with mypy narrows an item with isinstance() before using it as a parameter.
  • Parameters and bindings of generated constructs are typed too. ComputationItem and QuestionConstruct read r:InParameter, r:OutParameter and r:Binding as InParameter, OutParameter and Binding rather than as elements, and so do an Instruction's in_parameters and the generic item models that have them (Split, SplitJoin, RepeatUntil, RepeatWhile, MeasurementItem, MeasurementConstruct, DevelopmentStep, SampleStep, SamplingStage). Code that read these values as elements calls to_xml() on them; one read and written back unchanged is still written as read, and the lists still take raw elements. The generic models' annotations still say list[Element].
  • A language added to a name or label read from a file joins it. A string built in code used to start a container of its own next to the ones read, so adding fr to a name read in en wrote two d:ConstructName elements. It now joins the last container read when that container has no string in its language, keeping the container's attributes; a second string in the same language still starts a new container.
  • IndividualIdentificationFields.individual_names holds elements. An a:IndividualName is made of parts (a:FirstGiven, a:LastFamily...), not of r:Strings, but the code generator typed it as international strings and dropped the parts. The generator now asks whether a name's type derives from r:InternationalStringType.
  • Bumping a version refreshes versionDate. On an item that has a versionDate, every increment sets it to now, in Colectica's format; pass touch=False to keep the old date. Items without one are unchanged.

  • Neutral conditions use all of Colectica's operator codes. Operator(0) is NONE, not UNKNOWN_0, and a code that was read as an unknown one before (2, 4 to 6, 8 to 10, 13, 15 to 17) is now a named member. A ContainsAny or ContainsAll statement with a value but no selected codes reads back as unverifiable, where it read as =. compile_condition() writes !=, <, <=, >= and answered() as Neutral where it wrote Blaise.

  • A missing or unreadable schema fails loudly. If the packaged XSD was missing or could not be read, validation fell back to a stand-in that only checked the root element and the identification fields, so a broken install passed invalid files. get_schema() now raises FileNotFoundError for a missing schema and lets xmlschema's own error through otherwise.

  • An error in an on_register callback reaches the caller. The registry ignored it. The class is still registered before the callbacks run.
  • The example builder writes to the current folder. python -m ddi_l.examples.build_and_validate wrote into the installed package by default, and put the package folder itself on sys.path, where ddi_l/io.py could shadow the standard io module. make example passes the packaged paths, so it still refreshes the bundled files.
  • A FragmentInstance is written in Colectica's layout by default. write_ddi(), DDIFragment.to_xml(), ddi roundtrip, ddi from-json, POST /v1/roundtrip and POST /v1/convert/xml wrote this library's layout, so a Colectica export written back through them changed (declaration, prefixes, byte-order mark) though nothing was lost. Only save() wrote Colectica's. Now the root decides: a FragmentInstance gets Colectica's layout and a DDIInstance this library's. layout="default" (--layout default, ?layout=default) gives the old output, as do pretty_print=False, xml_declaration=False or an encoding other than UTF-8, which only that layout has.

docs.title: Colectica exports
docs.text:
• Read, edit and write Colectica FragmentInstance exports. ddi.open_fragment() opens one; DDIFragment.items(), get(), top_level_item(), put() and remove() work with its items as typed models; DDIFragment.save() writes Colectica Designer's exact layout (UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, one item per <Fragment>, each item declaring its module as the default namespace, attributes in schema order), so an export opened and saved comes back byte for byte. DDIFragment.from_items() builds a new export with what Colectica writes on every item. Every other way of writing a FragmentInstance uses the same layout by default (see Behaviour changes), and so does the ddi_l.colectica module. See Work with Colectica exports.
  • A typed model for every fragment item type. All 161 item types a DDI 3.3 fragment can carry now parse with MaintainableBase.from_xml; the 91 without a hand-written class get one from ddi_l.models.items. A test builds a schema-valid sample of each from the XSDs and checks it round-trips exactly.
  • version_date reads and sets versionDate on any item.
  • Exports without a byte-order mark round-trip byte for byte. The Colectica layout always wrote a mark. Now DDIFragment.source_bom records whether the file had one and save(), to_colectica_bytes(), write_ddi(..., layout="colectica") and ddi roundtrip --layout colectica write the same; pass bom= to choose.
  • Inline XHTML keeps its spaces. In <b>Kind</b> <i>of</i> pet the space between the elements is text. It was read as indentation: lxml read "Kindof pet", and the stdlib backend wrote such a file differently. Both backends now keep it and write it back as read, with the default layout as with Colectica's; whitespace between XHTML blocks is layout. Such a file is parsed twice on lxml, so reading it takes up to twice as long. A <br> separates words, and text under xml:space="preserve" is written as read. iterparse_ddi() reads items as read_ddi() does. See Layout on the Colectica page.
  • ddi lint --profile colectica-questionnaire for Colectica exports. Its colectica.maintainable.labels accepts an item's name (ConstructName, QuestionItemName, r:Name) as well as r:Label, provided it holds text.
  • Read, edit and explain Colectica conditions. ddi_l.colectica_logic parses the logic Colectica stores in an r:Command: the Neutral JSON of its condition editor (Condition, with groups and statements), the fields of a Blaise5DataLookup (DataLookup), and native code kept as text (NativeCondition). It reads the condition of an IfThenElse and of each of its ElseIf branches, of a ComputationItem, and of a Loop, RepeatUntil or RepeatWhile (which= reaches a Loop's InitialValue and StepValue). An unchanged condition is written back byte for byte, and an edited one as Colectica writes JSON. The operator codes (all 18) and join codes are Colectica's; a code not listed is kept as read. render_synopsis() describes a condition from its logic, naming subjects after their questions and codes by value, where Colectica's stored synopsis can be stale and numbers codes by position. ddi explain-condition FILE ID shows both, the condition's description, and its used and unused inputs.
  • 25 lint rules for Colectica questionnaires, in the colectica-questionnaire profile: shared identifiers, dangling bindings, malformed, empty, impossible or native-invalid conditions (of every ElseIf branch and loop as well; a ComputationItem with outputs holds a program, which may span lines and assign them), unused inputs, stale synopses, gates wrapping only part of a page, code domains without a code list, domain labels and wording that do not fit the item, missing translations, template placeholders, pasted user-interface text, malformed or undeclared pipes, duplicate or suspicious lookup fields, lookup outputs their field list does not hold, compounded or malformed aliases, design notes shown as statements, values read before the flow asks or computes them (on each path to a reused page), and gates on one answer of a question with several, which Designer's routing view reports as broken. Heuristic rules report warnings at most; rules depending on an organisation's conventions are off until configured with the new LintConfiguration options (required_languages, known_names, ui_chrome_tokens, ...).
  • colectica.flow.unreachable: constructs no respondent reaches. With the logic extra, the solver works out each construct's ask-condition, the disjunction over the ways to it of the gates' conjunction, with the parts of the flow that many paths share encoded once, and reports a construct for which no answers meet it (PetAge > 10 and PetAge < 1, or a gate inside a branch it contradicts). Only the first construct on a way is reported. A condition it cannot read may hold or not. Without the extra, a flow with a gate gets one info finding saying it was not checked.
  • colectica.flow.read-before-computed names a respondent. With the logic extra, a finding adds a respondent who reaches the item before the question or computation ("For example, when PetCount is 0."). When there is none, because every way that reaches it first is ruled out, the finding is info: only Designer's routing view is affected. Each respondent given is checked by walking the flow with evaluate.
  • ddi lint --format table, --required-language, --known-names FILE and --lint-config FILE. configure_lint() accepts any LintConfiguration field by name.
  • A generated lint rule reference. The Lint rule reference page lists every registered rule with its severity, profiles and an example finding; register_rule() takes severity= and example=, and iter_rule_metadata() reports them.
  • Edit a questionnaire without leaving its references behind. DDIFragment.revise() gives items a new version and, with cascade, every item pinning them, up to the instrument, leaving late-bound references alone; dry_run=True returns the plan only. It versions as Colectica does: what an item declares (its parameters, its codes) takes the item's new version, a reference pinning one of those is re-pointed too, and the items of one call share one versionDate (version_date= sets it). rationale= records why, as every revised item's r:VersionRationale, as Colectica records a save's message; the rationale an item carried, which explained its previous version, is dropped. New items record the configured responsibility. move_construct(), insert_construct() and wrap_in_condition() edit sequences and return the items to revise. duplicate() copies an item with new IDs for everything it declares, and repair_shared_identifiables() (a dry run by default) re-identifies the copies of a shared parameter, reporting references it cannot attribute.
  • Typed parameters and bindings. InParameter and Binding join OutParameter in ddi_l.models. IfThenElse, Loop, StatementItem and Sequence hold theirs in in_parameters, out_parameters and bindings, so a new gate can declare the inputs its condition tests. Binding.between(source, target, late_bound=False) links two parameters, and to_reference() refers to one without an r:URN, as Colectica writes it. A parameter reads its r:ParameterName, r:Description, r:DefaultValue, isArray and any representation.
  • Record who changed a version. The increment_* methods take responsibility=, and ddi.configure(version_responsibility=...) sets a default for it. ddi.configured() scopes a setting to a with block, and ddi.reset_configuration() restores the defaults.

docs.title: Load DDI from spreadsheets
docs.text:
• Bulk-load a study's metadata from CSV files, a zip of them, or an Excel workbook. One table per kind of item, rows linked by id, covering what most organizations document:
  • the study, its groups, organizations and people (studies, groups, organizations, individuals);
  • concepts, universes, unit types and the variable cascade (conceptual_variables, represented_variables, variables);
  • code lists, including hierarchical classifications (codes.parent);
  • questions with instructions, grids, blocks and question groups, worded per language and per audience (question_texts);
  • questionnaires and their flow (instruments, flow): sequences, statements, if-then-else and loops;
  • variable groups, data files (datasets) and n-cubes;
  • methodology, processing events, quality statements and comparison maps.

Text goes in one column per language (label@en, label@fr) and custom:<name> columns are stored as r:UserAttributePair. ddi_l.tables.load_tables() returns typed models; to_fragment() writes a Colectica FragmentInstance holding every item, valid against the DDI 3.3 schema, and to_study() a DDI study for tables a study document can hold. The items the rows imply are written too: a data collection per study, sequences for the flow, a data relationship per data file. Identifiers are derived from the agency and your ids, so loading again gives the same items. Every problem is reported at once with its file, row and column. Also ddi tables template and ddi tables import, and Document.attach() to place an item built elsewhere into a study. Excel workbooks are read and written with the standard library: no new dependency. See Load DDI from spreadsheets and Spreadsheet templates, which has blank and example templates to download.

docs.title: Spec conformance
docs.text:
• Check a questionnaire against a spec. A spec lists, in YAML or JSON, a survey's modules, the questions and statements in each, their response domains and code lists, the gates on modules and questions, the edit checks, and the variables a data lookup supplies or the instrument computes. ddi conform INSTRUMENT --spec SPEC (and ddi_l.spec.conform()) compares an instrument with it and reports, with a rule id and a severity, modules and items that are missing, extra, misplaced or ambiguous, codes and labels, languages, domains, gates and edits that differ. Output is JSON or a table; --fail-severity sets what fails the run, and exit code 2 means it could not run. Ids are found where the spec's match block says, and an id found on several constructs is reported, never guessed. An item reached by several paths is compared where the spec puts it, a gate is read from the bindings of each item's latest version, and referenced and mixed domains are compared. With gate_scope: page, each statement of the module must sit under its page gate too. See Check a questionnaire against a spec.
  • ddi spec validate|schema|example checks a spec against its JSON Schema and against itself (every problem with its path, in document order), writes the schema, or writes the example (a fictional Pet survey). YAML is read as YAML 1.2: repeated keys and merge keys are errors.
  • An expression language for gates and edits (ddi_l.spec.expression): comparisons, and, or, not, arithmetic, dates and the predicates answered(), missing(), empty(), refused() and today(). normalise() compares two gates without calculating: x > 3 and x >= 4 stay different. So does equivalent() without the logic extra (below). An answer test beside a comparison of the same question is dropped (answered(x) and x > 3 is x > 3), so such a gate compiles to Neutral.
  • Compile a gate for Colectica (compile_condition()): a Neutral condition when Colectica's operator codes can hold it, else Blaise code with fallback_reason saying why. !=, <, <= and >= have codes of their own, answered(x) is NotEmpty and NotRefused, and x != 2 on a coded question is ContainsNone; a not in front of a comparison, dates, arithmetic, two questions compared and and and or mixed in a group are still Blaise. Reading a condition back has a branch for every code, and a DontKnow test is reported as unverifiable. The Blaise words for empty, refused, today and dates have no defaults: a BlaiseDialect or the spec's blaise block sets them, and a date template must read back without doubt. parse_blaise() and condition_to_expression() read either form back; comparable() makes a quoted plain number that number, since Neutral stores "2" and 2 alike. Numbers keep every digit, however long. A choice among one coded question's codes is one ContainsAny statement wherever it sits, so a and (x = 2 or x = 3) or b compiles to Neutral. Each compiled condition is read back and compared with the gate, by normal form and then with the logic extra when it is installed: CompiledCondition.verified records the result, and compile_condition(validate=True) raises when they differ, naming a respondent they disagree on.
  • Edits are reported as not verifiable by default, since where an instrument stores them is not known in general; --edits strict compares them once the spec's match.edits says how they are marked.
  • Decide whether two gates hold for the same respondents (decide(), with the new logic extra, pip install 'ddi-l[logic]', which adds the Z3 solver). When they do not, the verdict gives a respondent they disagree on: x > 3 and x >= 4 differ when x is 3.25, and agree with types={"x": "integer"}. A respondent leaves each question empty, refuses it or answers it, and an answer may have no value to compare (a don't-know); a comparison holds only when the questions it reads have values. What cannot be modelled, such as text compared by order, is unknown, with the reason. evaluate() tells whether an expression holds for one respondent, and each different verdict is checked with it. A work limit, not a clock, bounds the solver, so a verdict is the same on every run, and import ddi_l.spec does not load it.
  • A new spec extra, pip install 'ddi-l[spec]', adds PyYAML and jsonschema to read specs. The expression language and its compilers need only the standard library, and import ddi_l loads none of it.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
• Lint options per request. POST /v1/lint takes ?rule=, ?skip_rule= and ?lint_config= (the JSON object --lint-config reads), and POST /v1/validate takes ?lint_config=. They apply to that request alone, so concurrent requests no longer share one process-wide setting.
  • Colectica exports round-trip byte for byte. POST /v1/roundtrip writes a FragmentInstance as Colectica Designer does, so an unchanged export comes back identical and a diff shows only what a parse lost. Before, every Colectica file looked changed; ?layout=default gives this library's layout.
  • Load metadata tables over HTTP. POST /v1/tables/import takes an .xlsx workbook or a .zip of CSV files and answers with a Colectica FragmentInstance (or, with ?study=, a study). Tables with problems are a 422 whose extra lists every problem with its file, row and column. GET /v1/tables/template downloads the blank or example tables, and GET /v1/tables describes every table and column as JSON. Uploads are read in memory, within limits on their size, number of files, and rows and columns.
  • load_tables() also reads a zip of CSV files, or the bytes of a workbook or a zip. So does ddi tables import.

docs.title: Native XML core
docs.text:
• pip install ddi-l brings a compiled XML core, the ddi-l-native package (Rust, built with PyO3), which ddi-l uses before lxml. It has wheels for Linux (x86_64, aarch64), macOS and Windows (x64), on CPython 3.11 and later; anywhere else pip installs a pure-Python stand-in of the same name and version, which ddi-l does without, so installing ddi-l never compiles anything. Its parser builds the tree the standard library's builds and its elements behave like the standard library's; the tree keeps the bytes it was read from and caches each element's content digest, cleared only on the path from a change to the root. DDI_L_XML_BACKEND=native|lxml|stdlib picks a backend; see Installation.
  • The same results on every backend. The whole test suite runs on the native backend. The parser is checked against the standard library's on every fixture, on crafted inputs and on random and damaged XML: it reads the same documents into the same trees and refuses the same ones, and it also refuses any document type declaration.
