Its digests and its source index are checked against the pure-Python ones after random edits, and the writer writes the same bytes with either.
  • Faster where it counts. On a 9 MB export: read_ddi 0.13 s (lxml 0.33 s); writing it back unchanged 0.01 s (0.28 s), or after an edit 0.04 s (0.31 s); the colectica-questionnaire profile 0.67 s (1.74 s). The parse runs at 185 MB/s (lxml 124 MB/s, standard library 41 MB/s), far from memory bandwidth: making the tree's nodes costs most of it. Writing a document with a fresh layout is slower than with lxml (0.80 s against 0.26 s); see Performance.
  • Schema validation in one pass, with lines, on the native backend. A new native validation backend, the default there, checks a document in one pass against a compiled form of the schema (ddi_l/schemas/ir/, made by codegen/schema_ir.py from the bundled XSDs). A valid document never loads xmlschema. Each element that may be wrong is checked by xmlschema alone, so the messages and paths are xmlschema's, and the issues carry the line each element starts on, as on the lxml backend. On a 9 MB export: 0.09 s valid; 0.13 s with an error (2.6 s on the first call), where libxml2 then xmlschema take 6.5 s. Tested against xmlschema on every fixture and on 300 randomly damaged documents per run: the same errors, in the same order.
  • Linting again costs what changed, on the native backend. A lint run keeps what it read from each item under the item's content digest, and a later run on the same document reads again only the items whose digest changed. On a 9 MB export, the colectica-questionnaire profile takes 0.13 s after an edit, against 0.8 s for a first run, with the same findings. Rules that follow the whole flow (colectica.flow.read-before-computed, colectica.ifthenelse.partial-gate) still walk it each time. A first run costs about 0.04 s more: it works out the digests, which a later write reuses. Tested after random edits against a run that reads everything.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• revise no longer scans every item for each item it revises. It finds who refers to a revised item in an index built once per call (kept per item on the native backend), and a dry run makes its changes and takes them back instead of copying the fragment; repair_shared_identifiables does the same. On a 9 MB export, revising one question with its six ancestors takes 0.02 s on the native backend (0.20 s before; a dry run 0.38 s) and 0.14 s on lxml (0.41 s; a dry run 0.49 s). Tested after random edits against the cascade as it was: the same plan and the same document.
  • One lint run builds each index once. The rules of a run share what they build from the document: its items and their latest versions, the reference resolutions, the bindings and the parsed conditions; conform does the same. Each was rebuilt by every rule that needed it, and the innermost items of a DDIInstance were found by searching every item's subtree. The colectica-questionnaire profile on a 9 MB export (4,478 items) went from 6.1 s to 2.0 s, with the same findings.
  • colectica.flow.read-before-computed no longer walks every path. A page reached by several paths was walked again on each, so a flow of chained gates took time doubling with every gate. A construct reached again now replays what it found the first time, for the same bindings above it; the findings are the same. A flow with 20 chained gates (a million paths) takes milliseconds. A flow that loops back on itself is still walked path by path.
  • conform no longer walks every path to a construct. A construct is one node for each run of sequences above it, which counts the paths to it and keeps the gates of the first; whether the paths agree on a gate is found without walking them one by one. The reports are the same. A question below 16 chained gates (65,536 paths) took 9.1 s and now takes 13 ms; below 20 gates, 17 ms. An instrument that loops back on itself is still walked path by path.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• DDIReferenceWarning can be made again from its arguments, as pickle, copy and pytest-xdist do: its argument is the records, and its text is unchanged.
  • An attribute set in code on a new <Fragment> is written. Colectica's layout wrote every <Fragment> start tag from a template, so an attribute on a copied or added one was lost; one on a fragment read from a file was kept.
  • A dry run of revise given an element picks the item the real run picks. It looked the item up by its ID alone, so with two items of that ID under different agencies it could plan for the other one.
  • A document type declaration is refused on both backends. The stdlib backend accepted <!DOCTYPE root><root/>, which lxml refused; both now refuse it with the same message. iterparse_ddi refuses one too, and a caller can no longer relax its parser: resolve_entities=True, load_dtd=True, no_network=False, a forbid_*=False or a parser raise ValueError.
  • Questions added to an opened file are saved. A data collection or question scheme read from a file wrote back only the questions it was read with: one added after open_ddi() was dropped on save with no warning, and one removed came back.
  • validate_document(doc) on a Document no longer detaches the models the caller holds; edits made to them afterwards were lost on save.
  • --debug works on every command; tables, spec, conform, explain-condition, versions and serve rejected it.
  • ddi.citation.title.languages is registered, listed and documented as the warning it reports, not as an error.
  • DDIDocument.validate(raise_error=True) is documented as raising DDIValidationError, which it does.
  • colectica.statement.logic-note skips Notes. A statement Colectica types as a Note (extension:TypeOfStatement = Note) is not shown, so a flow condition written in one is where it belongs, and is no longer reported as shown to respondents.
  • A str is read as the text it is. read_ddi() reads XML given as a string whatever encoding its declaration names; it was decoded again under that encoding, or refused.
  • Names built in code are schema-valid. A name set in code (construct_names, names and every other …Name field of a generated model) was written with r:Content, which the schema forbids in a name, so validate() rejected items such as ComputationItem, QuestionConstruct, Category, Universe and every scheme and group. Names are written with r:String. A name read from a file keeps its tag, unless it was the invalid r:Content.
  • ConceptualComponent keeps its module names. A c:ConceptualComponentModuleName set in code was never written, and one read from a file was kept only as unmapped content; both now go through conceptual_component_module_names.
  • Two item types can no longer silently share one generated ID. A DataCollection gives each item built with a non-UUID identifier the ID uuid5(agency:identifier), so a DataCollection and a CollectionEvent both called main came out with the same r:ID, as did a CollectionEvent called main added to that DataCollection after reading it back. Serializing now raises ModelValidationError naming both types. Versions of one item still share their ID, and identifiers an item already has are written as given.
  • A study in a fragment no longer warns about its references. DDIFragment.from_items() and put() reported every reference of a StudyUnit as unresolved, since in a fragment the items it references sit in fragments of their own.
  • The typed models no longer lose content. Reading an item and writing it back used to drop versionDate, r:VersionResponsibility and the r:BasedOnObject lineage on hand-written models (Variable, CodeList, RepresentedVariable, DataRelationship, StudyUnit and others); split a bilingual r:Label or name into one element per language; drop audienceLanguage and d:ConditionalText from question text, user attribute pairs and attributes inside references, attributes on r:URN/r:ID, controlled-vocabulary attributes, and the scheme-level metadata of inline schemes; and wrote some content out of schema order (QuestionItem, Sequence), which the schema rejects.
  • Text with markup is kept. A label, description or other multilingual text whose r:Content holds XHTML (<b>Kind</b> of pet) was cut to the text before its first element whenever its item was written from its model (put(), to_xml()), and its blocks could be reordered (a <ul> moved before the <p> it followed). Such a string now holds its whole text ("Kind of pet", with a space between blocks) and is written back as read while unchanged; an edited one is written as its text, and the other languages keep their markup. Parameters keep the attributes of their r:URN when edited.
  • DDIFragment.from_items() drops every restated reference URN. It skipped the reference after each one it removed, so an item with several references kept some r:URNs Colectica does not write.
  • References are written as read. A reference read without an r:URN no longer gains one; a reference built in code still does.
  • xs:boolean "1" is true. Several wrappers read it as false and wrote "false". Values keep their original spelling while unchanged.
  • Identifiers read from a file are kept. DataCollection rewrote non-UUID r:IDs (its own and those of everything inside it) into generated UUIDs, breaking references from other items; it now does so only for objects built in code.
  • Validation of fragments no longer forgives real errors. An error inside a fragment's StudyUnit (and a few other real DDI items) was passed over, and validation stopped there, hiding any error after it. Only the library's own extension types are exempt now, and every error is checked.
  • ConceptualComponent always writes concepts, universes, conceptual variables and unit types inside their schemes; written bare they were invalid.
  • d:Methodology writes d:MethodologyName in the DDI 3.3 namespace.
  • r:ExternalURLReference, r:ExternalURNReference and a few other elements named *Reference are no longer read as DDI references (which emptied them).
  • A schema-valid value that does not parse as its declared number type no longer stops an item from loading.
  • Building a fragment is linear in its size (it was quadratic: 53 s for a 4,478-item export, now under 3 s).

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• A page on working with other tools. "Work with other tools" shows, with examples that run, how ddi-l exchanges metadata with XML and schema tools (xmllint), linked-data tools (rdflib and SPARQL), JSON, spreadsheets, R, any language over HTTP, DDI Codebook files (for example Dataverse's export, converted through the tables import), DDI 3.2 tools and open-source questionnaire generators, and what to check before exchanging a file.
  • Measurable learning objectives in every module. Each of the 17 modules opens with three to six objectives that say what the learner can do ("write a script that...", "run ddi lint and name one finding"), tags every exercise and quiz question with the objective it practises, gives the expected output of each exercise, and ends with a "Check yourself" list. Every objective now has an exercise and a quiz question; quiz answers are spread across A to D (B was the answer to 42 of 72 questions). Modules 12, 14, 15 and 16 keep six objectives or fewer and move the rest to "Going further". The capstone rubric scores each track's techniques, and all four tracks have a sample solution. Ten stale copies of renumbered modules, in both languages, are removed.
  • Cross-references render on the API page. Docstrings wrote them as Sphinx roles (:func:...``), which showed raw; they are now code spans.
  • A curriculum module on advanced questionnaire specification. Module 16 teaches spec writers to write a questionnaire spec, give gates and edit checks the meaning they intend on a missing answer, replace "go to" and "otherwise" with gates, fit gates to a tool's condition editor without changing their meaning, keep one variable per idea in two languages, and check an instrument with ddi conform. The capstone projects are now Module 17, and the old address redirects to them.
  • One colour scheme that works in every mode. The site uses one brand blue for the header, links and buttons, with orange only for the keyboard focus ring, and every text colour meets WCAG AA in light, dark and high contrast. Dark mode now uses the site's own colours rather than Material's defaults, and its buttons are readable: the outline buttons were 2.3:1, and a download button in a page was 1.1:1, navy on black. High contrast has a black header, visible navigation tabs and readable code, and its notes and tips are dark like the page instead of white boxes whose tables were white on white. The logo follows the header colour instead of drawing in black, and the palette menu sits in the header beside the light/dark toggle instead of overlapping the search icon on phones. The three colour-vision palettes are gone: the blue-and-orange scheme already suits those readers.
  • Links without a version no longer 404. The README and issue template link through /latest/, and the site root now serves a 404.html that sends any unversioned path (/ddi-l/server/) to the same page under /latest/ and maps renamed curriculum pages to their new names.
  • Install from PyPI everywhere. Pages that said pip install . or pip install -e . now say pip install ddi-l, and the install tabs add uv add ddi-l.
  • One place to learn. The site is organized as Learn (the curriculum), How-to guides, Reference and About. The authoring tutorial, training labs and persona tracks are folded into the curriculum, which now has a single set of learner profiles and an automation track.
  • Curriculum order. Opening files and command-line validation move up to Modules 6 and 7, and Module 3 now checks its work with doc.validate() and doc.lint(), so learners validate from the start. Modules 6 to 13 become 8 to 15.
  • Answers under each exercise. Every exercise has a collapsible answer. The answer-key page for instructors is generated from the modules, so it can no longer drift from them.
  • Homepage. A lint-clean first example, what DDI is, DDI 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 scope, a study diagram, a Learn tile, an R / HTTP API tile and a "Cite ddi-l" section. Every page now has its own search description.

docs.title: Tooling and packaging
docs.text:
• Tests run on every core. pytest runs with pytest-xdist (-n auto, a new dev dependency); -n 0 runs in one process. On four cores the lxml suite takes 58 s instead of 3 min 20 s (without coverage); with coverage, lxml takes 1 min 43 s, the standard library 2 min 49 s and native 3 min 45 s.
  • The test suite runs without warnings. A test whose items refer to items outside its document now says so, and any other DDIReferenceWarning fails it; the two curriculum pages that warn on purpose must still warn. Five skips are gone: two generator bugs (a fixed element value, a content model that must occur twice) left three item types untested, and a deliberately truncated fixture is no longer fed to tests that need well-formed XML. The skips left depend on the environment (no R, no native core, the other XML backend) or on the generic engine not reading substitution-group members.
  • Python 3.15. ddi-l is tested on Python 3.15 too: a pull request tests 3.11 and 3.15, a push to main tests 3.11 to 3.15, both XML backends each time. CI pins uv 0.13.7, the first uv series that installs 3.15.
  • One command sets the version. scripts/set_version.py 0.3.0 (or patch, minor, major) writes the version in all 11 files that state it, with the release date and the citations' year, then runs uv lock; it writes nothing unless every file matches. A test fails when another file starts stating the version.
  • A link to a missing heading fails the docs build. mkdocs build --strict now checks anchors (validation: anchors: warn). It found two cheat-sheet links to a Module 15 section that had moved, now fixed.
  • Mutation runs draw fewer examples, the same each time. Under mutmut a property test draws at most 30 examples, derandomized, instead of 300 (or Hypothesis's 100), since it runs once for each mutant it covers; a mutant is caught on every run or none. The suite still draws 300.
  • The native core in CI and releases. A CI job checks the Rust code (cargo fmt, cargo clippy) and runs the whole suite on the native backend. A release builds ddi-l-native wheels (one stable-ABI wheel per platform: Linux x86_64 and aarch64, macOS universal2, Windows x64) and its sdist, plus the pure-Python stand-in wheel (native/fallback/), and publishes them with ddi-l; PyPI needs this repository set up as a trusted publisher for the ddi-l-native project too. The monthly job fuzzes the parser against the standard library's, 300,000 inputs per test. In the repository, uv.lock installs the stand-in, so no contributor needs Rust; the ddi-l sdist carries it and the crate's sources.
  • Test fixtures ship in the sdist only. The wheel carried 250 test files under ddi_l/examples/tests/. It keeps the two samples the CLI recipes run; the rest live in tests/fixtures/, and scripts/check_distributions.py fails if they reach the wheel again.
  • A mutation-testing gate. mutmut now covers fifteen modules, and the monthly job fails when a mutant survives that tests/mutation_baseline.txt does not list, or when a listed one no longer survives (scripts/check_mutation.py, make mutation). The latest full run caught 12,290 of 14,542 mutants (84.5 %). The list holds the 2,252 survivors: 239 with the reason no test can catch them, and 2,013 not looked at yet. New tests caught about 500 survivors, most in validation, the operations, the condition compiler, I/O and conformance. In the four modules new in this release (the fact base, the instrument index, the evaluator and the solver encoding), 1,237 of 1,282 mutants are caught, and each of the 45 survivors has its reason.
  • Ruff and the dependency audit run once in CI instead of on all eight test legs.
  • A pull request tests Python 3.11 and 3.14 on both backends; a push to main still tests all four versions.
  • Removed code nothing used, merged five copies of the version sort key, and replaced the serializer's strategy classes with one function.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
• ddi validate exits 1 when it reports any issue, including one of warning severity.
  • A study moved into a Group (Document.add_group()) is missing from iter_study_units(), and so from the index built from it.
  • Without lxml, output written with pretty_print=False spells empty elements <tag />, where lxml writes <tag/>.
  • A DDI 3.2 DDIInstance is written back with generated prefixes (ns0: with lxml, p0: without) and with r: bound to the 3.3 namespace. The XML means the same, but no longer reads as the source did. A 3.2 FragmentInstance is written in Colectica's layout, with r: and ddi: bound to the 3.2 namespaces.
The first release of ddi-l: a Python toolkit for creating, reading, updating, and validating DDI Lifecycle 3.3 XML documents, with a simple CRUD API over an XSD-generated model layer.

docs.title: Authoring
docs.text:
• Simple CRUD API: ddi.new_study(), ddi.open_ddi(), and the Document class with add_question(), add_variable(), add_concept(), add_universe(), add_code_list(), add_item(), find(), remove(), save(), and validate(). Every add_* helper takes an optional label= (and label_lang=), so an item can be labelled where it is created rather than in a second pass. That is the difference between output that lints clean and output that warns about itself.
  • Generic add_item() / items(): 30 DDI item types (QuestionItem, Variable, Category, Instrument, Concept, Universe, and more) through a single type registry.
  • Variable representations: Variable.set_numeric(), set_coded(), set_text(), and set_datetime() declare what kind of values a variable holds, with optional numeric ranges (low_inclusive / high_inclusive), missing_values, blank_is_missing_value, or a code-list reference. The setters chain onto add_variable().
  • Custom properties: set_property(), get_property(), properties, and remove_property() on any DDI item.
  • Versioning: increment_major_version(), increment_minor_version(), increment_subversion(), version rationales, and version responsibility.
  • Multilingual support: a lang= parameter on every add_* method, and InternationalString for additional translations.

docs.title: Study structure
docs.text:
• Multi-study series: doc.add_study() adds further studies to the group. doc.study(identifier) returns a StudyCursor whose add_variable(), add_question(), and other add_* helpers target that specific study, so non-primary studies are editable through the high-level API. doc.study() with no argument targets the primary study.
  • Study groups: doc.add_group() organizes a study into a <g:Group> (a study series or publication package). The document stays fully editable, and group-organized files open and round-trip.
  • Instance-level packages: doc.add_resource_package() and doc.add_local_holding_package() attach a ResourcePackage (reusable metadata) or a LocalHoldingPackage (a local holding of a deposited study, referencing the primary study by default) directly on the DDIInstance; doc.resource_packages / doc.local_holding_packages read them back.
  • Archive: doc.add_archive() attaches an Archive module (archive lifecycle metadata) to the primary study; doc.archives reads them back.
  • Translation information: doc.add_translation_information(languages=..., description=...) sets the instance's TranslationInformation; doc.translation_information reads it back.
  • Comparisons: doc.add_comparison() records harmonization maps between items across studies or versions: add_variable_map(), add_concept_map(), add_managed_item_map(), add_representation_map(), a correspondence() builder, and source_scheme / target_scheme / correspondence arguments on the map helpers.
  • DDI profiles: doc.add_ddi_profile() attaches a DDIProfile declaring which DDI elements a system uses, via add_used() / add_not_used() XPath statements.

docs.title: Data description
docs.text:
• Data relationships: doc.add_data_relationship() builds a DataRelationship whose add_logical_record() declares which variables make up one case (the rectangular-file default).
  • NCubes: doc.add_ncube() builds a multidimensional cube; add_dimension(variable_ref) adds an axis, add_measure(variable_ref) adds a measured value, and add_attribute() adds a qualifying variable. add_coordinate_region() and add_dimension_value() describe a region of a cube, and add_attribute(..., attachment_region=) attaches to one.
  • Physical instances: PhysicalInstance is a first-class add_item type at the study level, describing a concrete data file with set_data_file(), set_record_count(), and set_citation_title().
  • Record layouts: doc.add_record_layout() maps variables to positions in a data file via add_data_item(variable_ref, start_position=, width=), which also accepts storage_format, delimiter, and decimal_positions. Pass logical_record= to tie the backing structure to a modeled logical record. PhysicalStructure.link_logical_record(..., key_variable=) declares a segment key.
  • Inline datasets: doc.add_dataset() stores data values directly in the document, in ItemSet (add_item_value()), RecordSet (set_variable_order() / add_record()), or VariableSet (add_variable_item()) form.

docs.title: Questionnaires
docs.text: • Flow constructs: QuestionConstruct, Sequence, IfThenElse, StatementItem, ComputationItem, and Loop are first-class add_item() types, stored in a ControlConstructScheme that is built, serialized, and round-tripped automatically, and linked to one another with .to_reference().

docs.title: Validation and quality
docs.text:
• Offline schema validation: the DDI 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3 XSDs ship inside the package, so doc.validate() and ddi validate work with no network access and no separate download.
  • Reads DDI 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3: read_ddi(), ddi validate, ddi lint, ddi to-json and ddi roundtrip detect the version a document declares. The Document authoring API and the typed models target DDI 3.3; 3.1 and 3.2 documents are worked with as XML through DDIDocument.root.
  • Lint engine: ddi lint and Document.lint() check reference integrity, missing labels and citation completeness. The label rule follows the schema: it only asks for a label where the element's content model has an r:Label slot (174 of DDI 3.3's 1247 elements). The citation-language rule matches language ranges per RFC 4647, so a required en is satisfied by en, en-CA or en-Latn-CA, but not by eng.
  • Lint-clean output by default: the Document API labels the modules, schemes and physical wrappers it creates, and every add_* helper accepts label=. set_scheme_label() labels any generated scheme wrapper. Documents you parse are never modified.
  • Lint defaults suit a published library: the agency allow-list is opt-in (configure_lint(allowed_agencies=[...]) or --allowed-agency); a missing agency is always an error. ddi lint exits non-zero on errors only; pass --fail-severity warning for a strict gate.
  • Labels only where the schema allows them: label support is derived from the XSDs. Setting a label on a type with no r:Label slot warns instead of producing an invalid document.
  • Reference checks: Document.save() reports references to items the study does not contain as a single DDIReferenceWarning.
  • Clear errors: malformed XML raises DDIParseError with the parser's line and column; unresolvable references raise DDIReferenceError (a LookupError); duplicate identifiers raise DuplicateIdentifierError, and empty or non-string names are rejected when an item is added. Schema failures raise SchemaValidationError, a DDIValidationError, whose .issues carries the individual problems.
  • Examples that pass our own gates: the bundled example_instance.xml and Quality_of_Life.xml are schema-valid and free of lint errors; example_instance.xml has no findings at any severity.
  • Methodology uses DDI's own namespace: <Methodology> is written in ddi:datacollection:3_3, as DDI 3.3 declares it.
  • Extension types are visibly ours: the few Process and Methodology helper types that no DDI Lifecycle release defines serialize into urn:ddi-l:extension:*, so nothing can be mistaken for an official DDI namespace.
  • Round-trip fidelity: unknown XML elements and attributes are preserved when opening and re-saving files.
  • The lxml backend is a speed choice, not a dialect: documents ddi-l authors serialize to byte-identical output with and without ddi-l[full]. A third-party file whose namespaces are laid out differently (a prefixed root plus per-element xmlns= redeclarations, as in Quality_of_Life.xml) can differ in prefix spelling between backends; its content is identical.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• import ddi_l loads names on first use, so importing the package and starting the ddi command take a few hundredths of a second.
  • read_ddi() builds its resolver index lazily.
  • With ddi-l[full], validation first checks the document with libxml2 and runs the detailed xmlschema validator only when that check fails: valid documents validate in milliseconds, and reported issues are identical on both backends.
  • iter_variables(), iter_questions() and iterparse_ddi() stream large documents and yield fully populated objects.
  • See Performance for measured timings.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
• Optional Litestar service: pip install 'ddi-l[server]' then ddi serve exposes validate, lint and convert over HTTP, with OpenAPI docs at /schema. Every endpoint is a thin wrapper over ddi_l.operations, which the CLI also calls, so the two cannot disagree about whether a document is valid.
  • Self-describing OpenAPI: /schema serves Swagger UI, and a browser opening the root is redirected there. Every endpoint declares its request body, query parameters and a typed response schema with a captured example; "Try it out" arrives prefilled with a valid DDI instance.
  • Service-appropriate defaults: a 32 MiB request body cap, a bounded number of concurrent jobs (--max-jobs, 503 beyond it), the default schema preloaded at startup, no disk writes, CORS off unless origins are named, and the same XML hardening as the library.
  • JSON-LD output: POST /v1/convert/jsonld and ddi to-jsonld render a study as linked data using the DDI Alliance's own DDI-RDF Discovery vocabulary ("Disco"), with Dublin Core and SKOS for labels and DDI URNs as IRIs. Covers DDI's discovery subset and is one-way by design, as the Disco specification intends; to-json remains the lossless, round-trippable format (XML to JSON and back returns the bytes it was given, and so does /v1/roundtrip).
  • ddi_l.operations: the transport-neutral core, usable directly when embedding ddi-l in another application.

docs.title: Model layer
docs.text:
• XSD-driven model generation: every model class is generated from the official DDI 3.3 XSD, the single source of truth for fields, element ordering, namespaces, and documentation. All 508 XSD complex types are covered.
  • Generic XML engine: from_xml() / to_xml() driven by the generated _FIELD_XML_MAP, _ATTR_XML_MAP, and _ELEMENT_ORDER tables, emitting children in XSD-declared order.
  • Stable DDI namespace prefixes: output uses the canonical r:, s:, d:, l:, c:, a:, p:, pr: (ddiprofile), and prc: (process) prefixes rather than generated ns0/p0 names, and serialization prefers a namespace's registered prefix over an auto-generated one.
  • Namespace constants: exported for every DDI module, including DDI_PROFILE_NS and DATASET_NS.
  • Typed: ships py.typed; the public API is fully annotated.

docs.title: Tooling and distribution
docs.text:
• CLI: ddi validate, ddi lint, ddi to-json, ddi to-jsonld, ddi from-json, ddi roundtrip, ddi versions, and ddi serve. Commands take -o/--output and --ddi-version; ddi validate --format json prints a JSON array (empty when valid) for scripts.
  • Optional lxml backend: pip install ddi-l[full] enables faster parsing of large documents.
  • Generated API reference built from the source docstrings, alongside the guides.
  • Every documented code sample is executed in CI, including the R examples.
  • Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14 supported and tested in CI.
  • PyPI publishing via GitHub OIDC trusted publishing.
  • Bilingual documentation in English and French, including a guide to using ddi-l from R through reticulate.
  • Training curriculum: a 16-module progressive course with exercises, quizzes, an instructor guide, answer keys, and a bilingual cheat sheet.

docs.title: Schema coverage
docs.text: This page is an honest map of how much of the DDI Lifecycle 3.3 schema ddi-l supports, and at which level. "Support" means three different things, so the table separates them into three tiers.

docs.title: The three tiers
docs.text:
1. High-level API: you can create and manage these with the simple Document API: new_study(), add_question(), add_variable(), add_item(), items(), find(), remove(). This is the easy, one-line path most authoring needs.
  2. Typed model: every type in the module is a typed Python class with full from_xml() / to_xml() support, so you can read, build, and edit it precisely from ddi_l.models.* even when there is no one-line helper.
  3. Round-trip preserved: opening a file and saving it again keeps the content byte-for-byte faithful, even for parts the library does not model in detail. Unrecognized elements are preserved verbatim.

Nothing is lost

All of DDI 3.3 is modeled and validated: the model layer is generated from the official XSD (about 500 types), and doc.validate() checks against the real instance_3_3.xsd. Round-trip fidelity is complete: a 100,000-element production file re-saves with zero element loss. The only thing that varies by module is ergonomics: how much typing you do.

The typed models are as faithful. Each of the 161 item types a ddi:Fragment can carry has a model, and reading an item with from_xml() and writing it with to_xml() returns it unchanged: same elements, attributes, text and order. The test suite checks this for every type against samples built from the XSD, and byte for byte against real Colectica exports (see Work with Colectica exports).

docs.title: Coverage by module
docs.text:
DDI module High-level API Typed model Round-trip Study Unit Yes Yes Yes Conceptual Component (concepts, universes, unit types) Yes Yes Yes Data Collection (questions, instruments, questionnaire flow) Yes Yes Yes Logical Product (variables, code lists, data relationships, NCubes) Yes Yes Yes Reusable (shared types: references, names, dates…) n/a Yes Yes Archive (citations, coverage, provenance) Yes Yes Yes Methodology (data collection methodology) Yes Yes Yes Process types (urn:ddi-l:extension:process:1) No Yes Yes Comparative (harmonization maps) Yes Yes Yes Physical Data Product: record layouts Yes Yes Yes Physical Data Product: structures, NCube Yes Yes Yes Physical Instance (data files) Yes Yes Yes Group (study series) Yes Yes Yes Resource / Local Holding Packages Yes Yes Yes Translation information Yes Yes Yes DDI Profile (usage declaration) Yes Yes Yes Dataset (inline data) Yes Yes Yes

"No" in the High-level API column means there is no one-line helper; use the typed model instead. n/a means not applicable.

About the Process types

ddi_l.models.process models Process, ProcessStep, ProcessControl, ProcessMethod and their schemes. DDI Lifecycle does not define these: they appear in none of the 3.1, 3.2 or 3.3 schemas, neither as elements nor as complexTypes. They are a ddi-l extension, and they serialize into urn:ddi-l:extension:process:1 so that is unmistakable in the output. Other DDI tools will not recognise them. Build them from ddi_l.models.process when you want the modelling; do not expect them to interoperate.

DDI's own process vocabulary is ProcessingEvent, ProcessingInstruction and ControlConstruct, which live in ddi:datacollection:3_3 and are modeled separately. Questionnaire and data-capture flow in DDI 3.3 instead lives in Data Collection as control constructs (QuestionConstruct, Sequence, IfThenElse, StatementItem, ComputationItem, Loop), which are first-class add_item types.

docs.title: What "add_item" covers
docs.text:
add_item() / items() currently recognize 30 item types, including the full questionnaire-flow set (QuestionConstruct, Sequence, IfThenElse, StatementItem, ComputationItem, Loop; see Module 10), PhysicalInstance, RecordLayout, DataRelationship, and NCube. A physical instance describes one data file; a record layout maps variables to positions within it.

The samples on this page all continue from this setup:

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Health Survey", agency="example.org")
age = doc.add_variable(name="age")
income = doc.add_variable(name="income")
year = doc.add_variable(name="year")
region = doc.add_variable(name="region")
population = doc.add_variable(name="population")
footnote = doc.add_variable(name="footnote")
age_2020 = doc.add_variable(name="age_2020")
age_2021 = doc.add_variable(name="age_2021")
sex_codes = doc.add_code_list(name="Sex Codes")

from ddi_l.models.physical import PhysicalInstance

pi = doc.add_item(PhysicalInstance, name="2021 Microdata File")
pi.set_data_file("https://example.org/health-2021.csv")
pi.set_record_count(15000)

# Map variables to fixed-width columns
rl = doc.add_record_layout()
rl.add_data_item(age.to_reference(), start_position=1, width=2)
rl.add_data_item(income.to_reference(), start_position=3, width=8)

# Logical records (which variables make up one case)
dr = doc.add_data_relationship()
dr.add_logical_record()  # all variables, one rectangular record

# Multidimensional (cube) data (with a coordinate region for an attribute)
cube = doc.add_ncube(name="Population by year and region")
cube.add_dimension(year.to_reference())
cube.add_dimension(region.to_reference())
cube.add_measure(population.to_reference())
region = cube.add_coordinate_region()
cube.add_attribute(footnote.to_reference(), attachment_region=region)

# Variable types: numeric / coded / text / datetime
# (numeric ranges take inclusivity flags and missing values)
doc.add_variable(name="age").set_numeric(
    "Integer", low=0, high=120, low_inclusive=True, missing_values=["-9"]
)
doc.add_variable(name="sex").set_coded(sex_codes)

docs.title: Reaching the model layer
docs.text: When a module has no one-line helper, you still have full typed access. Build the object from ddi_l.models.* and attach it, or read it back after open_ddi(). For example, the physical data layer lives in ddi_l.models.physical, the archive layer in ddi_l.models.archive, and so on. Because every type round-trips, you can also open an existing file, reach the part you need, edit it, and save; nothing else in the document changes.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A document can be organized as a Group (a study series / publication package). doc.add_group() moves the study under a <g:Group>, and the document stays fully editable. Group-organized files open and round-trip:

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Wave 1", agency="example.org")
doc.add_variable(name="age")
doc.add_group()  # organize the study into a group
doc.add_variable(name="income")  # still edits the (now grouped) study

Add more studies with doc.add_study(title=...), and relate items across them with a Comparison:

doc.add_study(title="Wave 2")  # a second study in the series
cmp = doc.add_comparison(name="2020 to 2021")
cmp.add_variable_map(age_2020.to_reference(), age_2021.to_reference())

The high-level add_* helpers edit the primary study by default. To edit a different study in the series, use its cursor: doc.study(identifier) returns a StudyCursor whose add_* helpers target that study:

wave2 = doc.add_study(title="Wave 2")
doc.study(wave2.identifier).add_variable(name="income")  # edits wave 2
doc.study().add_variable(name="age")  # edits the primary study

docs.title: Instance-level packages, archive, and translation
docs.text:
Beyond the study, a DDIInstance can carry reusable and holding packages, an archive, and translation information, each with a one-line helper:

doc.add_archive()  # archive lifecycle metadata on the study
doc.add_resource_package()  # reusable metadata shared across studies
doc.add_local_holding_package()  # a local holding of a deposited study
doc.add_translation_information(  # which languages the instance was translated between
    languages=["en", "fr"], description="Translated from French."
)

Read them back with doc.archives, doc.resource_packages, doc.local_holding_packages, and doc.translation_information. Packages and translation information are serialized into their correct positions in the DDIInstance content model on save.

docs.title: Coverage summary
docs.text: The high-level API spans every DDI Lifecycle 3.3 instance module: study units, concepts, data collection and questionnaire flow, logical products (variables with typed representations including inclusivity flags and missing values, code lists, data relationships, NCubes with dimensions/measures/attributes and coordinate regions), physical instances, structures and record layouts (including segment keys and storage/decimal details), inline datasets (item, record, and variable sets), study groups with multi-study series (doc.study(id)) and the full set of comparison maps (variable/concept/… maps plus managed-item and representation maps), instance-level packages (resource, local-holding, archive, translation), and DDI profiles. The one group that is model-layer-only is the Process types (urn:ddi-l:extension:process:1), which DDI does not define at all. Everything in every actual DDI module is modeled, validated, and round-tripped.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
ddi-l ships an optional HTTP service that exposes the same validate, lint and convert operations as the CLI. It is built on Litestar.

Use it when DDI validation has to be reachable from somewhere that is not Python (a deposit form, a Java pipeline, a CI job in another language) without each of those reimplementing DDI handling.

It is the same code

Every endpoint is a thin wrapper over ddi_l.operations, which is also what the ddi CLI calls, so both give the same answer for the same document.

docs.title: Install and run
docs.text:
The server is an optional extra, so a plain install never pays for Litestar:

pip install 'ddi-l[server]'
ddi serve

That binds to 127.0.0.1:8000: this machine only. To accept connections from elsewhere:

ddi serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080

docs.title: Interactive documentation
docs.text:
Open the port in a browser and you land on Swagger UI at /schema: http://localhost:8000/schema. A browser hitting / is redirected there, so there is nothing to remember.

It is generated from the code, not written by hand, and it documents both directions of every call:

  • What to send. Each POST declares its request body, and "Try it out" arrives prefilled with a valid DDI instance. Press Execute and you get a real validation response without composing a request first.
  • Query parameters. ?version=, ?lint= and ?profile= appear as fields you can fill in rather than as prose you have to notice.
  • What comes back. Every response carries a captured example, including the failure cases: what a schema error looks like, and the {"status_code", "detail"} envelope a 400, 413, 503 or 504 returns.

The examples are captured responses, and the test suite checks them against a running service.

Path Serves /schema Swagger UI; start here /schema/redoc ReDoc, read-only reference /schema/elements, /schema/rapidoc Alternative renderings /schema/openapi.json, /schema/openapi.yaml The raw document, for client generators /schema/fr Swagger UI with the descriptions in French /schema/openapi.fr.json The raw document in French

An API client that requests / without Accept: text/html is not redirected; it gets a JSON index of the endpoints instead.

docs.title: The French rendering
docs.text:
/schema/fr serves the same API with its prose translated: endpoint summaries, parameter and field descriptions, example captions. What it does not translate is anything a client parses: field names, enum values and the sample documents are byte-identical to the English spec, because they are the contract rather than the documentation. info.title stays ddi-l for the same reason.

Swagger UI's own buttons ("Try it out", "Execute", "Parameters") remain in English. swagger-ui has no i18n support, and neither do ReDoc, RapiDoc or Stoplight, so a French reader gets French prose in an English-chromed page.

Kept in step with the English

The test suite checks that every string in the live spec has a French entry, and that every French entry still matches its English source.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method Path Does GET / Service index: version and the available endpoints. GET /health Liveness probe; returns the running version. GET /v1/versions Bundled DDI schema releases and the default. POST /v1/validate Schema validation plus lint findings. POST /v1/lint Lint rules only. POST /v1/convert/json DDI XML → JSON (lossless, round-trippable). POST /v1/convert/jsonld DDI XML → JSON-LD (linked data, one-way). POST /v1/convert/xml JSON → DDI XML. POST /v1/roundtrip Re-serialize a document through the model layer. GET /v1/tables The metadata tables and their columns, as JSON. GET /v1/tables/template The tables to fill in: a workbook, or a zip of CSV files. POST /v1/tables/import Metadata tables → DDI XML.

The document endpoints take the document as the raw request body: a DDIInstance, or a Colectica FragmentInstance. They accept ?version=3.1|3.2|3.3 to pin the schema release instead of using the one the document declares. /v1/tables/import takes a workbook or a zip instead; see Load metadata tables.

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
curl --data-binary @my-study.xml http://localhost:8000/v1/validate

{
  "valid": true,
  "schema_issues": [],
  "lint_findings": [ ... ],
  "messages": [ ... ]
}

valid answers the caller's actual question and reflects errors only: warnings are reported but do not make a document invalid, matching what ddi lint does with its exit status. Add ?lint=false for schema validation alone.

docs.title: Lint
docs.text:
curl --data-binary @my-study.xml http://localhost:8000/v1/lint
curl --data-binary @my-study.xml 'http://localhost:8000/v1/lint?profile=DDI_PROFILE_DEFAULT'

The options ddi lint takes travel with the request: ?rule= (repeated) runs only those rules, ?skip_rule= leaves out their findings, and ?lint_config= takes the JSON object --lint-config reads. They apply to that request alone; POST /v1/validate takes ?lint_config= too. A FragmentInstance is linted as a fragment, as ddi lint does.

curl --data-binary @my-study.xml --get \
  --data-urlencode 'lint_config={"allowed_agencies": ["example.org"]}' \
  --data-urlencode 'skip_rule=ddi.citation.present' \
  -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/lint

docs.title: Convert
docs.text:
curl --data-binary @my-study.xml http://localhost:8000/v1/convert/json > study.json
curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @study.json \
  http://localhost:8000/v1/convert/xml > study.xml

docs.title: JSON-LD (linked data)
docs.text:
/v1/convert/jsonld renders the document as JSON-LD using the DDI Alliance's own DDI-RDF Discovery vocabulary ("Disco"), served as application/ld+json:

curl --data-binary @my-study.xml http://localhost:8000/v1/convert/jsonld > study.jsonld

{
  "@context": {"disco": "http://rdf-vocabulary.ddialliance.org/discovery#", "...": "..."},
  "@graph": [
    {
      "@id": "urn:ddi:example.org:8f3a...:1",
      "@type": "disco:Study",
      "dcterms:title": "Household Survey",
      "disco:variable": [{"@id": "urn:ddi:example.org:1c9d...:1"}]
    },
    {
      "@id": "urn:ddi:example.org:1c9d...:1",
      "@type": "disco:Variable",
      "skos:prefLabel": [{"@value": "Age", "@language": "en"}],
      "disco:question": [{"@id": "urn:ddi:example.org:44b1...:1"}]
    }
  ]
}

This is a semantic mapping, not a transcription of the XML. Studies, variables, questions and universes become Disco terms with Dublin Core and SKOS for labels, so the result loads straight into a triple store. @id values are the DDI URNs the library already mints, which are valid IRIs.

Lossy and one-way, by design

Disco covers DDI's discovery subset: what a dataset is about, so it can be found and compared. It has no vocabulary for questionnaire flow logic, record layouts, NCubes or processing instructions, and those are dropped rather than approximated. Its specification is explicit that the reverse transformation "is not intended", so there is no JSON-LD → XML endpoint.

Use /v1/convert/json when the payload has to come back as XML. That format is an exact transcription and round-trips through /v1/convert/xml.

A Colectica FragmentInstance has no study to describe, so this endpoint answers 400 for one.

docs.title: Colectica exports
docs.text:
Validate, lint and the JSON conversion take a Colectica FragmentInstance as they take a DDIInstance. To check that an export survives a parse, round-trip it: a file comes back with its unchanged parts as they were posted, so an unchanged export comes back byte for byte:

curl --data-binary @export.xml http://localhost:8000/v1/roundtrip > back.xml
cmp export.xml back.xml && echo unchanged

?layout=default writes this library's layout instead (no byte-order mark, its own namespace prefixes), which differs from the export even when nothing was lost. A DDIInstance always comes back in this library's layout. POST /v1/convert/xml follows the same rule. See Work with Colectica exports.

docs.title: Load metadata tables
docs.text:
/v1/tables/import loads metadata kept in spreadsheets, laid out as in Load DDI from spreadsheets: an .xlsx workbook with one sheet per table, or a .zip of CSV files. It answers with a Colectica FragmentInstance holding every item:

curl --data-binary @my-survey.xlsx http://localhost:8000/v1/tables/import > my-survey.xml
curl --data-binary @my-survey.zip  http://localhost:8000/v1/tables/import > my-survey.xml
Query parameter Does agency the agency of every item; overrides settings item_version the version of items without their own; overrides settings language the language of names; overrides settings study a title: answer with a DDIInstance study instead of a fragment

Tables that were read but have problems are a 422. Every problem is listed at once, each with its file (or sheet), row and column:

{
  "status_code": 422,
  "detail": "The tables have 1 problem; `extra` lists them.",
  "extra": [
    {
      "where": "variables.csv, row 2, column question",
      "message": "no row in questions has id 'Q_AGE'"
    }
  ]
}

A body that is not a workbook or a zip at all is a 400, like any other malformed body.

The tables to fill in come from /v1/tables/template, as an attachment:

curl -OJ http://localhost:8000/v1/tables/template                          # blank workbook
curl -OJ 'http://localhost:8000/v1/tables/template?format=zip&example=true' # the example, as CSV files
curl -OJ 'http://localhost:8000/v1/tables/template?lang=en&lang=iu'         # columns for English and Inuktitut

/v1/tables describes every table and column as JSON (what goes in it, whether it is required, whether it takes one column per language, which table it points to), for building a form or checking a file before sending it.

docs.title: Running it safely
docs.text:
A library parses what its caller chose to open. A service parses whatever reaches the port, so the defaults are deliberately conservative.

  • Request bodies are capped at 32 MiB. Change it with --max-body-mb. Without a cap, one request can exhaust a worker's memory.
  • XML parsing is hardened, and the server adds no parser of its own. It goes through the same code as the library, which disables entity resolution and network access and routes standard-library parsing through defusedxml. Entity-expansion ("billion laughs") and external-entity (XXE) payloads are rejected; tests/test_server.py asserts both over HTTP.
  • Requests are bounded at 60 seconds by default. This caps how long a client waits, not how long the work runs: validation happens in a worker thread and a running Python thread cannot be cancelled, so on timeout the caller gets 504 while that thread finishes. The body cap is what bounds the work itself.
  • Concurrent work is bounded. At most --max-jobs documents are processed at once (default: the number of CPUs); further requests get 503 with Retry-After. The default schema is loaded at startup, so the first request does not pay for it.
  • Nothing is written to disk. Documents and tables are read from memory.
  • Workbooks and zips are read within limits. Their files may expand to 256 MiB in all, there may be 10,000 of them, and a workbook cell past Excel's last row or column is refused, so a small upload cannot make the reader allocate without end.
  • CORS is off. Enable named origins with --cors-allow-origin; there is deliberately no wildcard flag.
  • /schema can be turned off with --no-openapi for an internet-facing deployment.

Validation is CPU-bound

Schema-validating a large instance occupies a worker for the duration. Run behind a reverse proxy that enforces its own timeouts and rate limits, and size the worker pool for your largest expected document, not your median one.

POST /v1/validate reports every schema error up to ServerConfig.max_schema_issues (100 by default), then a warning that it stopped.

docs.title: Embedding it
docs.text:
ddi serve is a convenience. For a real deployment, build the app yourself and run it under any ASGI server:

from ddi_l.server import ServerConfig, create_app

app = create_app(
    ServerConfig(
        max_body_bytes=8 * 1024 * 1024,
        cors_allow_origins=("https://metadata.example.org",),
        enable_openapi=False,
    )
)

uvicorn myapp:app --workers 4

docs.title: Check a questionnaire against a spec
docs.text:
A spec says what a questionnaire should contain: its modules, the questions and statements in each, their response domains and code lists, the gates that decide who sees what, and the edit checks. ddi conform compares an instrument with it and reports every difference, with a rule id, a severity, and the module and item it is about.

The spec is a YAML or JSON file you write, or generate from your own design documents. ddi-l reads nothing else: how you get from your organisation's documents to a spec is yours to decide.

Reading a spec needs the spec extra:

pip install 'ddi-l[spec]'

Without it, ddi spec and ddi conform print that line and exit with 1. The expression language and its compilers need nothing beyond the standard library.

docs.title: Write a spec
docs.text:
ddi spec example writes the example, a spec for the fictional Pet survey; ddi spec schema writes the JSON Schema a spec is checked against, for an editor that completes and checks YAML.

ddi spec example > pet-survey.spec.yaml
ddi spec validate pet-survey.spec.yaml

The example in full:

spec: pet-survey
version: "1"
description: A small bilingual survey about the pets of a household.
languages: [en, fr]

# The words of your Blaise version, for gates that compile to Blaise.
# ddi-l assumes none of them.
blaise:
  empty: EMPTY
  refused: REFUSAL
  today: SYSDATE

code_lists:
  Species:
    values:
      1: {en: Dog, fr: Chien}
      2: {en: Cat, fr: Chat}
      3: {en: Bird, fr: Oiseau}

imported_variables:
  - {name: OwnerName, type: text, source: register}
derived_variables:
  - {name: HasPets, type: numeric, values: [0, 1]}

modules:
  - id: household
    questions:
      - id: PetCount
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 20, decimals: 0}}

  - id: pets
    gate: PetCount > 0
    statements: [PetsIntro]
    questions:
      - id: PetKind
        domain: {code: {list: Species}}
      - id: PetName
        domain: {text: {max_length: 50}}
        gate: answered(PetKind)
      - id: PetAge
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 40, decimals: 0}}

  - id: visits
    required: false
    questions:
      - id: VisitDate
        domain: {date: {type: Date}}

edits:
  - id: age_range
    when: PetAge > 30
    module: pets
    message:
      en: Is the pet really over 30?
      fr: L’animal a-t-il vraiment plus de 30 ans ?
    severity: warning

The parts:

Key What it holds spec, version, description The spec's name and your own version and notes. instrument The instrument to check when the file has several: its name, label, user ID or ID. languages The languages every question text and code label must be in (en matches en-CA). A label written without a language is in the first of them. blaise The Blaise words for empty, refused, today and dates, for gates that are Blaise code. match Where to find each id in the instrument (below). severities A severity for a rule, replacing its default: {spec.module.extra: error}. code_lists Code lists that a question names with list:. imported_variables, derived_variables Variables a data lookup supplies, and variables the instrument computes. modules Each module: its id, whether it is required (default true), its gate and gate_scope (module, the default, or page), its statements and its questions. edits Each edit check: its id, the condition it fires on (when), its module, message and severity.

A question has an id, a domain and a gate of its own, which applies on top of its module's. A domain is one of:

Domain Options code values (each value and its label), or list (a code_lists entry). numeric min, max, min_inclusive and max_inclusive (default true), decimals. text min_length, max_length. date type: the DDI DateTypeCode (Date, DateTime, Year...).

ddi spec validate checks a spec against the schema, then against itself: ids appear once, every list: names a code list, every gate and edit parses and names only the spec's questions and variables, min is below max, labels are in the spec's languages, and severities names real rules. Each problem says where it is:

pet-survey.spec.yaml: modules[1].questions[2].gate: 'PetAgee' is not a question or variable of the spec

YAML is read strictly, as YAML 1.2. A key given twice is an error, and so is a merge key (<<); 01 stays the string "01", a code, not the number 1; only true and false are booleans, so no and off stay strings; dates and = stay strings; and a whole number written 4e1 is 40. A spec must be UTF-8, JSON's NaN and Infinity are refused, and a gate may nest parentheses, not and minus 50 deep at most.

docs.title: Gates and edits: the expression language
docs.text:
A gate or an edit condition is an expression:

PetCount > 0 and answered(PetKind)
not refused(OwnerAge) or OwnerAge >= 18
VisitDate <= today()

From the loosest binding to the tightest:

Operators Meaning or, \|\| either side and, && both sides not negation = == != < <= > >= one comparison; they do not chain: write 1 < x and x < 3, not 1 < x < 3 + - addition, subtraction * / multiplication, division - negation of a number

Operands are numbers (3, 2.5), strings ("text" or 'text', a quote doubled inside), ISO dates (2024-05-31: write spaces around a minus to subtract), the ids of questions and variables, parentheses, and five functions:

Function True when answered(x) x has an answer: neither empty nor refused missing(x) x has no answer: empty or refused empty(x) x was not answered refused(x) x was refused today() (a value) the date of the interview

Keywords and function names are case-insensitive; ids are not. A number is compared as a number, so 01 is 1: write a code whose leading zero matters as a string, "01". identifiers() lists the ids an expression uses, in order of first use, and walk() yields each of its nodes.

Two gates are compared after normalising them: missing(x) becomes empty(x) or refused(x) and answered(x) its negation, a value compared with a question goes on the right, not moves inward over and and or, and the parts of an and or an or are sorted. In an and, an answer test beside a comparison of the same question goes, since a comparison is false without an answer: answered(x) and x > 3 is x > 3. In a gate stored as Colectica's Neutral form, which stores "2" and 2 alike, a quoted plain number compares as that number (x = "2" matches x = 2); "02", "+2" or " 2" stay text, and in Blaise code a quoted number is always text.

from ddi_l.spec import equivalent, format_expression, normalise, parse_expression

gate = parse_expression("not (answered(PetKind) and 3 < PetCount)")
print(format_expression(normalise(gate)))
print(equivalent("answered(x)", "not missing(x)"))
print(equivalent("x > 3", "x >= 4"))

The last line prints False. Normalising calculates nothing, so x > 3 and x >= 4 have different normal forms. Without the logic extra that is all equivalent() knows, so a gate reported as different may still be right; the report shows both normal forms so you can tell. With the extra, equivalent() decides the rest: these two still differ, for an x between 3 and 4, and agree when x is a whole number. Nor is not (x > 3) the same as x <= 3: an unanswered x makes the first true and the second false.

docs.title: Decide whether two gates agree
docs.text:
With the logic extra (pip install 'ddi-l[logic]', which adds the Z3 solver), decide() tells whether two gates hold for the same respondents. When they do not, it gives a respondent they disagree on:

from ddi_l.spec import decide

verdict = decide("answered(x)", "x > 3 or x <= 3")
print(verdict.outcome)  # -> different
print(verdict.example.describe())  # -> x is answered with no value
print(decide("x > 3", "x >= 4", types={"x": "integer"}).outcome)  # -> equivalent
print(decide('Owner = "Ana"', 'Owner < "B"').reason)  # -> compares text by order

A respondent leaves each question empty, refuses it or answers it, and an answer may have no value to compare, such as a don't-know. A comparison holds only when every question it reads has a value and nothing in it divides by zero. How each name is read:

  • a question compared only with = and != may take several answers: x = 1 holds when 1 is among them, x != 1 when it has answers and 1 is not one;
  • a question that is ordered (<...), calculated, or compared with a date or today() takes one value;
  • numbers may be fractions unless types says integer, and dates are whole days. types gives each name one of numeric, integer, date, text or code.

The verdict is equivalent, different with its example, or unknown with a reason: text compared by order, a condition compared as a value, a name compared with numbers and with text, or two names compared when either may take several answers. Two gates that differ only for a question answered with several codes are unknown too, since that depends on the question. evaluate() tells whether an expression holds for one respondent, and every different verdict is checked with it. A work limit, not a clock, bounds the solver, so a verdict is the same on every run.

docs.title: Write a gate for Colectica
docs.text:
compile_condition() turns a gate into what Colectica stores in an r:Command. Its condition editor's JSON (Neutral) holds what Colectica's operator codes (listed in Work with Colectica exports) can say:

Expression Statement x = 3, x != 3 (x has no codes) Equal, NotEqual 3 x > 3, x >= 3, x < 3, x <= 3 GreaterThan, GreaterThanOrEqual, LessThan, LessThanOrEqual 3 empty(x), not empty(x) Empty, NotEmpty refused(x), not refused(x) Refused, NotRefused x = 2, x = 2 or x = 3 (x is coded) ContainsAny those codes x = 2 and x = 3 (x is coded) ContainsAll those codes x != 2, x != 2 and x != 3 (x is coded) ContainsNone those codes

So answered(x), which is not empty(x) and not refused(x), is two statements, and missing(x) is Empty or Refused. Statements are joined in one group by and or or, or in groups joined by one and or or ((a or b) and c). A choice among one coded question's codes is one statement wherever it sits, so a and (x = 2 or x = 3) or b fits too.

ddi-l reads every comparison statement as the expression language reads a comparison: false when the question has no answer. Whether Colectica does is not known. It matters most for NotEqual and ContainsNone, which a reader could also take to hold when nothing was answered; check such a gate in a preview.

from ddi_l.colectica_logic import serialize_condition
from ddi_l.spec import BlaiseDialect, compile_condition

subjects = {
    "PetCount": "urn:ddi:example.org:in-count:1",
    "PetKind": "urn:ddi:example.org:in-kind:1",
}
codes = {"PetKind": {"2": "urn:ddi:example.org:code-cat:1"}}
compiled = compile_condition(
    "PetCount > 0 and PetKind = 2", subjects=subjects, codes=codes
)
print(compiled.condition.language, compiled.inputs)
print(serialize_condition(compiled.condition))

subjects gives the r:InParameter of the item that each id is bound to, and codes gives the l:Code of each coded value.

Anything else is written as Blaise code, and fallback_reason says why: - a not in front of a comparison: not (x = 3) holds when x has no answer, and whether NotEqual does is not known; - arithmetic, dates or today(); - one question compared with another, or text compared with <, <=, > or >=; - and and or mixed inside a group (other than a choice among one coded question's codes), since in what order Colectica evaluates them is not documented.

Blaise names inputs as {{name}} and puts every comparison in parentheses. The words it uses for empty, refused, today and dates come from a BlaiseDialect, which has no defaults. Without the word it needs, nothing is compiled, and the reason names the setting. A date template must read back without doubt: {year}, {month} and {day} each once, text before the first field that does not end with a digit, something other than digits between fields, no digit right after a field, and format specs only of the form 0Nd ({month:02d}; a width pads, so a wider value still reads back), so TODATE({year}, {month}, {day}) is fine and {year}{month:02d}{day:02d} is refused:

dialect = BlaiseDialect(empty="EMPTY", refused="REFUSAL")
gate = "answered(PetKind) and not (PetCount = 0)"
compiled = compile_condition(gate, subjects=subjects, dialect=dialect)
print(compiled.condition.text)
print(compiled.fallback_reason)

unset = compile_condition(gate, subjects=subjects)
print(unset.condition, unset.missing_settings)

parse_blaise() and condition_to_expression() read the two forms back into expressions; ddi conform uses them to compare an instrument's gates with the spec's. compile_condition() uses them too: it reads back what it compiled and compares that with the gate, by normal form and then with the logic extra when it is installed. compiled.verified is True when they agree, False when they do not, and None when it could not tell; compile_condition(..., validate=True) raises instead of returning a condition that differs, and names a respondent it differs on.

print(compiled.verified)  # -> True

docs.title: Check an instrument
docs.text:
ddi conform instrument.xml --spec pet-survey.spec.yaml --format table

pet-survey: Instrument 55555555 (Pet survey instrument)
module     severity  rule                             item       message
---------  --------  -------------------------------  ---------  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
household  info      spec.item.id-sources-differ      PetCount   The question PetCount is found by its construct_alias; its item_name is 'HouseholdPets'.
pets       error     spec.code.missing                PetKind    The question PetKind does not offer the code(s) 3.
pets       error     spec.code.extra                  PetKind    The question PetKind offers the code(s) 4, which the spec does not list.
pets       warning   spec.code.label                  PetKind    Code 2 of PetKind is labelled 'Chats' in fr; the spec says 'Chat'.
pets       error     spec.domain.length               PetName    The maximum length of PetName is 40; the spec says 50.
pets       warning   spec.language.missing            PetAge     The question text of PetAge has no fr.
pets       error     spec.domain.range                PetAge     The range of PetAge is [0, 30]; the spec says [0, 40].
pets       warning   spec.domain.decimals             PetAge     PetAge allows 1 decimal(s); the spec says 0.
pets       warning   spec.gate.extra                  PetAge     Question PetAge is gated by PetCount > 1; the spec gates it with nothing.
pets       warning   spec.item.extra                  PetColour  Module pets has the question QuestionConstruct 55555555 (PetColour), which the spec does not list.
visits     warning   spec.item.misplaced              VisitDate  The question VisitDate belongs in module visits, but is in module pets.
-          warning   spec.module.extra                feedback   The instrument has the module Sequence 55555555 (feedback), which the spec does not list.
-          error     spec.variable.derived-is-lookup  HasPets    The derived variable HasPets is a data lookup field: it is imported, not computed.
pets       info      spec.edit.unverifiable           age_range  The edit age_range: not verifiable (edit storage unknown).
5 error(s), 7 warning(s), 2 info.
Option Effect --spec SPEC The spec (required). --module ID Compare one module only; modules the spec does not list and variables are then not checked, and an item the module holds that the spec lists in another module is reported as extra. --instrument NAME The instrument to compare when the file has several. --edits off\|info\|strict How to check edits (below). Default: info. --format json\|table JSON (default): the spec, the instrument, a summary, each module's result and the findings; or a table. -o PATH, --indent N Where to write, and the JSON indentation. --fail-severity info\|warning\|error The least severe finding that fails the run. Default: error.

ddi conform exits with:

  • 0: no finding reaches --fail-severity;
  • 1: one does, or the spec extra is not installed;
  • 2: the comparison cannot run: the spec does not read or pass its checks, --module names no module of the spec, --edits strict and the spec has no match.edits, or the instrument file does not read.

From Python:

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.spec import conform, load_spec

report = conform(ddi.read_ddi("instrument.xml"), load_spec("pet-survey.spec.yaml"))
print(report.summary)
for finding in report.findings:
    print(
        finding.severity, finding.rule_id, finding.module, finding.item, finding.message
    )

docs.title: Where ids are found
docs.text:
Each id is looked for in the places match lists, in order. The first place that holds an id anywhere in the instrument is the one used. An id found there on several constructs is reported as ambiguous, never guessed.

Key Default Places question_id [construct_alias, item_name, item_alias, construct_name] the alias of the question construct's r:OutParameter, the question item's name, its output alias, the construct's name statement_id [construct_name, label, user_id] the statement's ConstructName, r:Label, r:UserID module_id [construct_name, label, user_id] the same, on a sequence module_depth any depth the depth of module sequences: the instrument's own sequence is 1, its children 2 edits none how edit checks are stored, for --edits strict lookup_types none a data lookup field type and the spec type it stands for: {Text: text, Integer: numeric}

A module is a sequence. A sequence typed ConditionalChildContainer is the body of an IfThenElse branch, never a module or a page; a page is any other sequence inside a module. When several places hold different ids for one question (its construct alias and its item name, say), the question is found by the first, and spec.item.id-sources-differ says what the others hold.

A module found on several sequences is spec.module.ambiguous; none of its candidates is reported as an extra module, and the items inside them are neither misplaced nor gate-checked. An item referenced from several places is compared where the spec puts it: it is misplaced only when none of its places is in its module, and each other module holding it reports it as spec.item.extra. A referenced domain (a ManagedNumericRepresentation, say) is compared like an inline one; of a StructuredMixedResponseDomain, the one domain of the spec's kind is compared.

docs.title: Gates
docs.text:
A module's gate is every condition on the way from the instrument to the module; a question's own gate is every condition between its module and the question. The Then branch of an IfThenElse adds its condition; an ElseIf branch adds its condition and the negation of those before it; the Else branch adds the negation of them all. With gate_scope: page, the module's gate is expected on each page instead of on the module. A statement has no gate of its own in a spec: with gate_scope: page, its page gate must be one of the gates between its module and it (spec.gate.missing or spec.gate.different otherwise), and a further gate of its own is not compared.

When the paths to an item inside its module carry gates that are not equivalent, its gate is spec.gate.unverifiable.

With the logic extra, gates and edits are decided as decide() does after their normal forms are compared, so a gate written differently that always agrees with the spec's is not reported. The spec's response domains and variable types say what each name is: a numeric domain with no decimals is a whole number, so PetCount > 0 and PetCount >= 1 agree. A gate or an edit that differs names a respondent the two disagree on, in the message and in the finding's example:

Module pets is gated by PetCount > 0; the spec says PetCount > 1 (they differ when PetCount is 1).

--semantics syntactic (conform(semantics="syntactic")) compares normal forms only, as without the extra; --semantics smt fails without it.

A Neutral condition's subjects are followed through their bindings, those of each item's latest version, to the question they come from. A question the spec does not list is named by its first id, so a gate bound to the wrong question reads as that question; one output of a question with several (a grid's cell) is named by its alias, or, when the spec does not know that alias, by the spec variable an alias on the way names. A subject bound to no question is named by the output its bindings end at (a data lookup's field): an alias never hides which question, output or field a gate is bound to. Blaise code is read with the spec's blaise words, its {{name}} inputs named the same way.

docs.title: Edits
docs.text:
Where an instrument stores its edit checks is not known in general, so by default each edit is reported as info: not verifiable (edit storage unknown). --edits off leaves edits out.

--edits strict looks for them, once the spec says how they are stored. An edit check is a ComputationItem marked by a user attribute; its id is in one of its construct_name, label or user_id:

match:
  edits: {attribute: kind, value: EditCheck, id: construct_name}

Colectica, for instance, marks its computations with an r:UserAttributePair whose r:AttributeKey reads x:TypeOfComputation: set attribute and value to what your exports hold. An edit with no such check is spec.edit.missing; one whose condition differs from when is spec.edit.different.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Rule Default Reported when spec.instrument.missing error No instrument in the file matches the spec's instrument, or the file has none. spec.instrument.ambiguous error Several instruments match; name one with instrument or --instrument. spec.module.missing error A required module is not in the instrument. spec.module.ambiguous error Several sequences carry a module's id. spec.module.extra warning A sequence at the modules' depth that the spec does not list. spec.item.missing error A question or statement is not found. spec.item.ambiguous error Several constructs carry a question's or statement's id. spec.item.extra warning A question or statement in a module that the spec does not list there, or lists in another module. spec.item.misplaced warning A question or statement found only in other modules than the spec's. spec.item.id-sources-differ info The id sources of a question disagree (its construct name and its item name, say). spec.code.missing error A code the spec lists is not offered. spec.code.extra error A code is offered the spec does not list. spec.code.label warning A code's category label differs from the spec's, in one language. spec.language.missing warning A question's or statement's text, or a code's label, lacks one of the spec's languages. spec.domain.type error The response domain is of another kind (code, numeric, text, date), or a mixed domain holds none of the spec's kind. spec.domain.length error A text domain's minimum or maximum length differs. spec.domain.range error A numeric domain's bounds, or whether they are included, differ. spec.domain.decimals warning A numeric domain's decimals differ. spec.domain.unverifiable info The question's domain cannot be read (several, a mixed domain with several of the spec's kind, a reference not in the file, a code list that cannot be resolved). spec.gate.missing error The spec gates a module or question, and nothing gates it. spec.gate.different error The gate differs from the spec's; both normal forms are shown. spec.gate.extra warning A module or question is gated, and the spec gates it with nothing. spec.gate.scope error The gate wraps each page where the spec says the module, or the reverse. spec.gate.unverifiable warning The stored gate cannot be read back into an expression (an operator code not listed, a don't-know test, and and or mixed, malformed Neutral JSON, native code this reader does not know), or paths to the item carry different gates. spec.edit.unverifiable info Not verifiable (edit storage unknown): reported for each edit unless --edits strict or off. spec.edit.missing error With --edits strict, no edit check carries the edit's id. spec.edit.different error With --edits strict, the edit check's condition differs from when. spec.variable.import-undeclared error An imported variable is not a field of any data lookup the instrument reaches. spec.variable.import-type warning An imported variable's lookup field type differs (with match.lookup_types). spec.variable.derived-is-lookup error A derived variable is a data lookup field: it is imported, not computed.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only the operator codes' names are known. A code not listed, and DontKnow and NotDontKnow (the expression language has no "don't know"), are reported as unverifiable.
  • How a statement treats a question with no answer is not known. ddi-l reads every comparison as false without an answer, as the expression language does.
  • The order of and and or inside a group is not known. Gates that mix them in one group are reported as unverifiable, and none is compiled that way.
  • Without the logic extra, nothing is calculated. Normalising does not prove arithmetic equivalence: x > 3 and x >= 4 are reported as different even for a whole-number question. With it, what decide() cannot model, such as text compared by order, is still compared by normal form.
  • A question compared only with = and != may take several answers, unless its domain says otherwise. Two gates that differ only for several answers (x = 1 and x = 2 and x = 1 and x = 3) are reported as different, without a respondent.
  • Where edits are stored is not known in general, hence --edits info by default.
  • A comparison under not is kept as written, since it differs from its opposite when the question has no answer.

docs.title: Load DDI from spreadsheets
docs.text:
Many teams keep their metadata in spreadsheets: one row per variable, one per question, one per code. ddi-l loads those spreadsheets into DDI in one step, as long as they follow the layout on this page: one table per kind of item, with rows that point at each other by id.

The tables can be a folder of CSV files, the same zipped, or one Excel workbook with a sheet per table. The result is a FragmentInstance laid out as Colectica Designer writes one, or a DDI study.

Start from a template: the spreadsheet templates page has blank tables and a filled-in bilingual example, as CSV files and as an Excel workbook.

docs.title: What the tables cover
docs.text:
The tables cover what most organizations document about a study, from its citation to its questionnaire, variables and data files.

Area Tables DDI items The study studies, groups, organizations, individuals StudyUnit, Group, Organization, Individual Concepts concepts, universes, unit_types Concept, Universe, UnitType Variables conceptual_variables, represented_variables, variables ConceptualVariable, RepresentedVariable, Variable Codes code_lists, codes CodeList (flat or hierarchical), Category Questions instructions, questions, question_texts, question_grids, question_blocks, question_groups Instruction, QuestionItem, QuestionGrid, QuestionBlock, QuestionGroup Questionnaire instruments, flow Instrument, Sequence, QuestionConstruct, StatementItem, IfThenElse, Loop Data variable_groups, datasets, ncubes VariableGroup, PhysicalInstance, DataRelationship, NCube Methods and quality methodologies, processing_events, quality_statements Methodology, ProcessingEvent, QualityStatement Comparison comparisons ConceptMap, UniverseMap, QuestionMap, VariableMap, CategoryMap

settings holds the agency, version and language every table uses.

Use the tables you need and leave out the rest: a folder with only settings, concepts and variables is fine.
