Some things are not in the tables: column positions of fixed-width files, classification levels and families, geography, sampling plans, derivation and computation code, and managed missing-value schemes. Load the tables, then add those to the typed models in Python, or in Colectica.

docs.title: How the tables fit together
docs.text:
A column that points at another table holds that table's ids. The diagrams show every link, one area at a time. A crow's foot marks the side that can have many rows; a column that holds several ids (a|b) makes a many-to-many link. In DDI each link is a reference, such as a variable's r:QuestionReference or a universe's r:DefiningConceptReference.

docs.title: Rules every table follows
docs.text:
• One file or sheet per table, named as in the tables above: concepts.csv, or a sheet called concepts. The first row holds the column names; every other row is one item.
  • id is your key. Give every row an id, unique within its table: the variable name, a question number, anything without spaces. Other tables use it to point at the row: a variable's question column holds a question's id.
  • Several ids in one cell are separated by |: Q_AGE|Q_AGE_PROXY.
  • Empty cells are fine. Only the columns marked required below must be filled.
  • Notes columns are ignored. A column whose name starts with # or _ is yours, for comments or working notes.
  • Unknown columns are errors, so a misspelled lable@en is caught rather than silently dropped.
  • One study needs no study column. When studies has a single row, instruments, data files, methodologies, processing events and quality statements with an empty study belong to it.

docs.title: Identifiers and versions
docs.text:
Every item gets a DDI identifier (a UUID). Leave ddi_id empty and one is derived from the agency, the table and the row's id, so loading the same tables again gives the same identifiers, and a re-import updates items instead of duplicating them. Fill ddi_id with an existing identifier to update an item that is already in Colectica.

Every item takes the version from settings, unless its own version column says otherwise.

docs.title: Names and labels
docs.text: name is the item's short name, such as AGE or Q_AGE, written in the language set in settings. It defaults to id. label and description are for people, in as many languages as you have.

docs.title: Several languages
docs.text:
Text that people read goes in one column per language: the column name, @, and a language tag.

Column Meaning label@en, label@fr the label in English and in French description@fr-CA the description in Canadian French text@en, text@fr a question's wording in English and in French

Any BCP 47 tag works: en, fr, fr-CA, iu. Add a column per language you document; a cell left empty means that language has no text for that row. All the languages of one row are written into one DDI element, as Colectica writes them.

docs.title: Question wording for different audiences
docs.text:
text@en is the wording everyone sees. When a question is worded differently for some respondents (asked of a proxy, or read by an interviewer), add one row per wording to question_texts:

question language audience text Q_WORK en proxy Last week, did this person work at a job or business? Q_WORK fr proxy La semaine dernière, cette personne a-t-elle travaillé à un emploi ou à une entreprise? Q_AGE en intvwr INTERVIEWER: Record the age in completed years.

Each wording becomes its own d:QuestionText. DDI 3.3 records who a wording is for in its audienceLanguage attribute, a language tag, so the audience is added to the language as a private-use subtag:

Wording audienceLanguage text@en in questions en proxy wording in English en-x-proxy intvwr wording in French fr-x-intvwr

Because it goes into a language tag, an audience is letters and digits, at most 8 between hyphens: proxy, intvwr, self-resp. A question can have one wording per language and audience.

docs.title: Custom properties
docs.text:
Any property DDI has no column for goes in a column named custom: and the property name: custom:Steward, custom:Sensitivity, custom:Mode. Each filled cell becomes an r:UserAttributePair on the item, with the key extension: and the property name, which is how Colectica Designer stores its custom fields. A name that already has a prefix, such as custom:x:Source, keeps it as it is.

Every table whose rows are items takes custom columns. Four tables do not: settings, codes (a category can be shared by several codes), question_texts and comparisons.

docs.title: The questionnaire flow
docs.text:
An instrument's content is in flow, one row per step, in the order the steps run. type says what a step is:

type What it is Needs question asks a question, grid or block question statement shows a text text@<language> sequence holds the steps whose parent it is, in order if runs its then steps when condition holds, else its else steps condition loop repeats its steps while condition holds condition

A step without a parent is at the top of its instrument. A step inside an if says which side it is on with branch (then by default, or else). The example's flow:

id type parent branch question condition F_INTRO statement F_DEMO sequence F_AGE question F_DEMO Q_AGE F_SEX question F_DEMO Q_SEX F_IF_15 if AGE >= 15 F_WORK question F_IF_15 then Q_WORK F_IF_WORKED if F_IF_15 then WORKED = 1 F_JOBS loop F_IF_WORKED job <= JOB_COUNT F_JOB question F_JOBS B_JOB F_TOO_YOUNG statement F_IF_15 else F_END statement

Conditions are text, recorded with the language named in condition_language (pseudo-code by default): write them in the syntax your collection system uses.

docs.title: What the tables add
docs.text:
Some items follow from the rows without a table of their own. Their identifiers are derived like a row's, so they too are the same on every load.

From Comes each code a category holding its labels, or the one its category key shares each study a data collection holding its instruments, methodology and processing events each study's processing events a processing event scheme listing them each instrument a sequence holding its top-level flow steps each if and loop a sequence for each of its branches or its body each dataset a data relationship with a logical record listing its variables each map of comparisons one map holding its rows

A unit type with no concept gets the placeholder concept reference Colectica writes, since the DDI 3.3 schema requires one by mistake.

docs.title: Each table, column by column
docs.text: Columns marked required must be present and filled on every row.

docs.title: settings
docs.text:
Two columns, setting and value, one row per setting:

setting Meaning Default agency the maintenance agency of every item, such as org.example required version the version of every item without its own 1 language the language of names en

docs.title: Columns most tables have
docs.text:
Every table whose rows are items, except studies, groups, organizations and individuals, starts with these:

Column Required What goes in it id yes your key for the row ddi_id an existing DDI identifier to keep version the item's version, if not the one in settings name the short name; defaults to id label@<language> a short label, per language description@<language> a longer definition, per language custom:<name> a property of your own

studies, groups, organizations and individuals have id, ddi_id, version and custom columns too, and the columns listed for each.

docs.title: studies
docs.text:
One row per study: a survey cycle, a census, an administrative source.

Column What goes in it title@<language> the study's title; defaults to id subtitle@<language> a subtitle alternate_title@<language> another title, such as an acronym abstract@<language> what the study is about purpose@<language> why it was done creator who made it: organizations or individuals ids, or names publisher who publishes it: ids or names, as for creator publication_date when it was published: 2024, 2024-05 or 2024-05-31 kind_of_data Survey data, Administrative records... analysis_unit Persons, Households, Businesses... universe who the study covers, as a universes id concept the concept that defines the study, as a concepts id keywords@<language> topics, separated by vertical bars start_date, end_date the period covered: 2024-01-01 countries country codes covered, such as CA funder who funds it, as organizations ids grant_number the funding grant numbers

A creator or publisher that is an id in organizations or individuals becomes a reference to it; anything else is written as a name.

docs.title: groups
docs.text:
One row per group of studies, such as every cycle of a survey.

Column What goes in it title@<language> the group's title; defaults to id abstract@<language> what the group holds purpose@<language> why the studies are grouped type the kind of group: Series, Program... studies the studies in it, as studies ids parent the group it sits in, as a groups id

docs.title: organizations
docs.text: Column Required What goes in it name@<language> yes the organization's name, per language abbreviation a short name or acronym email a contact email address url its web site description@<language> a description, per language

docs.title: individuals
docs.text:
Column What goes in it first_name given name last_name family name email a contact email address url a web page description@<language> a description, per language, such as the role

At least one of first_name and last_name is needed.

docs.title: concepts
docs.text: Column What goes in it parent the broader concept(s) this one narrows, as concepts ids

docs.title: universes
docs.text: Column What goes in it concept the concept that defines the universe, as a concepts id

docs.title: unit_types
docs.text:
The kinds of unit described: person, household, business.

Column What goes in it concept the concept of the unit, as a concepts id

docs.title: conceptual_variables
docs.text:
A concept measured on a unit type, with no representation yet.

Column What goes in it concept the concept, as a concepts id universe who it describes, as universes ids unit_type the kind of unit, as a unit_types id

docs.title: represented_variables
docs.text:
A conceptual variable with a representation, shared by the variables that record it the same way.

Column What goes in it conceptual_variable the conceptual variable, as a conceptual_variables id concept, unit_type without a conceptual_variable: the concept and unit type representation required: code, numeric, text or datetime code_list, numeric_type, min, max, max_length, date_type as for questions

docs.title: code_lists
docs.text: Only the columns most tables have. The codes go in codes.

docs.title: codes
docs.text:
One row per code, in the order the codes are listed. Each code gets a category holding its labels.

Column Required What goes in it code_list yes the code list, as a code_lists id value yes the code as stored in the data: 1, 01, M label@<language> the category label, per language description@<language> a longer definition, per language category a key to share one category between code lists missing true for a missing-value code, such as Refusal parent for a hierarchy: the value of the code this one sits under

Codes with the same category key share one category, labelled from the first of them: a "Not stated" category used by every code list, for example.

A classification is a code list whose codes nest: give each code below the top level the value of its parent, in the same code list, and list the parent first.

code_list value label@en parent OCCUPATIONS 1 Management OCCUPATIONS 11 Senior managers 1 OCCUPATIONS 12 Middle managers 1 OCCUPATIONS 2 Sales and service

docs.title: instructions
docs.text:
Instructions to respondents or interviewers, attached to questions with their instruction column.

Column What goes in it text@<language> the instruction, per language

docs.title: questions
docs.text: Column What goes in it text@<language> the wording, per language concept the concept the question measures, as a concepts id response the kind of answer: code, numeric, text or datetime code_list for code: the code list, as a code_lists id numeric_type for numeric: Integer, Decimal, Float, Double, Long or Short min for numeric: the lowest valid value max for numeric: the highest valid value max_length for text: the longest valid answer, in characters date_type for datetime: Date, DateTime, Time, Year, YearMonth or Duration instruction instructions shown with it, as instructions ids group the question groups it belongs to, as question_groups ids

docs.title: question_texts
docs.text: Column Required What goes in it question yes the question, as a questions id language yes the wording's language audience who the wording is for; empty for everyone text yes the wording

docs.title: question_grids
docs.text:
A question asked for each row of a grid: rows from one code list, columns from another if any, and one response per cell.

Column What goes in it text@<language> the question, per language rows required: the rows, as a code_lists id columns the columns, as a code_lists id response and its details the answer in each cell, as for questions concept, instruction, group as for questions

docs.title: question_blocks
docs.text:
Questions presented together.

Column What goes in it intent@<language> what the block is for questions its questions in order, as questions or question_grids ids concept, instruction, group as for questions

docs.title: question_groups
docs.text:
Groups of questions, such as the modules of a questionnaire. Questions, grids and blocks join with their group column.

Column What goes in it type the kind of group: Module, Topic... parent the group it sits in, as a question_groups id concept the concept it covers, as a concepts id

docs.title: instruments
docs.text:
One row per questionnaire. Its content is in flow.

Column What goes in it study the study, as a studies id type the kind of instrument: CAWI, CATI, Paper...

docs.title: flow
docs.text:
The steps of each instrument, as explained in The questionnaire flow.

Column Required What goes in it instrument yes the instrument, as an instruments id type yes question, statement, sequence, if or loop parent the sequence, if or loop it is inside, as a flow id branch inside an if: then or else; defaults to then question for question: a questions, question_grids or question_blocks id text@<language> for statement: the text shown condition for if and loop: the condition, such as AGE >= 15 condition_language the language of the condition; defaults to pseudo-code

docs.title: variables
docs.text:
Column What goes in it concept the concept the variable measures, as a concepts id universe who the variable describes, as universes ids question the question(s) its values come from, as questions ids representation how values are recorded: code, numeric, text or datetime code_list, numeric_type, min, max, max_length, date_type as for questions unit_type the kind of unit, as a unit_types id conceptual_variable its conceptual variable, as a conceptual_variables id represented_variable its represented variable, as a represented_variables id dataset the data file(s) it is a column of, as datasets ids group its variable groups, as variable_groups ids

A variable with an empty representation takes the one of its represented variable, or else the response of its first question, so a variable fed by a coded question does not repeat the code list. A data file lists its variables in the order of the variables table.

docs.title: variable_groups
docs.text:
Groups of variables, such as topics. Variables join with their group column.

Column What goes in it type the kind of group: Topic, Derived... parent the group it sits in, as a variable_groups id concept the concept it covers, as a concepts id universe who its variables describe, as universes ids

docs.title: datasets
docs.text:
One row per data file. Variables join with their dataset column.

Column What goes in it title@<language> the file's title; defaults to name file where the file is: a path or URL study the study, as a studies id

In DDI a physical instance has no label, so label and description describe the file's record of variables (its logical record).

docs.title: ncubes
docs.text:
Multidimensional tables of aggregates.

Column What goes in it dimensions required: its dimensions in order, as variables ids purpose@<language> what the n-cube is for universe who it describes, as universes ids

docs.title: methodologies
docs.text:
How a study's data were collected. A study has at most one methodology.

Column What goes in it study the study, as a studies id data_collection@<language> how data were collected time_method@<language> cross-section, panel, time series... sampling@<language> how the sample was drawn deviation@<language> how the sample departs from its design weighting@<language> how weights were derived

docs.title: processing_events
docs.text:
What was done to a study's data after collection.

Column What goes in it study the study, as a studies id control@<language> checks made on the data cleaning@<language> how the data were cleaned or edited weighting@<language> how the data were weighted appraisal@<language> response rates, sampling error...

docs.title: quality_statements
docs.text: Column What goes in it study the study, as a studies id text@<language> the statement

docs.title: comparisons
docs.text:
How items compare, across studies or cycles: one row per pair. Rows with the same map form one map.

Column Required What goes in it map yes your key for the map the row belongs to type yes what is compared: concept, universe, question, variable or category source yes the item compared from, as an id in that table target yes the item compared to, as an id in that table commonality@<language> what they share difference@<language> how they differ weight how alike they are, from 0 to 1

For category, write code_list/value (SEX_CODES/1), or a category key of codes.

docs.title: Load the tables
docs.text:
From Python, load_tables() reads a folder of CSV files or a workbook and gives back typed models you can check or edit before writing:

from ddi_l.tables import load_tables, write_table_templates

# The bilingual example from the templates page, written to a folder.
write_table_templates("my-survey", example=True)

tables = load_tables("my-survey")
print(len(tables.variables))  # -> 5
print(tables.get("variables", "AGE").labels[1].text)  # -> Âge en années
print(len(tables.tables["flow"]))  # -> 16

# A Colectica FragmentInstance, one item per fragment.
tables.to_fragment().save("my-survey.xml")

tables.tables holds the items of each table, and those it implies, in row order: the 16 items of flow are its 11 steps and the 5 sequences they imply. tables.items holds them all.

The same tables as one Excel workbook load the same way:

from pathlib import Path

write_table_templates("my-survey.xlsx", example=True, layout="xlsx")
tables = load_tables("my-survey.xlsx")

# A zip of the CSV files, at its top or in one folder, loads too.
write_table_templates("my-survey.zip", example=True, layout="zip")
tables = load_tables("my-survey.zip")

# So do the bytes of a workbook or a zip, received from an upload: they are
# read in memory, and problems name them workbook.xlsx or tables.zip.
tables = load_tables(Path("my-survey.xlsx").read_bytes())

load_tables() takes agency=, version= and language= to override settings.

docs.title: A fragment or a study document
docs.text:
to_fragment() writes every item, whatever the tables. Its top-level item is the only group, or else the only study; pass top_level= to choose another.

to_study() puts the items inside a new study of a DDIInstance document. A study document has one study and no place for groups, people, variable groups, processing events, quality statements or comparisons, so it takes the other tables only, and says which tables to remove otherwise:

from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("questionnaire")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(folder / "settings.csv").write_text(
    "setting,value\nagency,example.org\n", encoding="utf-8"
)
(folder / "concepts.csv").write_text("id,label@en\nAGE,Age\n", encoding="utf-8")
(folder / "variables.csv").write_text(
    "id,concept,representation,numeric_type\nAGE,AGE,numeric,Integer\n",
    encoding="utf-8",
)

study = load_tables(folder).to_study("Labour Force Survey")
print(study.validate())  # -> []
study.save("labour-force-survey.xml")

From the command line:

ddi tables template my-survey --example        # the example, as CSV files
ddi tables import my-survey -o my-survey.xml   # a Colectica FragmentInstance
ddi tables import questionnaire --study "Labour Force Survey" -o study.xml

Over HTTP, ddi serve offers the same: POST /v1/tables/import takes a workbook or a zip and answers with the fragment, or with every problem as a 422; GET /v1/tables/template gives the templates, and GET /v1/tables describes every table and column as JSON.

docs.title: When something is wrong
docs.text:
Loading checks every table before writing anything, and reports every problem at once, each with its file (or sheet), row and column:

Error: my-survey has 3 problems:
  - variables.csv, row 4, column question: no row in questions has id 'Q_AGEE'
  - codes.csv, row 7, column missing: 'maybe' is not true or false
  - flow.csv, row 6, column parent: 'F_AGE' is a question step; only a
    sequence, if or loop holds other steps

Row numbers are the spreadsheet's, header included, so row 4 is the fourth row you see in Excel.

docs.title: Excel tips
docs.text:
• Keep codes and dates as text. Excel turns 01 into the number 1 and 2024-05 into a date. The template workbooks format every cell as text; in your own workbook, format the columns as Text before typing.
  • Save CSV as "CSV UTF-8", so accented letters survive. Files saved with semicolons by a French-language Excel are read too.
  • One workbook or one folder. In a workbook, a sheet named README, or with a name starting with _, is ignored; any other sheet must be one of the tables.

docs.title: Into Colectica
docs.text: The FragmentInstance from to_fragment() is written the way Colectica Designer writes an export, with one item per <Fragment>, for importing into a Colectica repository; try the import in a test repository first. See Work with Colectica exports for reading and editing such files. Because identifiers are derived from your ids, loading the same tables again after editing them gives the same items with the same identifiers: bump version in settings (or per row) and import again.

docs.title: Spreadsheet templates
docs.text: Templates for the tables described in Load DDI from spreadsheets. Each comes as an Excel workbook (one sheet per table, plus a README sheet listing every column) and as a zip of CSV files (one file per table, plus README.txt).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A small bilingual (English and French) labour survey with every table filled in: the study with its series, agency and manager; concepts, a universe, a unit type and the variable cascade; code lists sharing a "Not stated" category and a two-level occupation classification; questions with proxy and interviewer wordings, an instruction, a grid, a block and modules; a web questionnaire with a sequence, nested conditions and a loop; variables in groups and in a data file; an n-cube; methodology, processing and quality; a concept comparison across cycles; and custom properties.

Example workbook Example CSV files

Load it as it is to see what each row becomes:

ddi tables import ddi-tables-example.xlsx -o example.xml
ddi tables import ddi-tables-example.zip -o example.xml   # the zip loads as it is

docs.title: Blank
docs.text:
The same tables with headers only, with label, description and text columns for English and French. Fill agency in settings, delete the tables you do not need, and add rows.

Blank workbook Blank CSV files

docs.title: Other languages
docs.text:
For other languages, generate the blank tables with the columns you need:

ddi tables template my-tables --lang en --lang fr --lang iu --format xlsx

Or from Python:

from ddi_l.tables import write_table_templates

write_table_templates("my-tables", languages=("en", "es"))

--format (or layout=) is csv for a folder of CSV files, zip for the same zipped, or xlsx for a workbook.

docs.title: What is in a template
docs.text:
Sheet or file One row per README column, with what goes in it (workbook only; README.txt in the zip) settings setting: agency, version, language studies study groups group of studies organizations organization individuals person concepts concept universes universe unit_types kind of unit conceptual_variables conceptual variable represented_variables represented variable code_lists code list codes code instructions instruction questions question question_texts extra wording of a question, by language and audience question_grids grid question question_blocks block of questions question_groups question group or module instruments questionnaire flow step of a questionnaire variables variable variable_groups variable group datasets data file ncubes n-cube methodologies methodology processing_events processing event quality_statements quality statement comparisons pair of compared items

Every cell of the workbooks is formatted as text, so codes such as 01 keep their leading zero. The CSV files are UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, so Excel opens accented letters correctly.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
This guide walks you through the main features of the ddi-l CRUD API. Each section is self-contained, so you can jump to the workflow you need.

Prerequisites

  • Python 3.11 or newer with ddi-l installed (pip install ddi-l).
  • No XML knowledge is required for the simple API.

docs.title: Create a study
docs.text:
Use ddi.new_study() to create a new DDI document with a study unit:

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="example.org")
print(doc.agency)  # -> example.org

The function returns a Document object. It automatically creates the DDI instance, study unit, and all required identification metadata.

docs.title: Add questions
docs.text:
Use doc.add_question() to add questions to the study:

q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="How old are you?")
q3 = doc.add_question(text="What is your household income?")

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> 3

Each question is a QuestionItem in a QuestionScheme inside the DataCollection module.

docs.title: Add variables
docs.text:
Use doc.add_variable() to add variables, optionally linking them to questions or concepts:

age_concept = doc.add_concept(name="Age")

doc.add_variable(name="Gender", question=q1)
doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q2, concept=age_concept)
doc.add_variable(name="Household Income", question=q3)

print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> 3

When you pass a question= or concept= argument, ddi-l automatically creates the DDI reference linking the variable to that item.

docs.title: Add concepts and universes
docs.text:
demo_concept = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
doc.add_universe(name="Canadian adults aged 18+")

print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")  # -> 2
print(f"Universes: {len(doc.universes)}")  # -> 1

docs.title: Add code lists
docs.text:
cl = doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")  # -> 1

docs.title: Work with any item type
docs.text:
The add_item() method supports all 30 DDI item types registered in the type registry. Use it for types that do not have a dedicated convenience method:

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, RepresentedVariable
from ddi_l.models.datacollection import Instrument

doc.add_item(Category, name="Male")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Female")
doc.add_item(RepresentedVariable, name="Gender Representation")
doc.add_item(Instrument, name="CAWI Questionnaire")

# Query items by type
print(f"Categories: {len(doc.items(Category))}")  # -> 2

docs.title: Find and remove items
docs.text:
Every item gets a unique identifier when created. Use find() to look up an item by its identifier, and remove() to delete it:

cat = doc.add_item(Category, name="Not specified")
print(cat.identifier)

found = doc.find(cat.identifier)
print(found)  # Prints the Category object

doc.remove(cat.identifier)
print(doc.find(cat.identifier))  # -> None

docs.title: Save to XML
docs.text:
doc.save("household-survey.xml")

The output uses proper DDI namespace prefixes (r:, s:, d:, l:, c:, a:, p:), not generic ns0/ns1.

docs.title: Open an existing file
docs.text:
doc = ddi.open_ddi("household-survey.xml")

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")

for v in doc.variables:
    print(f"  {v.identifier}")

Save it again and the parts you did not change are written as they were read, byte for byte; only what you added or changed is laid out, with the file's own indentation. To lay the whole file out afresh, use ddi.write_ddi(doc, "out.xml", layout="default").

Pass validate=True to run schema validation on load:

doc = ddi.open_ddi("household-survey.xml", validate=True)

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
Call doc.validate() to check the document against the DDI schema:

issues = doc.validate()
if issues:
    for issue in issues:
        print(f"[{issue.severity}] {issue.message}")
else:
    print("Document is valid!")

For more validation options, see the validation guide.

docs.title: Advanced: working with the model layer
docs.text:
The generated model classes under ddi_l.models are the advanced layer. You can import and use them directly for fine-grained control:

from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString, Reference
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Variable

var = Variable(
    agency="example.org",
    identifier="var-age",
    version="1.0",
    names=[InternationalString(text="Age", lang="en")],
)

See the models reference for a complete list of available types.

docs.title: Validate and lint DDI content
docs.text:
ddi-l checks documents in two ways: schema validation against the DDI XSDs, and lint rules for problems the schema allows (missing labels, broken references, agency rules).

Prerequisites

  • Python 3.11 or newer with ddi-l installed.
  • Access to the bundled schemas (installed automatically with the package).

docs.title: Validate on load
docs.text:
Pass validate=True when opening a document to run schema validation immediately:

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.open_ddi("my-study.xml", validate=True)

If the document fails validation, a DDIValidationError is raised.

docs.title: Validate an existing document
docs.text:
Call doc.validate() on any Document to check it against the DDI schema:

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Test", agency="example.org")
doc.add_question(text="How old are you?")

issues = doc.validate()
if issues:
    for issue in issues:
        print(f"[{issue.severity}] {issue.message}")
else:
    print("Document is valid!")

docs.title: How schema validation runs
docs.text:
Every error is reported, with the same message and path whichever way it runs. schema_loader.validate(..., backend=...) picks the way for one call; the best available is the default:

  • native, on the native backend: one pass over the document checks it against a compiled form of the schema. A valid document is done; xmlschema is not even loaded. For each element that may be wrong, xmlschema checks that element alone and words its errors, which also carry the line the element starts on. On a 9 MB export: 0.09 s when it is valid, 0.13 s with an error (2.6 s on the first call, which loads xmlschema).
  • lxml, with lxml installed: libxml2 confirms a valid document quickly; if it finds a problem, xmlschema validates the whole document again to report it (6.5 s with one error on the same export).
  • python: xmlschema validates the whole document.

docs.title: High-level validation
docs.text:
The ddi_l.validation module provides validate_document() for combined schema and lint validation:

from ddi_l.validation import validate_document

report = validate_document(doc)
print(f"Schema issues: {len(report.schema_issues)}")
print(f"Lint findings: {len(report.lint_findings)}")

if report.has_errors():
    print("Document has errors!")

docs.title: Model-level validation
docs.text:
Individual model objects can be validated with their .validate() method:

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Variable
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

var = Variable(
    agency="example.org",
    identifier="var-1",
    version="1.0",
    labels=[InternationalString(text="Age")],
)
var.validate()  # raises ModelValidationError on failure

docs.title: Lint rules
docs.text:
The lint engine runs configurable rules against documents. Use run_lint() to check referential integrity and other quality rules:

from ddi_l.document import DDIDocument
from ddi_l.lint import run_lint

doc = DDIDocument.from_xml("my-study.xml")
findings = run_lint(doc, rules=["ddi.reference.integrity"])
for f in findings:
    print(f"[{f.severity}] {f.message}")

Without rules=, run_lint() runs the default profile, DDI_PROFILE_DEFAULT. run_profile(doc, name) runs a named profile instead; ddi lint --list-profiles lists them.

Rule Severity Reports ddi.agency.allowed error A missing agency, or one outside the configured allow-list ddi.citation.present error A DDIInstance without a citation ddi.citation.title.present error A citation without a title ddi.citation.title.languages warning A citation title missing a required language ddi.maintainable.labels warning An item without an r:Label ddi.reference.integrity error (warning in a fragment) A reference whose item is not in the file ddi.reference.version warning A reference whose item is in the file, but not at the version named ddi.reference.provenance-external info A BasedOn or user-attribute reference to an item outside the file colectica.maintainable.labels warning An item with no label or name with text (colectica-questionnaire profile only)

Every finding has one of three severities: error, warning or info. info reports something worth knowing that is not a defect, and never fails ddi lint unless you pass --fail-severity info. A rule that yields any other severity raises ValueError.

A rule you add with register_rule() joins the default profile unless you pass default=False, for a rule meant only for a named profile. The colectica-questionnaire profile is for Colectica exports; see Work with Colectica exports. The lint rule reference lists every rule.

docs.title: CLI validation
docs.text:
From the command line:

ddi validate my-study.xml              # Schema validation
ddi lint my-study.xml                  # Lint checks
ddi lint export.xml --profile colectica-questionnaire
ddi lint my-study.xml --fail-severity warning   # Fail on warnings too
ddi validate *.xml                     # Validate multiple files

ddi lint exits non-zero when a finding reaches --fail-severity: error (the default), warning or info.

The output is JSON with message, xpath, and context fields for each issue found.

docs.title: Error types
docs.text:
Exception When it is raised DDIValidationError Schema validation fails (via validate=True or validate_document()) ModelValidationError A model object fails business rule checks DDIReadError The instance cannot be read DDIParseError The XML is malformed (a DDIReadError; carries line and column) DDIWriteError Serialization cannot complete DDIReferenceError A reference or study identifier cannot be resolved (a LookupError) DuplicateIdentifierError An item is added with an identifier already in the document (a ValueError)

Document.save() also issues a DDIReferenceWarning when a reference in the study points at an item the document does not contain. Filter it like any warning category:

import warnings

from ddi_l import DDIReferenceWarning

warnings.simplefilter("error", DDIReferenceWarning)  # fail instead of warn

docs.title: Documentation assets
docs.text: Branding and styling assets used by MkDocs.

docs.title: Logo and favicon
docs.text:
The header mark lives at docs/overrides/.icons/ddi/logo.svg: stacked records wrapped by an open circular arrow, for a dataset moving through the DDI Lifecycle. It is drawn entirely in currentColor, so it takes the header's foreground in every palette, including high contrast, without a second asset. That only works because theme.icon.logo makes Material inline it; set as theme.logo it would load as an <img>, where currentColor is black. Do not add palette-specific fills to it.

favicon.svg is a separate file rather than the same one reused. A browser tab renders at 16–32px against the browser's chrome, not the site's, so there is no inherited colour to take: it carries its own ground and drops the lifecycle arc, which turns to mud at that size.

docs.title: Colours
docs.text:
There is one brand colour, blue: a deep blue for the header, the same family for links and buttons. Orange marks only the keyboard focus ring. Code blocks and inline code sit on a neutral grey with no border.

There are three palettes: light (default), dark (slate) and high-contrast. Blue with a sparingly used orange is a pairing that readers with any common colour-vision deficiency can tell apart, so there are no separate colour-vision palettes. Every palette entry in mkdocs.yml declares primary: custom and accent: custom; without them Material's default indigo rules override palette.css in dark mode.

docs.title: Stylesheets
docs.text:
File Purpose palette.css Colour tokens for the three palettes, headings, buttons, code and note/info boxes. accessibility.css Skip link, focus ring, screen-reader-only utility, reduced-motion overrides, the version banner, and the palette menu. landing.css Call-to-action buttons and the card grid, used only by index.*.md.

Light and dark are on the header toggle. High contrast is chosen from the palette menu beside it, which lists all three palettes: Material cycles its toggle through every palette that declares one, and in high contrast the toggle has nothing to show, so the menu is also the way back. See the comments in mkdocs.yml and docs/overrides/partials/palette.html.

docs.title: Answer keys
docs.text:
Every exercise solution and quiz answer in the curriculum, on one page, for instructors. Learners working through a module can open the answer under each exercise and question instead.

This page is built from the modules each time the site is generated, so it always matches them.

docs.title: Module 1: What is metadata and why does it matter?
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Any three of these, or similar:

  1. What does each column mean? (Is A an age? In years or months?)
  2. What unit is column C in? (Dollars? Euros? Per year or per month?)
  3. Who was surveyed? (Students? Adults? Everyone?)
  4. When was the data collected?

Exercise 2

  1. Metadata is information that describes data: what it means, where it came from, and how it was collected.
  2. Metadata: any two of the title "Campus Sleep Study 2025", the collection date (September 2025), the population (first-year students), the column name sleep_hrs, or its meaning (hours of sleep on a typical school night). Data: any of the values 7, 6, or 8.

Exercise 3

1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a.

  • Findable (c): the catalog can only find what is described in structured fields.
  • Accessible (d): a standard, open format needs no special software.
  • Interoperable (b): a shared code list means the same code has the same meaning in both surveys, so the data can be combined.
  • Re-usable (a): a new user knows exactly what the data contains.

Exercise 4

For example: "DDI, the Data Documentation Initiative, is an international standard for describing surveys, censuses, and datasets in XML. National statistics offices, data archives, universities, and research teams use it so that others can find, understand, and reuse their data."

Any two of these kinds of organizations are correct: national statistics offices, data archives or national libraries, universities and their research repositories, research teams.

Exercise 5

Does: 1, 3, and 5. Does not: 2 and 4.

For example: "ddi-l creates, reads, updates, and validates DDI metadata from Python, but it does not collect survey answers."

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): A spreadsheet has a column headed Age (years) with the values 34, 28, and 45. Which of these is metadata?

B. Metadata is information about data. The header tells you what the numbers mean and how they are measured. The values themselves, and anything computed from them, are data.

Question 2 (O2): A colleague sends a table with columns A, B, and C and no notes. Column C holds values like 52000. You want to report the average income. Which question must you answer first?

D. Without knowing that C is income, and whether it is in dollars or euros, per year or per month, any average you report could be wrong. The other questions do not change what the numbers mean.

Question 3 (O3): Which sentence best describes DDI?

A. DDI is a standard: a set of agreed rules for documentation. Option C confuses DDI with tools; ddi-l is a Python package that works with DDI, and it does not compute statistics.

Question 4 (O4): Your survey and a survey in France use the same DDI code list for gender, so the two datasets can be merged. Which FAIR principle does this support most directly?

C. Interoperable means data works with other data. A shared code list gives each code the same meaning in both datasets, so they can be combined and compared.

Question 5 (O4): A data catalog reads the title, agency, and concepts in your DDI file, so a search for 'mental health survey' lists your dataset. Which FAIR principle does this support?

A. Findable means people can discover the data. Structured DDI fields give catalogs something reliable to index and search.

Question 6 (O5): Which of these tasks does ddi-l NOT do?

B. ddi-l works with metadata: it creates, reads, updates, and validates DDI documents. Collecting answers is the job of a survey tool.

docs.title: Module 2: Set up your Python environment
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

For example, Python 3.12.3: yes, because 3.12 is 3.11 or newer. If you see Python 3.10.12 or older, the answer is no: install a newer Python from https://www.python.org/downloads/ before you continue.

Exercise 2

The last line starts with Successfully installed and lists ddi-l-... among the packages (the version may vary). If the packages were already installed, pip says Requirement already satisfied instead. Both mean you are ready. A line starting with ERROR means the install failed.

Exercise 3

The installed version, such as 0.1.0 or later. If you see ModuleNotFoundError instead, ddi-l is not installed in this Python: go back to Exercise 2.

Exercise 4

  1. validate ("Validate an XML document against the DDI schema.")
  2. lint ("Lint a DDI document and report findings as JSON.")
  3. versions ("List supported DDI schema releases.")

Exercise 5

  1. Python REPL: it is the quickest way to run one line you do not need to keep.
  2. Script file: it saves your code, and python my_script.py runs it again from the top.
  3. Notebook: it shows notes, code, and output together, step by step.

Other choices are fine if your reason holds up; for example, a notebook also saves your code for task 2.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): python --version prints Python 3.10.12. What should you do before you install ddi-l?

B. ddi-l requires Python 3.11 or newer, and 3.10 is older. Install a newer Python, then install ddi-l with it.

Question 2 (O2): The last line of pip install ddi-l pandas openpyxl reads Requirement already satisfied. What does this mean?

D. Requirement already satisfied means the package is already there. A failed install ends with a line that starts with ERROR.

Question 3 (O3): You run import ddi_l as ddi and get ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddi_l'. What is the most likely cause?

A. Python cannot find the package, so it is not installed for this Python. Run pip install ddi-l again, or python3 -m pip install ddi-l if you start Python with python3. Option B is not valid Python: a hyphen cannot appear in an import name, which is why the module is called ddi_l.

Question 4 (O4): You want to check a file against the DDI schema from the terminal. Which command from the ddi --help list do you use?

C. Its description reads "Validate an XML document against the DDI schema." roundtrip re-writes a file, to-json converts it, and serve runs the HTTP API.

Question 5 (O5): You will build a study over several days and want to run the whole thing again from the top with one command after each change. Which workspace fits best?

B. A script file keeps your code, and one command runs all of it again. The REPL forgets what you typed when you close it.

docs.title: Module 3: Create your first DDI study
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Student Well-Being Survey", agency="university.edu")

q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your health?")
q3 = doc.add_question(text="How many hours do you sleep per night?")

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 3
for q in doc.questions:
    print(q.identifier)

doc.save("well-being.xml")

Exercise 2

The question text sits in a <d:Text> element, inside <d:LiteralText> inside <d:QuestionText>:

<d:Text xml:lang="en" isPlainText="true">What is your age?</d:Text>

Exercise 3

from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

print(f"Schema problems: {len(doc.validate())}")  # -> Schema problems: 0
print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")  # -> Lint findings: 3

q1.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Age", lang="en"))
q2.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Self-rated health", lang="en"))
q3.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Hours of sleep", lang="en"))

print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")  # -> Lint findings: 0
doc.save("well-being.xml")

The three warnings were "Maintainable element is missing a label.", one per question. A label fixes each one.

Exercise 4

q1.question_texts.append(InternationalString(text="Quel est votre âge ?", lang="fr"))
q1.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Âge", lang="fr"))

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 3
print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")  # -> Lint findings: 0
doc.save("well-being.xml")

The count stays at 3 because both translations belong to q1. In the XML, the first question now reads:

<r:Label>
  <r:Content xml:lang="en">Age</r:Content>
  <r:Content xml:lang="fr">Âge</r:Content>
</r:Label>
<d:QuestionText>
  <d:LiteralText>
    <d:Text xml:lang="en" isPlainText="true">What is your age?</d:Text>
  </d:LiteralText>
  <d:LiteralText>
    <d:Text xml:lang="fr">Quel est votre âge ?</d:Text>
  </d:LiteralText>
</d:QuestionText>

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): You run doc = ddi.new_study(title='Sleep Survey') and get a TypeError. Why?

B. ddi.new_study() requires both title= and agency=. The error message says so: "missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'agency'".

Question 2 (O1): After q1 = doc.add_question(text='What is your age?'), what is q1?

C. doc.add_question() adds a question item to the study and returns that question object. Keeping it in a variable lets you work with it later.

Question 3 (O2): A study has three questions. You add a fourth with doc.add_question(), then run print(len(doc.questions)). What is printed?

A. doc.questions is the list of every question in the study, and len() counts them: three plus the new one.

Question 4 (O3): You open the file written by doc.save('well-being.xml'). Where do you find the text of your first question?

A. doc.save() writes the whole study, and each question's text sits in <d:Text>, inside <d:LiteralText>, inside <d:QuestionText>.

Question 5 (O4): You want the first question, q1, in both English and French. Which line does it?

C. Appending an InternationalString with the new language stores both versions in the same question item. Option A creates a brand-new, separate question, not a translation of q1.

Question 6 (O5): doc.validate() returns an empty list, but doc.lint() reports warnings. Is the document valid DDI?

D. An empty list from doc.validate() means the document follows the DDI schema. Lint warnings are worth fixing, but they do not make the document invalid.

Question 7 (O5): doc.lint() reports 'Maintainable element is missing a label.' once for each of your three questions. Which change clears the warnings?

B. The warning names the problem: the questions have no label. Saving or validating does not change the document, and adding the questions again with the same code brings the same warnings back.

docs.title: Module 4: Add variables and link them to questions
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

For example: "A variable is one column of a data file, such as SleepHours, which holds every student's answer to the same question: how many hours they sleep per night."

Exercise 2

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Student Well-Being Survey", agency="university.edu")

q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?", label="Age")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your health?", label="Self-rated health")
q3 = doc.add_question(
    text="How many hours do you sleep per night?", label="Hours of sleep"
)

v1 = doc.add_variable(name="Age", label="Age in years", question=q1)
v2 = doc.add_variable(
    name="HealthRating", label="Self-rated health, 1 to 5", question=q2
)
v3 = doc.add_variable(name="SleepHours", label="Hours of sleep per night", question=q3)

print(f"Schema problems: {len(doc.validate())}")  # -> Schema problems: 0
print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")  # -> Lint findings: 0

If doc.lint() reports "Maintainable element is missing a label.", one of your questions or variables has no label=.

Exercise 3

print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 3
for v in doc.variables:
    print(v.identifier)

Each identifier is a UUID, such as a1b2c3d4-....

Exercise 4

For example: "The link leads to the question 'How would you rate your health?', so my colleague knows the values are each student's own rating of their health. Without it, they might guess wrongly, for example that the values were measured by a doctor, or that 1 means the best health."

Exercise 5

doc.save("well-being.xml")
print(q1.identifier)

The variable's name is in <l:VariableName>:

<l:VariableName>
  <r:String xml:lang="en">Age</r:String>
</l:VariableName>

The <r:ID> inside the <r:QuestionReference> a few lines below is the same identifier that print(q1.identifier) shows. That shared identifier is the link from the variable to the question.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): In a table with the columns Age, HealthRating, and SleepHours, which of these is a variable?

C. A variable is like a column. Each column holds one type of information, such as a health rating, for every person in the dataset. A row is one person; a value is one answer.

Question 2 (O2): What happens when you run doc.add_variable(name='Age', question='What is your age?')?

B. question= needs the object that doc.add_question() returned. A plain string is not a question, so the call fails with an AttributeError. Pass q1 instead.

Question 3 (O2): What does question=q2 do in doc.add_variable(name='HealthRating', question=q2)?

A. The question= argument stores a link between the variable and the question that collected the data. You can see it in the XML as <r:QuestionReference>.

Question 4 (O3): Which code prints the identifier of every variable in the study?

D. doc.variables is a list, so you loop through it and print each variable's identifier. Option A fails because a list has no identifier, and option C loops through the questions, not the variables.

Question 5 (O4): A data user sees the column SleepHours and wants to know exactly what was asked. How does the link from the variable to its question help?

B. This is traceability: the link takes the user from the data column back to the exact question that collected the data.

Question 6 (O5): In the saved XML, which element links a variable to the question that collected it?

C. <r:QuestionReference> sits inside the <l:Variable> element and holds the question's identifier. <l:VariableName> holds the variable's name, and <d:QuestionText> belongs to the question itself.

docs.title: Module 5: Organize with concepts and universes
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

  • Nutrition: concept.
  • Adults aged 18+ in Canada: universe.
  • Sleep quality: concept.
  • Public schools in Ontario: universe.
  • Employment: concept.
  • Children aged 6 to 11 living in private households: universe.

A concept is the idea that a variable measures, such as "Nutrition". A universe is the group of people or things a study covers, such as "Adults aged 18+ in Canada".

Exercise 2

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Health Survey", agency="health.gc.ca")

demo = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
activity = doc.add_concept(name="Physical Activity")
nutrition = doc.add_concept(name="Nutrition")

doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18+ in Canada")

print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")  # -> Concepts: 3
print(f"Universes: {len(doc.universes)}")  # -> Universes: 1

Exercise 3

q1 = doc.add_question(text="How old are you?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="What is your weight in kg?")
q3 = doc.add_question(text="How many days per week do you exercise?")
q4 = doc.add_question(text="How many servings of fruit do you eat per day?")

doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q1, concept=demo)
weight = doc.add_variable(name="Weight", question=q2, concept=demo)
doc.add_variable(name="ExerciseFrequency", question=q3, concept=activity)
doc.add_variable(name="FruitServings", question=q4, concept=nutrition)

linked = weight.concept_references[0].identifier == demo.identifier

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 4
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 4
print(f"Weight is linked to Demographics: {linked}")
print(f"Schema problems: {len(doc.validate())}")  # -> Schema problems: 0

Exercise 4

print("Concepts:")
for concept in doc.concepts:
    print(f"  {concept.names[0].text}")

print("Universes:")
for universe in doc.universes:
    print(f"  {universe.names[0].text}")

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): Which phrase is the universe of this study?

A. The universe says who is studied. "Sleep quality" and "Stress" say what is measured, so they are concepts. A question is neither.

Question 2 (O1): Which sentence correctly explains a concept?

C. A concept is an abstract idea that variables measure. Option A describes a universe, and option B describes a code list.

Question 3 (O2): What does this code print?

D. Two calls to doc.add_concept() add two concepts, and one call to doc.add_universe() adds one universe.

Question 4 (O3): The variable Age is not linked to its concept. Which call fixes it?

B. Pass the concept with concept= when you call doc.add_variable(). The other calls do not exist.

Question 5 (O4): Which loop prints the name of every universe?

C. Each universe keeps its name in names; names[0].text is the text. Option A prints the whole object, option B fails because a list has no names, and option D loops over the concepts.

docs.title: Module 6: Open, modify, and re-save existing DDI files
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

import ddi_l as ddi

# Create and save
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Census 2024", agency="stats.example.org")
q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
v1 = doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q1)
v2 = doc.add_variable(name="Gender", question=q2)
doc.save("census-2024.xml")
print("Saved.")

# Re-open and inspect
doc2 = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024.xml")
print(f"Questions: {len(doc2.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 2
print(f"Variables: {len(doc2.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 2

Exercise 2

try:
    ddi.open_ddi("census-2024-broken.xml", validate=True)
except ddi.DDIValidationError as error:
    print(f"Not valid: {error}")

unchecked = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024-broken.xml")
print(f"Opened without checking: {len(unchecked.questions)} questions")

The path after at points to the Version element directly under DDIInstance. Its value, one, does not match the pattern for versions: [0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)* means digits, optionally followed by more groups of a dot and digits, such as 1 or 1.0.0.

Without validate=True, the broken file opens with no complaint. Only validation tells you that the file breaks the DDI rules.

Exercise 3

q3 = doc2.add_question(text="What is your marital status?")
q4 = doc2.add_question(text="How many people live in your household?")
v3 = doc2.add_variable(name="MaritalStatus", question=q3)
v4 = doc2.add_variable(name="HouseholdSize", question=q4)

doc2.questions[0].question_texts[0].text = "What was your age at your last birthday?"

statuses = doc2.add_code_list(name="Marital Status Codes")
v3.set_coded(statuses)

errors = doc2.validate()
if errors:
    print("Validation errors:", errors)
else:
    print("Document is valid.")
    doc2.save("census-2024-updated.xml")
    print("Saved updated file.")

Exercise 4

doc3 = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024-updated.xml")
print(f"Questions: {len(doc3.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 4
print(f"Variables: {len(doc3.variables)}")
print(f"Code lists: {len(doc3.code_lists)}")
print(f"First question: {doc3.questions[0].question_texts[0].text}")

original = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024.xml")
print(f"Original questions: {len(original.questions)}")

The counts grew in the new file, and the original kept its two questions: saving under a new filename left it untouched.

Exercise 5

partner = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024-partner.xml", validate=True)
partner.add_variable(name="Region")
partner.save("census-2024-partner-updated.xml")

saved = Path("census-2024-partner-updated.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print("Persons living in private households" in saved)  # -> True

The element survives: ddi-l keeps XML it does not model exactly as it was, so opening and saving a file never deletes content you did not touch. This is the round-trip guarantee.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): What does this code print for a file with 3 questions and 5 variables?

D. ddi.open_ddi() reads the whole file. doc.questions and doc.variables list its questions and variables, in that order in the print() call.

Question 2 (O2): What is wrong with this file?

B. The path after at names the element: Version, under DDIInstance. The first part of the message says its value does not match the pattern for version numbers.

Question 3 (O3): Which line codes the variable v with the code list levels?

C. set_coded() is a method of the variable, and it takes the code list as its argument. doc.add_code_list() creates a new list; it does not code a variable.

Question 4 (O4): What does my-study.xml contain afterwards?

A. Changes live only in memory until you call doc.save(). The file on disk is unchanged.

Question 5 (O5): What happens to an element that ddi-l does not model?

D. This is the round-trip guarantee: content that ddi-l does not recognize passes through the read-and-write cycle untouched.

docs.title: Module 7: Validate from the command line
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

ddi validate census-2024.xml

The output says Document is valid., so the file follows all the DDI schema rules.

Exercise 2

cp census-2024.xml broken.xml
# edit line 5 of broken.xml, then:
ddi validate broken.xml
  • What: the value one does not match the pattern for versions. [0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)* means digits, optionally followed by more groups of a dot and digits, such as 1 or 1.0.0.
  • Where: the path after at ends with DDIInstance, then Version: the Version element directly under the root, which is the one on line 5. The context: line confirms the value found: one.

Exercise 3

ddi lint census-2024.xml --format table

One finding: severity warning, rule ddi.maintainable.labels, message "Maintainable element is missing a label." The file has four of them: its two questions and two variables have no label. To fix them, pass label= when you add each item, as in Section 9 of Module 3. The file is still valid: warnings point to quality, not to schema errors.

Exercise 4

ddi to-json census-2024.xml --indent 2 > census-2024.json
wc -l census-2024.json

The wc -l command counts the number of lines in a file (on Windows PowerShell, use (Get-Content census-2024.json).Count). A file with two questions and two variables gives about 200 lines; more content gives more lines.

Exercise 5

ddi roundtrip census-2024.xml --output census-2024-roundtrip.xml
ls -l census-2024.xml census-2024-roundtrip.xml

The ls -l command shows the file sizes (use dir on Windows). A file that ddi-l wrote itself comes back with exactly the same size. A file from another tool may differ a little, because of spacing; that is the normalization at work.

Exercise 6

ddi validate census-2024.xml
echo $?
ddi validate broken.xml
echo $?
# edit line 5 of broken.xml back to <r:Version>1</r:Version>, then:
ddi validate broken.xml
echo $?

A valid file gives exit code 0. A file with a schema error gives 1, and the fixed file gives 0 again, with Document is valid. above it. A script that runs ddi validate can use these codes to stop before it publishes a broken file.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): What does this output tell you?

A. ddi validate checks the schema only. Lint findings are a separate check (ddi lint), so option B does not follow.

Question 2 (O2): Where is the problem in this output?

C. The path after at ends with QuestionItem[1], the first question item, which holds the problem; the message names the unexpected element. A file that is not well-formed gives a mismatched tag error instead.

Question 3 (O3): What do these two results tell you about the file?

B. Validation checks the schema; lint checks quality rules beyond it. A warning alone does not fail ddi lint: it returns 0 unless you pass --fail-severity warning.

Question 4 (O4): Which command writes a JSON copy of my-study.xml to my-study.json?

D. ddi to-json converts DDI XML to JSON, and > saves the output in a file. ddi roundtrip writes XML, and the ddi validate command in option B saves the validation report, not the document.

Question 5 (O4): Why would you run ddi roundtrip on a file from another tool?

B. A round-trip reads the file and writes it back out in a normalized format. ddi-l keeps the elements it does not model, so nothing is deleted.

Question 6 (O5): What does this script print?

C. ddi validate returns 1 when the file has any schema error, however many there are. The exit code says "failed", not how many problems were found.

docs.title: Module 8: From a CSV or Excel table to DDI
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

import csv
import ddi_l as ddi

with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    columns = reader.fieldnames

# The question each column records, worded the way respondents saw it
QUESTIONS = {
    "age": "How old are you?",
    "gender": "What is your gender?",
    "income": "What was your total income last year, before taxes?",
    "education_level": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
}

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")
for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    # A column nobody was asked about, such as respondent_id, gets no question
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q)

doc.save("household-survey.xml")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 5

Exercise 2

Only the lines that read the column names change. QUESTIONS is the lookup table from Exercise 1.

import pandas as pd
import ddi_l as ddi

# Make a workbook from the sample CSV (once)
pd.read_csv("survey_sample.csv").to_excel("survey_sample.xlsx", index=False)

df = pd.read_excel("survey_sample.xlsx")
columns = list(df.columns)

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")
for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q)
doc.save("household-survey-excel.xml")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")

Exercise 3

Continuing from Exercise 1 (columns and QUESTIONS):

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")

demo = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
econ = doc.add_concept(name="Economics")
educ = doc.add_concept(name="Education")
doc.add_universe(name="Canadian households, 2024")

CONCEPTS = {
    "age": demo,
    "gender": demo,
    "income": econ,
    "education_level": educ,
}

for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q, concept=CONCEPTS.get(col))

linked = [v for v in doc.variables if v.concept_references]
print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")  # -> Concepts: 3
print(f"Universes: {len(doc.universes)}")  # -> Universes: 1
print(f"Linked variables: {len(linked)}")  # -> Linked variables: 4

Exercise 4

from pathlib import Path

from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

# The first question asks for the respondent's age, the second for their gender
doc.questions[0].question_texts.append(
    InternationalString(text="Quel âge avez-vous ?", lang="fr")
)
doc.questions[1].question_texts.append(
    InternationalString(text="Quel est votre genre ?", lang="fr")
)
doc.concepts[0].names.append(
    InternationalString(text="Démographie", lang="fr", child_tag="String")
)
doc.save("household-survey-bilingual.xml")

saved = Path("household-survey-bilingual.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print("How old are you?" in saved, "Quel âge avez-vous ?" in saved)  # -> True True

You can also open the XML in a text editor and look for xml:lang="fr" next to the English text.

Exercise 5

The message names the lang attribute and its value, fr_CA. The pattern [a-zA-Z]{1,8}(-[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,8})* means letters, optionally followed by groups of a hyphen and letters or digits. An underscore is not allowed, so write fr-CA (or just fr):

doc.questions[2].question_texts[-1].lang = "fr-CA"

issues = doc.validate()
if issues:
    for issue in issues:
        print(issue.message)
else:
    print("Document is valid.")  # -> Document is valid.
    doc.save("household-survey-bilingual.xml")

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): How many variables does the document hold?

D. The loop adds one variable per column, and there are three columns. A column with no question, such as id, still gets a variable.

Question 2 (O1): Why does the script take question text from the QUESTIONS lookup table?

B. A column name such as education_level is shorthand. The question text in DDI should be the wording from the questionnaire.

Question 3 (O2): How do you get column names from a pandas DataFrame?

C. Use df.columns to get the column names from a pandas DataFrame. Wrap it in list() to get a plain list. fieldnames belongs to csv.DictReader, not to pandas.

Question 4 (O3): Which call adds the income variable and links it to the Economics concept econ?

A. Pass the concept with concept= when you add the variable. In a loop, concept=CONCEPTS.get(col) does the same for every column.

Question 5 (O4): How can you confirm that French wording was saved?

D. The saved XML is what other people receive, so check it: open it in a text editor, or read it with Path(...).read_text() and test "Quel âge avez-vous ?" in saved. The CSV holds data, not metadata.

Question 6 (O5): doc.validate() reports this issue. What is the fix?

A. The pattern allows letters joined by hyphens, not underscores. A schema issue makes the document invalid, so fix it before you save.

docs.title: Module 9: Build code lists and controlled vocabularies
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A sample answer: "A code list is the fixed set of allowed answers to a question, and each allowed answer (such as Employed or Retired) is a category. If the census uses the same code list as the labour survey, every answer falls into the same categories in both, so we can count and compare them directly instead of cleaning free text such as 'M', 'emp.' or 'working'."

Exercise 2

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Census", agency="census.gc.ca")

doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Male")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Female")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Other")

doc.add_code_list(name="Employment Status Codes")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Employed")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Unemployed")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Retired")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Student")

doc.add_code_list(name="Housing Type Codes")
doc.add_item(Category, name="House")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Apartment")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Other Housing")

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")
print(f"Categories: {len(doc.items(Category))}")

Exercise 3

for cat in doc.items(Category):
    print(cat.names[0].text)

The categories come back in the order you added them.

Exercise 4

doc.add_code_list(name="Marital Status Codes")
for status in ("Single", "Married", "Separated", "Widowed"):
    doc.add_item(Category, name=status)

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")
print(f"Categories: {len(doc.items(Category))}")

One new code list makes 3 + 1 = 4. Four new categories make 10 + 4 = 14. The counts cover the whole document, not just the list you added last.

Exercise 5

Python's built-in csv module is enough; a set keeps one copy of each value:

import csv

with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    levels = sorted({row["education_level"] for row in csv.DictReader(f)})

doc.add_code_list(name="Education Level Codes")
for level in levels:
    doc.add_item(Category, name=level)

print(f"Education levels: {len(levels)}")

The file has five rows but only four distinct levels, because "Bachelor" appears twice. With pandas, df["education_level"].dropna().unique() gives the same values, as in Section 7.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): Why is Survey 2 easier to compare?

D. A code list fixes the allowed answers. Two surveys that share it put every answer into the same categories, so their counts line up. Free text such as "M", "emp." or "working" has to be cleaned first.

Question 2 (O2): Which fix makes this script run?

A. Category is a class that you import before you use it. doc.add_category() does not exist, add_code_list() would create a code list called "Male", and add_item() needs the class itself, not its name as a string.

Question 3 (O3): What does this script print?

C. The script creates two code lists and five categories. items(Category) counts every category in the document, whichever list you meant it for.

Question 4 (O3): Which loop prints the name of every category in doc?

B. doc.items(Category) returns every category, and names[0].text is the first name of each one. Option A prints the code list names, doc.categories does not exist, and items() takes the class, not a string.

Question 5 (O4): How many categories does a CSV column give?

A. The distinct non-blank values are Female, Male and Other. With pandas, df["gender"].dropna().unique() returns exactly those three.

docs.title: Module 10: Map a questionnaire to DDI flow logic
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

  • Intro → a StatementItem.
  • T1, T2 and T3 → one question each, wrapped in a QuestionConstruct.
  • "ask only if T1 = Yes" → an IfThenElse whose condition tests T1 and whose "then" branch runs T2's QuestionConstruct.
  • "repeat for each trip" → a Loop that points to T3's QuestionConstruct (or to a Sequence that holds it).
  • The order of the steps → the main Sequence.
  • The whole questionnaire → an Instrument that points to the main Sequence.

Exercise 2

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.datacollection import QuestionConstruct, Sequence

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Health Survey", agency="health.gc.ca")
q_age = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q_gender = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
q_employed = doc.add_question(text="Are you currently employed?")
q_occupation = doc.add_question(text="What is your occupation?")
q_health = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your general health?")
q_smoke = doc.add_question(text="Do you smoke?")

qc_age = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Age", question_reference=q_age.to_reference()
)
qc_gender = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Gender", question_reference=q_gender.to_reference()
)
qc_employed = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct,
    name="Ask Employed",
    question_reference=q_employed.to_reference(),
)
qc_occupation = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct,
    name="Ask Occupation",
    question_reference=q_occupation.to_reference(),
)
qc_health = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Health", question_reference=q_health.to_reference()
)
qc_smoke = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Smoke", question_reference=q_smoke.to_reference()
)

seq_demographics = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section A - Demographics",
    control_construct_references=[qc_age.to_reference(), qc_gender.to_reference()],
)
seq_employment = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section B - Employment",
    control_construct_references=[qc_employed.to_reference()],
)
seq_health = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section C - Health",
    control_construct_references=[qc_health.to_reference(), qc_smoke.to_reference()],
)

print(f"QuestionConstructs: {len(doc.items(QuestionConstruct))}")
print(f"Sequences: {len(doc.items(Sequence))}")
print(f"Steps in Section A: {len(seq_demographics.control_construct_references)}")

Exercise 3

from ddi_l.models.datacollection import IfThenElse

skip_employment = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Age gate for employment")
skip_employment.set_condition("age >= 16", description="Working age")
skip_employment.then_construct_reference = seq_employment.to_reference()

ask_occupation = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Occupation routing")
ask_occupation.set_condition("employed == 1", description="Employed")
ask_occupation.then_construct_reference = qc_occupation.to_reference()
seq_employment.control_construct_references.append(ask_occupation.to_reference())

print(f"IfThenElse: {len(doc.items(IfThenElse))}")
print(f"Steps in Section B: {len(seq_employment.control_construct_references)}")

Exercise 4

from ddi_l.models.datacollection import Loop

roster_loop = doc.add_item(Loop, name="Household roster loop")
roster_loop.control_construct_reference = seq_demographics.to_reference()

print(f"Loops: {len(doc.items(Loop))}")
repeats_a = (
    roster_loop.control_construct_reference.identifier == seq_demographics.identifier
)
print(f"Repeats Section A: {repeats_a}")

Exercise 5

from ddi_l.models.datacollection import Instrument, StatementItem

intro_a = doc.add_item(StatementItem, name="Welcome to the National Health Survey")
main_seq = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Main Survey Flow",
    control_construct_references=[
        intro_a.to_reference(),
        seq_demographics.to_reference(),
        skip_employment.to_reference(),
        seq_health.to_reference(),
        roster_loop.to_reference(),
    ],
)
instrument = doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Health Survey Instrument")
instrument.control_construct_reference = main_seq.to_reference()

print(f"Steps in main flow: {len(main_seq.control_construct_references)}")
print(f"Instruments: {len(doc.items(Instrument))}")
print(f"Validation errors: {len(doc.validate())}")

Exercise 6

Answers vary. Check that every QuestionConstruct references a question, that each Sequence lists its steps in the order respondents see them, and that the Instrument points to the top-level Sequence. Run doc.validate() before you save: it should return [].

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): Which constructs does this spec line need?

A. "Ask only if" is a condition, so it is an IfThenElse. Its "then" branch runs the QuestionConstruct that asks B2.

Question 2 (O2): What is wrong with this Sequence?

C. A Sequence orders control constructs. The question holds the content; the QuestionConstruct is the instruction "ask it now", and that is what a Sequence lists.

Question 3 (O3): A 12-year-old reaches this gate. What happens next?

D. The condition age >= 16 is false, and the gate has no "else" branch, so nothing runs inside it. The main Sequence then moves on to its next step, Section C.

Question 4 (O4): Which line makes the roster repeat Section A?

B. A Loop points to the one construct it repeats through control_construct_reference. Option A would put the loop inside Section A, which is the wrong way round.

Question 5 (O5): What if the Instrument is not linked to the flow?

C. The schema does not require the link, so the file is valid. But only control_construct_reference connects the questionnaire's entry point to the flow. Always set it, then validate.

docs.title: Module 11: Document data files and variable lineage
Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A sample answer: "The collection file holds the raw answers exactly as respondents gave them, such as age and health_rating. The production file keeps those cleaned variables and adds derived ones computed from them, such as age_group and health_score. The master file keeps only the derived variables that are ready for release, and it is the file the public receives."

Exercise 2

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Health Survey", agency="health.gc.ca")

q_age = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q_gender = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
q_employed = doc.add_question(text="Are you currently employed?")
q_occupation = doc.add_question(text="What is your occupation?")
q_health = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your general health?")
q_smoke = doc.add_question(text="Do you smoke?")

v_age = doc.add_variable(name="age", question=q_age)
v_gender = doc.add_variable(name="gender", question=q_gender)
v_employed = doc.add_variable(name="employed", question=q_employed)
v_occupation = doc.add_variable(name="occupation", question=q_occupation)
v_health = doc.add_variable(name="health_rating", question=q_health)
v_smoke = doc.add_variable(name="smoker", question=q_smoke)

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")
print(f"age question references: {len(v_age.question_references)}")

Exercise 3

v_age.set_numeric("Integer", low=0, high=120)

cl_gender = doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
for name in ("Male", "Female", "Other"):
    doc.add_item(Category, name=name)
v_gender.set_coded(cl_gender)

v_occupation.set_text()

rep = v_age.variable_representation
print(f"age: {rep.numeric_representation.numeric_type_code}")
rep = v_gender.variable_representation
print(f"gender is coded: {rep.code_representation is not None}")
rep = v_occupation.variable_representation
print(f"occupation is text: {rep.text_representation is not None}")

gender gets a code list because its answers come from a fixed set. occupation is text because any job title is possible.

Exercise 4

cl_age_group = doc.add_code_list(name="Age Group Codes")
for group in ("0-15", "16-24", "25-44", "45-64", "65+"):
    doc.add_item(Category, name=group)
