docs.title: Instructor guide
docs.text: This guide helps facilitators deliver the ddi-l training curriculum in classrooms, workshops, or online sessions. It also works for self-paced learners who want facilitation context.

docs.title: Classroom vs. self-paced
docs.text:
The curriculum works in both modes:

  • Classroom: An instructor demonstrates each concept live, then learners complete the exercises. Use the timing and facilitation tips below.
  • Self-paced: Learners read each module, follow the code examples, and check their work against the answer keys.

docs.title: Suggested schedules
docs.text:
The workshop rows add up the instructor-led times the modules give, and the self-paced row their self-paced times, without breaks or setup. The course overview gives both totals for each format.

Format Modules Time Covers Half-day workshop 1-5 3 h 20 min What metadata is, setup, a first study, variables, concepts and universes Full-day workshop 1-9 6 h 30 min All of Tier 1 (including opening files and validation), CSV to DDI and code lists Three-day intensive 1-17 16 h, about 5 h 20 min a day Full curriculum with capstone Self-paced One module per session 12 h 20 min to 12 h 50 min 17 sessions of 20 to 90 min, about 3 to 4 weeks

docs.title: Using the learning objectives
docs.text:
Every module opens with numbered learning objectives (O1, O2, ...), tags each exercise and quiz question with the objectives it practises, and ends with a Check yourself list, one line per objective. Use them to run each session:

  • Open with the objectives. Read the module's objectives aloud, or show the box, at the start of the session. Learners then know what they will be able to do by the end, and you know what to check.
  • Pick exercises by tag. Short on time? Choose one exercise per objective rather than the first few in the list. If a learner struggles with one objective, give them another exercise with the same tag.
  • Close with Check yourself as an exit ticket. In the last five minutes, learners tick the lines they can do. A line many learners leave unticked tells you what to revisit at the start of the next session. In Module 17, the rubric and the presentation do the same job.

docs.title: Environment setup checklist
docs.text:
Before the session, make sure every learner has:

  • Python 3.11 or newer installed
  • ddi-l installed (pip install ddi-l)
  • pandas and openpyxl installed (pip install pandas openpyxl)
  • A text editor or IDE (VS Code, PyCharm, or even Notepad)
  • The sample CSV file, survey_sample.csv (capstone tracks also use thesis-data.csv, health-survey.csv and census-data.csv)
  • A terminal or command prompt

Have a fallback plan: a cloud notebook (Google Colab, JupyterHub) or a pre-built container with everything installed.

docs.title: Module 1: What is metadata?
docs.text:
• Start with the "messy table" exercise before defining metadata. Let learners discover the problem.
  • For NSO audiences, use the census example. For students, use the thesis example.
  • FAIR principles: Walk through the Dr. Chen example in section 4. Ask learners which FAIR letter is hardest to achieve without a standard like DDI. Most will say Interoperable or Findable; use this to motivate the rest of the curriculum.
  • Time: 45 min including discussion.

docs.title: Module 2: Set up your environment
docs.text:
• Budget 30 min: environment issues are the #1 classroom time sink.
  • Walk around and help with PATH issues, wrong Python versions, and virtual environments.
  • If installs fail, switch to the fallback environment immediately.

docs.title: Module 3: Create your first study
docs.text:
• This is the "aha" moment. Type the code live and show the XML output.
  • Common mistake: forgetting quotes around strings.
  • Section 9 introduces doc.validate() and doc.lint(). Ask learners to run both at the end of every later module, before they save.
  • Time: 45 min with live demo.

docs.title: Module 4: Variables and questions
docs.text:
• Draw the mental model on a whiteboard: Question → Variable → Data column.
  • Common mistake: passing the question text string instead of the question object to question=.
  • Time: 40 min.

docs.title: Module 5: Concepts and universes
docs.text:
• Use a diagram: Universe = "who", Concept = "what", Variable = "how it is measured", Question = "how it is asked".
  • Time: 40 min.

docs.title: Module 6: Open and modify files
docs.text:
• This is the archivist workflow: receive → inspect → enrich → validate → save.
  • Time: 40 min.

docs.title: Module 7: Validate from the command line
docs.text:
• For NSO audiences, spend extra time on batch validation and exit codes.
  • Time: 40 min.

docs.title: Module 8: From CSV/Excel to DDI
docs.text:
• This is the most important module for researchers and NSO staff. Demonstrate the full workflow: open a CSV, run the script, show the DDI XML output.
  • Emphasize: the CSV is the data. The DDI XML is documentation about the data. They are two different files.
  • Skip the SQL section for non-technical audiences.
  • Time: 60 min with exercises.

docs.title: Module 9: Code lists
docs.text:
• Show a real-world code list (ISO country codes, employment classifications).
  • Common mistake: forgetting to import Category.
  • Time: 50 min.

docs.title: Module 10: Questionnaire flows
docs.text:
• Start with a paper spec on screen. Have learners circle questions, underline skip rules, and box repeat instructions before touching code.
  • Draw the flowchart on a whiteboard. Map each box to a DDI construct.
  • Key confusion: "Why both a Question and a QuestionConstruct?" Explain content vs. flow separation.
  • Time: 60 min.

docs.title: Module 11: Data lineage
docs.text:
• Use the "recipe" analogy: raw ingredients (collection), cooking (production), plated dish (master). Provenance is the recipe.
  • Draw the three-file pipeline. For each variable, ask learners to trace it back to the original question.
  • Clarify: question_references = "what was asked", source_variable_references = "what data was used to compute this".
  • The numeric-to-coded derivation (age → age_group) is the most relatable example for all audiences.
  • For NSO staff: this is audit trail documentation that regulators need.
  • Time: 75 min.

docs.title: Module 12: Data linkage
docs.text:
• Anchor with the burden argument: reuse the tax file instead of re-asking income. Linkage creates new information from existing data.
  • Draw two files sharing one column (anon_id): the linkage key.
  • Contrast deterministic (one reliable key) vs probabilistic (several noisy fields, weighted agreement, clerical review).
  • Stress that source_variable_references crossing study boundaries is the technical heart of linkage; the save-time warning is expected.
  • For NSO staff: connect to their own organization's linkage environment and approval rules (for example, linkages that are pre-approved and those that need a review).
  • Always end a linkage on de-identification and, often, synthetic data.
  • Time: 75 min.

docs.title: Module 13: Properties, find, and validate
docs.text:
• Demonstrate that custom properties survive XML round-trips.
  • Show passing a code list object as a property value (stores URN).
  • Common mistake: trying to find() by name instead of by identifier.
  • Time: 50 min.

docs.title: Module 14: Custom fields
docs.text:
• Open with the "side spreadsheet" problem: local metadata kept outside the file always drifts out of sync. Custom fields keep it in the DDI.
  • Make the openness point explicit: DDI provides a standardized extension point. Show the UserAttributePair XML so learners see it is still valid DDI.
  • Contrast with Module 13: that module taught the set_property mechanics; this one governs extensions: namespaces, catalogs, controlled values, audit.
  • Clarify UserID vs custom property: identify vs describe.
  • For NSO/archive staff: connect to real governance (retention schedules, security classifications, data stewards), and the Section 9 audit loop.
  • Caution: do not reinvent built-in DDI; custom fields are for genuine gaps.
  • Time: 55 min.

docs.title: Module 15: Update and version
docs.text:
• Key module for archivists and NSO staff managing long-running surveys.
  • Show the XML before and after versioning so learners see the version number and rationale in the file.
  • Time: 75 min.

docs.title: Module 16: Advanced questionnaire specification
docs.text:
• For spec writers and NSO staff who move from screen designs and workbooks to a spec that instruments are checked against.
  • Put the missing-answer table of section 2 on the board first, and let learners fill in the last row before you show it.
  • Stress that a gate kept in the tool's own code is a correct result, and that an undocumented format is never guessed: the operators to use are the ones the tool's documentation lists.
  • Time: 90 min.

docs.title: Module 17: Capstone projects
docs.text:
• Let learners choose their persona track. If in a mixed group, form teams by role.
  • Ask to see each learner's plan (objective O1) before they write code.
  • Budget 90 min including the 5-minute presentations at the end (O6). Tracks B and D record two techniques each and run longest.
  • Score with the self-assessment rubric in the module: 80 points for the skills every track shares, and 20 for the track's own techniques (flow, lineage, linkage, custom fields or specification).

docs.title: Common mistakes across all modules
docs.text: Mistake Module Fix Forgetting quotes around strings 3 Show the error message and explain Passing text instead of object to question= 4 Show the difference between "age" and q1 Forgetting to import Category/Instrument 9, 10 Show the import line explicitly Confusing Question with QuestionConstruct 10 Question = content, QuestionConstruct = flow step Confusing question_references with source_variable_references 11 question_ref = what was asked, source_var_ref = what data was used Using find() with a name instead of identifier 13 Print item.identifier first Writing not x > 30 where x <= 30 was meant 16 Fill in the missing-answer table: they differ when x has no answer Not validating before saving 3 onwards Make validation a habit: always validate before save

docs.title: Adapting for each audience

docs.title: Module 1: What is metadata and why does it matter?
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Define metadata in one sentence and point to two pieces of metadata that describe a given table.
  • O2. List three questions a reader must answer before using an undocumented table.
  • O3. Describe what DDI is in two sentences and name two kinds of organizations that use it.
  • O4. Match each FAIR principle to one way DDI metadata supports it.
  • O5. State what ddi-l does and one thing it does not do.

Prerequisites: None.

Time: 30 min self-paced / 45 min instructor-led.

New in this module: no functions or commands yet. This module sets out the ideas the rest of the course builds on.

docs.title: 1. What is metadata?
docs.text:
Metadata is information about your data. Think of a library card catalog. The catalog does not contain the full text of every book. Instead, it tells you the title, author, subject, and where to find each book. Metadata does the same thing for data files. It tells you what the data is about without showing you all the data.

Here are a few examples of metadata:

  • The title of a survey.
  • The date the data was collected.
  • The meaning of each column in a table.

Without metadata, a data file is just rows and columns of numbers. No one knows what those numbers mean.

docs.title: 2. Real-world example: a household survey table
docs.text:
Look at the table below. It comes from a household survey.

Column A Column B Column C 34 Female 52 000 28 Male 41 000 45 Female 67 000 22 Male 29 000 51 Other 73 000

Without documentation you might ask:

  • What do the numbers in Column A mean? Ages? ID numbers?
  • Is Column C in dollars, euros, or another currency?
  • Who was surveyed? Adults only? Everyone?
  • When was the survey done?

With documentation we add metadata:

Age Gender Annual Income (CAD) 34 Female 52 000 28 Male 41 000 45 Female 67 000 22 Male 29 000 51 Other 73 000
  • Study title: Canadian Household Income Survey 2024
  • Population: Canadian adults aged 18 and older.
  • Collection period: January-March 2024.

Now the data makes sense. Metadata is the difference between confusion and clarity.

docs.title: 3. What is DDI?
docs.text:
DDI stands for Data Documentation Initiative. It is an international standard (a set of agreed-upon rules) for describing surveys, censuses, and datasets. Governments, universities, and research organizations around the world use DDI to document their data so that others can find it, understand it, and reuse it.

Key facts about DDI:

  • It is maintained by the DDI Alliance.
  • It uses XML (a structured text format) to store the documentation.
  • It covers the full life of a dataset, from planning and collection to archiving and sharing.

docs.title: 4. How DDI makes data FAIR
docs.text:
FAIR is a set of four principles that help people share and reuse data. The letters stand for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Re-usable. Good data should follow all four. DDI-Lifecycle helps you meet each one.

Principle What it means How DDI helps Findable People can search for and discover the data. DDI gives every item a unique identifier and stores structured fields like title, agency, and concepts. Data catalogs can index these fields so users find your dataset in a search. Accessible People can get the data and its documentation. DDI files are standard XML. Any tool that reads XML can open them. No special software is required. Interoperable Data works with other data and tools. DDI uses shared code lists and controlled vocabularies. When two surveys use the same code list for gender or employment status, their data can be combined and compared. Re-usable People understand the data well enough to use it correctly. DDI records who collected the data, when, how, and what each variable means. A researcher in another country can read the DDI file and know exactly what the data contains.

docs.title: Example: FAIR in action
docs.text:
Imagine Dr. Chen publishes a health survey to an open data repository. Without DDI metadata, a visitor sees a file called health-2024.csv and has no idea what is inside.

With DDI metadata:

  • Findable: The repository indexes the DDI title, concepts ("Physical Health", "Mental Health"), and agency ("health-research.example.org"). A student searching for "mental health survey data" finds it.
  • Accessible: The DDI XML file is published next to the CSV. Anyone can download both files with no login or special tool.
  • Interoperable: The DDI file uses a standard code list for gender (Male / Female / Other). Another team in France uses the same code list, so both datasets can be merged for cross-country analysis.
  • Re-usable: The DDI file says the data was collected from adults aged 18+ in 2024, that "bmi" is body mass index in kg/m², and that income is in Canadian dollars. A new researcher can use the data correctly without asking the original team.

Without DDI, the data sits in a file that nobody finds, nobody understands, and nobody reuses. With DDI, the data becomes a shared resource.

docs.title: 5. What is ddi-l?
docs.text:
ddi-l is a Python package (a tool you install and use in the Python programming language) that lets you create, read, update, and validate DDI documents. You do not need to know XML to use it. You write a few lines of Python, and ddi-l handles the XML for you.

What ddi-l can do:

  • Create a new DDI study with questions and variables.
  • Read an existing DDI file and inspect its contents.
  • Update a DDI document by adding or removing items.
  • Validate a document to make sure it follows the DDI rules.

What ddi-l does not do:

  • It does not collect answers. You still run your survey with your own survey tool; ddi-l describes the survey and its data.
  • It does not analyze your data. It does not compute averages or tables from the values in your data file. It records what those values mean.

docs.title: 6. The big picture
docs.text:
Here is the typical workflow when you use ddi-l:

flowchart LR
    A["Your data\n(CSV / Excel)"] --> B["Your script\n(Python + ddi-l)"]
    B --> C["DDI XML file"]
    C --> D["Validation"]
    D --> E["Archive / Publish"]
  1. You start with a data file (for example, a CSV or Excel spreadsheet).
  2. You write a short Python script that uses ddi-l to describe the data.
  3. ddi-l creates a DDI XML file.
  4. You validate the file to make sure everything is correct.
  5. You archive or publish the file so others can find and understand your data.

docs.title: 7. Who uses DDI? Four stories
docs.text:
Maya, university student. Maya just finished her thesis on student stress. She needs to deposit her survey data in the university's research repository. DDI metadata helps future students find and understand her dataset.

Dr. Chen, researcher. Dr. Chen runs a multi-country health study. He publishes data to an open repository. DDI makes his datasets discoverable and comparable across countries.

Fatima, archivist. Fatima manages a data collection at a national library. She uses DDI to catalog thousands of datasets so researchers can search and browse the collection.

Jean-Pierre, National Statistics Office (NSO) staff. Jean-Pierre works at a government statistics office. His team documents every census and survey with DDI so the public can access reliable, well-documented data.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Scenario

You receive a data file with no documentation. The file has five rows and the columns are labeled A, B, and C. The values look like numbers and short words.

Exercise 1 (O2). Look at the table below.

A B C 34 Female 52000 28 Male 41000 45 Female 67000 22 Male 29000 51 Other 73000

Write down 3 questions a new person would need answered before they could use this data. For example: What does column A measure?

Expected output: a list of three questions.

Answer

Any three of these, or similar:

  1. What does each column mean? (Is A an age? In years or months?)
  2. What unit is column C in? (Dollars? Euros? Per year or per month?)
  3. Who was surveyed? (Students? Adults? Everyone?)
  4. When was the data collected?

Exercise 2 (O1). The same researcher now sends a documented version of another file:

Campus Sleep Study 2025. Collected in September 2025 from first-year students. sleep_hrs is the hours of sleep on a typical school night.

sleep_hrs 7 6 8
  1. Write a one-sentence definition of metadata.
  2. Name two pieces of metadata in this file, and one piece of data.

Expected output: one sentence, then three short items.

Answer
  1. Metadata is information that describes data: what it means, where it came from, and how it was collected.
  2. Metadata: any two of the title "Campus Sleep Study 2025", the collection date (September 2025), the population (first-year students), the column name sleep_hrs, or its meaning (hours of sleep on a typical school night). Data: any of the values 7, 6, or 8.

Exercise 3 (O4). Match each FAIR principle (1 to 4) with the DDI feature (a to d) that supports it.

FAIR principle DDI feature 1. Findable a. The DDI file records who was surveyed, when, and what each variable means. 2. Accessible b. Two surveys use the same DDI code list for employment status. 3. Interoperable c. A data catalog indexes the title, agency, and concepts stored in the DDI file. 4. Re-usable d. The DDI file is plain XML, published next to the data, that any XML tool can open.

Expected output: four pairs, such as 1-?.

Answer

1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a.

  • Findable (c): the catalog can only find what is described in structured fields.
  • Accessible (d): a standard, open format needs no special software.
  • Interoperable (b): a shared code list means the same code has the same meaning in both surveys, so the data can be combined.
  • Re-usable (a): a new user knows exactly what the data contains.

Exercise 4 (O3). A new colleague asks you: "What is DDI?" Write a two-sentence answer. Name two kinds of organizations that use it.

Expected output: two sentences.

Answer

For example: "DDI, the Data Documentation Initiative, is an international standard for describing surveys, censuses, and datasets in XML. National statistics offices, data archives, universities, and research teams use it so that others can find, understand, and reuse their data."

Any two of these kinds of organizations are correct: national statistics offices, data archives or national libraries, universities and their research repositories, research teams.

Exercise 5 (O5). For each task below, write does if ddi-l does it, or does not if it does not.

  1. Write a DDI XML file from a short Python script.
  2. Send a questionnaire to respondents and collect their answers.
  3. Check a DDI document against the DDI rules.
  4. Calculate the average income from the values in a CSV file.
  5. Open an existing DDI file and list its questions.

Then write one sentence that says what ddi-l does and one thing it does not do.

Expected output: five answers, then one sentence.

Answer

Does: 1, 3, and 5. Does not: 2 and 4.

For example: "ddi-l creates, reads, updates, and validates DDI metadata from Python, but it does not collect survey answers."

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): A spreadsheet has a column headed Age (years) with the values 34, 28, and 45. Which of these is metadata?

A. The value 34.

B. The header Age (years), which says what the values mean and their unit.

C. The sum of the three values.

D. The second row.

Answer

B. Metadata is information about data. The header tells you what the numbers mean and how they are measured. The values themselves, and anything computed from them, are data.

Question 2 (O2): A colleague sends a table with columns A, B, and C and no notes. Column C holds values like 52000. You want to report the average income. Which question must you answer first?

A. Which font was used to type the table?

B. How many rows does the file have?

C. What is the name of the file?

D. What does column C measure, and in which currency and period?

Answer

D. Without knowing that C is income, and whether it is in dollars or euros, per year or per month, any average you report could be wrong. The other questions do not change what the numbers mean.

Question 3 (O3): Which sentence best describes DDI?

A. An international standard for describing surveys, censuses, and datasets, used by national statistics offices, data archives, and universities.

B. A survey tool that sends questionnaires to respondents.

C. A Python package that computes statistics from data files.

D. A database that stores survey answers.

Answer

A. DDI is a standard: a set of agreed rules for documentation. Option C confuses DDI with tools; ddi-l is a Python package that works with DDI, and it does not compute statistics.

Question 4 (O4): Your survey and a survey in France use the same DDI code list for gender, so the two datasets can be merged. Which FAIR principle does this support most directly?

A. Findable

B. Accessible

C. Interoperable

D. Re-usable

Answer

C. Interoperable means data works with other data. A shared code list gives each code the same meaning in both datasets, so they can be combined and compared.

Question 5 (O4): A data catalog reads the title, agency, and concepts in your DDI file, so a search for 'mental health survey' lists your dataset. Which FAIR principle does this support?

A. Findable

B. Accessible

C. Interoperable

D. Re-usable

Answer

A. Findable means people can discover the data. Structured DDI fields give catalogs something reliable to index and search.

Question 6 (O5): Which of these tasks does ddi-l NOT do?

A. Create a DDI study from a Python script.

B. Collect answers from survey respondents.

C. Validate a DDI document against the DDI rules.

D. Open an existing DDI file and inspect its contents.

Answer

B. ddi-l works with metadata: it creates, reads, updates, and validates DDI documents. Collecting answers is the job of a survey tool.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can define metadata in one sentence and point to two pieces of metadata that describe a table. (O1)
  • I can list three questions a reader must answer before using an undocumented table. (O2)
  • I can describe DDI in two sentences and name two kinds of organizations that use it. (O3)
  • I can match each FAIR principle to one way DDI metadata supports it. (O4)
  • I can state what ddi-l does and one thing it does not do. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Opening activity: Start with the "messy table" exercise (Exercise 1). Give learners the unlabeled table and ask them to guess what the data means. This builds motivation for the rest of the module.
  • Audience adaptation: For the messy table, you can show a few rows of the course's sample datasets with the headers removed: census-data.csv for NSO audiences and thesis-data.csv for university students. Both come back in the Module 17 capstone.
  • Discussion prompt: Ask learners to share a time they received a file with no documentation. What questions did they have?
  • FAIR matching (Exercise 3): Ask which FAIR letter is hardest to achieve without a standard like DDI. Most will say Interoperable or Findable.
  • Closing: Reinforce that ddi-l makes documentation easy: you write Python, and the tool creates the standard XML for you.

docs.title: Module 2: Set up your Python environment
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Run python --version and decide whether your Python is new enough for ddi-l (3.11 or newer).
  • O2. Install ddi-l, pandas, and openpyxl with pip and read the last line of the output to confirm the install.
  • O3. Run a two-line Python test that prints the installed ddi-l version.
  • O4. Run ddi --help and find the command that does a given task, such as validating a file.
  • O5. Choose a workspace (Python REPL, script file, or notebook) for a given task and give a one-sentence reason.

Prerequisites: Module 1

Time: 20 min self-paced / 30 min instructor-led.

New in this module: python --version, pip install, ddi --help, import ddi_l as ddi, ddi.__version__

docs.title: 1. What you need: Python 3.11 or newer
docs.text:
Python is a programming language. ddi-l runs inside Python, so you must have Python installed on your computer.

Open a terminal (also called a command prompt) and type:

python --version

You should see something like:

Python 3.12.3

The version number must be 3.11 or higher. Read the first two numbers: 3.12 is newer than 3.11, so it works; 3.10 or 3.9 is too old. If your version is older, visit https://www.python.org/downloads/ and install a newer version.

Common issue

On some systems the command is python3 instead of python. If python --version does not work, try python3 --version.

docs.title: 2. Install ddi-l
docs.text:
In your terminal, run:

pip install ddi-l

This command downloads ddi-l from the internet and installs it. The word pip is Python's package installer. It is the standard way to add new tools to your Python setup.

Next, install two helper packages you will need in later modules:

pip install pandas openpyxl
  • pandas is a popular tool for working with tables of data.
  • openpyxl lets Python read and write Excel files.

You can install everything in one line if you prefer:

pip install ddi-l pandas openpyxl

The last line of the output tells you how it went:

  • Successfully installed followed by package names means pip installed them.
  • Requirement already satisfied means a package was already there, so pip had nothing to do.
  • A line starting with ERROR means the install failed. Read the message, fix the cause (often the Python version or a network problem), and run the command again.

docs.title: 3a. Test the command-line tool
docs.text:
ddi-l includes a command-line tool called ddi. Run:

ddi --help

You should see a list of available commands. This confirms the tool is installed and ready to use. Each command has a one-line description. The start of the list looks like this:

positional arguments:
    validate            Validate an XML document against the DDI schema.
    to-json             Convert a DDI instance document to JSON.
    ...

To find the command for a task, read the descriptions, not just the names. For example, the command that checks a file against the DDI rules is the one whose description says "Validate". You will use these commands in Module 7.

docs.title: 3b. Test in Python
docs.text:
Open a Python session by typing python in your terminal. Then type:

import ddi_l as ddi

print(ddi.__version__)

You should see a version number printed, such as 0.1.0 or later. This confirms that Python can find and load the ddi-l package.

If you see ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddi_l' instead, ddi-l is not installed in the Python you are running. Run pip install ddi-l again, using the same python or python3 command you used above (for example, python3 -m pip install ddi-l).

Type exit() to leave the Python session.

docs.title: 4. Choose your workspace
docs.text:
You can write Python code in several ways. Pick the one that feels most comfortable:

Workspace How to start Best for Python REPL Type python in the terminal. Quick tests and exploring. Script file Create a file like my_script.py. Saving your work. Jupyter Notebook Run jupyter notebook in terminal. Step-by-step exploration.
  • REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop. It is an interactive prompt where you type one line of Python at a time and see the result right away.
  • A script file is a plain text file ending in .py that you run all at once.
  • A Jupyter Notebook is a tool that lets you mix text, code, and output in one document. It is not installed with ddi-l: run pip install notebook first if you want to use one.

How to choose:

  • Use the REPL for a one-off check you do not need to keep, such as printing the version.
  • Use a script file when you want to keep your code and run it again from the top with one command, such as python my_script.py.
  • Use a notebook when you want to see notes, code, and output together, step by step, for example to walk a colleague through your work.

For this curriculum, any of the three options will work.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Scenario

You are setting up a new laptop for a training workshop. You need to make sure Python and ddi-l are ready to go before the workshop starts.

Exercise 1 (O1). Run python --version (or python3 --version) in your terminal. Write down the version, and say whether it is new enough for ddi-l.

Expected output: one line such as Python 3.12.3, and a yes or no.

Answer

For example, Python 3.12.3: yes, because 3.12 is 3.11 or newer. If you see Python 3.10.12 or older, the answer is no: install a newer Python from https://www.python.org/downloads/ before you continue.

Exercise 2 (O2). Run the following command in your terminal:

pip install ddi-l pandas openpyxl

Paste the last line of the output, and say what it means.

Expected output: a line that starts with Successfully installed or Requirement already satisfied.

Answer

The last line starts with Successfully installed and lists ddi-l-... among the packages (the version may vary). If the packages were already installed, pip says Requirement already satisfied instead. Both mean you are ready. A line starting with ERROR means the install failed.

Exercise 3 (O3). Open a Python session and run:

import ddi_l as ddi

print(ddi.__version__)

Write down the version number you see.

Expected output: one version number, such as 0.1.0.

Answer

The installed version, such as 0.1.0 or later. If you see ModuleNotFoundError instead, ddi-l is not installed in this Python: go back to Exercise 2.

Exercise 4 (O4). Run ddi --help in your terminal. Read the descriptions and write down the command you would use for each task:

  1. Check a DDI file against the DDI schema.
  2. Report quality problems in a DDI file, such as missing labels.
  3. List the DDI schema releases that ddi-l supports.

Expected output: three command names.

Answer
  1. validate ("Validate an XML document against the DDI schema.")
  2. lint ("Lint a DDI document and report findings as JSON.")
  3. versions ("List supported DDI schema releases.")

Exercise 5 (O5). Choose a workspace for each task, and give a one-sentence reason:

  1. Check once that import ddi_l works on the new laptop.
  2. Write the study you will build in Module 3, so you can run it again next week after you change it.
  3. Show a colleague, step by step, how the study is built, with notes between the pieces of code.

Expected output: three workspaces, each with a reason.

Answer
  1. Python REPL: it is the quickest way to run one line you do not need to keep.
  2. Script file: it saves your code, and python my_script.py runs it again from the top.
  3. Notebook: it shows notes, code, and output together, step by step.

Other choices are fine if your reason holds up; for example, a notebook also saves your code for task 2.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): python --version prints Python 3.10.12. What should you do before you install ddi-l?

A. Nothing. Any Python 3 version works.

B. Install Python 3.11 or newer.

C. Run pip install ddi-l twice.

D. Switch to Python 2.7.

Answer

B. ddi-l requires Python 3.11 or newer, and 3.10 is older. Install a newer Python, then install ddi-l with it.

Question 2 (O2): The last line of pip install ddi-l pandas openpyxl reads Requirement already satisfied. What does this mean?

A. The install failed and must be run again.

B. pip needs administrator rights.

C. The packages must be removed first.

D. The package was already installed, so pip had nothing to do.

Answer

D. Requirement already satisfied means the package is already there. A failed install ends with a line that starts with ERROR.

Question 3 (O3): You run import ddi_l as ddi and get ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddi_l'. What is the most likely cause?

A. ddi-l is not installed in the Python you are running.

B. The import must be written import ddi-l.

C. You must call ddi.__version__ before the import.

D. The package only works in a notebook.

Answer

A. Python cannot find the package, so it is not installed for this Python. Run pip install ddi-l again, or python3 -m pip install ddi-l if you start Python with python3. Option B is not valid Python: a hyphen cannot appear in an import name, which is why the module is called ddi_l.

Question 4 (O4): You want to check a file against the DDI schema from the terminal. Which command from the ddi --help list do you use?

A. roundtrip

B. to-json

C. validate

D. serve

Answer

C. Its description reads "Validate an XML document against the DDI schema." roundtrip re-writes a file, to-json converts it, and serve runs the HTTP API.

Question 5 (O5): You will build a study over several days and want to run the whole thing again from the top with one command after each change. Which workspace fits best?

A. The Python REPL, typing each line again.

B. A script file, such as build_study.py, run with python build_study.py.

C. A text document that you copy and paste into the REPL.

D. The terminal, running ddi --help.

Answer

B. A script file keeps your code, and one command runs all of it again. The REPL forgets what you typed when you close it.

docs.title: Going further (optional)
docs.text: For advanced setups (such as installing with uv or Poetry, or adding the optional lxml backend for faster parsing), see the full Installation guide.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can run python --version and decide whether my Python is new enough for ddi-l. (O1)
  • I can install ddi-l, pandas, and openpyxl with pip and read the last line of the output. (O2)
  • I can run a two-line Python test that prints the ddi-l version. (O3)
  • I can run ddi --help and find the command for a given task. (O4)
  • I can choose a workspace for a task and give a one-sentence reason. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Budget extra time for environment issues. Python version problems, permission errors, and network issues are common in live workshops.
  • Have a fallback ready: a cloud notebook (such as Google Colab) or a pre-built container with everything installed.
  • Why install pandas now? Installing it here avoids disruption in Module 8, where learners will load CSV and Excel files. Getting the install out of the way early keeps later modules focused on DDI.
  • Exercise 4: The number of commands grows from one release to the next, so ask learners to find commands by their description rather than count them.
  • Pair up learners who finish early with those who need help. Setup problems are easier to solve with a partner.

docs.title: Module 3: Create your first DDI study
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Write a script that creates a study with ddi.new_study() and adds three questions with doc.add_question().
  • O2. Count the questions in a study with len(doc.questions) and print each question's identifier.
  • O3. Save the study to an XML file with doc.save() and find a question's text in the saved file.
  • O4. Add a French version of an existing question's text and label, so that one question holds both languages.
  • O5. Check a study with doc.validate() and doc.lint(), and fix the lint warnings until both report nothing.

Prerequisites: Module 2

Time: 30 min self-paced / 45 min instructor-led.

New in this module: ddi.new_study(), doc.add_question(), doc.questions, doc.save(), InternationalString, doc.validate(), doc.lint()

docs.title: 1. What is a "study" in DDI?
docs.text:
A study is a container that holds all the information about one survey or research project. Think of it like a folder that keeps everything together: the title, the organization that ran the survey, the questions that were asked, and the data that was collected.

In ddi-l, you create a study first, and then you add items (like questions and variables) to it.

docs.title: 2. Create a study
docs.text:
Open a Python session or create a new script file. Type the following:

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="Student Well-Being Survey",
    agency="university.edu",
)

What this does:

  • import ddi_l as ddi loads the ddi-l package and gives it the short name ddi.
  • ddi.new_study() creates a new DDI document. It returns a Document object, which we store in the variable called doc.
  • title= sets the name of the study.
  • agency= sets the organization responsible for the study. It is required: without it, ddi.new_study() raises a TypeError.

docs.title: 3. What is an "agency"?
docs.text:
An agency is the organization responsible for the study. It could be a university, a government department, a research institute, or any group that runs the survey. Its agency ID goes into every item it creates, beside the item's own identifier and version, so that together they name the item.

  • Registered. So that no two organizations share an agency ID, each registers its own with the DDI Agency ID Registry. It can then add sub-agencies after a dot, for example one per division.
  • Format. Letters, digits and hyphens, in parts joined by dots, each part at most 63 characters. doc.validate() checks the format, not whether the ID is registered.
  • In this course. IDs such as "university.edu" and "stats.example.org" are made up. In a real document, use the ID your organization registered.

docs.title: 4. Add questions
docs.text:
A survey asks questions. In DDI, each question is stored as a separate item. Let us add three questions to our study:

q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your health?")
q3 = doc.add_question(text="How many hours do you sleep per night?")

Each call to doc.add_question() creates a new question inside the study and returns a question object. We save each object in a variable (q1, q2, q3) so we can use it later, for example, to link a variable to it.

docs.title: 5. Questions in more than one language
docs.text:
Many surveys are conducted in more than one language. For example, a Canadian survey might be in both English and French. DDI can store the same question in multiple languages inside a single document.

Every add_question() call accepts a lang= argument. The default is lang="en" (English), so the questions you added above are in English. To create a question in French, pass lang="fr", as in doc.add_question(text="Quel est votre âge ?", lang="fr").

To add a French translation of the same question, append it to the question's question_texts list:

from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

q1.question_texts.append(InternationalString(text="Quel est votre âge ?", lang="fr"))

An InternationalString is a piece of text together with its language code ("en", "fr", and so on). Now q1 contains the question text in both English and French. When someone opens the DDI file, they can see both versions.

The lang= argument works on all add_* methods: add_variable(), add_concept(), add_universe(), and add_code_list(). You can also append translations to their names list the same way. Module 8 shows a complete bilingual workflow.

docs.title: 6. Check your questions
docs.text:
You can see how many questions the study contains:

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")

Expected output:

Questions: 3

You can also loop through all the questions and print their identifiers:

for q in doc.questions:
    print(q.identifier)

An identifier is a unique label that DDI assigns to each item. It helps you find and refer to specific items in the document.

docs.title: 7. Save to XML
docs.text:
To save your study to a file, use the save() method:

doc.save("well-being.xml")

This creates a file called well-being.xml in your current folder. The file contains your study in DDI XML format, a structured text format that follows the DDI standard.

docs.title: 8. Look inside the XML
docs.text:
Open well-being.xml in a text editor (such as Notepad, VS Code, or any plain-text editor). You will see XML tags: words wrapped in angle brackets like <QuestionItemName>.

Look for the text of your first question. You should find something like:

<d:QuestionText>
  <d:LiteralText>
    <d:Text>What is your age?</d:Text>
  </d:LiteralText>
</d:QuestionText>

You do not need to understand all the XML. The point is that ddi-l turned your five lines of Python into a complete, standards-compliant DDI document.

Cross-reference: User guide: Create a study

docs.title: 9. Check your work
docs.text:
Get into the habit of checking a study before you share it. ddi-l runs two kinds of check:

  • Validation compares the document with the DDI schema: the official rules for which elements are allowed, where they go, and which ones are required. A document that fails validation is not valid DDI.
  • Linting looks for problems the schema allows but that are usually mistakes, such as an item with no label.
issues = doc.validate()
print(f"Schema problems: {len(issues)}")

findings = doc.lint()
print(f"Lint findings: {len(findings)}")
for finding in findings:
    print(f"  [{finding.severity}] {finding.message}")

Expected output:

Schema problems: 0
Lint findings: 3
  [warning] Maintainable element is missing a label.
  [warning] Maintainable element is missing a label.
  [warning] Maintainable element is missing a label.

The study is valid DDI. The three warnings say that your questions have no label: a short name that catalogues and other tools show instead of the full question text. Add a label to each question and check again:

q1.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Age", lang="en"))
q2.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Self-rated health", lang="en"))
q3.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Hours of sleep", lang="en"))

print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")
doc.save("well-being.xml")

Expected output:

Lint findings: 0

A label can have more than one language, just like the question text. Append a French label to the same labels list:

q1.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Âge", lang="fr"))

When you add a new item, you can give it a label straight away. Every add_* method accepts label=:

q4 = doc.add_question(text="Do you exercise every week?", label="Weekly exercise")

Warnings do not make a document invalid; schema errors do. Check your work like this at the end of every module. Module 7 runs the same checks from the command line.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Scenario

You are a research assistant. Your professor asks you to document a Student Well-Being Survey with three questions about age, health, and sleep. You will use ddi-l to create the documentation.

Exercise 1 (O1, O2). Create a study titled "Student Well-Being Survey" with agency "university.edu". Add three questions:

  1. "What is your age?"
  2. "How would you rate your health?"
  3. "How many hours do you sleep per night?"

Print the question count, then the identifier of each question. Save the study as well-being.xml.

Expected output: Questions: 3, then three identifiers, one per line (yours will differ).

Questions: 3
4f0c9a5e-...
9b1d2e7c-...
c3a8f610-...
Answer 
import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Student Well-Being Survey", agency="university.edu")

q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your health?")
q3 = doc.add_question(text="How many hours do you sleep per night?")

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 3
for q in doc.questions:
    print(q.identifier)

doc.save("well-being.xml")

Exercise 2 (O3). Open well-being.xml, the file you saved in Exercise 1, in a text editor. Find the text of your first question inside the XML. Write down the XML tag that wraps the question text.

Expected output: the name of one XML tag.

Answer

The question text sits in a <d:Text> element, inside <d:LiteralText> inside <d:QuestionText>:

<d:Text xml:lang="en" isPlainText="true">What is your age?</d:Text>

Exercise 3 (O5). Continue from Exercise 1. Check the study with doc.validate() and doc.lint(), and print how many problems each reports. Then give each question an English label ("Age", "Self-rated health", "Hours of sleep"), check again, and save.

Expected output:

Schema problems: 0
Lint findings: 3
Lint findings: 0
Answer 
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

print(f"Schema problems: {len(doc.validate())}")  # -> Schema problems: 0
print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")  # -> Lint findings: 3

q1.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Age", lang="en"))
q2.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Self-rated health", lang="en"))
q3.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Hours of sleep", lang="en"))

print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")  # -> Lint findings: 0
doc.save("well-being.xml")

The three warnings were "Maintainable element is missing a label.", one per question. A label fixes each one.

Exercise 4 (O4). Add French to the first question: the text "Quel est votre âge ?" and the label "Âge". Do not create a new question. Print the question count and the lint count, save the file again, and check the XML for both languages.

Expected output:

Questions: 3
Lint findings: 0

In the XML, the first question has xml:lang="en" and xml:lang="fr" entries for both its label and its text.

Answer 
q1.question_texts.append(InternationalString(text="Quel est votre âge ?", lang="fr"))
q1.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Âge", lang="fr"))

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 3
print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")  # -> Lint findings: 0
doc.save("well-being.xml")

The count stays at 3 because both translations belong to q1. In the XML, the first question now reads:

<r:Label>
  <r:Content xml:lang="en">Age</r:Content>
  <r:Content xml:lang="fr">Âge</r:Content>
</r:Label>
<d:QuestionText>
  <d:LiteralText>
    <d:Text xml:lang="en" isPlainText="true">What is your age?</d:Text>
  </d:LiteralText>
  <d:LiteralText>
    <d:Text xml:lang="fr">Quel est votre âge ?</d:Text>
  </d:LiteralText>
</d:QuestionText>

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): You run doc = ddi.new_study(title='Sleep Survey') and get a TypeError. Why?

A. The title is too short.

B. agency= is missing. Every study needs the organization responsible for it.

C. You must import InternationalString first.

D. new_study() takes no arguments.

Answer

B. ddi.new_study() requires both title= and agency=. The error message says so: "missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'agency'".

Question 2 (O1): After q1 = doc.add_question(text='What is your age?'), what is q1?

A. The string "What is your age?".

B. The number of questions in the study.

C. A question object stored in the study, which you can use later, for example to translate it or to link a variable to it.

D. The XML text of the question.

Answer

C. doc.add_question() adds a question item to the study and returns that question object. Keeping it in a variable lets you work with it later.

Question 3 (O2): A study has three questions. You add a fourth with doc.add_question(), then run print(len(doc.questions)). What is printed?

A. 4

B. 3

C. 1

D. An error, because doc.questions is not a list.

Answer

A. doc.questions is the list of every question in the study, and len() counts them: three plus the new one.

Question 4 (O3): You open the file written by doc.save('well-being.xml'). Where do you find the text of your first question?

A. In a <d:Text> element inside <d:QuestionText>.

B. Only in the file name.

C. In the <r:Agency> element.

D. Nowhere: save() writes only the study title.

Answer

A. doc.save() writes the whole study, and each question's text sits in <d:Text>, inside <d:LiteralText>, inside <d:QuestionText>.

Question 5 (O4): You want the first question, q1, in both English and French. Which line does it?

A. doc.add_question(text="Quel est votre âge ?", lang="fr")

B. q1.lang = "fr"

C. q1.question_texts.append(InternationalString(text="Quel est votre âge ?", lang="fr"))

D. None: DDI cannot store more than one language in one question.

Answer

C. Appending an InternationalString with the new language stores both versions in the same question item. Option A creates a brand-new, separate question, not a translation of q1.

Question 6 (O5): doc.validate() returns an empty list, but doc.lint() reports warnings. Is the document valid DDI?

A. No. Any finding makes a document invalid.

B. Only after you save it.

C. It depends on the language of the questions.

D. Yes. Validation checks the schema; lint warnings point to quality problems, such as a missing label, that the schema allows.

Answer

D. An empty list from doc.validate() means the document follows the DDI schema. Lint warnings are worth fixing, but they do not make the document invalid.

Question 7 (O5): doc.lint() reports 'Maintainable element is missing a label.' once for each of your three questions. Which change clears the warnings?

A. Save the document again with doc.save().

B. Give each question a label, for example q1.labels.append(InternationalString(text="Age", lang="en")), or pass label= when you call doc.add_question().

C. Delete the questions and add them again with the same code.

D. Call doc.validate() before doc.lint().

Answer

B. The warning names the problem: the questions have no label. Saving or validating does not change the document, and adding the questions again with the same code brings the same warnings back.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can write a script that creates a study with ddi.new_study() and adds three questions with doc.add_question(). (O1)
  • I can count the questions with len(doc.questions) and print each question's identifier. (O2)
  • I can save the study with doc.save() and find a question's text in the XML file. (O3)
  • I can add a French version of an existing question's text and label without creating a new question. (O4)
  • I can check a study with doc.validate() and doc.lint() and fix the lint warnings until both report nothing. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • This is the "aha" module. Five lines of Python create a real, standards-compliant XML document. Demo it live to make the impact clear.
  • Live coding: Type the code on screen, line by line. Let learners follow along. Pause after each step to let people catch up.
  • Common mistake: Learners often forget the quotes around strings. For example, they type text=What is your age? instead of text="What is your age?". Watch for this during exercises.
  • Common mistake: In Exercise 4, some learners call doc.add_question(..., lang="fr"). Ask them to print len(doc.questions): a count of 4 shows they created a second question instead of translating the first.
  • Explore the XML together: Open the saved file on screen and scroll through it. Point out the question text inside the tags. Emphasize that learners did not need to write any of this XML by hand.
  • Extension activity: Ask fast finishers to add two more questions of their own, each with a label=, then check with doc.lint() and save the file again.

docs.title: Module 4: Add variables and link them to questions
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Explain in one sentence what a variable is, using a spreadsheet column as the example.
  • O2. Write a script that adds a labelled variable for each question with doc.add_variable() and links it with question=, so that doc.validate() and doc.lint() report nothing.
  • O3. Count the variables with len(doc.variables) and print each variable's identifier.
  • O4. Explain in two sentences why linking a variable to its question matters, using one data column as the example.
  • O5. Find a variable's name and its link to its question (<r:QuestionReference>) in the saved XML.

Prerequisites: Module 3

Time: 30 min self-paced / 40 min instructor-led.

New in this module: doc.add_variable() (with name=, label=, and question=), doc.variables

docs.title: 1. What is a variable?
docs.text:
A variable is like a column in a spreadsheet. If you have a spreadsheet of survey results, each column holds one piece of information for every person who answered the survey. For example:

Age HealthRating SleepHours 19 4 7 21 3 6 20 5 8

In this table, Age, HealthRating, and SleepHours are the three variables. Each one stores the answers to one question from the survey.

docs.title: 2. The connection between questions and variables
docs.text:
Every variable comes from a question. The question asks for information, and the variable stores the answers.

Question: "What is your age?"   --->   Variable: Age
Question: "Rate your health?"   --->   Variable: HealthRating
Question: "Hours of sleep?"     --->   Variable: SleepHours

In DDI, you can link a variable to the question that produced it. This link is stored inside the DDI document so anyone reading the metadata can follow the chain from a data column back to the exact question that collected the data.

docs.title: 3. Add variables linked to questions
docs.text:
Let us continue with the Student Well-Being Survey from Module 3. First, create the study and add the questions, each with a label as you learned in Module 3:

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="Student Well-Being Survey",
    agency="university.edu",
)

q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?", label="Age")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your health?", label="Self-rated health")
q3 = doc.add_question(
    text="How many hours do you sleep per night?", label="Hours of sleep"
)

Now add three variables. Each one is linked to a question using the question= argument:

v1 = doc.add_variable(name="Age", label="Age in years", question=q1)
v2 = doc.add_variable(
    name="HealthRating", label="Self-rated health, 1 to 5", question=q2
)
v3 = doc.add_variable(name="SleepHours", label="Hours of sleep per night", question=q3)

What this does:

  • doc.add_variable() creates a new variable inside the study.
  • name= gives the variable a short name, like a column header.
  • label= gives it a human-readable label, as you did for questions in Module 3. Without a label, doc.lint() reports a warning.
  • question= links the variable to the question object that collected the data. Notice that you pass the question object (like q1), not the question text string. Passing the text, as in question="What is your age?", raises an error.

docs.title: 4. List all variables
docs.text:
You can count the variables and loop through them, just like you did with questions:

print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")

Expected output:

Variables: 3

To print the identifier of each variable:

for v in doc.variables:
    print(v.identifier)

Each variable gets a unique identifier (a label assigned by DDI) so it can be found and referenced inside the document.

docs.title: 5. Why linking matters
docs.text:
Linking variables to questions creates traceability. Traceability means you can follow the path from any piece of data back to where it came from.

Imagine you are looking at a column called SleepHours in a dataset. You wonder: "What exactly did the survey ask?" Because the variable is linked to the question, you can look up the question and see: "How many hours do you sleep per night?"

This is important for:

  • Researchers who need to understand how data was collected.
  • Archivists who preserve data for future use.
  • Auditors who verify that data was collected properly.

Without the link, you would have to guess which question produced which column. With DDI, the connection is clear and automatic.

docs.title: 6. Check, save, and inspect
docs.text:
Check your work, as you learned in Module 3, then save the complete document:

print(f"Schema problems: {len(doc.validate())}")
print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")
doc.save("well-being.xml")

Expected output:

Schema problems: 0
Lint findings: 0

Open well-being.xml in a text editor. Look for a variable element. You should see something like:

<l:Variable>
  <r:ID>c4eefbc3-...</r:ID>
  <l:VariableName>
    <r:String xml:lang="en">Age</r:String>
  </l:VariableName>
  <r:Label>
    <r:Content xml:lang="en">Age in years</r:Content>
  </r:Label>
  <r:QuestionReference>
    <r:ID>86aed7cf-...</r:ID>
    <r:TypeOfObject>QuestionItem</r:TypeOfObject>
  </r:QuestionReference>
</l:Variable>

<l:VariableName> holds the name. <r:QuestionReference> is the link: the <r:ID> inside it is the identifier of the question q1, so a reader can find the exact question. ddi-l created all of this for you.

Cross-reference: User guide: Add variables

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Scenario

You are continuing your work on the Student Well-Being Survey from Module 3. The professor now asks you to define the data columns (variables) and connect each one to the question that collected it.

Exercise 1 (O1). A first-year student shows you this extract from her data file:

StudentID SleepHours ExerciseDays S001 6.9 7 S002 7.6 7 S003 6.6 2

Write one sentence that explains what a variable is, using SleepHours as your example.

Expected output: one sentence.

Answer

For example: "A variable is one column of a data file, such as SleepHours, which holds every student's answer to the same question: how many hours they sleep per night."

Exercise 2 (O2). Build on Module 3. Create the study and add three questions, each with a label. Then add three variables, each with a label and linked to its question:

  • Age linked to the age question.
  • HealthRating linked to the health question.
  • SleepHours linked to the sleep question.

Check your work with doc.validate() and doc.lint().

Expected output:

Schema problems: 0
Lint findings: 0
Answer 
import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Student Well-Being Survey", agency="university.edu")

q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?", label="Age")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your health?", label="Self-rated health")
q3 = doc.add_question(
    text="How many hours do you sleep per night?", label="Hours of sleep"
)

v1 = doc.add_variable(name="Age", label="Age in years", question=q1)
v2 = doc.add_variable(
    name="HealthRating", label="Self-rated health, 1 to 5", question=q2
)
v3 = doc.add_variable(name="SleepHours", label="Hours of sleep per night", question=q3)

print(f"Schema problems: {len(doc.validate())}")  # -> Schema problems: 0
print(f"Lint findings: {len(doc.lint())}")  # -> Lint findings: 0

If doc.lint() reports "Maintainable element is missing a label.", one of your questions or variables has no label=.

Exercise 3 (O3). Print the number of variables, then the identifier of each variable using a for loop.

Expected output: Variables: 3, then three unique identifiers, one per line (yours will differ).

Answer 
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 3
for v in doc.variables:
    print(v.identifier)

Each identifier is a UUID, such as a1b2c3d4-....

Exercise 4 (O4). A colleague finds the column HealthRating, with values from 1 to 5, in your data file. Write two sentences: what the link from HealthRating to its question tells your colleague, and what could go wrong if the link were missing.

Expected output: two sentences.

Answer

For example: "The link leads to the question 'How would you rate your health?', so my colleague knows the values are each student's own rating of their health. Without it, they might guess wrongly, for example that the values were measured by a doctor, or that 1 means the best health."

Exercise 5 (O5). Save the document with doc.save("well-being.xml"). Open the XML file in a text editor and find the <l:Variable> element for Age. Write down:

  1. The variable name inside <l:VariableName>.
  2. The <r:ID> inside its <r:QuestionReference>.

Then run print(q1.identifier) and compare.

Expected output: the name Age, and an identifier that matches the one print(q1.identifier) shows.

Answer 
doc.save("well-being.xml")
print(q1.identifier)

The variable's name is in <l:VariableName>:

<l:VariableName>
  <r:String xml:lang="en">Age</r:String>
</l:VariableName>

The <r:ID> inside the <r:QuestionReference> a few lines below is the same identifier that print(q1.identifier) shows. That shared identifier is the link from the variable to the question.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): In a table with the columns Age, HealthRating, and SleepHours, which of these is a variable?

A. The row for the first respondent.

B. The value 4 in the second column.

C. The column HealthRating, which holds every respondent's answer to one question.

D. The name of the spreadsheet tab.

Answer

C. A variable is like a column. Each column holds one type of information, such as a health rating, for every person in the dataset. A row is one person; a value is one answer.

Question 2 (O2): What happens when you run doc.add_variable(name='Age', question='What is your age?')?

A. ddi-l finds the question by its text and links it.

B. It raises an error, because question= expects the question object (like q1), not the question text.

C. The variable is created with no link to a question.

D. A new question with that text is created.

Answer

B. question= needs the object that doc.add_question() returned. A plain string is not a question, so the call fails with an AttributeError. Pass q1 instead.

Question 3 (O2): What does question=q2 do in doc.add_variable(name='HealthRating', question=q2)?

A. It records, in the DDI document, a reference from the variable to the question q2.

B. It prints the question text on the screen.

C. It deletes q2 from the study.

D. It renames the question to HealthRating.

Answer

A. The question= argument stores a link between the variable and the question that collected the data. You can see it in the XML as <r:QuestionReference>.

Question 4 (O3): Which code prints the identifier of every variable in the study?

A. print(doc.variables.identifier)

B. doc.list_variables()

C. for v in doc.questions: print(v.identifier)

D. for v in doc.variables: print(v.identifier)

Answer

D. doc.variables is a list, so you loop through it and print each variable's identifier. Option A fails because a list has no identifier, and option C loops through the questions, not the variables.

Question 5 (O4): A data user sees the column SleepHours and wants to know exactly what was asked. How does the link from the variable to its question help?

A. It converts the hours into minutes.

B. The user can follow the link to the question "How many hours do you sleep per night?" instead of guessing.

C. It hides the column from users who do not need it.

D. It makes the data file smaller.

Answer

B. This is traceability: the link takes the user from the data column back to the exact question that collected the data.

Question 6 (O5): In the saved XML, which element links a variable to the question that collected it?

A. <l:VariableName>

B. <r:Agency>

C. <r:QuestionReference>

D. <d:QuestionText>

Answer

C. <r:QuestionReference> sits inside the <l:Variable> element and holds the question's identifier. <l:VariableName> holds the variable's name, and <d:QuestionText> belongs to the question itself.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can explain in one sentence what a variable is, using a spreadsheet column as the example. (O1)
  • I can write a script that adds a labelled variable for each question and links it with question=, so that doc.validate() and doc.lint() report nothing. (O2)
  • I can count the variables with len(doc.variables) and print each variable's identifier. (O3)
  • I can explain in two sentences why linking a variable to its question matters. (O4)
  • I can find a variable's name and its <r:QuestionReference> in the saved XML. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Visual aid: Draw this diagram on the board or screen: Question --> Variable --> Data column. Walk through one example: "What is your age?" leads to the variable Age, which becomes the Age column in the spreadsheet.
  • Common mistake: Learners sometimes pass the question text (a string like "What is your age?") instead of the question object (q1). Remind them that question= expects the object returned by doc.add_question(), not the text.
  • Hands-on check: After Exercises 2 and 3, ask learners to share their output. Everyone should see Lint findings: 0 and Variables: 3.
  • Extension activity: Ask fast finishers to add a fourth question and a fourth variable, then check, save, and inspect the updated XML.
  • Reinforce the concept: Ask the group: "If you only had the data file with no links to questions, how would you know what each column means?" This drives home the value of traceability (Exercise 4).

docs.title: Module 5: Organize with concepts and universes
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Explain, in one sentence each, what a concept and a universe describe, and sort example phrases into concepts and universes.
  • O2. Add concepts and a universe to a document with doc.add_concept() and doc.add_universe().
  • O3. Link each variable to the concept it measures by passing concept= to doc.add_variable(), and check the link.
  • O4. Print the names of all the concepts and universes in a document, using doc.concepts and doc.universes.

Prerequisites: Module 4.

Time: 30 min self-paced / 40 min instructor-led.

New in this module: doc.add_concept(), doc.add_universe(), the concept= argument of doc.add_variable(), doc.concepts, doc.universes, concept_references, names[0].text.

docs.title: 1. What is a concept?
docs.text:
A concept is an abstract idea that a variable measures. Think of it as a label for a group of related variables.

For example, the variable "Age" measures the concept "Demographics." The variable "Fruit servings per day" measures the concept "Nutrition."

Concepts help you organize your survey. When someone reads your metadata, they can quickly see which variables belong together.

docs.title: 2. What is a universe?
docs.text:
A universe is the group of people or things being studied. It answers the question: "Who does this survey cover?"

For example: "Adults aged 18+ in Canada."

A single survey usually has one universe, but some surveys study more than one group.

Concept or universe? A quick test

Ask two questions about a phrase:

  • Does it say what is measured? Then it is a concept ("Nutrition", "Sleep quality").
  • Does it say who or what is measured? Then it is a universe ("Adults aged 18+ in Canada", "Public schools in Ontario").

docs.title: 3. Add concepts
docs.text:
Use doc.add_concept(name=) to add a concept to your document. The method returns a concept object that you can use later.

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Health Survey", agency="health.gc.ca")

demo = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
activity = doc.add_concept(name="Physical Activity")
nutrition = doc.add_concept(name="Nutrition")

print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")  # -> Concepts: 3

Each call creates one concept and adds it to the document. We save the return value in a variable so we can link it later.

docs.title: 4. Add universes
docs.text:
Use doc.add_universe(name=) to add a universe.

doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18+ in Canada")

print(f"Universes: {len(doc.universes)}")  # -> Universes: 1

The name should clearly describe who is being studied.

docs.title: 5. Link a variable to a concept
docs.text:
When you add a variable, you can pass a concept= argument. This links the variable to that concept in the DDI metadata.

q1 = doc.add_question(text="How old are you?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="How many days per week do you exercise?")
q3 = doc.add_question(text="How many servings of fruit do you eat per day?")

doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q1, concept=demo)
doc.add_variable(name="Exercise Frequency", question=q2, concept=activity)
doc.add_variable(name="Fruit Servings", question=q3, concept=nutrition)

print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 3

Now each variable is connected to its concept. Anyone who reads the DDI file can see that "Age" belongs to "Demographics."

To check a link, look at the variable's concept_references list. Each entry is a reference: a pointer that holds the identifier of the concept. If the identifier matches the concept's, the link is right:

age = doc.variables[0]
print(age.concept_references[0].identifier == demo.identifier)  # -> True

A variable added without concept= has an empty concept_references list.

docs.title: 6. List concepts and universes
docs.text:
Use doc.concepts and doc.universes to see all items in the document.

print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")  # -> Concepts: 3
print(f"Universes: {len(doc.universes)}")  # -> Universes: 1

These properties return lists, so you can loop over them. Each item keeps its name in a list called names, with one entry per language. names[0].text is the text of the first name:

for concept in doc.concepts:
    print(concept.names[0].text)

Expected output:

Demographics
Physical Activity
Nutrition

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Scenario

A national health authority surveys adults about diet and exercise. They need three concepts: Nutrition, Physical Activity, and Demographics. The universe is Adults aged 18+ in Canada. Your job is to build this structure in code.

Exercise 1 (O1). For each phrase below, write "concept" or "universe". Then write one sentence that explains what a concept describes and one sentence that explains what a universe describes.

  • Nutrition
  • Adults aged 18+ in Canada
  • Sleep quality
  • Public schools in Ontario
  • Employment
  • Children aged 6 to 11 living in private households
Answer
  • Nutrition: concept.
  • Adults aged 18+ in Canada: universe.
  • Sleep quality: concept.
  • Public schools in Ontario: universe.
  • Employment: concept.
  • Children aged 6 to 11 living in private households: universe.

A concept is the idea that a variable measures, such as "Nutrition". A universe is the group of people or things a study covers, such as "Adults aged 18+ in Canada".

Exercise 2 (O2). Create a document with the title "National Health Survey" and the agency "health.gc.ca". Add three concepts (Demographics, Physical Activity, Nutrition) and one universe (Adults aged 18+ in Canada). Keep each concept in a Python variable: you link to them in Exercise 3. Print the counts.

Expected output:

Concepts: 3
Universes: 1
Answer 
import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Health Survey", agency="health.gc.ca")

demo = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
activity = doc.add_concept(name="Physical Activity")
nutrition = doc.add_concept(name="Nutrition")

doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18+ in Canada")

print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")  # -> Concepts: 3
print(f"Universes: {len(doc.universes)}")  # -> Universes: 1

Exercise 3 (O3). Continue with the same document.

  1. Add four questions:

    • "How old are you?"
    • "What is your weight in kg?"
    • "How many days per week do you exercise?"
    • "How many servings of fruit do you eat per day?"

  2. Add four variables. Link each one to its matching concept:

    • Age -> Demographics
    • Weight -> Demographics
    • ExerciseFrequency -> Physical Activity
    • FruitServings -> Nutrition

  3. Check that Weight is linked to Demographics, then check the document against the schema with doc.validate().

Expected output:

Questions: 4
Variables: 4
Weight is linked to Demographics: True
Schema problems: 0
Answer 
q1 = doc.add_question(text="How old are you?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="What is your weight in kg?")
q3 = doc.add_question(text="How many days per week do you exercise?")
q4 = doc.add_question(text="How many servings of fruit do you eat per day?")

doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q1, concept=demo)
weight = doc.add_variable(name="Weight", question=q2, concept=demo)
doc.add_variable(name="ExerciseFrequency", question=q3, concept=activity)
doc.add_variable(name="FruitServings", question=q4, concept=nutrition)

linked = weight.concept_references[0].identifier == demo.identifier

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 4
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 4
print(f"Weight is linked to Demographics: {linked}")
print(f"Schema problems: {len(doc.validate())}")  # -> Schema problems: 0

Exercise 4 (O4). Print the name of every concept and every universe in the document, under a heading for each kind.

Expected output:

Concepts:
  Demographics
  Physical Activity
  Nutrition
Universes:
  Adults aged 18+ in Canada
Answer 
print("Concepts:")
for concept in doc.concepts:
    print(f"  {concept.names[0].text}")

print("Universes:")
for universe in doc.universes:
    print(f"  {universe.names[0].text}")

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): Which phrase is the universe of this study?

A report says: "We asked adults aged 18+ in Canada about their sleep quality and their stress."

A. Adults aged 18+ in Canada

B. Sleep quality

C. Stress

D. The question "How many hours do you sleep?"

Answer

A. The universe says who is studied. "Sleep quality" and "Stress" say what is measured, so they are concepts. A question is neither.

Question 2 (O1): Which sentence correctly explains a concept?

A. A concept is the group of people a study covers.

B. A concept is a list of allowed answers.

C. A concept is the idea a variable measures, such as "Nutrition"; several variables can share one concept.

D. A concept is a file format for surveys.

Answer

C. A concept is an abstract idea that variables measure. Option A describes a universe, and option B describes a code list.

Question 3 (O2): What does this code print? 
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Sleep Study", agency="example.org")
doc.add_concept(name="Sleep quality")
doc.add_concept(name="Stress")
doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18+ in Canada")
print(len(doc.concepts), len(doc.universes))

A. 3 0

B. 1 2

C. 0 0

D. 2 1

Answer

D. Two calls to doc.add_concept() add two concepts, and one call to doc.add_universe() adds one universe.

Question 4 (O3): The variable Age is not linked to its concept. Which call fixes it?

After age = doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q1), age.concept_references is an empty list.

A. doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q1, universe=demo)

B. doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q1, concept=demo)

C. doc.add_concept(name="Age", variable=q1)

D. doc.link(q1, demo)

Answer

B. Pass the concept with concept= when you call doc.add_variable(). The other calls do not exist.

Question 5 (O4): Which loop prints the name of every universe?

A. for u in doc.universes: print(u)

B. print(doc.universes.names)

C. for u in doc.universes: print(u.names[0].text)

D. for u in doc.concepts: print(u.names[0].text)

Answer

C. Each universe keeps its name in names; names[0].text is the text. Option A prints the whole object, option B fails because a list has no names, and option D loops over the concepts.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can explain, in one sentence each, what a concept and a universe describe, and sort phrases into the two. (O1)
  • I can add concepts and a universe with doc.add_concept() and doc.add_universe(). (O2)
  • I can link a variable to its concept with concept= and check the link. (O3)
  • I can print the names of all the concepts and universes in a document. (O4)

Instructor notes

  • Draw a diagram on the board: Concept at the top, with arrows pointing down to its variables. This helps visual learners.
  • Ask the class: "If you had a survey about schools, what would your universe be?" (e.g., "All public schools in Ontario.")
  • Run Exercise 1 as a quick class poll before anyone writes code. The "what versus who" test in Section 2 settles most disagreements.
  • Common mistake: students forget to save the concept object in a variable. Remind them that doc.add_concept() returns something they need to keep.
  • Emphasize that concepts and universes are about describing the data; they do not change the data itself.

See also: User guide: Concepts and universes

docs.title: Module 6: Open, modify, and re-save existing DDI files
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Open an existing DDI file with ddi.open_ddi() and print how many questions and variables it holds.
  • O2. Open a file with validate=True, catch the ddi.DDIValidationError that a broken file raises, and name the element its message points to.
  • O3. Add new items to an opened document, reword an existing question, and code a variable with a code list.
  • O4. Save the changed document under a new filename and re-open it to confirm that your changes were kept and the original file is unchanged.
  • O5. Predict what happens to XML that ddi-l does not model when you open and save a file, and check your prediction.

Prerequisites: Module 5.

Time: 30 min self-paced / 40 min instructor-led.

New in this module: ddi.open_ddi(), open_ddi(..., validate=True), ddi.DDIValidationError, question_texts, doc.add_code_list(), variable.set_coded().

docs.title: 1. Open an existing file
docs.text:
First, get a file to open

This module works on a file called my-study.xml. If you do not have one yet, create it now, or reuse well-being.xml from Module 3 and change the filename in the examples below.

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="My Study", agency="example.org")
doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
doc.add_variable(name="Age")
doc.save("my-study.xml")
