The function ddi.open_ddi() reads a DDI XML file from your computer and gives you a Document object. A Document is the main object you use to view and change DDI content.

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.open_ddi("my-study.xml")

The argument is the path: the location of the file on your computer. It can be a simple filename (like "my-study.xml") if the file is in the same folder as your script, or a full path (like "/home/user/data/my-study.xml").

After this line runs, the variable doc holds the entire DDI document in memory. You can now read its contents or make changes.

docs.title: 2. Explore what is inside
docs.text:
Once you open a document, you can count and list what it contains. The Document object has properties (shortcuts) for the most common item types:

  • doc.questions: a list of all questions.
  • doc.variables: a list of all variables.
  • doc.concepts: a list of all concepts.
  • doc.universes: a list of all universes.
  • doc.code_lists: a list of all code lists.

Here is how to count items and print their identifiers:

doc = ddi.open_ddi("my-study.xml")

print(f"Questions:  {len(doc.questions)}")
print(f"Variables:  {len(doc.variables)}")
print(f"Concepts:   {len(doc.concepts)}")

# Print each question's identifier
for q in doc.questions:
    print(f"  Question: {q.identifier}")

# Print each variable's identifier
for v in doc.variables:
    print(f"  Variable: {v.identifier}")

An identifier is a unique name that DDI assigns to each item. It is like a student ID number: no two items share the same one.

docs.title: 3. Open with validation
docs.text:
You can ask ddi-l to check the file against the DDI rules while it loads. This is called validation. If the file has errors, you will see them right away instead of discovering them later.

doc = ddi.open_ddi("my-study.xml", validate=True)

The validate=True option tells open_ddi() to run the DDI schema check during loading. A schema is a set of rules that says which elements are allowed and how they must be arranged.

  • If the file is valid, open_ddi() returns the document as usual.
  • If the file breaks a schema rule, open_ddi() raises an exception: a Python error that stops the script unless you catch it. For a schema problem the exception is ddi.DDIValidationError.

To report the problem instead of stopping, catch the exception with try/except:

try:
    doc = ddi.open_ddi("my-study.xml", validate=True)
except ddi.DDIValidationError as error:
    print(f"Not valid: {error}")

The message has two parts. The first part names the rule that is broken. The part in parentheses, after at, is the path to the element with the problem, from the root of the file down. For example, (at /{ddi:instance:3_3}DDIInstance/{ddi:reusable:3_3}Version) points to the Version element directly under DDIInstance. You can ignore the parts in curly braces: they name the DDI namespace each element belongs to.

If the file is not even well-formed XML (for example, a closing tag is missing), open_ddi() raises ddi.DDIParseError instead, with or without validate=True.

Validating on load is helpful when you receive a file from someone else and want to make sure it follows the DDI standard before you start working with it.

docs.title: 4. Add new items to an existing document
docs.text:
You can add questions, variables, concepts, universes, and code lists to an existing document. The methods are the same ones you used when you created a new document:

doc = ddi.open_ddi("my-study.xml")

# Add a new question
q = doc.add_question(text="What is your highest level of education?")

# Add a new variable linked to the question
v = doc.add_variable(name="Education", question=q)

# Add a concept
c = doc.add_concept(name="Educational Attainment")

# Add a universe
u = doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18 and over")

Each add_* method returns the new item. You can use that item later, for example, to link a variable to a question or to set a custom property.

docs.title: Edit items that are already there
docs.text:
The items you get back, and the ones in doc.questions, doc.variables and the other lists, are live objects. Change a field and the change is saved with the document. A question keeps its wording in question_texts, a list with one entry per language, so question_texts[0].text is the first wording.

A variable can also be coded: its values come from a code list, the set of allowed answers to a question (for example "High school", "College", "University"). Two calls are enough for now:

  • doc.add_code_list(name=...) creates a new, empty code list in the document and returns it.
  • v.set_coded(code_list) records that the values of variable v come from that code list. Calling it again with another list switches the variable to that list.

Module 9 covers code lists in depth, including how to fill a list with its answers.

# Reword the question added above
q.question_texts[0].text = "What is the highest level of education you have completed?"

# Code the variable with a code list; calling set_coded() again switches lists
levels = doc.add_code_list(name="Education Levels")
v.set_coded(levels)

In a published file, an edit like this is a new version of the item. Later in the course, Module 15 shows the whole workflow for rewording a question and switching a variable to another code list, including the version bump and the references you must update.

docs.title: 5. Save the modified document
docs.text:
After you make changes, save the document to a file. You can save to the same filename (to overwrite) or to a new filename (to keep both copies). Your changes live only in memory until you call doc.save().

# Save to a new file; this keeps the original unchanged
doc.save("my-study-updated.xml")

It is usually best to save to a new filename. That way you always have the original file as a backup.

# Overwrite the original (use with care)
doc.save("my-study.xml")

To confirm that a save worked, open the new file again and count what is inside, as in Section 2.

docs.title: 6. The round-trip guarantee
docs.text:
ddi-l makes a promise: it will not delete content it does not understand. This is called the round-trip guarantee.

DDI XML files can contain many elements. ddi-l knows how to read and write the most common ones (questions, variables, concepts, code lists, and more). But if the file contains extra elements that ddi-l does not recognize, those elements are kept exactly as they are. They pass through the read-and-write cycle untouched.

This means you can safely open a file that was created by another tool, add your metadata, and save it. The parts you did not touch will stay the same.

Original file           ddi-l                  Saved file
┌──────────────┐        ┌────────────┐            ┌──────────────┐
│ Known items  │──────▶ │ Parsed     │──────────▶ │ Known items  │
│ Unknown XML  │──────▶ │ Preserved  │──────────▶ │ Unknown XML  │
└──────────────┘        └────────────┘            └──────────────┘

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Scenario

An archivist receives a DDI file from a research team. They need to check its contents, add missing metadata, validate the file, and save an updated copy.

Exercise 1 (O1). Create a study with two questions and two variables (or use a file from an earlier module). Save it to disk. Then re-open it with open_ddi() and print the question and variable counts.

Expected output:

Saved.
Questions: 2
Variables: 2
Answer 
import ddi_l as ddi

# Create and save
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Census 2024", agency="stats.example.org")
q1 = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q2 = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
v1 = doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q1)
v2 = doc.add_variable(name="Gender", question=q2)
doc.save("census-2024.xml")
print("Saved.")

# Re-open and inspect
doc2 = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024.xml")
print(f"Questions: {len(doc2.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 2
print(f"Variables: {len(doc2.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 2

Exercise 2 (O2). Files from other people are not always valid. Run this code to make a broken copy of census-2024.xml: the first version number becomes the word one.

from pathlib import Path

text = Path("census-2024.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
broken = text.replace("<r:Version>1</r:Version>", "<r:Version>one</r:Version>", 1)
Path("census-2024-broken.xml").write_text(broken, encoding="utf-8")

Then:

  1. Open census-2024-broken.xml with validate=True. Catch the ddi.DDIValidationError and print its message.
  2. From the message, name the element that is wrong and say what is wrong with it.
  3. Open the same file without validate=True and print its question count. What does this tell you?

Expected output:

Not valid: value doesn't match any pattern of ['[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)*'] (at /{ddi:instance:3_3}DDIInstance/{ddi:reusable:3_3}Version)
Opened without checking: 2 questions
Answer 
try:
    ddi.open_ddi("census-2024-broken.xml", validate=True)
except ddi.DDIValidationError as error:
    print(f"Not valid: {error}")

unchecked = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024-broken.xml")
print(f"Opened without checking: {len(unchecked.questions)} questions")

The path after at points to the Version element directly under DDIInstance. Its value, one, does not match the pattern for versions: [0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)* means digits, optionally followed by more groups of a dot and digits, such as 1 or 1.0.0.

Without validate=True, the broken file opens with no complaint. Only validation tells you that the file breaks the DDI rules.

Exercise 3 (O3). Work on the document you re-opened in Exercise 1 (doc2):

  1. Add two new questions and two new variables linked to them (MaritalStatus and HouseholdSize).
  2. Reword the first question to "What was your age at your last birthday?".
  3. Create a code list called "Marital Status Codes" and code the MaritalStatus variable with it.
  4. Validate the document. If it is valid, save it as census-2024-updated.xml.

Expected output:

Document is valid.
Saved updated file.
Answer 
q3 = doc2.add_question(text="What is your marital status?")
q4 = doc2.add_question(text="How many people live in your household?")
v3 = doc2.add_variable(name="MaritalStatus", question=q3)
v4 = doc2.add_variable(name="HouseholdSize", question=q4)

doc2.questions[0].question_texts[0].text = "What was your age at your last birthday?"

statuses = doc2.add_code_list(name="Marital Status Codes")
v3.set_coded(statuses)

errors = doc2.validate()
if errors:
    print("Validation errors:", errors)
else:
    print("Document is valid.")
    doc2.save("census-2024-updated.xml")
    print("Saved updated file.")

Exercise 4 (O4). Re-open census-2024-updated.xml. Print its question, variable and code list counts, and the wording of its first question. Then re-open the original census-2024.xml and confirm that it still has two questions.

Expected output:

Questions: 4
Variables: 4
Code lists: 1
First question: What was your age at your last birthday?
Original questions: 2
Answer 
doc3 = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024-updated.xml")
print(f"Questions: {len(doc3.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 4
print(f"Variables: {len(doc3.variables)}")
print(f"Code lists: {len(doc3.code_lists)}")
print(f"First question: {doc3.questions[0].question_texts[0].text}")

original = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024.xml")
print(f"Original questions: {len(original.questions)}")

The counts grew in the new file, and the original kept its two questions: saving under a new filename left it untouched.

Exercise 5 (O5). A partner's copy of your file contains an element that ddi-l does not model: a description of the units the study covers. Run this code to make that copy:

from pathlib import Path

text = Path("census-2024.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
extra = (
    '<r:AnalysisUnitsCovered><r:String xml:lang="en">'
    "Persons living in private households"
    "</r:String></r:AnalysisUnitsCovered>"
)
Path("census-2024-partner.xml").write_text(
    text.replace("<d:DataCollection>", extra + "<d:DataCollection>", 1),
    encoding="utf-8",
)

Before you go further, write down your prediction in one sentence: if you open census-2024-partner.xml, add a variable called Region, and save it as census-2024-partner-updated.xml, will the saved file still contain "Persons living in private households"? Then do it, and check by searching the saved file for that sentence.

Expected output:

True
Answer 
partner = ddi.open_ddi("census-2024-partner.xml", validate=True)
partner.add_variable(name="Region")
partner.save("census-2024-partner-updated.xml")

saved = Path("census-2024-partner-updated.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print("Persons living in private households" in saved)  # -> True

The element survives: ddi-l keeps XML it does not model exactly as it was, so opening and saving a file never deletes content you did not touch. This is the round-trip guarantee.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): What does this code print for a file with 3 questions and 5 variables?

doc = ddi.open_ddi("survey.xml"), then print(len(doc.questions), len(doc.variables))

A. 5 3

B. 0 0, because a file must be validated before you can count its items.

C. 8

D. 3 5

Answer

D. ddi.open_ddi() reads the whole file. doc.questions and doc.variables list its questions and variables, in that order in the print() call.

Question 2 (O2): What is wrong with this file?

ddi.open_ddi("partner.xml", validate=True) raises a ddi.DDIValidationError with this message:

value doesn't match any pattern of ['[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)*'] (at /{ddi:instance:3_3}DDIInstance/{ddi:reusable:3_3}Version)

A. The file partner.xml does not exist.

B. The Version element directly under DDIInstance holds a value that is not a version number such as 1 or 1.0.0.

C. The file has too many questions.

D. ddi-l cannot read DDI 3.3 files.

Answer

B. The path after at names the element: Version, under DDIInstance. The first part of the message says its value does not match the pattern for version numbers.

Question 3 (O3): Which line codes the variable v with the code list levels?

A. levels.set_coded(v)

B. doc.add_code_list(v)

C. v.set_coded(levels)

D. v.code_list = "levels"

Answer

C. set_coded() is a method of the variable, and it takes the code list as its argument. doc.add_code_list() creates a new list; it does not code a variable.

Question 4 (O4): What does my-study.xml contain afterwards?

You open my-study.xml, add a variable, and close Python without calling doc.save().

A. The original content, without the new variable.

B. The original content and the new variable.

C. Nothing: the file is emptied.

D. A backup copy of the original.

Answer

A. Changes live only in memory until you call doc.save(). The file on disk is unchanged.

Question 5 (O5): What happens to an element that ddi-l does not model?

A partner's file contains an element that ddi-l does not model. You open the file, add a variable, and save it under a new name.

A. It is deleted, because ddi-l writes only what it understands.

B. It is moved to the end of the file.

C. It is turned into a note.

D. It is kept unchanged in the saved file.

Answer

D. This is the round-trip guarantee: content that ddi-l does not recognize passes through the read-and-write cycle untouched.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can open an existing DDI file with ddi.open_ddi() and print how many questions and variables it holds. (O1)
  • I can open a file with validate=True, catch ddi.DDIValidationError, and name the element its message points to. (O2)
  • I can add items to an opened document, reword a question, and code a variable with a code list. (O3)
  • I can save the changed document under a new filename and re-open it to confirm my changes and the untouched original. (O4)
  • I can predict what happens to XML that ddi-l does not model when I open and save a file, and check it. (O5)

See also:

  • User guide: Open an existing file
  • From XML to objects

Instructor notes

  • Hands-on first. Have learners bring a DDI file from a previous module. If they do not have one, create a quick file together as a group. The goal is to practice the open-modify-save workflow with a real file.
  • Validate on load. Demonstrate what happens when you open a broken file with validate=True. Change a version number to a word, as in Exercise 2, to show a schema error (ddi.DDIValidationError). Delete a closing tag in a text editor to show a parse error (ddi.DDIParseError), which appears even without validate=True.
  • Round-trip demo. Exercise 5 adds an element that ddi-l does not model. Open the saved file in a text editor and show the element in place. This builds trust in the tool.
  • Common mistake: Learners sometimes forget to save after making changes. Remind them that changes live only in memory until doc.save() is called.
  • Code lists come later. This module uses add_code_list() and set_coded() with an empty list. If learners ask how to add the answers, point them to Module 9.
  • Extension activity: Ask advanced learners to open a file, add items, version the study (Module 15, later in the course), and save, combining both modules into one workflow.

docs.title: Module 7: Validate from the command line
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Run ddi validate on a DDI file and state from its output whether the file is valid.
  • O2. Interpret a ddi validate error: say what is wrong and where, using the message and the path after at, then fix the file so it validates.
  • O3. Run ddi lint on a file and name one finding by its severity, rule and message.
  • O4. Convert a DDI file to JSON with ddi to-json and write a normalized copy with ddi roundtrip.
  • O5. Check the exit code of a command after a valid and an invalid file, and predict the code (0 or 1) a script will get.

Prerequisites: Module 6.

Time: 30 min self-paced / 40 min instructor-led.

New in this module: ddi validate, ddi validate --format json, ddi lint, ddi lint --format table, ddi to-json, ddi roundtrip, echo $? (and echo %ERRORLEVEL% or $LASTEXITCODE on Windows).

docs.title: 1. Why use the command line?
docs.text:
So far you have written Python scripts to work with DDI files. But sometimes you just want to check a file quickly without writing code. The command line (also called a terminal or shell) lets you do that.

The command line is also useful when you need to:

  • Process many files at once. You can validate 20 files with one command.
  • Automate checks. You can add validation to a script that runs every night.
  • Plug into CI/CD pipelines. A CI/CD pipeline is an automated system that builds and tests software. Many teams use pipelines to catch errors early.

ddi-l includes a command-line tool called ddi. You installed it when you installed the ddi-l package (see Module 2).

The exercises use census-2024.xml, the file you saved in Exercise 1 of Module 6. Run the commands from the folder that holds it.

docs.title: 2. Validate a file
docs.text:
The ddi validate command checks whether a DDI XML file follows the DDI schema rules. A schema is a set of rules that says which elements are allowed, what order they must appear in, and which ones are required.

ddi validate my-study.xml

If the file is valid, you see:

Document is valid.

If the file has errors, you see one entry per problem. For example, here is the output for a file in which someone misspelled <r:Abstract> as <r:Abstrct>:

error: Unexpected child with tag '{ddi:reusable:3_3}Abstrct' at position 5.
    at /{ddi:instance:3_3}DDIInstance/{ddi:studyunit:3_3}StudyUnit
    context: <s:StudyUnit>
1 issue found.

Each error tells you:

  • what went wrong: the message after error:. Here, an element called Abstrct appears where the schema does not allow it.
  • where: the path after at. Read it from left to right, from the root of the file down to the element that holds the problem: DDIInstance, then StudyUnit. You can ignore the parts in curly braces, such as {ddi:reusable:3_3}: they name the DDI namespace each element belongs to. A number in square brackets, such as QuestionItem[2], means "the second QuestionItem".
  • what was found: the context: line shows the element (and its value, when it has one).

The last line counts the problems. For scripts, add --format json to get the same information as a JSON list (an empty list [] when the file is valid).

docs.title: 3. Reading the output
docs.text:
When you see "Document is valid.", it means the file follows all the DDI schema rules. No action is needed.

When you see errors, read each message carefully. The most common messages are:

The message says What it means Unexpected child with tag '...' An element is in the wrong place, is misspelled, or a required element before it is missing. value doesn't match any pattern of ... A text value breaks a rule, such as a version number that is not made of digits. Error: mismatched tag: line N, column M The file is not well-formed XML: a tag is not closed. The line and column say where.

The last kind of error stops ddi before the schema check: it cannot read the file at all.

Fix the errors in your Python script (or in the XML file directly), then run ddi validate again.

docs.title: 4. Lint a file
docs.text:
The ddi lint command checks quality rules that go beyond the schema. It runs the same rules as doc.lint(), which you used in Module 3. Linting means looking for problems that are technically allowed by the schema but are usually mistakes or bad practice.

ddi lint my-study.xml

For example, a lint rule might warn you that an item has no label, or that a reference points to an item that is not in the file. The file can still be valid XML, but the metadata is incomplete.

By default the output is JSON, for scripts. Add --format table for a table that is easier to read:

ddi lint my-study.xml --format table

severity  rule                     message
--------  -----------------------  ----------------------------------------
warning   ddi.maintainable.labels  Maintainable element is missing a label.
warning   ddi.maintainable.labels  Maintainable element is missing a label.

Each row is one finding, with three columns:

  • severity: how serious it is: error, warning or info.
  • rule: the name of the rule that found it, such as ddi.maintainable.labels. The lint rules page explains each rule.
  • message: what the rule found. Here, two items have no label.

docs.title: 5. Export to JSON
docs.text:
The ddi to-json command converts a DDI XML file into JSON format. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format that many tools and programming languages can read. It is easier for some people to read than XML.

ddi to-json my-study.xml --indent 2

The --indent 2 option adds spaces to make the output easier to read. Without it, the JSON is printed on one long line.

You can save the output to a file by using the > symbol:

ddi to-json my-study.xml --indent 2 > my-study.json

This creates a new file called my-study.json with the JSON content.

docs.title: 6. Round-trip
docs.text:
The ddi roundtrip command reads a DDI XML file and writes it back out. This is called a round-trip because the data travels in a circle: file to memory and back to file.

ddi roundtrip input.xml --output output.xml

Why is this useful?

  • Normalize formatting. Different tools may write XML with different spacing and ordering. A round-trip produces a clean, consistent format.
  • Test for data loss. If the output file is the same as the input, nothing was lost. You can compare the two files to check.

docs.title: 7. Exit codes
docs.text:
Every command-line tool returns an exit code when it finishes. An exit code is a number that tells you whether the command succeeded or failed.

Exit code Meaning 0 Success: everything is fine. 1 Failure: something went wrong.

ddi validate returns 1 when the file has at least one schema error. ddi lint returns 1 only when a finding has the severity error: warnings alone return 0. (Add --fail-severity warning to make warnings fail too.)

Why does this matter? Because scripts and pipelines can check the exit code to decide what to do next. For example:

ddi validate my-study.xml && echo "All good!" || echo "Fix the errors."

This line says: "Run ddi validate. If it succeeds (exit code 0), print 'All good!'. If it fails (exit code 1), print 'Fix the errors.'"

You can also print the exit code of the last command. On macOS and Linux, use $?:

ddi validate my-study.xml
echo $?

On Windows, use echo %ERRORLEVEL% in the Command Prompt, or $LASTEXITCODE in PowerShell.

If the file is valid, echo $? prints 0. If not, it prints 1.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Scenario

A national statistics office has 20 DDI XML files from different survey teams. They need to validate them all, check their quality, export one to JSON, and produce a normalized copy.

Exercise 1 (O1). Validate census-2024.xml from the Module 6 exercises (or any file from an earlier module) using ddi validate. Is the file valid?

Expected output:

Document is valid.
Answer 
ddi validate census-2024.xml

The output says Document is valid., so the file follows all the DDI schema rules.

Exercise 2 (O2). Break a file on purpose and read the error.

  1. Make a copy of census-2024.xml called broken.xml (cp census-2024.xml broken.xml on macOS and Linux, copy census-2024.xml broken.xml on Windows).
  2. Open broken.xml in a text editor. On line 5, change <r:Version>1</r:Version> to <r:Version>one</r:Version>. Save the file.
  3. Run ddi validate broken.xml.
  4. Write down what is wrong and where.

Keep broken.xml as it is: you fix it in Exercise 6.

Expected output:

error: value doesn't match any pattern of ['[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)*']
    at /{ddi:instance:3_3}DDIInstance/{ddi:reusable:3_3}Version
    context: <r:Version> one
1 issue found.
Answer 
cp census-2024.xml broken.xml
# edit line 5 of broken.xml, then:
ddi validate broken.xml
  • What: the value one does not match the pattern for versions. [0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)* means digits, optionally followed by more groups of a dot and digits, such as 1 or 1.0.0.
  • Where: the path after at ends with DDIInstance, then Version: the Version element directly under the root, which is the one on line 5. The context: line confirms the value found: one.

Exercise 3 (O3). Run ddi lint on census-2024.xml with --format table. Pick one finding and name its severity, its rule and its message. What would you change to make it go away?

Expected output:

severity  rule                     message
--------  -----------------------  ----------------------------------------
warning   ddi.maintainable.labels  Maintainable element is missing a label.
warning   ddi.maintainable.labels  Maintainable element is missing a label.
warning   ddi.maintainable.labels  Maintainable element is missing a label.
warning   ddi.maintainable.labels  Maintainable element is missing a label.
Answer 
ddi lint census-2024.xml --format table

One finding: severity warning, rule ddi.maintainable.labels, message "Maintainable element is missing a label." The file has four of them: its two questions and two variables have no label. To fix them, pass label= when you add each item, as in Section 9 of Module 3. The file is still valid: warnings point to quality, not to schema errors.

Exercise 4 (O4). Export census-2024.xml to JSON with ddi to-json. Count how many lines the JSON has.

Expected output: about 200 lines (wc -l prints the count followed by the filename).

Answer 
ddi to-json census-2024.xml --indent 2 > census-2024.json
wc -l census-2024.json

The wc -l command counts the number of lines in a file (on Windows PowerShell, use (Get-Content census-2024.json).Count). A file with two questions and two variables gives about 200 lines; more content gives more lines.

Exercise 5 (O4). Round-trip census-2024.xml. Compare the input and output sizes.

Expected output: two files of the same size, about 4 KB each.

Answer 
ddi roundtrip census-2024.xml --output census-2024-roundtrip.xml
ls -l census-2024.xml census-2024-roundtrip.xml

The ls -l command shows the file sizes (use dir on Windows). A file that ddi-l wrote itself comes back with exactly the same size. A file from another tool may differ a little, because of spacing; that is the normalization at work.

Exercise 6 (O5, O2). Check the exit codes.

  1. Run ddi validate census-2024.xml, then print the exit code (echo $? on macOS and Linux, echo %ERRORLEVEL% in the Windows Command Prompt, $LASTEXITCODE in PowerShell).
  2. Do the same with broken.xml from Exercise 2.
  3. Fix broken.xml (change one back to 1), validate it again, and print the exit code once more.

Expected output (the exit codes, in order):

0
1
0
Answer 
ddi validate census-2024.xml
echo $?
ddi validate broken.xml
echo $?
# edit line 5 of broken.xml back to <r:Version>1</r:Version>, then:
ddi validate broken.xml
echo $?

A valid file gives exit code 0. A file with a schema error gives 1, and the fixed file gives 0 again, with Document is valid. above it. A script that runs ddi validate can use these codes to stop before it publishes a broken file.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): What does this output tell you?

You run ddi validate study.xml and see Document is valid.

A. The file follows all the DDI schema rules; no action is needed.

B. The file has no lint findings either.

C. The file was converted to JSON.

D. The file was saved in a new, normalized format.

Answer

A. ddi validate checks the schema only. Lint findings are a separate check (ddi lint), so option B does not follow.

Question 2 (O2): Where is the problem in this output? 
error: Unexpected child with tag '{ddi:datacollection:3_3}QuestionTxt' at position 4.
    at /{ddi:instance:3_3}DDIInstance/{ddi:studyunit:3_3}StudyUnit/{ddi:datacollection:3_3}DataCollection/{ddi:datacollection:3_3}QuestionScheme/{ddi:datacollection:3_3}QuestionItem[1]
    context: <d:QuestionItem>
1 issue found.

A. In the title of the study.

B. The file is not well-formed XML.

C. Inside the first QuestionItem: it holds an element called QuestionTxt, which the schema does not allow there (it looks like a misspelled QuestionText).

D. On line 1 of the file.

Answer

C. The path after at ends with QuestionItem[1], the first question item, which holds the problem; the message names the unexpected element. A file that is not well-formed gives a mismatched tag error instead.

Question 3 (O3): What do these two results tell you about the file?

ddi validate data.xml prints Document is valid., and ddi lint data.xml --format table prints one row: warning ddi.maintainable.labels Maintainable element is missing a label.

A. The file breaks a schema rule.

B. The file is valid, but lint found a quality problem: an item has no label.

C. ddi lint and ddi validate check the same rules, so one of them is wrong.

D. The warning makes ddi lint return exit code 1.

Answer

B. Validation checks the schema; lint checks quality rules beyond it. A warning alone does not fail ddi lint: it returns 0 unless you pass --fail-severity warning.

Question 4 (O4): Which command writes a JSON copy of my-study.xml to my-study.json?

A. ddi roundtrip my-study.xml --output my-study.json

B. ddi validate my-study.xml > my-study.json

C. ddi lint my-study.json

D. ddi to-json my-study.xml --indent 2 > my-study.json

Answer

D. ddi to-json converts DDI XML to JSON, and > saves the output in a file. ddi roundtrip writes XML, and the ddi validate command in option B saves the validation report, not the document.

Question 5 (O4): Why would you run ddi roundtrip on a file from another tool?

A. To delete the elements that ddi-l does not model.

B. To write a copy with clean, consistent formatting, and to check that nothing is lost on the way.

C. To validate the file against the schema.

D. To convert the file to JSON.

Answer

B. A round-trip reads the file and writes it back out in a normalized format. ddi-l keeps the elements it does not model, so nothing is deleted.

Question 6 (O5): What does this script print?

broken.xml has three schema errors. A script runs:

ddi validate broken.xml
echo $?

A. 0

B. 3

C. 1 (after the list of errors)

D. -1

Answer

C. ddi validate returns 1 when the file has any schema error, however many there are. The exit code says "failed", not how many problems were found.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can run ddi validate on a file and say from the output whether it is valid. (O1)
  • I can read a ddi validate error, say what is wrong and where, and fix the file so it validates. (O2)
  • I can run ddi lint and name one finding by its severity, rule and message. (O3)
  • I can convert a file to JSON with ddi to-json and write a normalized copy with ddi roundtrip. (O4)
  • I can check the exit code after a valid and an invalid file, and predict what a script will get. (O5)

See also:

  • CLI recipes
  • Automation playbook
  • Lint rules

Instructor notes

  • Live demo. Run ddi validate, ddi lint, ddi to-json, and ddi roundtrip on a projector so learners can see the output in real time. Use files from previous modules.
  • Break a file on purpose. Exercise 2 changes a version number to a word, which gives a schema error. Also show a different break: delete a closing tag in a text editor and run ddi validate again. That gives Error: mismatched tag: line N, column M, because the file is no longer well-formed XML. Fix it and re-validate.
  • Batch validation. Show how to validate many files at once: for f in *.xml; do echo "--- $f ---"; ddi validate "$f"; done
  • Exit codes in practice. Write a short bash script that validates a file and prints a message based on the exit code. This prepares learners for CI/CD integration. Windows users print the code with echo %ERRORLEVEL% (Command Prompt) or $LASTEXITCODE (PowerShell).
  • Lint is not validation. Learners often expect lint warnings to make a file invalid. Use Exercise 3 and Question 3 to separate the two checks.
  • JSON as a bridge. Explain that JSON output can be loaded by other tools (R, JavaScript, data catalogs). This is useful for teams that do not use Python.
  • Timing note. This module is lighter on Python code and heavier on command-line skills. If your audience is less comfortable with the terminal, spend extra time on Section 1 and the exercises.

docs.title: Module 8: From a CSV or Excel table to DDI
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Write a script that reads the header of a CSV file and creates one DDI variable per column, with question text taken from a lookup table.
  • O2. Adapt the script to read the column names from an Excel sheet with pandas.
  • O3. Add concepts and a universe to the generated document and link each measured variable to its concept.
  • O4. Add question text in a second language and confirm that both wordings appear in the saved XML.
  • O5. Validate the generated document with doc.validate() and fix any error it reports before saving.

Prerequisites: Module 7.

Time: 45 min self-paced / 60 min instructor-led.

New in this module: csv.DictReader, reader.fieldnames, pd.read_excel(), df.columns, question_texts.append(), issue.message, issue.xpath.

docs.title: 1. The workflow overview
docs.text:
This is the key practical module. Most researchers already have data in a CSV or Excel file. They need DDI metadata that describes that data. This module teaches the real-world workflow: start from data you already have and produce a DDI document.

Already documenting in spreadsheets?

This module builds the DDI in code, one column at a time. If your study's concepts, questions, questionnaire, code lists, variables and data files are already in spreadsheets, lay them out as in Load DDI from spreadsheets and load them all in one step, in any number of languages. The spreadsheet templates are a starting point.

Your data lives in a CSV or Excel file. You want DDI metadata (an XML file) that describes it.

Here is the plan:

  1. Python reads the column names from your data file.
  2. For each column, it creates a variable in a DDI document.
  3. You link the variables to concepts, add a second language, and validate.
  4. You save the DDI document as XML.

The DDI file does not contain the data itself. It contains documentation about the data: variable names, questions, concepts, and more.

docs.title: 2. Step 1: Read column names from a CSV
docs.text:
A CSV file (Comma-Separated Values) is a plain-text file where each line is a row of data. The first line usually holds the column names.

Python has a built-in module called csv that can read these files. We use csv.DictReader to get the column names.

import csv

with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    columns = reader.fieldnames

print(columns)

Expected output:

['respondent_id', 'age', 'gender', 'income', 'education_level']

The variable columns is now a list of strings. Each string is a column name from your CSV file.

Sample file

Download the sample CSV and save it next to your script, or create your own file with these columns: respondent_id, age, gender, income, education_level.

Download survey_sample.csv

docs.title: 3. Step 2: Create one variable per column
docs.text:
Now we use ddi-l to build a DDI document. We loop over the column names and create one variable for each.

import csv
import ddi_l as ddi

# Read columns from CSV
with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    columns = reader.fieldnames

# The question each column records, worded the way respondents saw it
QUESTIONS = {
    "age": "How old are you?",
    "gender": "What is your gender?",
    "income": "What was your total income last year, before taxes?",
    "education_level": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
}

# Build the DDI document
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")

for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    # A column nobody was asked about, such as respondent_id, gets no question
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q)

doc.save("household-survey.xml")

print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")

Expected output:

Variables: 5

What happened:

  • We read 5 column names from the CSV.
  • For each column, we added a variable.
  • The four columns that record an answer also got a question, worded the way respondents saw it. respondent_id is assigned by the survey team, not asked, so its variable has no question.
  • We saved everything to an XML file.

Why a lookup table?

A column name such as education_level is shorthand, not a question. Building the text from it (f"What is the respondent's {col}?") produces "What is the respondent's education_level?", which nobody was ever asked. Copy the wording from your questionnaire into QUESTIONS instead, so the metadata records what respondents actually answered.

docs.title: 4. Step 3: Read the columns from Excel
docs.text:
If your data is in an Excel file (.xlsx), you can use the pandas library. Pandas is a popular Python tool for working with tables of data.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_excel("survey.xlsx")
columns = list(df.columns)

print(columns)

The variable df is a DataFrame: a table in memory. The columns property gives you the column names, just like csv.DictReader. pd.read_excel() reads the first sheet of the workbook; pass sheet_name="Data" to read the sheet called "Data" instead.

After this step, the rest of the code is the same as Step 2. Loop over columns, create variables, and save.

Installing pandas

If you do not have pandas, install it with: pip install pandas openpyxl

docs.title: 5. Link variables to concepts and a universe
docs.text:
Importing column names is a good start, but raw column names are not enough. Good metadata needs more detail. After importing, add:

  • Concepts to group related variables (see Module 5).
  • A universe to say who is being studied.

To link each variable to its concept inside the loop, create the concepts first and keep a second lookup table, CONCEPTS, that gives the concept for each measured column:

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")

# Concepts and the universe come first, so the loop can link to them
demo = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
econ = doc.add_concept(name="Economics")
doc.add_universe(name="Canadian households, 2024")

# The concept each measured column belongs to
CONCEPTS = {
    "age": demo,
    "gender": demo,
    "income": econ,
    "education_level": demo,
}

for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    # respondent_id measures nothing, so CONCEPTS.get() returns None: no link
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q, concept=CONCEPTS.get(col))

linked = [v for v in doc.variables if v.concept_references]
print(f"Linked variables: {len(linked)}")  # -> Linked variables: 4

This turns a bare list of column names into useful, shareable metadata. Code lists, which record the allowed answers to each question, are the subject of Module 9.

docs.title: 6. Documenting in more than one language
docs.text:
Many surveys serve bilingual or multilingual populations. For example, a Canadian survey might need metadata in both English and French. DDI stores multiple language versions inside the same document.

In Module 3 you learned that every add_* method accepts a lang= argument. Here is how to build a fully bilingual DDI document from a CSV file:

import csv
import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    columns = csv.DictReader(f).fieldnames

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")

# English and French wording for each question
QUESTIONS = {
    "age": ("How old are you?", "Quel âge avez-vous ?"),
    "gender": ("What is your gender?", "Quel est votre genre ?"),
    "income": (
        "What was your total income last year, before taxes?",
        "Quel a été votre revenu total l'an dernier, avant impôts ?",
    ),
    "education_level": (
        "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
        "Quel est le plus haut niveau de scolarité que vous avez atteint ?",
    ),
}

for col in columns:
    q = None
    if col in QUESTIONS:
        english, french = QUESTIONS[col]
        # Create the question in English (default)...
        q = doc.add_question(text=english)
        # ...and append the French wording to the same question
        q.question_texts.append(InternationalString(text=french, lang="fr"))

    # Create the variable with an English name
    v = doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q)

    # Append the French variable name
    v.names.append(InternationalString(text=col, lang="fr", child_tag="String"))

# Bilingual concepts
demo = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
demo.names.append(
    InternationalString(text="Démographie", lang="fr", child_tag="String")
)

econ = doc.add_concept(name="Economics")
econ.names.append(InternationalString(text="Économie", lang="fr", child_tag="String"))

# Bilingual universe
u = doc.add_universe(name="Canadian households, 2024")
u.names.append(
    InternationalString(text="Ménages canadiens, 2024", lang="fr", child_tag="String")
)

doc.save("household-survey-bilingual.xml")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")

Expected output:

Variables: 5

The pattern is the same for every item type:

  1. Create the item with add_*() (uses lang="en" by default).
  2. Append an InternationalString with lang="fr" to the item's text list (question_texts for questions, names for everything else).

You can add as many languages as you need. Just append one InternationalString per language.

To confirm that both languages were saved, open the XML file in a text editor: you will see both xml:lang="en" and xml:lang="fr" entries for each question, variable, concept, and universe. Or let Python check: read the saved file as text and look for both wordings of a question.

from pathlib import Path

saved = Path("household-survey-bilingual.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print("How old are you?" in saved, "Quel âge avez-vous ?" in saved)  # -> True True

docs.title: 7. Validate before you save
docs.text:
A script that builds metadata from a file can build something invalid without noticing: a typo in a lookup table is enough. Check the document with doc.validate() before you save it. It returns a list of issues, empty when the document follows the DDI schema. Each issue has:

  • issue.message: the rule that is broken.
  • issue.xpath: where, as a path from the root of the document, like the path after at in Module 7.
issues = doc.validate()
if issues:
    for issue in issues:
        print(issue.message)
        print(f"  at {issue.xpath}")
else:
    doc.save("household-survey-bilingual.xml")
    print("Document is valid. Saved.")  # -> Document is valid. Saved.

Only save when the list is empty; otherwise, read each message, fix the script, and run it again.

A common mistake: the language code

Language codes follow the BCP 47 standard: a language, then optionally a region, joined by a hyphen: fr, fr-CA, en-GB. Some software writes fr_CA, with an underscore. The DDI schema rejects it, and doc.validate() reports an issue whose message contains lang='fr_CA'.

docs.title: 8. A complete script
docs.text:
Here is the full CSV-to-DDI pipeline in one file. Copy this and change it to match your own data.

import csv
import ddi_l as ddi

# Step 1: Read column names
with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    columns = reader.fieldnames

# The question each column records, worded the way respondents saw it
QUESTIONS = {
    "age": "How old are you?",
    "gender": "What is your gender?",
    "income": "What was your total income last year, before taxes?",
    "education_level": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
}

# Step 2: Build the DDI document, with its concepts and universe
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")
demo = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
econ = doc.add_concept(name="Economics")
doc.add_universe(name="Canadian households, 2024")

# The concept each measured column belongs to
CONCEPTS = {
    "age": demo,
    "gender": demo,
    "income": econ,
    "education_level": demo,
}

# Step 3: One variable per column, linked to its question and concept
for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    # A column nobody was asked about, such as respondent_id, gets no question
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q, concept=CONCEPTS.get(col))

# Step 4: Validate, and save only a valid document
issues = doc.validate()
for issue in issues:
    print(issue.message)
if not issues:
    doc.save("household-survey.xml")

# Step 5: Verify
print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")
print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")
print(f"Universes: {len(doc.universes)}")
print(f"Schema problems: {len(issues)}")

Expected output:

Questions: 4
Variables: 5
Concepts: 2
Universes: 1
Schema problems: 0

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Scenario

A researcher has a CSV file called survey_sample.csv from a household survey. It has five columns: respondent_id, age, gender, income, education_level. They need to create DDI metadata for this dataset. Your job is to write a Python script that reads the CSV, builds the DDI document, links it to concepts and a universe, adds French wording, validates it, and saves it as XML.

  1. (O1) Download or create survey_sample.csv with these 5 columns: respondent_id, age, gender, income, education_level. Write a script that reads the CSV, creates a DDI document with one variable per column (with the question text from a lookup table), and saves it. Print the count.

    Expected output:

    Variables: 5
    Answer 
    import csv
import ddi_l as ddi

with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    columns = reader.fieldnames

# The question each column records, worded the way respondents saw it
QUESTIONS = {
    "age": "How old are you?",
    "gender": "What is your gender?",
    "income": "What was your total income last year, before taxes?",
    "education_level": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
}

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")
for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    # A column nobody was asked about, such as respondent_id, gets no question
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q)

doc.save("household-survey.xml")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 5

  2. (O2) (If pandas is installed) Adapt your Exercise 1 script to read the column names from an Excel sheet. To get a workbook, convert the sample CSV once with pd.read_csv("survey_sample.csv").to_excel("survey_sample.xlsx", index=False), or save it as survey_sample.xlsx from your spreadsheet program. Then use pd.read_excel() to get the columns, and create the variables the same way.

    Expected output:

    Variables: 5
    Answer

    Only the lines that read the column names change. QUESTIONS is the lookup table from Exercise 1.

    import pandas as pd
import ddi_l as ddi

# Make a workbook from the sample CSV (once)
pd.read_csv("survey_sample.csv").to_excel("survey_sample.xlsx", index=False)

df = pd.read_excel("survey_sample.xlsx")
columns = list(df.columns)

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")
for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q)
doc.save("household-survey-excel.xml")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")

  3. (O3) Rebuild the document from Exercise 1 with three concepts and one universe: Demographics (for age and gender), Economics (for income), Education (for education_level), and the universe "Canadian households, 2024". Link each measured variable to its concept; respondent_id gets no concept. Print the counts and the number of linked variables.

    Expected output:

    Concepts: 3
Universes: 1
Linked variables: 4
    Answer

    Continuing from Exercise 1 (columns and QUESTIONS):

    doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")

demo = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
econ = doc.add_concept(name="Economics")
educ = doc.add_concept(name="Education")
doc.add_universe(name="Canadian households, 2024")

CONCEPTS = {
    "age": demo,
    "gender": demo,
    "income": econ,
    "education_level": educ,
}

for col in columns:
    wording = QUESTIONS.get(col)
    q = doc.add_question(text=wording) if wording else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q, concept=CONCEPTS.get(col))

linked = [v for v in doc.variables if v.concept_references]
print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")  # -> Concepts: 3
print(f"Universes: {len(doc.universes)}")  # -> Universes: 1
print(f"Linked variables: {len(linked)}")  # -> Linked variables: 4

  4. (O4) Add French wording to the age and gender questions and a French name to the Demographics concept. Save the file as household-survey-bilingual.xml. Then read the saved file and confirm that both wordings of the age question are in it.

    Expected output:

    True True
    Answer 
    from pathlib import Path

from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

# The first question asks for the respondent's age, the second for their gender
doc.questions[0].question_texts.append(
    InternationalString(text="Quel âge avez-vous ?", lang="fr")
)
doc.questions[1].question_texts.append(
    InternationalString(text="Quel est votre genre ?", lang="fr")
)
doc.concepts[0].names.append(
    InternationalString(text="Démographie", lang="fr", child_tag="String")
)
doc.save("household-survey-bilingual.xml")

saved = Path("household-survey-bilingual.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print("How old are you?" in saved, "Quel âge avez-vous ?" in saved)  # -> True True

    You can also open the XML in a text editor and look for xml:lang="fr" next to the English text.

  5. (O5) This code adds French wording to the income question, but it has a mistake. Run it and read the issue that doc.validate() reports. Then fix the mistake, validate again, and save the document once it is valid.

    doc.questions[2].question_texts.append(
    InternationalString(
        text="Quel a été votre revenu total l'an dernier, avant impôts ?",
        lang="fr_CA",
    )
)
for issue in doc.validate():
    print(issue.message)

    Expected output (before the fix, then after it):

    attribute {http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace}lang='fr_CA': value doesn't match any pattern of ['[a-zA-Z]{1,8}(-[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,8})*']
Document is valid.
    Answer

    The message names the lang attribute and its value, fr_CA. The pattern [a-zA-Z]{1,8}(-[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,8})* means letters, optionally followed by groups of a hyphen and letters or digits. An underscore is not allowed, so write fr-CA (or just fr):

    doc.questions[2].question_texts[-1].lang = "fr-CA"

issues = doc.validate()
if issues:
    for issue in issues:
        print(issue.message)
else:
    print("Document is valid.")  # -> Document is valid.
    doc.save("household-survey-bilingual.xml")

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): How many variables does the document hold?

A CSV header is id,age,income. The script loops over reader.fieldnames and calls doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q) once per column.

A. 1

B. 2, because id was not asked of anyone.

C. 0, until you save the document.

D. 3

Answer

D. The loop adds one variable per column, and there are three columns. A column with no question, such as id, still gets a variable.

Question 2 (O1): Why does the script take question text from the QUESTIONS lookup table?

The alternative is to build it from the column name, with f"What is the respondent's {col}?".

A. Python cannot format strings that contain a column name.

B. So the metadata records the wording respondents actually saw, not a sentence made from a column name.

C. A lookup table makes the script run faster.

D. DDI does not allow question marks in generated text.

Answer

B. A column name such as education_level is shorthand. The question text in DDI should be the wording from the questionnaire.

Question 3 (O2): How do you get column names from a pandas DataFrame?

A. df.rows

B. df.fieldnames

C. df.columns

D. df.headers

Answer

C. Use df.columns to get the column names from a pandas DataFrame. Wrap it in list() to get a plain list. fieldnames belongs to csv.DictReader, not to pandas.

Question 4 (O3): Which call adds the income variable and links it to the Economics concept econ?

A. doc.add_variable(name="income", question=q, concept=econ)

B. doc.add_concept(name="income", concept=econ)

C. econ.add_variable("income")

D. doc.add_universe(name="income")

Answer

A. Pass the concept with concept= when you add the variable. In a loop, concept=CONCEPTS.get(col) does the same for every column.

Question 5 (O4): How can you confirm that French wording was saved?

You appended French wording to a question with q.question_texts.append(InternationalString(text=french, lang="fr")) and saved the document.

A. Count the variables in the document.

B. Run doc.validate(): it lists the languages in the document.

C. Open the CSV file and look for the French text.

D. Read the saved XML file and check that it contains the French wording, next to xml:lang="fr".

Answer

D. The saved XML is what other people receive, so check it: open it in a text editor, or read it with Path(...).read_text() and test "Quel âge avez-vous ?" in saved. The CSV holds data, not metadata.

Question 6 (O5): doc.validate() reports this issue. What is the fix?

attribute {http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace}lang='fr_CA': value doesn't match any pattern of ['[a-zA-Z]{1,8}(-[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,8})*']

A. Write the language code with a hyphen, fr-CA, or just fr.

B. Remove the French text from the document.

C. Save the file anyway: the issue is only a warning.

D. Rename the variable that holds the question.

Answer

A. The pattern allows letters joined by hyphens, not underscores. A schema issue makes the document invalid, so fix it before you save.

docs.title: Going further (optional)
docs.text: This section is for readers who store data in a SQL database. It has no objective, and you can skip it if you only use CSV or Excel files.

docs.title: Read column names from a SQL database
docs.text:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is a language for working with databases. We use Python's built-in sqlite3 module to connect to a SQLite database.

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("survey.db")
cursor = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM survey LIMIT 0")
columns = [desc[0] for desc in cursor.description]

print(columns)

The trick is LIMIT 0. It reads zero rows but still gives us the column names from cursor.description.

After this, the rest is the same: loop over columns and create variables.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can write a script that reads a CSV header and creates one variable per column, with question text from a lookup table. (O1)
  • I can adapt the script to read the column names from an Excel sheet with pandas. (O2)
  • I can add concepts and a universe and link each measured variable to its concept. (O3)
  • I can add question text in a second language and confirm that both wordings are in the saved XML. (O4)
  • I can validate the generated document and fix any error it reports before saving. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • This is the "aha" module for researchers and NSO staff. Many learners will recognize their own workflow here.
  • Key message: The CSV is the data. The DDI XML is documentation about the data. They are two separate files with two separate purposes.
  • Walk through the complete script line by line. Let learners type along.
  • The SQL example under "Going further" is optional. Skip it for non-technical audiences. It is there for database-savvy participants who ask "what about SQL?"
  • Exercise 5 plants a language code with an underscore (fr_CA). Many learners have seen that style in other software; let them find the fix from the message before you explain it.
  • If time allows, let learners try with their own CSV files. Real data makes the exercise more meaningful.
  • Common mistake: learners confuse the CSV file with the XML output. Remind them that doc.save() writes metadata, not data.

See also: Download the sample CSV file (survey_sample.csv).

docs.title: Module 9: Build code lists and controlled vocabularies
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Explain in two sentences what a code list and a category are, and why two surveys that share a code list can be compared.
  • O2. Write a script that creates code lists with doc.add_code_list() and adds their categories with doc.add_item(Category, name=...).
  • O3. Write a loop over doc.items(Category) that prints the name of every category, and predict the counts that len(doc.code_lists) and len(doc.items(Category)) return.
  • O4. Write a script that reads the distinct values of a CSV column and creates one category for each value.

Prerequisites: Module 8.

Time: 40 min self-paced / 50 min instructor-led.

New in this module: doc.add_code_list(), doc.code_lists, Category, doc.add_item(), doc.items(), item.names[0].text.

docs.title: 1. What is a code list?
docs.text:
A code list is a set of allowed answers for a question. It is also called a controlled vocabulary.

For example, the question "What is your gender?" might allow these answers:

  • Male
  • Female
  • Other

That set of three answers is a code list. Each answer in the list is called a category.

docs.title: 2. Why code lists matter
docs.text:
Code lists keep your data consistent. Without them, one person might type "M" and another might type "Male." The data becomes messy and hard to analyze.

Code lists also make surveys comparable. If two surveys use the same code list for employment status, you can compare their results.

National surveys often share standard code lists so that data from different countries can be combined.

docs.title: 3. Create a code list
docs.text:
Use doc.add_code_list(name=) to create a new code list.

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Census", agency="census.gc.ca")

cl_gender = doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
cl_employment = doc.add_code_list(name="Employment Status Codes")
cl_housing = doc.add_code_list(name="Housing Type Codes")

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")  # -> Code lists: 3

Each call creates one code list and adds it to the document.

docs.title: 4. Add categories
docs.text:
A category is one allowed answer in a code list. To add categories, use doc.add_item() with the Category type.

First, import Category:

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

Then add categories one at a time:

# Gender categories
doc.add_item(Category, name="Male")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Female")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Other")

# Employment status categories
doc.add_item(Category, name="Employed")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Unemployed")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Retired")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Student")

# Housing type categories
doc.add_item(Category, name="House")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Apartment")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Other Housing")

print(f"Categories: {len(doc.items(Category))}")  # -> Categories: 10

Categories and codes

doc.add_item(Category, ...) adds the category to the study. It does not yet place it inside one particular code list. In this module you build the code lists and their categories side by side. Module 14 shows how to put each category into its list as a code (a value such as 1 that points to the category).

docs.title: 5. The add_item() method
docs.text:
The add_item() method is a general tool. It works for any DDI item type, not just categories.

The pattern is always the same:

doc.add_item(SomeType, name="Some Name")

You pass the type as the first argument and the name as a keyword argument. This is how you add items that do not have their own convenience method like add_question() or add_variable().

docs.title: 6. Query items by type
docs.text:
Use doc.items(Category) to get a list of all categories in the document.

all_categories = doc.items(Category)
print(f"Total categories: {len(all_categories)}")  # -> Total categories: 10

for cat in all_categories:
    print(f"  - {cat.names[0].text}")

Each item keeps its names in a list called names, because an item can have a name in more than one language. names[0] is the first name, and .text is its text. The loop prints Male, Female, Other, and so on, in the order you added them.

This works for any registered type. Pass the type you want, and you get back a list of all items of that type.

docs.title: 7. Build code lists from CSV column values
docs.text:
In Module 8, you learned to read columns from a CSV file. You can go further: read the unique values in a column and turn them into categories.

This is useful when your data already has coded answers. The examples use the Module 8 sample file:

Download survey_sample.csv

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("survey_sample.csv")

# Get unique values from the "gender" column
unique_genders = df["gender"].dropna().unique()
print(unique_genders)  # -> ['Female' 'Male' 'Other']

# Create a code list and add one category per unique value
cl = doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
for val in unique_genders:
    doc.add_item(Category, name=str(val))

print(f"Categories: {len(doc.items(Category))}")

The dropna() call removes missing values. The unique() call returns only distinct values, with no duplicates.

Without pandas, Python's built-in csv module and a set do the same job: a set keeps one copy of each value. Exercise 5 uses that approach.

docs.title: 8. Real-world example
docs.text:
National statistical offices use standard code lists for employment classification. For example, the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO) defines hundreds of job categories.

When multiple countries use the same code list, their employment data can be compared. This is the power of controlled vocabularies: they make data interoperable.

In ddi-l, you build these code lists the same way: one category at a time, or by importing from a data file.

Scenario

You are building metadata for a national census. You need code lists for Gender (Male, Female, Other), Employment Status (Employed, Unemployed, Retired, Student), and Housing Type (House, Apartment, Other).

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (O1) A colleague asks why the census should reuse the employment status code list from last year's labour survey instead of letting interviewers type each answer. Write your answer in two sentences.

    Answer

    A sample answer: "A code list is the fixed set of allowed answers to a question, and each allowed answer (such as Employed or Retired) is a category. If the census uses the same code list as the labour survey, every answer falls into the same categories in both, so we can count and compare them directly instead of cleaning free text such as 'M', 'emp.' or 'working'."

  2. (O2) Create a census study with the title "National Census" and agency "census.gc.ca". Add 3 code lists (Gender Codes, Employment Status Codes, Housing Type Codes) and their categories (10 total). Print the counts.

    Expected output:

    Code lists: 3
Categories: 10
    Answer 
    import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Census", agency="census.gc.ca")

doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Male")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Female")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Other")

doc.add_code_list(name="Employment Status Codes")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Employed")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Unemployed")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Retired")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Student")

doc.add_code_list(name="Housing Type Codes")
doc.add_item(Category, name="House")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Apartment")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Other Housing")

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")
print(f"Categories: {len(doc.items(Category))}")

  3. (O3) List all category names. Loop over doc.items(Category) and print each category's name.

    Expected output:

    Male
Female
Other
Employed
Unemployed
Retired
Student
House
Apartment
Other Housing
    Answer 
    for cat in doc.items(Category):
    print(cat.names[0].text)

    The categories come back in the order you added them.

  4. (O2, O3) The census also asks about marital status. Add a code list "Marital Status Codes" with four categories: Single, Married, Separated, Widowed. Before you run your script, write down the two counts it will print. Then run it and check your prediction.

    Expected output:

    Code lists: 4
Categories: 14
    Answer 
    doc.add_code_list(name="Marital Status Codes")
for status in ("Single", "Married", "Separated", "Widowed"):
    doc.add_item(Category, name=status)

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")
print(f"Categories: {len(doc.items(Category))}")

    One new code list makes 3 + 1 = 4. Four new categories make 10 + 4 = 14. The counts cover the whole document, not just the list you added last.

  5. (O4) Generate categories from a CSV column's unique values. Read survey_sample.csv, get the unique values from the education_level column, and create a category for each one.

    Expected output:

    Education levels: 4
    Answer

    Python's built-in csv module is enough; a set keeps one copy of each value:

    import csv

with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    levels = sorted({row["education_level"] for row in csv.DictReader(f)})

doc.add_code_list(name="Education Level Codes")
for level in levels:
    doc.add_item(Category, name=level)

print(f"Education levels: {len(levels)}")

    The file has five rows but only four distinct levels, because "Bachelor" appears twice. With pandas, df["education_level"].dropna().unique() gives the same values, as in Section 7.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): Why is Survey 2 easier to compare?

Survey 1 lets interviewers type employment status as free text. Survey 2 uses the code list Employed / Unemployed / Retired / Student. Why is Survey 2 easier to compare with other surveys?

A. Its data file is smaller.

B. Python needs a code list before it can save a variable.

C. DDI cannot store free-text answers.

D. Every answer is one of a fixed set of categories, so another survey that uses the same code list counts exactly the same answers.

Answer

D. A code list fixes the allowed answers. Two surveys that share it put every answer into the same categories, so their counts line up. Free text such as "M", "emp." or "working" has to be cleaned first.

Question 2 (O2): Which fix makes this script run?

A script calls doc.add_item(Category, name="Male") and stops with NameError: name 'Category' is not defined. Which fix makes it run?

A. Add from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category at the top of the script.

B. Replace the call with doc.add_category(name="Male").

C. Call doc.add_code_list(name="Male") instead.

D. Put the type in quotes: doc.add_item("Category", name="Male").

Answer

A. Category is a class that you import before you use it. doc.add_category() does not exist, add_code_list() would create a code list called "Male", and add_item() needs the class itself, not its name as a string.

Question 3 (O3): What does this script print? 
import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

census = ddi.new_study(title="Census", agency="example.org")
census.add_code_list(name="Yes/No")
census.add_item(Category, name="Yes")
census.add_item(Category, name="No")
census.add_code_list(name="Tenure")
census.add_item(Category, name="Owner")
census.add_item(Category, name="Renter")
census.add_item(Category, name="Other")
print(len(census.code_lists), len(census.items(Category)))

A. 2 2

B. 5 5

C. 2 5

D. 7 0

Answer

C. The script creates two code lists and five categories. items(Category) counts every category in the document, whichever list you meant it for.

Question 4 (O3): Which loop prints the name of every category in doc?

A. for cat in doc.code_lists: print(cat.names[0].text)

B. for cat in doc.items(Category): print(cat.names[0].text)

C. for cat in doc.categories: print(cat)

D. for cat in doc.items("Category"): print(cat.identifier)

Answer

B. doc.items(Category) returns every category, and names[0].text is the first name of each one. Option A prints the code list names, doc.categories does not exist, and items() takes the class, not a string.

Question 5 (O4): How many categories does a CSV column give?

A CSV gender column holds Female, Male, Female, (blank), Other, Male. You keep one copy of each value, skip the blank, and add one category per value. How many categories do you add?

A. 3

B. 4

C. 5

D. 6

Answer

A. The distinct non-blank values are Female, Male and Other. With pandas, df["gender"].dropna().unique() returns exactly those three.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can explain in two sentences what a code list and a category are, and why a shared code list makes surveys comparable. (O1)
  • I can write a script that creates code lists with doc.add_code_list() and adds categories with doc.add_item(Category, name=...). (O2)
  • I can write a loop over doc.items(Category) that prints every category's name, and predict what len(doc.code_lists) and len(doc.items(Category)) return. (O3)
  • I can write a script that turns the distinct values of a CSV column into categories. (O4)

Instructor notes

  • Start by asking: "Have you ever seen a survey with a dropdown menu? That dropdown is a code list."
  • Show a real example: the gender dropdown on a government form. Point out that the choices are fixed. That is a controlled vocabulary.
  • The add_item() pattern can feel abstract. Remind learners: "You are telling Python what type to create and what to name it."
  • Exercise 4 asks learners to predict before they run. Collect a few predictions first. A common wrong prediction is Categories: 4, from learners who think the count covers only the new list.
  • Exercise 5 connects Module 8 (CSV) to Module 9 (code lists). Faster learners can repeat it for the gender column.
  • If learners ask how a category gets inside a particular code list in the DDI XML: each list holds codes, and each code points to a category. Module 14 builds them. For now, learners create the lists and the categories side by side.

See also: User guide: Code lists | User guide: Any item type

docs.title: Module 10: Map a questionnaire to DDI flow logic
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Identify the questions, sections, skip rules and repeat rules in a questionnaire spec, and name the DDI construct for each (QuestionConstruct, Sequence, IfThenElse, Loop, StatementItem, Instrument).
  • O2. Write a script that wraps each question in a QuestionConstruct and lists the constructs, in order, in one Sequence per section with .to_reference().
  • O3. Add an IfThenElse that sets its condition with set_condition() and runs a section or question only when the condition is true.
  • O4. Add a Loop that repeats a section, such as a household roster, by pointing it at that section.
  • O5. Create an Instrument that points to the main Sequence, and check that doc.validate() returns [] for the whole flow.

Prerequisites: Module 9.

Time: 50 min self-paced / 60 min instructor-led.

New in this module: QuestionConstruct, Sequence, StatementItem, IfThenElse, set_condition(), Loop, Instrument, .to_reference().

docs.title: 1. From paper to DDI
docs.text:
Most questionnaires start as a written specification. The spec lists the questions in order and describes skip patterns: rules like "If the respondent is under 18, skip to Section C."

Your job is to turn that spec into DDI metadata so that the flow logic is machine-readable. This module teaches you how.

docs.title: 2. A sample questionnaire spec
docs.text:
Here is a simple health survey specification. Read it carefully; we will map every part to DDI.

Health Survey Spec

Section A: Demographics

  • A1. What is your age? (numeric)
  • A2. What is your gender? (code list: Male, Female, Other)

Section B: Employment (skip if age < 16)

  • B1. Are you currently employed? (Yes / No)
  • B2. What is your occupation? (text, ask only if B1 = Yes)

Section C: Health

  • C1. How would you rate your general health? (code list: Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor)
  • C2. Do you smoke? (Yes / No)

Household Roster (repeat Section A for each household member)

docs.title: 3. The DDI building blocks
docs.text:
Each part of the spec maps to a DDI control construct:

Spec element DDI construct What it does A section intro StatementItem Shows text without asking a question A question QuestionConstruct Asks one question An ordered section Sequence Groups steps in order "Skip if..." IfThenElse Branches based on a condition "Ask only if..." IfThenElse Same; the condition decides which path "Repeat for each..." Loop Repeats a section for a list of items The whole questionnaire Instrument Points to the top-level Sequence

All of these live in the ddi_l.models.datacollection module:

from ddi_l.models.datacollection import (
    Instrument,
    Sequence,
    QuestionConstruct,
    IfThenElse,
    Loop,
    StatementItem,
)

Two things to remember

  • You create every construct with the same doc.add_item(<Type>, name="...") call you already use for categories in Module 9.
  • You link constructs to one another with .to_reference(). A reference says "this construct points to that one". It carries the target's identifier and type so the file stays valid.

docs.title: 4. Step 1: Create the study and questions
docs.text:
First, create the study and all the questions from the spec. Each question becomes a DDI question item.

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Health Survey", agency="health.gc.ca")

# Section A
q_age = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q_gender = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")

# Section B
q_employed = doc.add_question(text="Are you currently employed?")
q_occupation = doc.add_question(text="What is your occupation?")

# Section C
q_health = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your general health?")
q_smoke = doc.add_question(text="Do you smoke?")

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 6

docs.title: 5. Step 2: Create QuestionConstructs
docs.text:
A QuestionConstruct wraps a question so it can be placed in a Sequence. Think of it as the instruction "now ask this question."

Add one for each question, and point it at the question with .to_reference():

qc_age = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Age", question_reference=q_age.to_reference()
)
qc_gender = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Gender", question_reference=q_gender.to_reference()
)
qc_employed = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Employed", question_reference=q_employed.to_reference()
)
qc_occupation = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct,
    name="Ask Occupation",
    question_reference=q_occupation.to_reference(),
)
qc_health = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct,
    name="Ask Health Rating",
    question_reference=q_health.to_reference(),
)
qc_smoke = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Smoke", question_reference=q_smoke.to_reference()
)

print(f"QuestionConstructs: {len(doc.items(QuestionConstruct))}")
# -> QuestionConstructs: 6

docs.title: 6. Step 3: Build Sequences for each section
docs.text:
The spec has three sections (A, B, C). Each section becomes a Sequence that lists its steps in order. You list the steps with control_construct_references, one reference per step:

seq_demographics = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section A - Demographics",
    control_construct_references=[qc_age.to_reference(), qc_gender.to_reference()],
)
seq_employment = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section B - Employment",
    control_construct_references=[qc_employed.to_reference()],
)
seq_health = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section C - Health",
    control_construct_references=[qc_health.to_reference(), qc_smoke.to_reference()],
)

print(f"Steps in Section A: {len(seq_demographics.control_construct_references)}")
# -> Steps in Section A: 2

A Sequence lists constructs, not questions: it points to qc_age, the instruction to ask, not to q_age, the question's content.

You can also add a StatementItem to introduce a section. It shows a message instead of asking a question:

intro_a = doc.add_item(StatementItem, name="Welcome to the National Health Survey")

docs.title: 7. Step 4: Model skip patterns with IfThenElse
docs.text:
The spec says: "Skip Section B if age < 16." In DDI, this becomes an IfThenElse construct.

An IfThenElse has up to three parts:

  • If condition: the rule to check (age >= 16)
  • Then: which construct to run if the rule is true (Section B)
  • Else (optional): which construct to run if it is false

Create it with add_item(), set the rule with set_condition(), then connect the "then" branch with .to_reference():

skip_employment = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Age gate for employment")
skip_employment.set_condition("age >= 16", description="Working age")
skip_employment.then_construct_reference = seq_employment.to_reference()
