The age gate needs no "else" branch. When the respondent is under 16, nothing runs, and the flow simply continues with the next step of the main Sequence (Section C, in Step 7). When you do need an else branch, set else_construct_reference the same way.

docs.title: 8. Step 5: Model "ask only if" with a nested IfThenElse
docs.text:
The spec says: "Ask B2 (occupation) only if B1 = Yes." This is another IfThenElse, this time inside Section B. The "then" path runs the occupation QuestionConstruct; there is no "else" path, so the question is skipped when the condition is false:

ask_occupation = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Occupation routing")
ask_occupation.set_condition("employed == 1", description="Employed")
ask_occupation.then_construct_reference = qc_occupation.to_reference()

# Section B asks B1, then runs this gate
seq_employment.control_construct_references.append(ask_occupation.to_reference())

print(f"Steps in Section B: {len(seq_employment.control_construct_references)}")
# -> Steps in Section B: 2

docs.title: 9. Step 6: Model a household roster with Loop
docs.text:
The spec says: "Repeat Section A for each household member." DDI represents this with a Loop construct.

A Loop repeats a control construct (usually a Sequence) for each item in a list. For example, it runs the demographics section once per household member. Add it like any other construct, and point it at the section it repeats with control_construct_reference:

from ddi_l.models.datacollection import Loop

roster_loop = doc.add_item(Loop, name="Household roster loop")
roster_loop.control_construct_reference = seq_demographics.to_reference()

print(roster_loop.control_construct_reference.identifier == seq_demographics.identifier)
# -> True

Note the difference: a Sequence lists many steps (control_construct_references, plural), while a Loop repeats one (control_construct_reference, singular).

docs.title: 10. Step 7: Build the main Sequence and Instrument
docs.text:
The main Sequence defines the overall flow of the questionnaire. It references the welcome statement, the section sequences, the IfThenElse gate, and the loop, in order.

main_seq = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Main Survey Flow",
    control_construct_references=[
        intro_a.to_reference(),
        seq_demographics.to_reference(),
        skip_employment.to_reference(),
        seq_health.to_reference(),
        roster_loop.to_reference(),
    ],
)

The order is:

  1. StatementItem: Welcome
  2. Sequence: Section A (Demographics)
  3. IfThenElse: Age gate (→ Section B, or skip it)
  4. Sequence: Section C (Health)
  5. Loop: Household roster

Finally, create an Instrument that points to the main Sequence. The Instrument is the top-level entry point: it says "this is the questionnaire."

instrument = doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Health Survey Instrument")
instrument.control_construct_reference = main_seq.to_reference()
print(f"Instruments: {len(doc.items(Instrument))}")  # -> Instruments: 1

# The whole flow is valid DDI:
assert doc.validate() == []

The second line is the one that matters. Without it the Instrument has a name and nothing else (a questionnaire that administers nothing), and the document is still perfectly valid, because the schema does not require the link. Only the ControlConstructReference connects the entry point to the flow you just built.

docs.title: 11. The complete mapping
docs.text:
Here is the full spec mapped to DDI, as a diagram. Each arrow is a reference in the XML. A Sequence's numbered steps run in order. An IfThenElse runs its "then" construct only when its condition holds; neither gate has an "else", and DDI has no "go to". When a construct ends, the flow continues with the next step of the Sequence that holds it.

flowchart TD
    I["Instrument: Health Survey"] -->|ControlConstructReference| M["Sequence: Main Flow"]
    M -->|1| W["StatementItem: Welcome"]
    M -->|2| SA["Sequence: Section A"]
    M -->|3| ITE1["IfThenElse: Age >= 16?"]
    M -->|4| SC["Sequence: Section C"]
    M -->|5| L["Loop: Household Roster"]
    SA -->|1| QC1["QuestionConstruct: Ask Age"]
    SA -->|2| QC2["QuestionConstruct: Ask Gender"]
    ITE1 -->|then| SB["Sequence: Section B"]
    SB -->|1| QC3["QuestionConstruct: Ask Employed"]
    SB -->|2| ITE2["IfThenElse: Employed = Yes?"]
    ITE2 -->|then| QC4["QuestionConstruct: Ask Occupation"]
    SC -->|1| QC5["QuestionConstruct: Ask Health"]
    SC -->|2| QC6["QuestionConstruct: Ask Smoke"]
    L -->|repeats| SA

docs.title: 12. Mapping steps
docs.text:
Follow these steps when you map any questionnaire spec to DDI:

  1. List all questions → add_question(), then add_item(QuestionConstruct, ...) for each.
  2. Identify sections → add_item(Sequence, ...) for each.
  3. Find "skip if..." rules → add_item(IfThenElse, ...) for each.
  4. Find "ask only if..." rules → add_item(IfThenElse, ...) for each.
  5. Find "repeat for each..." rules → add_item(Loop, ...) for each.
  6. Find section introductions → add_item(StatementItem, ...) for each.
  7. Build the main Sequence that ties everything together.
  8. Create the Instrument that points to the main Sequence, and run doc.validate().

Scenario

You received the Health Survey spec above from your research team. Your task: create the DDI document with all questions, build the flow logic with Sequences, IfThenElse gates and a Loop, and connect everything to an Instrument.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (O1) Read this short spec. For each line, name the DDI construct (or constructs) you would use. Do not write code yet.

    • Intro: "This survey asks about your trips to work."
    • T1. Do you travel to a workplace? (Yes / No)
    • T2. How do you usually travel? (ask only if T1 = Yes)
    • T3. How many minutes did the trip take? (repeat for each trip you made last week)
    Answer
    • Intro → a StatementItem.
    • T1, T2 and T3 → one question each, wrapped in a QuestionConstruct.
    • "ask only if T1 = Yes" → an IfThenElse whose condition tests T1 and whose "then" branch runs T2's QuestionConstruct.
    • "repeat for each trip" → a Loop that points to T3's QuestionConstruct (or to a Sequence that holds it).
    • The order of the steps → the main Sequence.
    • The whole questionnaire → an Instrument that points to the main Sequence.

  2. (O2) Create a study for the Health Survey and add its 6 questions. Wrap each question in a QuestionConstruct, then add a Sequence for each section (A, B, C) that lists its constructs in order. Print the counts and the number of steps in Section A.

    Expected output:

    QuestionConstructs: 6
Sequences: 3
Steps in Section A: 2
    Answer 
    import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.datacollection import QuestionConstruct, Sequence

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Health Survey", agency="health.gc.ca")
q_age = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q_gender = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
q_employed = doc.add_question(text="Are you currently employed?")
q_occupation = doc.add_question(text="What is your occupation?")
q_health = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your general health?")
q_smoke = doc.add_question(text="Do you smoke?")

qc_age = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Age", question_reference=q_age.to_reference()
)
qc_gender = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Gender", question_reference=q_gender.to_reference()
)
qc_employed = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct,
    name="Ask Employed",
    question_reference=q_employed.to_reference(),
)
qc_occupation = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct,
    name="Ask Occupation",
    question_reference=q_occupation.to_reference(),
)
qc_health = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Health", question_reference=q_health.to_reference()
)
qc_smoke = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Smoke", question_reference=q_smoke.to_reference()
)

seq_demographics = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section A - Demographics",
    control_construct_references=[qc_age.to_reference(), qc_gender.to_reference()],
)
seq_employment = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section B - Employment",
    control_construct_references=[qc_employed.to_reference()],
)
seq_health = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section C - Health",
    control_construct_references=[qc_health.to_reference(), qc_smoke.to_reference()],
)

print(f"QuestionConstructs: {len(doc.items(QuestionConstruct))}")
print(f"Sequences: {len(doc.items(Sequence))}")
print(f"Steps in Section A: {len(seq_demographics.control_construct_references)}")

  3. (O3) Add the two gates from the spec. The age gate runs Section B only when age >= 16. The occupation gate runs B2 only when employed == 1; place it in Section B, after B1. Print the number of IfThenElse items and the number of steps in Section B.

    Expected output:

    IfThenElse: 2
Steps in Section B: 2
    Answer 
    from ddi_l.models.datacollection import IfThenElse

skip_employment = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Age gate for employment")
skip_employment.set_condition("age >= 16", description="Working age")
skip_employment.then_construct_reference = seq_employment.to_reference()

ask_occupation = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Occupation routing")
ask_occupation.set_condition("employed == 1", description="Employed")
ask_occupation.then_construct_reference = qc_occupation.to_reference()
seq_employment.control_construct_references.append(ask_occupation.to_reference())

print(f"IfThenElse: {len(doc.items(IfThenElse))}")
print(f"Steps in Section B: {len(seq_employment.control_construct_references)}")

  4. (O4) Add the household roster: a Loop that repeats Section A. Print the number of loops, and check that the loop points to Section A.

    Expected output:

    Loops: 1
Repeats Section A: True
    Answer 
    from ddi_l.models.datacollection import Loop

roster_loop = doc.add_item(Loop, name="Household roster loop")
roster_loop.control_construct_reference = seq_demographics.to_reference()

print(f"Loops: {len(doc.items(Loop))}")
repeats_a = (
    roster_loop.control_construct_reference.identifier == seq_demographics.identifier
)
print(f"Repeats Section A: {repeats_a}")

  5. (O5) Add a welcome StatementItem and the main Sequence (welcome, Section A, age gate, Section C, roster loop). Create an Instrument that points to the main Sequence. Print the number of steps in the main flow, the number of instruments, and the number of validation errors.

    Expected output:

    Steps in main flow: 5
Instruments: 1
Validation errors: 0
    Answer 
    from ddi_l.models.datacollection import Instrument, StatementItem

intro_a = doc.add_item(StatementItem, name="Welcome to the National Health Survey")
main_seq = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Main Survey Flow",
    control_construct_references=[
        intro_a.to_reference(),
        seq_demographics.to_reference(),
        skip_employment.to_reference(),
        seq_health.to_reference(),
        roster_loop.to_reference(),
    ],
)
instrument = doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Health Survey Instrument")
instrument.control_construct_reference = main_seq.to_reference()

print(f"Steps in main flow: {len(main_seq.control_construct_references)}")
print(f"Instruments: {len(doc.items(Instrument))}")
print(f"Validation errors: {len(doc.validate())}")

  6. (O1, O5) (Optional) Draw a flowchart of your own survey (real or imaginary) on paper. Label each box with the DDI construct type. Then build it in Python with add_item(), link the constructs with .to_reference(), and validate it.

    Answer

    Answers vary. Check that every QuestionConstruct references a question, that each Sequence lists its steps in the order respondents see them, and that the Instrument points to the top-level Sequence. Run doc.validate() before you save: it should return [].

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): Which constructs does this spec line need?

The spec says: "B2. What is your occupation? (ask only if B1 = Yes)".

A. A QuestionConstruct for B2, run by the "then" branch of an IfThenElse whose condition tests B1.

B. A Loop that repeats B2 for each answer to B1.

C. A StatementItem that shows the text of B2.

D. A second Instrument for employed respondents.

Answer

A. "Ask only if" is a condition, so it is an IfThenElse. Its "then" branch runs the QuestionConstruct that asks B2.

Question 2 (O2): What is wrong with this Sequence? 

seq_a = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section A",
    control_construct_references=[q_age.to_reference(), q_gender.to_reference()],
)

A. Nothing. A Sequence can list questions directly.

B. A Sequence can hold only one step.

C. It lists the questions themselves. It should list the QuestionConstructs that ask them (qc_age, qc_gender).

D. .to_reference() must be called on the Sequence, not on its steps.

Answer

C. A Sequence orders control constructs. The question holds the content; the QuestionConstruct is the instruction "ask it now", and that is what a Sequence lists.

Question 3 (O3): A 12-year-old reaches this gate. What happens next?

The main Sequence is: welcome, Section A, skip_employment, Section C.

skip_employment = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Age gate for employment")
skip_employment.set_condition("age >= 16")
skip_employment.then_construct_reference = seq_employment.to_reference()

A. Section B, then Section C.

B. Section B only, then the survey ends.

C. Nothing more: the survey ends at the gate.

D. Section B is skipped, and the flow continues with Section C, the next step of the main Sequence.

Answer

D. The condition age >= 16 is false, and the gate has no "else" branch, so nothing runs inside it. The main Sequence then moves on to its next step, Section C.

Question 4 (O4): Which line makes the roster repeat Section A?

You want roster_loop to repeat Section A (seq_demographics) for each household member. Which line does that?

A. seq_demographics.control_construct_references.append(roster_loop.to_reference())

B. roster_loop.control_construct_reference = seq_demographics.to_reference()

C. roster_loop.set_condition("household members")

D. roster_loop = doc.add_item(Sequence, name="Household roster")

Answer

B. A Loop points to the one construct it repeats through control_construct_reference. Option A would put the loop inside Section A, which is the wrong way round.

Question 5 (O5): What if the Instrument is not linked to the flow?

You create the Instrument but forget instrument.control_construct_reference = main_seq.to_reference(). What is true?

A. doc.validate() reports an error about the missing link.

B. Python raises AttributeError when you save.

C. doc.validate() still returns [], but the Instrument points to no flow, so it administers nothing.

D. The Instrument finds the main Sequence on its own.

Answer

C. The schema does not require the link, so the file is valid. But only control_construct_reference connects the questionnaire's entry point to the flow. Always set it, then validate.

docs.title: Going further (optional)
docs.text: This section has no objective or quiz question. Read it when you need routing with more than two paths.

docs.title: Multi-way routing with ElseIf
docs.text:
Some specs route respondents to one of several sections: "if 65 or older, ask about retirement; if 16 to 64, ask about employment; otherwise skip both." One IfThenElse can hold extra conditions as ElseIf branches, added with add_elseif():

q_retired = doc.add_question(text="In what year did you retire?")
qc_retired = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct,
    name="Ask Retirement Year",
    question_reference=q_retired.to_reference(),
)
seq_retirement = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Section B2 - Retirement",
    control_construct_references=[qc_retired.to_reference()],
)

age_router = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Age router")
age_router.set_condition("age >= 65", description="Retirement age")
age_router.then_construct_reference = seq_retirement.to_reference()
age_router.add_elseif(seq_employment.to_reference(), command="age >= 16")

print(f"ElseIf branches: {len(age_router.else_if_branches)}")
# -> ElseIf branches: 1

The conditions are checked in order, so test the narrowest group first. If the first condition were age >= 16, a 70-year-old would match it and never reach the retirement branch. A respondent under 16 matches neither condition, so nothing runs; set else_construct_reference if that case needs its own branch.

Try it: add an "else" branch to age_router that runs a StatementItem thanking respondents under 16, then run doc.validate().

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can identify the questions, sections, skip rules and repeat rules in a spec, and name the DDI construct for each. (O1)
  • I can write a script that wraps each question in a QuestionConstruct and lists the constructs, in order, in one Sequence per section. (O2)
  • I can add an IfThenElse with set_condition() that runs a section or question only when its condition is true. (O3)
  • I can add a Loop that repeats a section, such as a household roster. (O4)
  • I can create an Instrument that points to the main Sequence, and check that doc.validate() returns []. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Start with the paper spec on screen. Ask learners to circle every question, underline every skip rule, and box every "repeat" instruction. This makes the mapping concrete before touching code.
  • Draw the flowchart on a whiteboard. Label each box with the DDI construct name. Then translate box-by-box to Python.
  • Stress the .to_reference() habit: every time one construct points to another (a Sequence to its steps, an IfThenElse to its branches), the link is a reference, not the object itself. References keep the file valid because they carry the target's identifier and type.
  • Common confusion: "Why do I need both a Question and a QuestionConstruct?" Answer: the Question is the content ("What is your age?"). The QuestionConstruct is the instruction ("now ask this question"). The Sequence says "ask these in this order." Separating content from flow lets you reuse the same question in different instruments. Quiz question 2 checks this.
  • A gate with only a "then" branch is how DDI says "skip". If learners add an "else" branch that points to Section C while Section C is also the next step of the main Sequence, respondents under 16 would see Section C twice. Ask them to trace a 12-year-old through the flow.
  • For the Loop: show a household roster form where the same section repeats per person. Ask: "How many times does this section run?" Answer: "It depends on how many people live in the household." That is a loop.
  • ElseIf is in "Going further". Use it with faster learners: "If 65+ → ask retirement. If 16-64 → ask employment. Otherwise → skip." Point out that the order of the conditions matters.
  • Exercise 6 (draw your own spec) is excellent for group work. Pairs can swap specs and map each other's questionnaires.

See also: Module 9: Code lists | User guide: Any item type

docs.title: Module 11: Document data files and variable lineage
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Explain in two or three sentences how a collection file, a production file and a master file differ, and which variables each one holds.
  • O2. Choose a representation for a variable from its values, and set it with set_numeric(), set_coded() or set_text().
  • O3. Link each collection variable to its source question with doc.add_variable(..., question=...).
  • O4. Record a derived variable's sources in source_variable_references, whether it has one source or several.
  • O5. Trace a master-file variable back to its original question by following source_variable_references and question_references with doc.find().

Prerequisites: Module 10.

Time: 60 min self-paced / 75 min instructor-led.

New in this module: set_numeric(), set_text(), variable_representation, source_variable_references, question_references, doc.find().

docs.title: 1. What happens after data collection?
docs.text:
In Module 10 you built a questionnaire. When respondents answer that questionnaire, the responses become data files.

But the raw data rarely goes straight to users. It passes through stages:

flowchart LR
    A["Collection File
(raw responses)"] --> B["Production File
(cleaned + derived)"]
    B --> C["Master File
(ready for release)"]

Each stage has its own set of variables. DDI lets you document every stage and track how each variable connects back to the others. This is called data lineage or provenance.

docs.title: 2. The three data files
docs.text:
We will use the Health Survey from Module 10 as our running example.

Three data files

Collection file: raw responses exactly as collected.

respondent_id age gender employed occupation health_rating smoker R001 34 Female Yes Teacher Good No R002 17 Male No Fair No R003 68 Female No Excellent Yes

Production file: cleaned data with both original and derived variables.

respondent_id age gender employed age_group employment_status_code health_score R001 34 2 1 3 1 3 R002 17 1 0 2 0 2 R003 68 2 0 5 0 4

Master file: only the final derived variables, ready for dissemination.

respondent_id age_group employment_status_code health_score R001 3 1 3 R002 2 0 2 R003 5 0 4

docs.title: 3. Set up the study
docs.text:
Start by creating the study and the questions from our Health Survey.

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="National Health Survey: Data Documentation",
    agency="health.gc.ca",
)

# Create the source questions
q_age = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q_gender = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
q_employed = doc.add_question(text="Are you currently employed?")
q_occupation = doc.add_question(text="What is your occupation?")
q_health = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your general health?")
q_smoke = doc.add_question(text="Do you smoke?")

docs.title: 4. Build the collection variables
docs.text:
Collection variables capture exactly what was asked. Each one has a representation (numeric, coded, or text) and a link back to its source question.

A representation tells users what kind of values the variable holds:

The values are... Call Examples Numbers you can count or measure set_numeric() age, income, nights in hospital One answer from a fixed set set_coded(code_list) gender, health rating, yes/no Free words set_text() occupation, comments

docs.title: Numeric variable: age
docs.text:
v_age = doc.add_variable(name="age", question=q_age)
v_age.set_numeric("Integer", low=0, high=120)

The question= parameter automatically creates a question_references entry linking this variable to the question it came from. set_numeric() records that the values are whole numbers ("Integer") from 0 to 120.

docs.title: Coded variable: gender
docs.text:
For coded variables, you first create a code list (Module 9), then point the variable at it with set_coded(), which you met in Module 6.

# Create the Gender code list
cl_gender = doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Male")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Female")
doc.add_item(Category, name="Other")

v_gender = doc.add_variable(name="gender", question=q_gender)
v_gender.set_coded(cl_gender)

docs.title: Text variable: occupation
docs.text:
v_occupation = doc.add_variable(name="occupation", question=q_occupation)
v_occupation.set_text()

docs.title: Check a representation
docs.text:
Each call fills the variable's variable_representation. It holds one kind of representation (numeric_representation, code_representation or text_representation), and the other two stay None:

print(v_age.variable_representation.numeric_representation.numeric_type_code)
# -> Integer
print(v_occupation.variable_representation.text_representation is not None)
# -> True

docs.title: Build all collection variables
docs.text:
v_employed = doc.add_variable(name="employed", question=q_employed)
v_health = doc.add_variable(name="health_rating", question=q_health)
v_smoke = doc.add_variable(name="smoker", question=q_smoke)

print(f"Collection variables: {len(doc.variables)}")
# -> Collection variables: 6

Every collection variable references its source question. This is the first link in the provenance chain.

docs.title: 5. What is a derived variable?
docs.text:
A derived variable is computed from one or more existing variables.

Examples:

Derived variable Source variable(s) Derivation age_group age Recode: 0-15→1, 16-24→2, 25-44→3, 45-64→4, 65+→5 employment_status_code employed Recode: Yes→1, No→0 health_score health_rating Recode: Excellent→4, Good→3, Fair→2, Poor→1

In DDI, you track this derivation with source_variable_references, a list of references pointing to the variables that were used to compute the derived value.

docs.title: 6. Create derived variables with source references
Step 1: Create the age_group code list
docs.text:
cl_age_group = doc.add_code_list(name="Age Group Codes")
doc.add_item(Category, name="0-15")
doc.add_item(Category, name="16-24")
doc.add_item(Category, name="25-44")
doc.add_item(Category, name="45-64")
doc.add_item(Category, name="65+")

docs.title: Step 2: Create the derived variable
docs.text:
v_age_group = doc.add_variable(name="age_group", question=q_age)
v_age_group.set_coded(cl_age_group)

docs.title: Step 3: Link it to its source variable
docs.text:
The key field is source_variable_references. It tells anyone reading the metadata: "This variable was derived from these other variables." Build each reference with .to_reference(), as you did for constructs in Module 10:

v_age_group.source_variable_references = [v_age.to_reference()]

Now age_group has two provenance links:

  • Question source: points to "What is your age?" (set by question=q_age)
  • Variable source: points to the collection variable age (set by source_variable_references)

docs.title: 7. Build all production variables
docs.text:
The production file has both the original collection variables and the derived variables.

# Derived: employment_status_code from employed
v_emp_code = doc.add_variable(name="employment_status_code", question=q_employed)
v_emp_code.source_variable_references = [v_employed.to_reference()]

# Derived: health_score from health_rating
v_health_score = doc.add_variable(name="health_score", question=q_health)
v_health_score.source_variable_references = [v_health.to_reference()]

print(f"Total variables (collection + derived): {len(doc.variables)}")
# -> Total variables (collection + derived): 9

docs.title: 8. The provenance chain
docs.text:
Every variable in the production file can be traced back to:

  1. Its source question → "What was asked?"
  2. Its source variable(s) → "What data was it computed from?"

And every collection variable can be traced to:

  1. Its source question → "What was asked?"

This creates a full lineage chain:

flowchart BT
    Q1["Question: What is your age?"]
    V1["Collection Variable: age\n(numeric)"]
    V2["Derived Variable: age_group\n(coded: 0-15, 16-24, ...)"]
    V3["Master Variable: age_group_master\n(dissemination)"]

    V1 -->|"QuestionReference\n(question_references)"| Q1
    V2 -->|"QuestionReference"| Q1
    V3 -->|"QuestionReference"| Q1
    V2 -->|"SourceVariableReference\n(source_variable_references)"| V1
    V3 -->|"SourceVariableReference"| V2

Reading from bottom to top, you can answer:

  • "Where does age_group_master in the master file come from?" → From the production variable age_group.
  • "Where does the production age_group come from?" → Derived from age in the collection file.
  • "Where does age come from?" → From the question "What is your age?"

docs.title: Follow the chain in code
docs.text:
A reference stores the identifier of its target. doc.find(identifier) returns the item that has that identifier, wherever it is in the document. Module 13 covers finding items in more depth. Follow age_group back one step, then to its question:

source = doc.find(v_age_group.source_variable_references[0].identifier)
print(source.names[0].text)  # -> age

question = doc.find(source.question_references[0].identifier)
print(question.question_texts[0].text)  # -> What is your age?

docs.title: 9. Build the master file variables
docs.text:
The master file contains only the derived variables that are ready for dissemination. These reference the production-stage derived variables as their source.

# Master file variables reference the production variables as source
v_master_age_group = doc.add_variable(name="age_group_master", question=q_age)
v_master_age_group.source_variable_references = [v_age_group.to_reference()]

v_master_emp = doc.add_variable(name="employment_status_master", question=q_employed)
v_master_emp.source_variable_references = [v_emp_code.to_reference()]

v_master_health = doc.add_variable(name="health_score_master", question=q_health)
v_master_health.source_variable_references = [v_health_score.to_reference()]

print(f"Total variables in document: {len(doc.variables)}")
# -> Total variables in document: 12

docs.title: 10. A variable with multiple sources
docs.text:
Some derived variables combine more than one source variable. For example, a Body Mass Index (BMI) variable is derived from both height and weight.

q_height = doc.add_question(text="What is your height in cm?")
q_weight = doc.add_question(text="What is your weight in kg?")

v_height = doc.add_variable(name="height_cm", question=q_height)
v_weight = doc.add_variable(name="weight_kg", question=q_weight)

v_bmi = doc.add_variable(name="bmi")
v_bmi.source_variable_references = [
    v_height.to_reference(),
    v_weight.to_reference(),
]

print(f"BMI sources: {len(v_bmi.source_variable_references)}")  # -> BMI sources: 2

The source_variable_references list contains two references. Anyone reading this metadata knows that BMI depends on both height and weight.

docs.title: 11. Numeric to coded: the derivation pattern
docs.text:
A common pattern in data processing: a numeric collection variable becomes a coded production variable.

Stage Variable Representation Example values Collection age Numeric (0-120) 34, 17, 68 Production age_group Coded (5 categories) "25-44", "16-24", "65+"

You documented this in three steps:

  1. v_age.set_numeric("Integer", low=0, high=120) gives age a numeric representation.
  2. v_age_group.set_coded(cl_age_group) gives age_group a code representation that points to the Age Group Codes list.
  3. v_age_group.source_variable_references points to age.

The representation tells users what kind of values the variable holds. The source reference tells them where those values came from.

docs.title: 12. The lineage model at a glance
docs.text:
File Variables Each one points to Collection age, gender, employed, occupation, health_rating, smoker its question (question_references) Production (derived) age_group, employment_status_code, health_score a collection variable (source_variable_references) Master age_group_master, employment_status_master, health_score_master a production variable (source_variable_references)

Every link is a Reference. Follow them from any master variable and you reach the original question.

Scenario

You are documenting the National Health Survey data pipeline. The collection file has 6 raw variables from the questionnaire. The production file adds 3 derived variables (age_group, employment_status_code, health_score). The master file has only the 3 derived variables for public release. Every variable must trace back to its source.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (O1) Look at the three tables in Section 2. In two or three sentences, explain how the collection, production and master files differ, and say which file a member of the public receives.

    Answer

    A sample answer: "The collection file holds the raw answers exactly as respondents gave them, such as age and health_rating. The production file keeps those cleaned variables and adds derived ones computed from them, such as age_group and health_score. The master file keeps only the derived variables that are ready for release, and it is the file the public receives."

  2. (O3) Create a study for the Health Survey. Add 6 questions and 6 collection variables, each linked to its source question. Print the counts and the number of question references on age.

    Expected output:

    Questions: 6
Variables: 6
age question references: 1
    Answer 
    import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Health Survey", agency="health.gc.ca")

q_age = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")
q_gender = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
q_employed = doc.add_question(text="Are you currently employed?")
q_occupation = doc.add_question(text="What is your occupation?")
q_health = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your general health?")
q_smoke = doc.add_question(text="Do you smoke?")

v_age = doc.add_variable(name="age", question=q_age)
v_gender = doc.add_variable(name="gender", question=q_gender)
v_employed = doc.add_variable(name="employed", question=q_employed)
v_occupation = doc.add_variable(name="occupation", question=q_occupation)
v_health = doc.add_variable(name="health_rating", question=q_health)
v_smoke = doc.add_variable(name="smoker", question=q_smoke)

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")
print(f"age question references: {len(v_age.question_references)}")

  3. (O2) Choose and set a representation for three of the collection variables: age holds whole numbers from 0 to 120, gender holds Male, Female or Other, and occupation holds free text. Then print a check for each one.

    Expected output:

    age: Integer
gender is coded: True
occupation is text: True
    Answer 
    v_age.set_numeric("Integer", low=0, high=120)

cl_gender = doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
for name in ("Male", "Female", "Other"):
    doc.add_item(Category, name=name)
v_gender.set_coded(cl_gender)

v_occupation.set_text()

rep = v_age.variable_representation
print(f"age: {rep.numeric_representation.numeric_type_code}")
rep = v_gender.variable_representation
print(f"gender is coded: {rep.code_representation is not None}")
rep = v_occupation.variable_representation
print(f"occupation is text: {rep.text_representation is not None}")

    gender gets a code list because its answers come from a fixed set. occupation is text because any job title is possible.

  4. (O4) Create the three production variables. age_group is coded with an "Age Group Codes" list (0-15, 16-24, 25-44, 45-64, 65+) and derived from age. employment_status_code is derived from employed, and health_score from health_rating. Record each source in source_variable_references. Print the total.

    Expected output:

    Variables: 9
    Answer 
    cl_age_group = doc.add_code_list(name="Age Group Codes")
for group in ("0-15", "16-24", "25-44", "45-64", "65+"):
    doc.add_item(Category, name=group)

v_age_group = doc.add_variable(name="age_group", question=q_age)
v_age_group.set_coded(cl_age_group)
v_age_group.source_variable_references = [v_age.to_reference()]

v_emp_code = doc.add_variable(name="employment_status_code", question=q_employed)
v_emp_code.source_variable_references = [v_employed.to_reference()]

v_health_score = doc.add_variable(name="health_score", question=q_health)
v_health_score.source_variable_references = [v_health.to_reference()]

print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")

  5. (O4) Create 3 master file variables (age_group_master, employment_status_master, health_score_master). Each should reference its production-stage derived variable as its source. Print the total, then print every variable that has a source.

    Expected output:

    Variables: 12
  age_group: 1 source(s)
  employment_status_code: 1 source(s)
  health_score: 1 source(s)
  age_group_master: 1 source(s)
  employment_status_master: 1 source(s)
  health_score_master: 1 source(s)
    Answer 
    v_master_ag = doc.add_variable(name="age_group_master", question=q_age)
v_master_ag.source_variable_references = [v_age_group.to_reference()]

v_master_emp = doc.add_variable(name="employment_status_master", question=q_employed)
v_master_emp.source_variable_references = [v_emp_code.to_reference()]

v_master_hs = doc.add_variable(name="health_score_master", question=q_health)
v_master_hs.source_variable_references = [v_health_score.to_reference()]

print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")

for v in doc.variables:
    sources = len(v.source_variable_references)
    if sources > 0:
        print(f"  {v.names[0].text}: {sources} source(s)")

  6. (O4) Create a BMI variable derived from two sources, height_cm and weight_kg. Print how many source references it has.

    Expected output:

    BMI sources: 2
    Answer 
    v_height = doc.add_variable(name="height_cm")
v_weight = doc.add_variable(name="weight_kg")

v_bmi = doc.add_variable(name="bmi")
v_bmi.source_variable_references = [
    v_height.to_reference(),
    v_weight.to_reference(),
]

print(f"BMI sources: {len(v_bmi.source_variable_references)}")

  7. (O5) Trace health_score_master back to its question. Start at that variable, print its name, and follow its first source reference with doc.find() until you reach a variable with no source. Then print the text of that variable's question.

    Expected output:

    health_score_master
health_score
health_rating
How would you rate your general health?
    Answer 
    current = v_master_hs
print(current.names[0].text)
while current.source_variable_references:
    current = doc.find(current.source_variable_references[0].identifier)
    print(current.names[0].text)

question = doc.find(current.question_references[0].identifier)
print(question.question_texts[0].text)

    The loop stops at health_rating, the collection variable. Only its question link is left to follow.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): Which file is this?

A file holds only respondent_id, age_group, employment_status_code and health_score, and it is ready for public release. Which file is it?

A. The collection file.

B. The production file.

C. The questionnaire.

D. The master file.

Answer

D. The master file keeps only the final derived variables, ready for dissemination. The production file would also hold age, gender and employed.

Question 2 (O2): Which call fits this variable?

A variable records how many nights a person spent in hospital last year, from 0 to 365. Which call sets the right representation?

A. v.set_numeric("Integer", low=0, high=365)

B. v.set_text()

C. v.set_coded(cl_nights), with one category for each possible number

D. None: a count needs no representation.

Answer

A. The values are whole numbers you can add and average, so the representation is numeric, with the valid range. A code list of 366 categories would hide that, and text would allow "three" or "a few".

Question 3 (O3): How do you record that smoker came from q_smoke?

A script creates the variable with v_smoke = doc.add_variable(name="smoker"). Which change records that its values answer the question q_smoke?

A. v_smoke.source_variable_references = [q_smoke.to_reference()]

B. Create it with doc.add_variable(name="smoker", question=q_smoke).

C. v_smoke.set_coded(q_smoke)

D. v_smoke.names.append(q_smoke)

Answer

B. The question= parameter adds the link to question_references. source_variable_references is for source variables, not questions.

Question 4 (O4): A BMI variable is computed from height and weight. How many source_variable_references does it have?

A. 0

B. 1

C. 2

D. 3

Answer

C. BMI has 2 source variable references, one for height and one for weight, because it is derived from both.

Question 5 (O4): What does source_variable_references track?

A. Which questions a variable came from.

B. Which other variables a derived variable was computed from.

C. Which code list a variable uses.

D. Which data file a variable belongs to.

Answer

B. source_variable_references is a list of references pointing to the variables that were used to compute a derived variable. Questions go in question_references, and the code list in the representation.

Question 6 (O5): What does this code print?

v_master_hs is health_score_master from Exercise 5.

current = v_master_hs
while current.source_variable_references:
    current = doc.find(current.source_variable_references[0].identifier)
print(current.names[0].text)

A. health_rating

B. health_score

C. health_score_master

D. How would you rate your general health?

Answer

A. The loop follows health_score_master → health_score → health_rating, and stops there because health_rating has no source variable. It prints a variable name; the question text needs one more step through question_references.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can explain in two or three sentences how the collection, production and master files differ. (O1)
  • I can choose a representation for a variable and set it with set_numeric(), set_coded() or set_text(). (O2)
  • I can link each collection variable to its source question with question=. (O3)
  • I can record a derived variable's sources in source_variable_references, for one source or several. (O4)
  • I can trace a master-file variable back to its question with doc.find(). (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Start with the analogy: "Think of a recipe. The collection file is the raw ingredients. The production file is the cooking process. The master file is the plated dish. Provenance is the recipe that tells you where every ingredient came from."
  • Draw the three-file pipeline on the whiteboard. For each variable, draw an arrow back to its source. Ask: "Can you trace this master variable back to the original question?" Exercise 7 does the same in code.
  • The concept of source_variable_references vs question_references can be confusing. Clarify: question_references says "what was asked." source_variable_references says "what data was used to compute this." Quiz questions 3 and 5 check the difference.
  • The numeric-to-coded pattern (age → age_group) is the most common derivation in national surveys. Show a real recoding table: "age 0-15 = group 1, 16-24 = group 2, ..."
  • For staff of national statistical offices (NSOs): emphasize that this lineage is what auditors and researchers look for. "If someone questions a number in your publication, can you trace it back to the original data?"
  • Exercise 6 (BMI from two sources) teaches multi-source derivation. This is common: BMI = weight / height², household income = sum of member incomes, etc.

See also: Module 10: Questionnaire flows | User guide: Add variables

docs.title: Module 12: Data linkage: combining records across datasets
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Explain in two or three sentences what microdata linkage is, and why a national statistical office or a researcher links existing files instead of collecting new data.
  • O2. Choose deterministic or probabilistic linkage for a pair of files, and justify the choice from the variables they share.
  • O3. Model each source dataset as its own study with doc.add_study(), and add its variables through doc.study().
  • O4. Tag the linkage key on both sides with set_property("linkage_role", "key"), and read it back with get_property().
  • O5. Add a Comparison that maps the two keys with add_variable_map() and a correspondence weight, and record the linkage method and match rate on it.
  • O6. Record a linked variable's sources in both studies with source_variable_references.

Prerequisites: Module 11.

Time: 60 min self-paced / 75 min instructor-led.

New in this module: doc.add_study(), doc.study(), set_property(), get_property(), doc.add_comparison(), correspondence(), add_variable_map(), doc.comparisons.

docs.title: 1. What is data linkage?
docs.text:
Data linkage (also called microdata linkage or record linkage) is the process of combining records from two or more files that refer to the same unit: an individual, a household, or a business.

Statistics Canada describes it this way:

Statistics Canada: Microdata linkage

Microdata linkage is an internationally recognized statistical method that maximizes the use of existing information by linking different files and variables to create new information. [...] We first link the different data records by using the variables they have in common. In order to protect confidentiality, all personal information is removed, so that the linked files are anonymized, or de-identified.

The key idea: instead of running a new survey to collect a variable, you link an existing survey to an existing administrative file and reuse what is already there.

flowchart LR
    A["Survey file
(health_rating)"] -->|"common key
(anon_id)"| C["Linked analytical file
(health_rating + hospital_visits)"]
    B["Admin file
(hospital_visits)"] -->|"common key
(anon_id)"| C
    C --> D["De-identified /
synthetic outputs"]

docs.title: 2. Why statistical offices and researchers link data
docs.text:
A national statistical office (NSO) is the government agency that produces a country's official statistics. NSOs and academic researchers link data for similar reasons:

Who Typical linkage Why NSO Survey → tax/administrative records Add income without re-asking; reduce burden NSO Census → health/education registers Study outcomes across domains NSO Same respondents across waves Build a longitudinal file Academic Survey → hospital admissions Research health outcomes Academic Birth records → school records Study life-course trajectories

For both, the payoff is the same: linkage turns two narrow files into one rich file that can answer questions neither file could answer alone, without asking respondents anything new.

docs.title: 3. Two ways to link: deterministic and probabilistic
docs.text:
Method How it matches When to use Deterministic Exact match on a unique key (e.g. an anonymized ID) A reliable common identifier exists Probabilistic Weighted agreement across several quasi-identifiers (name, date of birth, sex, postal code) with a decision threshold No single reliable key; some fields have errors or missing values

A quasi-identifier is a variable that does not identify a person on its own, but narrows the match when combined with others.

To choose, look at what the two files share. If both carry the same reliable ID, link deterministically. If they share only quasi-identifiers, or the ID has errors, link probabilistically.

Deterministic linkage is simpler and is what we model in detail below. Probabilistic linkage records the same structure but adds an agreement weight and marks several matching variables rather than one key.

docs.title: 4. Our running example
docs.text:
We will link two files from a health study:

Two source files

Survey file: collected from respondents.

anon_id age health_rating A17 34 Good A22 68 Excellent A31 17 Fair

Administrative file: hospital admissions register.

anon_id hospital_visits last_admission A17 2 2021-03 A22 5 2021-07 A31 0

Both files share the column anon_id, an anonymized linkage key. That common variable is what lets us join a respondent's health_rating to their hospital_visits to create a linked analytical file.

docs.title: 5. Model each source as its own study
docs.text:
In DDI, each source dataset is its own StudyUnit. When you add a second study, ddi-l automatically wraps both in a group (a study series). The first study is the survey; we add the administrative register as a second study.

import ddi_l as ddi

# Source 1: the survey (the primary study)
doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="Canadian Community Health Survey 2021",
    agency="statcan.gc.ca",
)
q_key = doc.add_question(text="Anonymized linkage key")
q_health = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your general health?")

survey_key = doc.add_variable(name="anon_id", question=q_key)
survey_health = doc.add_variable(name="health_rating", question=q_health)

print(f"Survey variables: {len(doc.variables)}")
# -> Survey variables: 2

Now add the administrative register as a second study and target it with a study cursor:

# Source 2: the administrative register (a second study in the group)
admin = doc.add_study(title="Hospital Admissions Register 2021")
admin_ds = doc.study(admin.identifier)

admin_key = admin_ds.add_variable(name="anon_id")
admin_visits = admin_ds.add_variable(name="hospital_visits")

doc.add_study() returns the new study. doc.study(identifier) returns a cursor for it: an object with the same add_* methods as doc, which add items to that study instead of the first one.

Where do the counts live?

doc.variables counts variables in the primary study only. The administrative register's variables live in its own study unit, reached through the cursor doc.study(admin.identifier). This mirrors reality: each source file is a separate, independently maintained dataset. doc.find() (Module 11) still finds an item in any study.

docs.title: 6. Tag the linkage keys
docs.text:
The linkage key is the common variable that connects the sources. Mark it on both sides so anyone reading the metadata knows which variable does the joining.

DDI has no dedicated field for "this is the linkage key", so you record it as a custom property: a key-value pair you attach to any item. Two methods are all you need here:

  • item.set_property(key, value) stores a value under a key.
  • item.get_property(key) reads it back, or returns None if the item has no such key.

Module 13 covers custom properties fully.

Tag both sides:

survey_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")
admin_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")

print(survey_key.get_property("linkage_role"))
# -> key
print(survey_health.get_property("linkage_role"))
# -> None

For probabilistic linkage you would instead tag several variables as "matching" (e.g. date_of_birth, sex, postal_code) and, optionally, the ones used to group candidate pairs as "blocking".

docs.title: 7. Record how the keys correspond: a Comparison
docs.text:
A Comparison is DDI's container for recording how items in different studies correspond. Add a variable map from the survey key to the admin key, and describe the match quality with a correspondence.

cmp = doc.add_comparison(name="Survey-to-Admin Microdata Linkage 2021")

# Describe the match: full commonality (weight 1.0) for an exact key
key_match = cmp.correspondence(
    commonality="Anonymized personal identifier common to both sources.",
    weight=1.0,
)

cmp.add_variable_map(
    survey_key.to_reference(),
    admin_key.to_reference(),
    correspondence=key_match,
)

print(f"Comparisons: {len(doc.comparisons)}")
# -> Comparisons: 1

For probabilistic linkage, set weight below 1.0 to record that agreement is partial, and add a variable map for each matching variable.

docs.title: 8. Record the linkage method and quality
docs.text:
Store the linkage method and quality indicators as custom properties on the comparison. These are exactly the facts an auditor, a data steward, or a future researcher will ask for.

cmp.set_property("linkage_method", "deterministic")
cmp.set_property("match_rate", "0.94")
cmp.set_property("false_match_rate", "0.01")

print(cmp.get_property("linkage_method"))
# -> deterministic

docs.title: 9. Build the linked variable with cross-source provenance
docs.text:
The linked analytical file holds variables drawn from both sources. Each linked variable records where it came from with source_variable_references, just like a derived variable in Module 11, except now the sources sit in different studies.

linked = doc.add_variable(name="health_by_hospital_use")
linked.source_variable_references = [
    survey_health.to_reference(),
    admin_visits.to_reference(),
]

print(f"Linked variable sources: {len(linked.source_variable_references)}")
# -> Linked variable sources: 2

Cross-study references warn on save

When you save, ddi-l may print a UserWarning that a source_variable_reference is "not present in the current document." That is expected for linkage: the source variable lives in a different study within the group. The reference is still written correctly: it is a full cross-study link, which is the whole point of data linkage.

docs.title: 10. Save the linkage document
docs.text:
doc.save("health-linkage-2021.xml")

The saved file records, in one place: both source studies, the linkage key on each side, the comparison that maps the keys, the linkage method and quality, and the linked variable's provenance to both sources.

docs.title: 11. The complete linkage model
docs.text:
The saved file holds one group with the comparison and both studies. The linked variable sits in the survey study, the primary one. Arrows point the way the XML refers: from the map's item map to the two keys, and from the linked variable to its two sources.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Group["Group"]
        subgraph Comparison["Comparison"]
            VM["VariableMap\nCorrespondence: CommonalityWeight 1.0"]
        end
        subgraph Survey["StudyUnit 1: Survey"]
            SK["anon_id\n(UserAttributePair linkage_role = key)"]
            SH["health_rating"]
            L["health_by_hospital_use"]
        end
        subgraph Admin["StudyUnit 2: Admin register"]
            AK["anon_id\n(UserAttributePair linkage_role = key)"]
            AV["hospital_visits"]
        end
    end

    VM -->|"ItemMap: SourceItemReference"| SK
    VM -->|"ItemMap: TargetItemReference"| AK
    L -->|SourceVariableReference| SH
    L -->|SourceVariableReference| AV

Every arrow is a Reference in DDI. Reading the model, anyone can see which variable joined the files, how good the match was, and where every value in the linked file came from.

Scenario

You are documenting a microdata linkage at a national statistical office. A health survey and a hospital admissions register share an anonymized identifier, anon_id. You link them deterministically to study health outcomes against hospital use. You must record: the two source datasets, the linkage key on each side, the map between the keys, the linkage method and match rate, and the provenance of the linked variable back to both sources.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (O1) Your manager asks why the team should link the health survey to the hospital register instead of adding a hospital-visits question to next year's survey. Answer in two or three sentences.

    Answer

    A sample answer: "Linkage combines records from the two files that describe the same person, using a variable they share. The register already holds every hospital visit, so linking gives us that information without asking respondents anything new, which reduces their burden. The counts also come from records rather than from memory, and the linked file can answer questions neither file answers alone, such as whether people who rate their health as poor visit hospital more often."

  2. (O2) For each pair of files, choose deterministic or probabilistic linkage, and give the reason in one sentence.

    • (a) A survey and a tax file that both carry the same anonymized person ID.
    • (b) A birth register and school records that share only name, date of birth, sex and postal code, with some typos in the names.
    • (c) Two waves of a panel survey that keep each respondent's ID from wave to wave.
    Answer
    • (a) Deterministic: both files carry the same reliable ID, so an exact match on it is enough.
    • (b) Probabilistic: there is no shared ID, and the names have errors, so you weigh agreement across several quasi-identifiers and apply a threshold.
    • (c) Deterministic: the respondent ID is stable across waves.

  3. (O3) Create the survey study with two variables (anon_id, health_rating). Add the hospital register as a second study with two variables (anon_id, hospital_visits). Print the number of survey variables, and check with doc.find() that hospital_visits is in the document.

    Expected output:

    Survey variables: 2
hospital_visits found: True
    Answer 
    import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="Canadian Community Health Survey 2021",
    agency="statcan.gc.ca",
)
q_key = doc.add_question(text="Anonymized linkage key")
q_health = doc.add_question(text="How would you rate your general health?")
survey_key = doc.add_variable(name="anon_id", question=q_key)
survey_health = doc.add_variable(name="health_rating", question=q_health)

admin = doc.add_study(title="Hospital Admissions Register 2021")
admin_ds = doc.study(admin.identifier)
admin_key = admin_ds.add_variable(name="anon_id")
admin_visits = admin_ds.add_variable(name="hospital_visits")

print(f"Survey variables: {len(doc.variables)}")
print(f"hospital_visits found: {doc.find(admin_visits.identifier) is not None}")

    doc.variables counts only the survey's two variables. The register's variables are in the second study, and doc.find() still reaches them.

  4. (O4) Tag anon_id as the linkage key in both studies. Print the linkage_role of both keys, and of health_rating.

    Expected output:

    Survey anon_id: key
Register anon_id: key
health_rating: None
    Answer 
    survey_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")
admin_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")

print(f"Survey anon_id: {survey_key.get_property('linkage_role')}")
print(f"Register anon_id: {admin_key.get_property('linkage_role')}")
print(f"health_rating: {survey_health.get_property('linkage_role')}")

    health_rating was never tagged, so get_property() returns None.

  5. (O5) Add a Comparison that maps the survey key to the register key with a correspondence weight of 1.0. Record the linkage method (deterministic) and a match_rate of 0.94 as properties on the comparison. Print the counts and the two properties.

    Expected output:

    Comparisons: 1
Variable maps: 1
deterministic, match rate 0.94
    Answer 
    cmp = doc.add_comparison(name="Survey-to-Admin Microdata Linkage 2021")
key_match = cmp.correspondence(
    commonality="Anonymized personal identifier common to both sources.",
    weight=1.0,
)
cmp.add_variable_map(
    survey_key.to_reference(),
    admin_key.to_reference(),
    correspondence=key_match,
)
cmp.set_property("linkage_method", "deterministic")
cmp.set_property("match_rate", "0.94")

print(f"Comparisons: {len(doc.comparisons)}")
print(f"Variable maps: {len(cmp.variable_maps)}")
method = cmp.get_property("linkage_method")
print(f"{method}, match rate {cmp.get_property('match_rate')}")

  6. (O6) Create a linked variable health_by_hospital_use with source_variable_references pointing to both health_rating (survey) and hospital_visits (register). Print how many sources it has.

    Expected output:

    Linked variable sources: 2
    Answer 
    linked = doc.add_variable(name="health_by_hospital_use")
linked.source_variable_references = [
    survey_health.to_reference(),
    admin_visits.to_reference(),
]

print(f"Linked variable sources: {len(linked.source_variable_references)}")

  7. (O2, O4, O5) (Optional) Model a probabilistic linkage instead. Add date_of_birth, sex and postal_code to both studies and tag each one with linkage_role="matching". Add a second comparison with the method probabilistic, and map each pair of variables with a correspondence weight of 0.85. Print the number of maps and the method.

    Expected output:

    Variable maps: 3
probabilistic
    Answer 
    prob = doc.add_comparison(name="Probabilistic Linkage")
prob.set_property("linkage_method", "probabilistic")
partial = prob.correspondence(
    commonality="Agreement across date of birth, sex, and postal code.",
    weight=0.85,
)

for name in ("date_of_birth", "sex", "postal_code"):
    survey_var = doc.add_variable(name=name)
    register_var = admin_ds.add_variable(name=name)
    survey_var.set_property("linkage_role", "matching")
    register_var.set_property("linkage_role", "matching")
    prob.add_variable_map(
        survey_var.to_reference(),
        register_var.to_reference(),
        correspondence=partial,
    )

print(f"Variable maps: {len(prob.variable_maps)}")
print(prob.get_property("linkage_method"))

    A weight below 1.0 records that agreement on these fields is strong evidence of a match, but not proof.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): Why link instead of asking a new question?

A team has a survey with health ratings and a hospital register. It wants to know whether people who rate their health as poor visit hospital more often. Why link the two files instead of adding a hospital-visits question to the survey?

A. Linking reuses records the register already holds, so respondents answer nothing new and the counts do not depend on memory.

B. DDI cannot store a question about hospital visits.

C. Linking makes the survey file smaller.

D. Linking removes the need for any common variable.

Answer

A. Linkage combines records about the same person from existing files. It reduces respondent burden and creates information that neither file holds alone. It still needs a common variable to join the records.

Question 2 (O2): Which linkage method fits these files?

Two files share no ID. Both hold name, date of birth, sex and postal code, and some names have typos. Which linkage fits?

A. Deterministic, on name.

B. Probabilistic: weigh agreement across several fields and apply a threshold.

C. None: files without a common ID cannot be linked.

D. Deterministic, on postal code.

Answer

B. With no reliable key and errors in some fields, an exact match on one field would miss true pairs (name typos) or join the wrong people (many share a postal code). Probabilistic linkage combines the evidence from several quasi-identifiers.

Question 3 (O3): How do you add a variable to the register study?

You added the register with admin = doc.add_study(title="Hospital Admissions Register 2021"). Which line adds hospital_visits to the register, not to the survey?

A. doc.add_variable(name="hospital_visits")

B. doc.add_study(title="hospital_visits")

C. doc.study(admin.identifier).add_variable(name="hospital_visits")

D. doc.variables.append("hospital_visits")

Answer

C. doc.study() returns a cursor for that study, and its add_* methods add items there. doc.add_variable() always adds to the primary study, the survey.

Question 4 (O4): What does this code print? 

survey_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")
print(
    survey_key.get_property("linkage_role"),
    survey_health.get_property("linkage_role"),
)

A. key key

B. None None

C. linkage_role key

D. key None

Answer

D. Only survey_key was tagged. get_property() returns the value stored under the key, or None when the item has no such key.

Question 5 (O5): Which call records that the two keys correspond exactly?

A. cmp.add_variable_map(survey_key.to_reference(), admin_key.to_reference(), correspondence=cmp.correspondence(weight=1.0))

B. survey_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")

C. cmp.set_property("match_rate", "1.0")

D. linked.source_variable_references = [survey_key.to_reference()]

Answer

A. A variable map in the Comparison records that the survey key corresponds to the register key, and the correspondence weight 1.0 says they are the same identifier. Option B tags one side only; option C records a quality figure; option D records provenance.

Question 6 (O6): How do you record that a linked variable draws on two source files?

A. Set question= twice.

B. Put both sources in source_variable_references.

C. Rename the variable.

D. Increase the version number.

Answer

B. source_variable_references holds a Reference to each source variable (here, one to the survey variable and one to the admin variable), even though they live in different studies.

docs.title: Going further (optional)
docs.text: This section has no objective or quiz question.

docs.title: Linkage environments
docs.text: Some national statistical offices run dedicated environments for linkage. Statistics Canada, for example, runs the Social Data Linkage Environment (SDLE), the Business – Linkable File Environment (B-LFE), and the Longitudinal Employee and Business Analytical Files (LEBAF), precisely to build linked analytical files without collecting additional data from Canadians.

docs.title: Record confidentiality and governance
docs.text:
Microdata linkage is governed by strict privacy rules. Statistics Canada's Directive on Microdata Linkage requires that the public value of a linkage outweigh any intrusion on privacy, and that personal identifiers be removed so the linked file is de-identified. Researchers often work with synthetic versions rather than the original records.

Record this governance context as custom properties so it travels with the metadata:

study = doc.study_unit
study.set_property(
    "confidentiality",
    "de-identified; synthetic file for researcher access",
)
study.set_property("governance", "Directive on Microdata Linkage")
cmp.set_property("approval", "Directive on Microdata Linkage - pre-approved")

print(study.get_property("confidentiality"))
# -> de-identified; synthetic file for researcher access

Save again after these calls, so the file carries the governance context too.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can explain in two or three sentences what microdata linkage is and why NSOs and researchers link existing files. (O1)
  • I can choose deterministic or probabilistic linkage for a pair of files, and say why. (O2)
  • I can model each source dataset as its own study with doc.add_study() and doc.study(). (O3)
  • I can tag the linkage key on both sides with set_property() and read it back with get_property(). (O4)
  • I can add a Comparison that maps the keys with a correspondence weight, and record the method and match rate. (O5)
  • I can record a linked variable's sources in both studies with source_variable_references. (O6)

Instructor notes

  • Anchor the concept with the burden argument: "Why ask people their income on a survey if the tax file already has it? Link instead." Linkage reuses existing data to create new information.
  • Draw two file icons sharing one column (anon_id). The shared column is the key. Everything else in the module hangs off that picture.
  • Contrast the two data-quality regimes: deterministic (one reliable key, weight 1.0) vs probabilistic (several noisy fields, weight < 1.0, clerical review). Exercise 2 asks learners to choose; ask which fits a file with typos in names.
  • Learners meet custom properties here only as a tool for tagging keys and recording the method. Keep it to set_property() and get_property(); Module 13 covers properties fully.
  • Emphasize that source_variable_references crossing study boundaries is the technical heart of linkage, and that the save-time warning is expected, not an error.
  • For NSO staff: "Going further" connects to real infrastructure (SDLE, B-LFE, LEBAF) and to governance: pre-approved linkages vs those needing a documented proposal and review under the Directive on Microdata Linkage.
  • For academics: stress reproducibility. A reviewer must be able to see which key joined the files, the match rate, and the provenance of every linked variable. That is exactly what this metadata captures.
  • Privacy framing matters: every real linkage ends with de-identification and, often, synthetic data for access. If you have time, do the "Going further" governance step in class as the last step, not an afterthought.

See also: Module 11: Data lineage | Module 13: Properties, find, and validate | User guide: Compare and harmonize studies

docs.title: Module 13: Custom properties, find, remove, and validate
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Add, read and remove custom properties on a DDI item with set_property(), get_property(), properties and remove_property().
  • O2. Find an item by its identifier with doc.find(), and predict what doc.find() returns when no item has that identifier.
  • O3. Remove an item with doc.remove(), and fix the broken reference that doc.lint() reports when another item still points at it.
  • O4. Fix a document that fails validation: read each issue's message and context, correct the cause, and run doc.validate() again until it returns an empty list.

Prerequisites: Module 12.

Time: 40 min self-paced / 50 min instructor-led.

New in this module: set_property(), get_property(), properties, remove_property(), doc.find(), doc.remove(), issue.message, issue.context.

docs.title: 1. Custom properties
docs.text:
Every DDI item can carry extra information as custom properties. A property is a key-value pair: a name and a value, like a label on a box.

For example, you might tag a question with:

  • "sensitivity" = "high" (this question asks about private information)
  • "data_source" = "administrative records" (this data comes from government files)

Properties let your team add notes and tags that the DDI standard does not have built-in fields for.

docs.title: 2. Set a property
docs.text:
Use item.set_property(key, value) to add a property to any item.

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="survey.example.org")

q_age = doc.add_question(text="How old are you?")
q_income = doc.add_question(text="What is your household income?")
q_name = doc.add_question(text="What is your full name?")

# Tag the income question as high sensitivity
q_income.set_property("sensitivity", "high")

# Tag the name question too
q_name.set_property("sensitivity", "high")
q_name.set_property("data_source", "self-reported")

You can set as many properties as you need on any item. Setting a key that the item already has replaces its value.

docs.title: 3. Read properties
docs.text:
Use item.get_property(key) to read one property. It returns the value as a string, or None if the key does not exist.

print(q_income.get_property("sensitivity"))  # -> high
print(q_age.get_property("sensitivity"))  # -> None

Use item.properties to get all properties as a dictionary.

print(q_name.properties)
# -> {'sensitivity': 'high', 'data_source': 'self-reported'}

A dictionary (also called a dict) is a Python data structure that maps keys to values.

properties gives you a new dictionary each time you read it. Changing that dictionary does not change the item: use the methods to do that.

docs.title: 4. Remove a property
docs.text:
Use item.remove_property(key) to delete a property. It returns True if the property was found and removed, or False if the key was not there.

removed = q_name.remove_property("data_source")
print(removed)  # -> True
print(q_name.properties)  # -> {'sensitivity': 'high'}

docs.title: 5. Find items by identifier
docs.text:
Every item in a DDI document gets a unique identifier when it is created. Think of it as a serial number.

Use doc.find(identifier) to look up any item by its identifier.

v1 = doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q_age)

# Save the identifier
age_id = v1.identifier
print(f"Identifier: {age_id}")

# Find it later
found = doc.find(age_id)
print(found.names[0].text)  # -> Age

If no item matches, doc.find() returns None. It does not raise an error, so check the result before you use it:

print(doc.find("not-an-identifier"))  # -> None

docs.title: 6. Remove items
docs.text:
Use doc.remove(identifier) to delete an item from the document. It returns True if the item was found and removed, and False if no item has that identifier.

print(f"Questions before: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> 3

# Remove the name question
doc.remove(q_name.identifier)

print(f"Questions after: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> 2

Be careful: removing is permanent. There is no undo.

docs.title: Removing leaves references behind
docs.text:
doc.remove() removes the item and nothing else. If another item refers to it, that reference (the link from one item to another, Module 4) stays, and now points at nothing. The variable Age refers to the age question. Remove the question and ask doc.lint() (Module 3) what it finds:

doc.remove(q_age.identifier)

for finding in doc.lint():
    if finding.severity == "error":
        print(finding.rule_id)  # -> ddi.reference.integrity

The rule ddi.reference.integrity means "this reference cannot be resolved to an item in the document". doc.validate() does not report it: the schema checks the shape of the file, not whether each reference finds its target. doc.save() warns about it too.

You have two ways to fix it. Drop the reference, so the variable no longer names a question. Or remove the variable as well, if it means nothing without the question. Here the variable stays and the reference goes:

v1.question_references = [
    ref for ref in v1.question_references if ref.identifier != q_age.identifier
]

errors = [finding for finding in doc.lint() if finding.severity == "error"]
print(f"Lint errors: {len(errors)}")  # -> Lint errors: 0

docs.title: 7. Read a validation issue
docs.text:
In Module 3 you ran doc.validate() on a correct study and got an empty list. Here is what a problem looks like.

A common mistake is a language tag written with an underscore, fr_CA. The standard writes it with a hyphen: fr-CA. Add a French text with the wrong tag and validate:

from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

q_income.question_texts.append(
    InternationalString(text="Quel est le revenu de votre ménage ?", lang="fr_CA")
)

issues = doc.validate()
print(f"Issues: {len(issues)}")  # -> Issues: 1
for issue in issues:
    print(issue.message)
    print(issue.context)

Expected output:

Issues: 1
attribute {http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace}lang='fr_CA': value doesn't match any pattern of ['[a-zA-Z]{1,8}(-[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,8})*']
<d:Text> Quel est le revenu de votre ménage ?

Each issue has two parts worth reading:

  • message says which rule the file breaks. Here an attribute, {http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace}lang (the long name of xml:lang), holds fr_CA. That value does not match the pattern the schema allows: letters, then optional parts that each start with a hyphen.
  • context shows the element and the start of its text: a <d:Text> holding the French text you just added. That tells you which item to fix.

If the context is not enough, issue.xpath gives the full path to the element in the file.

docs.title: 8. The validate-fix-validate loop
docs.text:
Before you publish or share a DDI file, follow this loop:

  1. Validate with doc.validate().
  2. Read each issue's message and context.
  3. Fix the cause in your document.
  4. Validate again, and go back to step 2 until the list is empty.
  5. Save the file.

Fix the language tag from section 7, validate again, and save:

q_income.question_texts[-1].lang = "fr-CA"

issues = doc.validate()
print(f"Issues: {len(issues)}")  # -> Issues: 0

doc.save("household-survey.xml")

Step 4 is not a formality. A fix can be wrong, and the validator does not always report every problem at once: when one error stops it checking the rest of an element, the next problem shows up only after you fix the first. Run doc.lint() as well, since validation does not see broken references (section 6).

Scenario

A survey team is preparing a household survey for publication. They need to tag some questions with sensitivity levels and data sources. Before publishing, they must remove a question they dropped, validate the document, fix any issues, and save a clean file.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (O1) Create a study with 3 questions: "How old are you?", "What is your household income?", and "What is your full name?". Set "sensitivity" = "high" on the income question. On the name question, set "sensitivity" = "high" and "data_source" = "self-reported", and print its properties. Then remove "data_source", print what remove_property() returns, and print the properties again.

    Expected output:

    {'sensitivity': 'high', 'data_source': 'self-reported'}
True
{'sensitivity': 'high'}
    Answer 
    import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="research.org")
q_age = doc.add_question(text="How old are you?")
q_income = doc.add_question(text="What is your household income?")
q_name = doc.add_question(text="What is your full name?")

q_income.set_property("sensitivity", "high")
q_name.set_property("sensitivity", "high")
q_name.set_property("data_source", "self-reported")
print(q_name.properties)
# -> {'sensitivity': 'high', 'data_source': 'self-reported'}

print(q_name.remove_property("data_source"))  # -> True
print(q_name.properties)  # -> {'sensitivity': 'high'}

  2. (O2) Add a variable named Age for the age question. Find it by its identifier and print its name. Then predict what doc.find("not-an-identifier") returns, and print it to check.

    Expected output:

    Found: Age
None
    Answer 
    v_age = doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q_age)

found = doc.find(v_age.identifier)
print(f"Found: {found.names[0].text}")  # -> Found: Age
print(doc.find("not-an-identifier"))  # -> None

    doc.find() returns None when nothing matches; it does not raise an error.

  3. (O3) Remove the name question and print the new question count. Then call doc.remove() again with the same identifier and print what it returns.

    Expected output:

    Questions: 2
False
    Answer 
    doc.remove(q_name.identifier)
print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")  # -> Questions: 2
print(doc.remove(q_name.identifier))  # -> False

    The second call finds nothing to remove, so it returns False.

  4. (O3) Remove the age question, which the Age variable refers to. Run doc.lint() and print the rule of each error. Fix the broken reference by dropping it from the variable, then print the number of lint errors.

    Expected output:

    ddi.reference.integrity
Lint errors: 0
    Answer 
    doc.remove(q_age.identifier)

for finding in doc.lint():
    if finding.severity == "error":
        print(finding.rule_id)  # -> ddi.reference.integrity

v_age.question_references = [
    ref for ref in v_age.question_references if ref.identifier != q_age.identifier
]
errors = [finding for finding in doc.lint() if finding.severity == "error"]
print(f"Lint errors: {len(errors)}")  # -> Lint errors: 0

    Removing the Age variable too (doc.remove(v_age.identifier)) is also a correct fix, if the variable means nothing without its question.

  5. (O4) The block below puts two mistakes in the income question. Run doc.validate() and print the number of issues and the context of the first one. Fix that cause, and validate again. Repeat until there are no issues, then save the document as household-clean.xml.

    from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

q_income.question_texts.append(
    InternationalString(text="Revenu du ménage ?", lang="fr_CA")
)
q_income.version = "1.a"

    Expected output:

    Issues: 1
<r:Version> 1.a
Issues: 1
<d:Text> Revenu du ménage ?
Issues: 0
    Answer 
    issues = doc.validate()
print(f"Issues: {len(issues)}")  # -> Issues: 1
print(issues[0].context)  # -> <r:Version> 1.a

# A version is numbers separated by dots
q_income.version = "1.1"
issues = doc.validate()
print(f"Issues: {len(issues)}")
print(issues[0].context)  # -> <d:Text> Revenu du ménage ?

# A language tag uses a hyphen, not an underscore
q_income.question_texts[-1].lang = "fr-CA"
issues = doc.validate()
print(f"Issues: {len(issues)}")  # -> Issues: 0

doc.save("household-clean.xml")

    The first run reports only the version. The language tag shows up once the version is fixed, which is why you validate again after every fix.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O1): What does print(q.properties) show after these two calls?

q.set_property("sensitivity", "high"), then q.set_property("sensitivity", "low").

A. {'sensitivity': 'high'}

B. {'sensitivity': ['high', 'low']}

C. {'sensitivity': 'low'}

D. An error, because the key already exists.

Answer
