report = conform(ddi.read_ddi("pet-instrument.xml"), spec, module="pets")
print(report.summary)  # -> {'error': 4, 'warning': 3, 'info': 1}

What the rules in this module mean (the full list is in Check a questionnaire against a spec):

Rule Severity What it means spec.gate.missing error The spec gates something the instrument shows to everyone. spec.gate.different error The gates differ; both normal forms are shown. spec.domain.type error The response domain is of another kind, or missing. spec.language.missing warning A text or label lacks one of the spec's languages. spec.item.extra warning The instrument has a question the spec does not list there. spec.gate.unverifiable warning The stored gate cannot be read back. Check it by hand. spec.edit.unverifiable info Where the instrument stores edit checks is not known. Check them by hand.

Errors are differences to resolve; warnings and info say what is extra or what was not compared. A clean run means 0 errors, not 0 findings.

The draft stores its gate as plain text, set with set_condition() in Module 10. ddi conform reads gates in the forms that questionnaire tools store; it cannot read this one back, so it says so with a warning rather than guess.

Spec or instrument? For each error, ask which of the two says what the survey needs. The spec is the record, so the instrument is usually the one to fix. But a spec can be wrong too: a question added on purpose that nobody wrote into the spec, or a bound typed wrong. Then fix the spec, give it a new version, and run the check again.

docs.title: 7. Version the change
docs.text:
A DDI reference names one exact version of an item (Module 15). When you fix an item, it gets a new version, so every item that refers to it must be revised to point at the new version, and so on up to the instrument. Items that refer to nothing you changed keep their versions. A new item, such as a new gate, starts at its first version, and the item that now refers to it is revised.

For example, fixing the condition of Ask PetName changes that IfThenElse. The pets sequence refers to it, so it is revised; the main sequence refers to pets, and the instrument refers to the main sequence, so both are revised too. The household sequence and the questions keep their versions.

Make the whole fix one release: one date (versionDate) and one responsibility (the person who made it) for every new and revised item, as in Module 15. Then run ddi conform again on the new version, and keep its output with the release.

docs.title: 8. Spec-writing checklist
docs.text:
• Every module and question has an id that does not depend on its number.
  • Every question has a domain, with bounds where the answer has bounds.
  • Every "go to" is a gate on what it skips; every "otherwise" is a second gate.
  • For each gate, you decided what happens when an answer is missing.
  • Every edit's when is the error, its message is in each language, its severity is set.
  • No variable has a language suffix.
  • ddi spec validate passes, and ddi conform reports 0 errors.
  • A copy of the spec with one gate or bound changed gives exactly one new error.

Scenario

The Pet survey team sends you a specification document and a spreadsheet of variables. Section 1 says: "Q1 How many pets live here? (0 to 20). If 0, go to Section 3." Section 2 says: "Q2 What kind of pet is it? (Dog, Cat, Bird). Q3 What is its name? (text, up to 50 characters; ask if Q2 is answered). Q4 How old is it? (0 to 40 years). If Q4 > 10, ask Q5 (vet visits last year, 0 to 50), otherwise ask Q6 (number of toys, 0 to 99)." Section 3 says: "Q7 When did you last visit a vet? (a date)." The spreadsheet lists KindText_en and KindText_fr for the pet kind piped into Q3's text, and an edit: "Q4 over 30: please confirm."

Your task: decide what each gate does with a missing answer, write the spec, and check an instrument against it.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (O2) Write the gates for Q5 and Q6 of the scenario. Q6 must show when the age is missing. Check their normal forms. Then predict whether the scenario's edit, when: PetAge > 30, fires for a pet aged 35, a pet aged 12, and a pet with no age.

    Expected output:

    PetAge > 10
not PetAge > 10
    Answer

    Q5 is PetAge > 10. Q6 shows when Q5 does not, including a missing age, so it is not PetAge > 10 (or, saying the same out loud, PetAge <= 10 or missing(PetAge); pick one form and keep it).

    print(normal("PetAge > 10"))  # -> PetAge > 10
print(normal("not PetAge > 10"))  # -> not PetAge > 10

    Had Q6 been PetAge <= 10, a respondent with no age would see neither Q5 nor Q6.

    The edit fires for 35 only. For 12 the comparison is false, and for a missing age a comparison is always false. To flag a missing age, you would write a second edit with when: missing(PetAge).

  2. (O3) A specification document for a housing survey says: "H1 Do you own your home? (1 Yes, 2 No). If No, go to H4. H2 How many years ago did you buy it? H3 Do you have a mortgage? H4 How many rooms are there?" The questions' ids are Own, YearsOwned, Mortgage and Rooms. (a) Write the gate on H2 and H3 that does exactly what the jump says, including when H1 has no answer. (b) The survey owner says H2 and H3 are for owners only. Write that gate. Check both with normal().

    Expected output:

    not Own = 2
Own = 1
    Answer

    (a) The jump fires only on "No". A respondent who did not answer H1 does not jump, so sees H2 and H3: the gate is not Own = 2. (b) Owners only: Own = 1. The two differ only when H1 has no answer, so write the one the survey means. H4 has no gate: everyone sees it.

    print(normal("not Own = 2"))  # -> not Own = 2
print(normal("Own = 1"))  # -> Own = 1

  3. (O4) Replace KindText_en and KindText_fr with one variable, and write the YAML of the code list it uses.

    Answer

    The pet kind comes from a closed list, so it is a code: the question PetKind itself, with the code list Species, whose labels are in English and French. Q3's English text pipes in PetKind, and so does its French text; each shows the label of its language (check once that your tool's piped text shows labels). No derived variable is needed, since the answer already is the value.

    code_lists:
  Species:
    values:
      1: {en: Dog, fr: Chien}
      2: {en: Cat, fr: Chat}
      3: {en: Bird, fr: Oiseau}

  4. (O1) Write my-pets.spec.yaml for the scenario: three modules (household, pets, visits), the seven questions with their domains, the gates of the pets module, of Q3 and of exercise 1, and the edit as a soft check. Name the questions PetCount, PetKind, PetName, PetAge, VetVisits, Toys and LastVisit. Run ddi spec validate my-pets.spec.yaml.

    Expected output:

    my-pets.spec.yaml: the spec 'my-pets' is valid: 3 module(s), 7 question(s), 1 edit(s).
    Answer 
    spec: my-pets
version: "1"
languages: [en, fr]

code_lists:
  Species:
    values:
      1: {en: Dog, fr: Chien}
      2: {en: Cat, fr: Chat}
      3: {en: Bird, fr: Oiseau}

modules:
  - id: household
    questions:
      - id: PetCount
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 20, decimals: 0}}

  - id: pets
    gate: PetCount > 0
    questions:
      - id: PetKind
        domain: {code: {list: Species}}
      - id: PetName
        domain: {text: {max_length: 50}}
        gate: answered(PetKind)
      - id: PetAge
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 40, decimals: 0}}
      - id: VetVisits
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 50, decimals: 0}}
        gate: PetAge > 10
      - id: Toys
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 99, decimals: 0}}
        gate: not PetAge > 10

  - id: visits
    questions:
      - id: LastVisit
        domain: {date: {type: Date}}

edits:
  - id: age_over_30
    when: PetAge > 30
    module: pets
    message:
      en: Is the pet really over 30?
      fr: L’animal a-t-il vraiment plus de 30 ans ?
    severity: warning

    "If 0, go to Section 3" becomes the gate of the module it skips, pets. If ddi spec validate reports a problem, its path says where: modules[1].questions[2] is the third question of the second module.

  5. (O5) Build the draft instrument of section 6 if you have not, and run ddi conform pet-instrument.xml --spec pet-survey.spec.yaml --module pets --format table. For each finding, say whether the spec or the instrument is wrong, and what to change. The survey owner tells you PetColour was added on purpose this wave. Then list the items that get a new version when you add PetAge's French text and the module gate.

    Expected output: the table of section 6, ending with:

    4 error(s), 3 warning(s), 1 info.
    Answer Finding Wrong What to change spec.gate.missing (module pets) instrument Show pets only when PetCount > 0: wrap it in an IfThenElse with that condition. spec.domain.type (PetKind, PetName, PetAge) instrument The draft's questions have no response domain. Give PetKind the Species codes, PetName text up to 50 characters, PetAge a number from 0 to 40. spec.gate.unverifiable (PetName) neither Check by hand: the draft's condition reads answered(PetKind), the spec's gate. Nothing to change. spec.language.missing (PetAge) instrument Add the French text of the question. spec.item.extra (PetColour) spec It was added on purpose: add PetColour and its domain to the pets module of the spec, and give the spec a new version. spec.edit.unverifiable (age_range) neither Not compared. Check the edit in the instrument by hand.

    Items with a new version after the two fixes: PetAge's question (new text); the PetAge construct, which refers to it; the pets sequence, which refers to the construct; the new IfThenElse for the module gate, at its first version; the main sequence, which now refers to that IfThenElse instead of to pets; and the instrument. The household sequence, the other questions and constructs, and Ask PetName keep their versions. All new and revised items share one versionDate and one responsibility.

  6. (O2, O5) For an instrument whose gates it can read, ddi conform reports: spec.gate.different Toys Question Toys is gated by PetAge <= 10; the spec says not PetAge > 10. Which one is right, and what do you change?

    Answer

    The scenario says Q6 shows when Q5 does not, so a missing age must show Q6: the spec (not PetAge > 10) is right. Change the instrument's gate. The two gates differ only for a missing age, which is why equivalent() and ddi conform treat them as different.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 (O2): PetAge has no answer. Which gate is true?

A. PetAge > 30

B. PetAge <= 30

C. not PetAge > 30

D. PetAge != 30

Answer

C. A comparison is false without an answer, so A, B and D are false, and not turns A's false into true.

Question 2 (O2): An edit check has when: PetAge > 30. A respondent skips PetAge. Does the check fire?

A. Yes: a missing answer is an error.

B. No: a comparison is false without an answer. To flag a missing age, write an edit with when: missing(PetAge).

C. Only if its severity is error.

D. Only in the French version.

Answer

B. The check fires when when is true, and PetAge > 30 is false when there is no answer.

Question 3 (O3): The document says: if Q4 > 10 ask Q5, otherwise Q6. A respondent with no age must see Q6. Which gate do you write for Q6?

A. PetAge <= 10

B. No gate: an else branch is enough.

C. PetAge < 10

D. not PetAge > 10

Answer

D. not PetAge > 10 is true when PetAge > 10 is false, including when the age is missing. A and C are false on a missing age (and C also hides Q6 from a pet aged exactly 10). A second gate reads the same in every tool, which an else branch does not.

Question 4 (O4): Why does a month need no language-specific copies of its variable?

A. A code's label is stored in each language, and piped text shows the label of the language in use.

B. Months are numbers.

C. French has no month names.

D. The data file holds both.

Answer

A. One code, two labels, one variable.

Question 5 (O1): ddi spec validate prints this. What do you fix? 
my.spec.yaml: modules[0].questions[1].domain.numeric: min is greater than max

A. The name of the first module.

B. The bounds of the second question of the first module.

C. The gate of the first question.

D. Nothing: it is a warning.

Answer

B. Positions count from 0, so modules[0].questions[1] is the second question of the first module, and its numeric min is above its max. ddi spec validate reports problems, not warnings: the spec does not load until you fix it.

Question 6 (O5): ddi conform reports 0 errors and 12 warnings. Is the instrument right?

A. No: warnings are errors.

B. Only if the warnings drop to 0.

C. It cannot tell.

D. Yes, as far as the spec says; the warnings say what is extra or was not compared.

Answer

D. Read the warnings: a shared module that another spec covers is a typical one, and an unverifiable gate needs a check by hand. To be sure the check is live, change one gate in a copy of the spec and expect exactly one new error.

Question 7 (O5): ddi conform reports spec.item.extra for PetColour, which the survey owner added on purpose. What do you change?

A. Remove PetColour from the instrument.

B. Nothing: warnings can be ignored.

C. Add PetColour to the spec and give the spec a new version.

D. Rename PetColour so it is not found.

Answer

C. Here the spec is the one that is wrong: it does not list a question the survey needs. Fix the record, version it, and run the check again.

Question 8 (O5): You fix the condition of the IfThenElse that gates PetName, inside the pets sequence. Which items get a new version?

A. The IfThenElse, the pets sequence, the main sequence and the instrument.

B. Only the IfThenElse.

C. Every item in the instrument.

D. Only the instrument.

Answer

A. The changed item and every item that refers to it, up to the instrument. Items that refer to nothing you changed, such as the household sequence, keep their versions.

docs.title: When your tool cannot say it
docs.text:
A questionnaire tool stores each gate in a form it can run. Many have a condition editor with a fixed set of operators, and fall back on code in a scripting language for anything else. A gate the editor holds stays editable by spec writers; a gate in code needs a programmer to change it. So write gates the editor can hold, as long as the meaning stays exactly the same.

Start from the operators the tool's documentation lists. An operator the documentation lists can be used as it describes; one you have only seen in an exported file is a guess. Documentation can be incomplete too: it may name an operator without saying what it does with a missing answer, and then a gate that depends on it should be checked in a preview.

Suppose your tool's editor offers =, >, "is empty", "is refused" and "any of" for a coded question, joined by and or or, and nothing else. Three rewrites keep the meaning exactly and let more gates fit:

  1. Drop an answer test a comparison already implies. answered(PetAge) and PetAge > 30 needs "is not empty", which the editor lacks. Its normal form (section 2) is PetAge > 30, which fits.
  2. Read a choice among one question's codes as one "any of". In PetCount > 1 and (PetKind = 1 or PetKind = 2), the part in parentheses is "PetKind is any of 1, 2": one condition, joined to the other by and.

  3. Use a value set the spec declares. HasPets is declared with the values 0 and 1, so HasPets != 1 is HasPets = 0. The expressions alone cannot tell you that:

    print(equivalent("HasPets != 1", "HasPets = 0"))  # -> False
print(spec.derived_variables[0].values)  # -> ('0', '1')

    The values come from the spec, so the rewrite is yours to make. Note beside the gate where the values come from, so whoever changes them knows to change the gate too.

Anything else stays in the tool's code, and that is fine: it is still exact. What you must never do is guess an undocumented part of a tool's format, an operator number say, to force a gate into the editor. A wrong guess is a wrong gate that looks right. If a gap matters, report it to the tool's maker with a fictional example, and keep the code until the answer comes.

Optional exercise. Your tool's editor offers what the paragraph above assumes. Which of these can it hold, after an exact rewrite where one exists? PetCount > 2, PetKind = 1 or PetKind = 3, answered(PetName), PetCount < 2, answered(PetCount) and PetCount > 2.

Answer
  • PetCount > 2: yes, as written.
  • PetKind = 1 or PetKind = 3: yes, as "PetKind is any of 1, 3".
  • answered(PetName): no. It is "not empty and not refused", and the editor has no "not". It stays in code.
  • PetCount < 2: yes, after a rewrite. The spec declares PetCount a whole number from 0, so PetCount < 2 is PetCount = 0 or PetCount = 1.
  • answered(PetCount) and PetCount > 2: yes. Its normal form drops the answer test.
domain = spec.module("household").questions[0].domain
print(domain.minimum, domain.maximum, domain.decimals)  # -> 0 20 0
print(normal("answered(PetCount) and PetCount > 2"))  # -> PetCount > 2

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can write a YAML spec for a short survey that ddi spec validate accepts with no errors. (O1)
  • I can predict whether a gate or an edit check is true when an answer is missing, and write the condition I mean. (O2)
  • I can rewrite "go to" and "otherwise" instructions as gates. (O3)
  • I can replace language-specific copies of a variable with one variable whose code list has labels in both languages. (O4)
  • I can run ddi conform, decide whether the spec or the instrument is wrong for each finding, and list the items that need a new version. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Start with the missing-answer table in section 2 on the board. Ask the room to fill in the last row before you show it; most people get not PetAge > 30 wrong.
  • Bring a real page of a specification document if you have one, with its jumps and "otherwise". Translating one page into gates together is the best exercise in the module.
  • Before learners run ddi conform in section 6, ask them to predict its findings from the draft's code. The problems are there on purpose: no module gate, no response domains, no French text for PetAge, an extra question.
  • Learners used to spreadsheets ask for one variable per language out of habit. Show the code list with two labels and the piped text in both languages.
  • Section 7 applies Module 15; if learners are fresh from it, go fast.
  • The Going further section is where tool knowledge meets spec writing. Stress that a gate kept in the tool's own code is a correct answer, and that guessing an undocumented format is the one thing never to do.

See also: Module 10: Questionnaire flows | Check a questionnaire against a spec

docs.title: Module 17: Real-world capstone projects
docs.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Write a project plan for your track's dataset: one row per column with its question (or why it has none), its type and its code list, plus the techniques your track needs.
  • O2. Build the DDI document from the data with ddi-l, so that each asked column is a variable linked to its question, coded columns use code lists with categories, and the study has concepts and a universe.
  • O3. Validate and lint your document so that doc.validate() returns no errors, doc.lint() reports no error, and ddi validate passes on every file you save.
  • O4. Record the questionnaire flow, lineage, linkage, custom fields or specification your track asks for, so that a reader of the XML can follow it without your script.
  • O5. Version a change: increment the version, record a rationale and who is responsible, and save each version to its own file.
  • O6. Present your project in 5 minutes and justify two design choices, naming for each the option you rejected and why.

Prerequisites: All previous modules, from Module 1 to Module 16. The table under "Choose your track" lists the modules each track leans on most.

Time: 60-90 min self-paced / 90 min instructor-led.

New in this module: nothing new. You combine what earlier modules taught, such as ddi.new_study(), doc.add_variable(), set_coded(), source_variable_references, doc.add_comparison(), set_property(), doc.lint(), load_spec(), ddi validate and ddi spec validate.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
You have now learned all the tools. You know how to create DDI documents, add metadata, validate files, manage versions, and use the command line. Now it is time to put everything together in a real project.

Choose the track that matches your role. Each track walks you through a complete workflow: plan the metadata, build it from a data file, record what your track needs, validate it, version it, and present your choices.

If you are not sure which track to pick, try Track A (University Student). It is the simplest starting point.

docs.title: Choose your track
docs.text:
Every track practises all six objectives. They differ in the data and in the techniques you record for objective O4:

Track For Data Techniques for O4 Modules to review A University students thesis-data.csv: 40 students, 12 columns Lineage: a derived stress index 11 B Researchers health-survey.csv: 40 respondents, 15 columns Lineage (body mass index) and linkage to a hospital register 11, 12 C Archivists Three small DDI files from three research teams Custom fields from a catalog, with an audit 6, 13, 14 D National statistical office staff census-data.csv: 55 people in 20 households, 22 columns Questionnaire flow and a specification 10, 16

docs.title: Plan your project
docs.text:
(O1) Good metadata starts on paper. Before you write any code, write a plan: a short table with one row per column of your data file, and a few lines under it. The plan is your first deliverable. It also saves time, because most mistakes in a capstone come from deciding these things halfway through the code.

For each column, decide:

  • Question: the exact wording the respondent saw, or why there is none. An identifier such as a student ID is assigned, and a score can be computed. Neither gets a question.
  • Type: numeric, coded (one answer from a fixed list), text, or date.
  • Code list: for a coded column, the list of allowed answers.
  • Concept: the idea the column measures, such as "Well-being".

Here are four rows of a plan for Track A:

Column Question, or why there is none Type Code list Concept StudentID None: assigned by the researcher Text None None Gender "What is your gender?" Coded Female, Male, Non-binary Demographics StressLevel "On a scale of 1 to 10, how stressed have you felt this term?" Numeric, 1 to 10 None Well-being AnxietyScore None: computed from a standard anxiety scale Numeric None Well-being

Under the table, write three short notes:

  • Techniques: which techniques your track needs (see the table above), and where each one applies. For Track A: "StressIndex is derived from StressLevel and AnxietyScore."
  • Versions: what changes in the next version, and why.
  • Two design choices you will present at the end (see "Present your project" below). For example: why Program is coded rather than free text.

docs.title: Track A: University Student: Document Your Thesis Dataset
docs.text:
Scenario

You just finished your thesis on student stress. Your dataset has 12 columns. You need to create a DDI document so your university's research repository can catalog your data.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. (O1) Plan the project. Download the sample thesis dataset (40 students, 12 columns) or use your own CSV file with at least 10 columns. Fill in the plan table for every column.

    Download thesis-data.csv

  2. (O2) Create a DDI study:

    import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="Student Stress Survey 2024",
    agency="university.example.org",
)

  3. (O2) Add variables from your CSV columns. Create one variable for each column. Link each variable to the question it came from. An identifier such as StudentID is assigned, and AnxietyScore is computed, so neither needs a question.

    q1 = doc.add_question(text="How many hours do you study per day?")
v1 = doc.add_variable(name="StudyHours", question=q1)
q2 = doc.add_question(
    text="On a scale of 1 to 10, how stressed have you felt this term?"
)
stress = doc.add_variable(name="StressLevel", question=q2)
# AnxietyScore is computed from a standard scale, so it has no question.
anxiety = doc.add_variable(name="AnxietyScore")
# Repeat for each column...

  4. (O2) Add 3 concepts and 1 universe:

    c1 = doc.add_concept(name="Academic Workload")
c2 = doc.add_concept(name="Mental Health")
c3 = doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
u1 = doc.add_universe(name="Undergraduate students aged 18-25")

  5. (O2) Add a code list with categories for each coded column. A code list is the set of allowed answers. Each answer is a category (its meaning) and a code (the value stored in the data) that points at the category. set_coded() tells the variable which code list holds its values.

    from uuid import uuid4

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem

gender_codes = doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")
for number, label in enumerate(["Female", "Male", "Non-binary"], start=1):
    category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
    gender_codes.codes.append(
        CodeItem(
            agency=gender_codes.agency,
            identifier=str(uuid4()),
            version=gender_codes.version,
            value=str(number),
            category=category.to_reference(),
        )
    )

q3 = doc.add_question(text="What is your gender?")
gender = doc.add_variable(name="Gender", question=q3)
gender.set_coded(gender_codes)
print(f"Gender codes: {len(gender_codes.codes)}")  # -> Gender codes: 3

  6. (O2) Set custom properties on at least 2 items. A custom property is extra metadata you define yourself, like a data source or collection date.

    v1.set_property("dataSource", "Online survey tool")
v1.set_property("collectionDate", "2024-03-15")
anxiety.set_property("scoring", "Sum of a standard 10-item anxiety scale")

  7. (O3) Validate, lint and save as version 1.0:

    errors = doc.validate()
lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"Validation errors: {len(errors)}, lint errors: {len(lint_errors)}")
# -> Validation errors: 0, lint errors: 0
doc.save("thesis-v1.xml")

    Lint may also report warnings, such as an item with no label. Read them, but only errors stop you from saving.

  8. (O4) Record the lineage of a derived variable. Add StressIndex, which combines StressLevel and AnxietyScore. It is computed, not asked, so it has no question. Instead, source_variable_references lists the variables it was computed from.

    stress_index = doc.add_variable(name="StressIndex")
stress_index.source_variable_references = [
    stress.to_reference(),
    anxiety.to_reference(),
]
print(f"StressIndex sources: {len(stress_index.source_variable_references)}")
# -> StressIndex sources: 2

  9. (O5) Version the change. Increment the version to 1.1, and record why and by whom.

    from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_minor_version(allow_dotted=True)
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[
            InternationalString(text="Added the derived StressIndex variable")
        ]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Thesis Author"
print(study.version)  # -> 1.1

  10. (O3) Validate, lint and save as version 1.1:

    errors = doc.validate()
lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
if not errors and not lint_errors:
    doc.save("thesis-v1.1.xml")

docs.title: Track B: Researcher: Package a Health Survey for Publication
docs.text:
Scenario

You lead a multi-country health study. Your data file has 15 columns of survey data. Your team also linked each respondent to a hospital admissions register. You need to package the metadata for an open data repository.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. (O1) Plan the project and read the data. Start from a data file with at least 15 columns. Download the sample health survey (40 respondents, 15 columns) or use your own. Fill in the plan table, then read the column names:

    Download health-survey.csv

    import csv

import ddi_l as ddi

with open("health-survey.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    columns = csv.DictReader(f).fieldnames

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="International Health Survey 2024",
    agency="health-research.example.org",
)
print(f"{len(columns)} columns")  # -> 15 columns

    If your data is in an Excel workbook, read the column names with pandas instead (see Module 8):

    import pandas as pd

columns = list(pd.read_excel("health-survey.xlsx").columns)

  2. (O2) Create the questions and variables from the columns. The first line below creates one question per entry of QUESTIONS. The second creates one variable per column and links it to its question. questions.get(col) gives None for a column with no question, such as RespondentID.

    # Copy the wording from your questionnaire. Columns left out, such as
# RespondentID, become variables without a question.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Age": "How old are you?",
    "SmokingStatus": "Which of these best describes your smoking?",
    "ExerciseFrequency": "How often do you exercise for at least 30 minutes?",
    "SelfRatedHealth": "In general, how would you rate your health?",
    # ...one entry for each column you asked about
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 15

  3. (O2) Add 4 concepts and a universe:

    doc.add_concept(name="Physical Health")
doc.add_concept(name="Mental Health")
doc.add_concept(name="Access to Healthcare")
doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18 and over in the participating countries")

  4. (O2) Add 2 code lists built from the values in the file. A code list is a set of allowed answers (like "Yes", "No", "Unsure"). {row[col] for row in rows} collects the distinct values of a column; each one becomes a category and a code, and set_coded() points the variable at the list.

    from uuid import uuid4

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem

with open("health-survey.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

for col in ["SmokingStatus", "ExerciseFrequency"]:
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col} Codes")
    for number, label in enumerate(sorted({row[col] for row in rows}), start=1):
        category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
        code_list.codes.append(
            CodeItem(
                agency=code_list.agency,
                identifier=str(uuid4()),
                version=code_list.version,
                value=str(number),
                category=category.to_reference(),
            )
        )
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")  # -> Code lists: 2

  5. (O4) Record lineage. Body mass index (BMI) is computed from height and weight. It gets no question; it lists its two sources instead (see Module 11):

    bmi = doc.add_variable(name="BMI", label="Body mass index")
bmi.source_variable_references = [
    variables["HeightCm"].to_reference(),
    variables["WeightKg"].to_reference(),
]

  6. (O4) Record the linkage. Your team joined the survey to a hospital admissions register on RespondentID. Record it as in Module 12: the register is a second study, the key is tagged on both sides, a Comparison maps the keys, and the linked variable names its sources in both studies.

    register = doc.add_study(title="Hospital Admissions Register 2024")
register_ds = doc.study(register.identifier)
register_key = register_ds.add_variable(name="RespondentID")
admissions = register_ds.add_variable(name="HospitalAdmissions")

variables["RespondentID"].set_property("linkage_role", "key")
register_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")

link = doc.add_comparison(name="Survey-to-register linkage 2024")
exact = link.correspondence(
    commonality="The same respondent identifier in both sources.",
    weight=1.0,
)
link.add_variable_map(
    variables["RespondentID"].to_reference(),
    register_key.to_reference(),
    correspondence=exact,
)
link.set_property("linkage_method", "deterministic")

linked = doc.add_variable(name="HealthByHospitalUse")
linked.source_variable_references = [
    variables["SelfRatedHealth"].to_reference(),
    admissions.to_reference(),
]
print(f"Comparisons: {len(doc.comparisons)}")  # -> Comparisons: 1

    When you save, ddi-l warns that a source variable is not in the current document. That is expected: it is in the register study.

  7. (O3) Validate and lint the document:

    errors = doc.validate()
lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"Validation errors: {len(errors)}, lint errors: {len(lint_errors)}")
# -> Validation errors: 0, lint errors: 0

  8. (O3) Save as version 1.0:

    doc.save("health-survey-v1.xml")

    Then export it to JSON from the command line:

    ddi to-json health-survey-v1.xml --indent 2 > health-survey-v1.json

  9. (O5) Update to version 1.1 with a rationale. Add a new variable or fix a label.

    from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

q_dentist = doc.add_question(
    text="How many times did you see a dentist in the last 12 months?"
)
doc.add_variable(name="DentistVisitsLastYear", question=q_dentist)
study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_minor_version(allow_dotted=True)
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[InternationalString(text="Added dental visit frequency question")]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Principal Investigator"
doc.save("health-survey-v1.1.xml")

    Check the new file from the command line with ddi validate health-survey-v1.1.xml.

docs.title: Track C: Archivist: Enrich and Version Existing DDI Files
docs.text:
Scenario

You manage a data collection at a national library. You receive 3 DDI files from different research teams. Some files are missing metadata. You need to check each file, add what is missing, record the archive's own facts about it, and create new versions.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. (O1) Prepare 3 DDI files and plan. Use files from earlier modules, or create 3 small studies now. Your plan has one row per file: what it holds, what is missing, and what you will add.

    import ddi_l as ddi

questions = [
    "How old are you?",
    "How many people live in your household?",
    "Did you vote in the last federal election?",
]
for i, text in enumerate(questions, start=1):
    doc = ddi.new_study(
        title=f"Research Study {i}",
        agency="library.example.org",
    )
    doc.add_question(text=text)
    doc.add_variable(name=f"Var{i}")
    doc.save(f"study-{i}.xml")

  2. (O3) For each file, check completeness. Open the file and list what it contains. The last line counts the variables linked to a question:

    doc = ddi.open_ddi("study-1.xml")
print(f"Questions:  {len(doc.questions)}")
print(f"Variables:  {len(doc.variables)}")
print(f"Concepts:   {len(doc.concepts)}")
print(f"Universes:  {len(doc.universes)}")
print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")
linked = sum(1 for v in doc.variables if v.question_references)
print(f"Variables linked to a question: {linked}")
# -> Variables linked to a question: 0

  3. (O2) Add missing metadata. If a file has no concepts, add one. If it has no universe, add one. If a variable is not linked to its question, link it. If a question has a fixed set of answers, such as the vote question in study 3, add a code list with categories and point the variable at it (the sample solution shows how).

    doc.add_concept(name="Social Sciences")
doc.add_universe(name="General population")

# Link the variable to the question it records
variable, question = doc.variables[0], doc.questions[0]
variable.question_references = [question.to_reference()]

  4. (O4) Add custom fields from a catalog. Your archive records the same facts about every file it accepts. Write them down once as a catalog: one namespace (archive:) and the meaning of each key (see Module 14). Set fields only through a function that checks the catalog, so a typo cannot create a new key. Then audit the file: count the items that carry your fields.

    ARCHIVE_FIELDS = {
    "archive:accession_date": "Date the archive received the file.",
    "archive:depositor": "Team that deposited the file.",
    "archive:retention": "How long the archive keeps the file.",
    "archive:access": "Who may use the data: open, registered or restricted.",
}


def set_archive_field(item, key, value):
    if key not in ARCHIVE_FIELDS:
        raise KeyError(f"{key!r} is not in the archive catalog")
    item.set_property(key, value)


def count_archive_fields(doc):
    items = [doc.study_unit, *doc.questions, *doc.variables]
    return sum(
        any(key.startswith("archive:") for key in item.properties) for item in items
    )


study = doc.study_unit
set_archive_field(study, "archive:accession_date", "2024-11-04")
set_archive_field(study, "archive:depositor", "Research team 1")
set_archive_field(study, "archive:retention", "permanent")
set_archive_field(variable, "archive:access", "open")
print(f"Items with archive fields: {count_archive_fields(doc)}")
# -> Items with archive fields: 2

  5. (O5) Increment the version with a rationale:

    from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

study.increment_minor_version(allow_dotted=True)
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[
            InternationalString(
                text="Enriched metadata: added concept, universe, question link and archive fields"
            )
        ]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Archive Metadata Team"

  6. (O3) Validate, lint and save:

    errors = doc.validate()
lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
if not errors and not lint_errors:
    doc.save("study-1-enriched.xml")
    print("Saved study-1-enriched.xml")  # -> Saved study-1-enriched.xml

  7. Repeat steps 2 to 6 for all 3 files.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• Your plan: one row per file.
  • 3 updated XML files (study-1-enriched.xml, study-2-enriched.xml, study-3-enriched.xml), all valid, each with a version rationale.
  • Your custom-field catalog, and the audit count for each file.
Sample solution

One loop over the three files from step 1.

from uuid import uuid4

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString, VersionRationale
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem

ARCHIVE_FIELDS = {
    "archive:accession_date": "Date the archive received the file.",
    "archive:depositor": "Team that deposited the file.",
    "archive:retention": "How long the archive keeps the file.",
    "archive:access": "Who may use the data: open, registered or restricted.",
}
YES_NO_FILES = {3}  # from the plan: study 3 asks a yes/no question


def set_archive_field(item, key, value):
    if key not in ARCHIVE_FIELDS:
        raise KeyError(f"{key!r} is not in the archive catalog")
    item.set_property(key, value)


def count_archive_fields(doc):
    items = [doc.study_unit, *doc.questions, *doc.variables]
    return sum(
        any(key.startswith("archive:") for key in item.properties) for item in items
    )


for i in (1, 2, 3):
    doc = ddi.open_ddi(f"study-{i}.xml")
    if not doc.concepts:
        doc.add_concept(name="Social Sciences")
    if not doc.universes:
        doc.add_universe(name="General population")
    variable, question = doc.variables[0], doc.questions[0]
    if not variable.question_references:
        variable.question_references = [question.to_reference()]
    if i in YES_NO_FILES:
        yes_no = doc.add_code_list(name="Yes/No")
        for value, label in (("1", "Yes"), ("2", "No")):
            category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
            yes_no.codes.append(
                CodeItem(
                    agency=yes_no.agency,
                    identifier=str(uuid4()),
                    version=yes_no.version,
                    value=value,
                    category=category.to_reference(),
                )
            )
        variable.set_coded(yes_no)

    study = doc.study_unit
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:accession_date", "2024-11-04")
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:depositor", f"Research team {i}")
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:retention", "permanent")
    set_archive_field(variable, "archive:access", "open")

    study.increment_minor_version(allow_dotted=True)
    study.version_rationales.append(
        VersionRationale(
            descriptions=[
                InternationalString(
                    text="Enriched metadata: added concept, universe, question link and archive fields"
                )
            ]
        )
    )
    study.version_responsibility = "Archive Metadata Team"

    lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
    print(
        f"study-{i}: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, "
        f"{len(lint_errors)} lint errors, "
        f"{count_archive_fields(doc)} items with archive fields"
    )
    doc.save(f"study-{i}-enriched.xml")
# -> study-3: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors, 2 items with archive fields

docs.title: Track D: NSO Staff: Build a Census Instrument
docs.text:
Scenario

You work at a national statistics office. Your census team has a large CSV file with 20+ columns. You need to build a complete DDI document, create code lists from the data, describe the questionnaire's flow and write its specification, manage multiple versions, and automate validation with a bash script.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. (O1) Plan the project and read the data. Start from a large CSV with 20+ columns. Download the sample census extract (55 people in 20 households, 22 columns, including the five coded columns used in step 3) or use your own. Fill in the plan table. Note that EmploymentType says "Not applicable" for children: that is a gate, which step 5 records.

    Download census-data.csv

    import csv

import ddi_l as ddi

with open("census-data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    columns = csv.DictReader(f).fieldnames

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="National Census 2024",
    agency="census.example.gov",
)
print(f"{len(columns)} columns")  # -> 22 columns

  2. (O2) Create 20+ variables from the CSV columns, each linked to its question:

    # Wording from the census questionnaire. HouseholdID and PersonNumber are
# assigned, not asked, so they are left out and get no question.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Province": "In which province or territory do you live?",
    "Age": "What was your age at your last birthday?",
    "Gender": "What is your gender?",
    "MaritalStatus": "What is your marital status?",
    "EmploymentType": "Last week, were you an employee, self-employed, or not working?",
    "HousingType": "What type of dwelling do you live in?",
    # ...one entry for each remaining column
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 22

  3. (O2) Build 5 code lists from the values in the file, each with one category and one code per value:

    from uuid import uuid4

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem

with open("census-data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

categorical_cols = [
    "Province",
    "Gender",
    "MaritalStatus",
    "EmploymentType",
    "HousingType",
]
for col in categorical_cols:
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col}Codes")
    for number, label in enumerate(sorted({row[col] for row in rows}), start=1):
        category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
        code_list.codes.append(
            CodeItem(
                agency=code_list.agency,
                identifier=str(uuid4()),
                version=code_list.version,
                value=str(number),
                category=category.to_reference(),
            )
        )
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")  # -> Code lists: 5

  4. (O2) Add concepts, a universe and custom properties. Set custom properties, such as a classification, on at least 2 items:

    doc.add_concept(name="Population")
doc.add_concept(name="Labour")
doc.add_universe(name="All persons usually resident in private dwellings")

variables["Occupation"].set_property("classification", "ISCO-08")
variables["AnnualIncome"].set_property("referencePeriod", "Calendar year 2023")

  5. (O4) Build the questionnaire flow. Everyone answers the person questions. Only people aged 15 and over answer the labour questions. Build the flow as in Module 10: a QuestionConstruct for each question, a Sequence for each section, an IfThenElse for the gate, and an Instrument that points at the main sequence.

    from ddi_l.models.datacollection import (
    IfThenElse,
    Instrument,
    QuestionConstruct,
    Sequence,
)

AGE_GATE = "Age >= 15"


def ask(col):
    """A QuestionConstruct that asks the question of column col."""
    return doc.add_item(
        QuestionConstruct, name=col, question_reference=questions[col].to_reference()
    )


person = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="person",
    control_construct_references=[
        ask("Age").to_reference(),
        ask("Gender").to_reference(),
    ],
)
labour = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="labour",
    control_construct_references=[ask("EmploymentType").to_reference()],
)
gate = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Working-age gate")
gate.set_condition(AGE_GATE, description="Persons aged 15 and over")
gate.then_construct_reference = labour.to_reference()

main = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Census flow",
    control_construct_references=[person.to_reference(), gate.to_reference()],
)
instrument = doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Census 2024 questionnaire")
instrument.control_construct_reference = main.to_reference()
print(f"Instruments: {len(doc.items(Instrument))}")  # -> Instruments: 1

  6. (O4) Write the specification. A spec says what the instrument must contain: its modules, their questions and the gates (see Module 16). Write it to a file, load it, and check that its gate says the same as the instrument's.

    from pathlib import Path

from ddi_l.spec import equivalent, load_spec

SPEC = """\
spec: census-2024
version: "1"
code_lists:
  Employment:
    values: {1: Employee, 2: Self-employed, 3: Unemployed, 4: Not in labour force}
modules:
  - id: person
    questions:
      - id: Age
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 120, decimals: 0}}
  - id: labour
    gate: Age >= 15
    questions:
      - id: EmploymentType
        domain: {code: {list: Employment}}
"""
Path("census.spec.yaml").write_text(SPEC, encoding="utf-8")

spec = load_spec("census.spec.yaml")
labour_gate = spec.module("labour").gate_text
print(labour_gate, equivalent(labour_gate, AGE_GATE))  # -> Age >= 15 True
print(equivalent(AGE_GATE, "not Age < 15"))  # -> False

    Decide what the gate does when Age has no answer, and write it in your plan. Age >= 15 is false when Age is missing, so a person with no age skips the labour questions. not Age < 15 would ask them, which is why equivalent() says the two differ. "Not applicable" is not in the spec's code list: it is what the data holds for people the gate skipped.

    Check the spec file from the command line too:

    ddi spec validate census.spec.yaml

  7. (O3) Validate, lint and save as version 1.0:

    errors = doc.validate()
lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"Validation errors: {len(errors)}, lint errors: {len(lint_errors)}")
# -> Validation errors: 0, lint errors: 0
doc.save("census-v1.xml")

  8. (O5) Update to version 1.1: add a new question and variable:

    from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

q_internet = doc.add_question(text="Do you have access to high-speed internet?")
doc.add_variable(name="HighSpeedInternet", question=q_internet)
study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_minor_version(allow_dotted=True)
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[InternationalString(text="Added internet access question")]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Census Content Team"
doc.save("census-v1.1.xml")

  9. (O5) Update to version 2.0: major redesign (add 5 new questions, retire 3 old ones). Retiring a question also retires the variable that recorded its answers; otherwise the variable would keep pointing at a question that is no longer in the file (see Module 15). Retire only questions the flow does not use. A version holds one rationale, so replace the one from version 1.1; census-v1.1.xml keeps it.

    # Add new questions
for text in [
    "What is your primary language at home?",
    "Do you identify as Indigenous?",
    "What is your highest degree?",
    "Do you have a disability?",
    "What is your annual household income?",
]:
    doc.add_question(text=text)

# Retire 3 old questions, and the variables that recorded their answers
for col in ["Province", "MaritalStatus", "HousingType"]:
    doc.remove(variables[col].identifier)
    doc.remove(questions[col].identifier)

study.increment_major_version()
study.version_rationales = [
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[
            InternationalString(
                text="Major redesign: added equity and income questions"
            )
        ]
    )
]
errors = [finding for finding in doc.lint() if finding.severity == "error"]
print(f"Lint errors: {len(errors)}")  # -> Lint errors: 0
print(f"Validation errors: {len(doc.validate())}")  # -> Validation errors: 0
doc.save("census-v2.xml")

  10. (O3) Batch validate all three files from the command line:

    ddi validate census-v1.xml
ddi validate census-v1.1.xml
ddi validate census-v2.xml

  11. (O3) Write a bash script that runs the full pipeline:

    #!/bin/bash
# validate.sh: check the spec, then validate all census DDI files.

echo "=== Checking the spec ==="
ddi spec validate census.spec.yaml

echo "=== Validating census files ==="
for f in census-v*.xml; do
    echo "--- $f ---"
    ddi validate "$f"
    if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
        echo "PASS"
    else
        echo "FAIL"
    fi
    echo ""
done
echo "=== Done ==="

    Make the script executable and run it:

    chmod +x validate.sh
./validate.sh

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• Your plan: one row per column, the three notes, and what the gate does with a missing age.
  • census-v1.xml: version 1.0, valid, with the instrument and its gate.
  • census.spec.yaml: the specification, passing ddi spec validate.
  • census-v1.1.xml: version 1.1, valid, with rationale.
  • census-v2.xml: version 2.0, valid, with rationale.
  • validate.sh: bash script that checks the spec and validates all files.
Sample solution

One complete script, using census-data.csv. Run validate.sh from step 11 after it.

import csv
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString, VersionRationale
from ddi_l.models.datacollection import (
    IfThenElse,
    Instrument,
    QuestionConstruct,
    Sequence,
)
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem
from ddi_l.spec import equivalent, load_spec


def add_codes(doc, code_list, labels):
    """Add one Category and one Code per label, numbered from 1."""
    for number, label in enumerate(labels, start=1):
        category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
        code_list.codes.append(
            CodeItem(
                agency=code_list.agency,
                identifier=str(uuid4()),
                version=code_list.version,
                value=str(number),
                category=category.to_reference(),
            )
        )


def rationale(text):
    return VersionRationale(descriptions=[InternationalString(text=text)])


with open("census-data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
columns = list(rows[0])

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Census 2024", agency="census.example.gov")
# HouseholdID and PersonNumber are assigned, not asked.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Province": "In which province or territory do you live?",
    "Age": "What was your age at your last birthday?",
    "Gender": "What is your gender?",
    "MaritalStatus": "What is your marital status?",
    "RelationshipToHead": "What is your relationship to Person 1?",
    "CountryOfBirth": "In which country were you born?",
    "Citizenship": "Of what country are you a citizen?",
    "MotherTongue": "What language did you first learn at home in childhood?",
    "HighestEducation": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
    "EmploymentType": "Last week, were you an employee, self-employed, or not working?",
    "Occupation": "What was your main kind of work last week?",
    "WeeklyHoursWorked": "How many hours did you work last week?",
    "AnnualIncome": "What was your total income last year?",
    "CommuteMode": "How did you usually get to work last week?",
    "HousingType": "What type of dwelling do you live in?",
    "Tenure": "Is this dwelling owned or rented by a member of this household?",
    "Rooms": "How many rooms are in this dwelling?",
    "YearBuilt": "In what year was this dwelling built?",
    "HouseholdSize": "How many people usually live here?",
    "InternetAccess": "Does this household have access to the internet at home?",
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}

for col in ("Province", "Gender", "MaritalStatus", "EmploymentType", "HousingType"):
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col}Codes")
    add_codes(doc, code_list, sorted({row[col] for row in rows}))
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

doc.add_concept(name="Population")
doc.add_concept(name="Labour")
doc.add_universe(name="All persons usually resident in private dwellings")
variables["Occupation"].set_property("classification", "ISCO-08")
variables["AnnualIncome"].set_property("referencePeriod", "Calendar year 2023")

# The flow: everyone answers the person section; the labour section has a gate
AGE_GATE = "Age >= 15"


def ask(col):
    return doc.add_item(
        QuestionConstruct, name=col, question_reference=questions[col].to_reference()
    )


person = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="person",
    control_construct_references=[ask(c).to_reference() for c in ("Age", "Gender")],
)
labour = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="labour",
    control_construct_references=[
        ask(c).to_reference()
        for c in ("EmploymentType", "Occupation", "WeeklyHoursWorked")
    ],
)
gate = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Working-age gate")
gate.set_condition(AGE_GATE, description="Persons aged 15 and over")
gate.then_construct_reference = labour.to_reference()
main = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Census flow",
    control_construct_references=[person.to_reference(), gate.to_reference()],
)
instrument = doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Census 2024 questionnaire")
instrument.control_construct_reference = main.to_reference()

# The spec of the same flow. A person with no age skips the labour section.
Path("census.spec.yaml").write_text(
    """\
spec: census-2024
version: "1"
modules:
  - id: person
    questions:
      - id: Age
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 120, decimals: 0}}
  - id: labour
    gate: Age >= 15
    questions:
      - id: EmploymentType
        domain: {text: {max_length: 40}}
      - id: Occupation
        domain: {text: {max_length: 60}}
      - id: WeeklyHoursWorked
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 168, decimals: 0}}
""",
    encoding="utf-8",
)
spec = load_spec("census.spec.yaml")
print(f"Gates agree: {equivalent(spec.module('labour').gate_text, AGE_GATE)}")
# -> Gates agree: True

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v1: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
doc.save("census-v1.xml")

# Version 1.1: one question added
q_internet = doc.add_question(text="Do you have access to high-speed internet?")
doc.add_variable(name="HighSpeedInternet", question=q_internet)
study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_minor_version(allow_dotted=True)
study.version_rationales.append(rationale("Added internet access question"))
study.version_responsibility = "Census Content Team"
doc.save("census-v1.1.xml")

# Version 2.0: five questions added, three retired with their variables
for text in [
    "What is your primary language at home?",
    "Do you identify as Indigenous?",
    "What is your highest degree?",
    "Do you have a disability?",
    "What is your annual household income?",
]:
    doc.add_question(text=text)
for col in ("Province", "MaritalStatus", "HousingType"):
    doc.remove(variables[col].identifier)
    doc.remove(questions[col].identifier)
study.increment_major_version()
study.version_rationales = [
    rationale("Major redesign: added equity and income questions")
]

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v2: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
# -> v2: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors
doc.save("census-v2.xml")

docs.title: Present your project
docs.text:
(O6) Finish with a 5-minute presentation to your group. If you work alone, write the same content as a one-page note. Keep to this order:

  1. The data and its readers (30 seconds): what the data is, and who will read the metadata.
  2. The plan (1 minute): show your plan table, and say which techniques your track needed.
  3. The proof (1 minute): run ddi validate on your last file. Show one place in the XML where your technique is recorded, such as a SourceVariableReference, a Comparison, a UserAttributePair or an IfThenElse.
  4. Two design choices (2 minutes): for each one, say what you chose, the option you rejected, and why.
  5. One thing you would change next time (30 seconds).

Choices worth justifying:

  • Coded or free text for a column such as Program or Occupation.
  • Which columns get a question, and which are assigned or computed.
  • A minor or a major version for your change.
  • A custom field, or a field DDI already has.
  • What a gate does when the answer it tests is missing (Track D).

docs.title: Capstone checklist (for all tracks)
docs.text:
Use this checklist to make sure your project is complete:

  • A written plan covers every column (Track C: every file) and names your track's techniques.
  • The document starts from a CSV or Excel file (Track C: from the DDI files you received).
  • Every variable a respondent answered is linked to its question.
  • Coded columns use code lists with categories.
  • At least one concept and one universe are defined.
  • Custom properties are set on at least 2 items.
  • Questionnaire flow (Track D): an Instrument points at a main Sequence that holds an IfThenElse gate.
  • Lineage (Tracks A and B): every derived variable lists its sources in source_variable_references.
  • Linkage (Track B): the register is a second study, the key is tagged on both sides, and a Comparison maps the keys.
  • Custom fields (Track C): every key comes from your catalog, and the audit counts the items that carry one.
  • Specification (Track D): the spec passes ddi spec validate, and its gate matches the instrument's.
  • The version was incremented at least once, with a rationale and a responsibility.
  • Document passes doc.validate() and doc.lint() with no errors.
  • Every saved file passes ddi validate.
  • Two design choices are ready to present.

docs.title: Self-assessment rubric
docs.text:
Use this table to score your own work, or a partner's. The rubric measures the six objectives of this module on your track's data. The maximum score is 100 points.

Criteria Objective Modules Points A plan, written before the code, covers every column and names your track's techniques O1 8 10 Every asked column is a variable linked to its question; assigned and computed columns have none O2 4, 8 10 At least one concept and one universe O2 5 5 Coded columns use code lists with categories O2 9 10 Custom properties on at least 2 items O2 13 5 No errors from doc.validate(), doc.lint() or ddi validate on any saved file O3 3, 7, 13 15 Your track's techniques (next table) O4 10, 11, 12, 14, 16 20 A version change with a rationale and a responsibility, each version in its own file O5 15 10 A 5-minute presentation that justifies two design choices against the options rejected O6 All 15

Track techniques (20 points). Score only the rows for your track. Each track's points add up to 20. Give half the points when a technique is there but incomplete, for example a derived variable that lists one of its two sources.

Technique Module Full points when A B C D Questionnaire flow 10 An Instrument points at a main Sequence, and an IfThenElse gate routes at least one section - - - 10 Lineage 11 Every derived variable lists all its source variables in source_variable_references 20 10 - - Linkage 12 Both sources are studies in one document, the key is tagged on both sides, a Comparison maps the keys, and the method is recorded - 10 - - Custom fields 14 Every key comes from a written catalog with one namespace, and an audit counts the items that carry them - - 20 - Specification 16 The spec passes ddi spec validate, its gates match the instrument's (equivalent()), and the plan says what each gate does with a missing answer - - - 10

Scoring guide:

  • 90-100: Excellent. You can take data from a file to a valid, versioned DDI document, record what your track needs, and explain your choices. The rubric checks these skills on one dataset; it does not test every part of ddi-l.
  • 70-89: Good. For each row where you lost points, review the modules listed beside it.
  • 50-69: Needs practice. Redo the exercises of the modules beside your weakest rows, and try again.
  • Below 50: Start with Track A and work through the steps slowly.

docs.title: Reflection questions
docs.text:
These are open-ended questions. There are no right or wrong answers. Write your thoughts in a notebook or discuss with your group.

  1. What was the hardest part of building your DDI document? What would you do differently next time?

  2. How would you explain DDI to a colleague who has never heard of it? Try to describe it in two or three simple sentences.

  3. Which part of the ddi-l API did you use the most? Why? Think about which methods you called again and again, and what that tells you about your workflow.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
• I can write a plan that gives every column of my dataset its question (or the reason it has none), its type and its code list, and names the techniques my track needs. (O1)
  • I can build the DDI document from the data, with each asked column linked to its question, code lists with categories, concepts and a universe. (O2)
  • I can get no errors from doc.validate(), doc.lint() and ddi validate on every file I save. (O3)
  • I can record the flow, lineage, linkage, custom fields or specification my track needs, and show where it is in the XML. (O4)
  • I can version a change with a rationale and a responsibility, and keep each version in its own file. (O5)
  • I can present my project in 5 minutes and justify two design choices against the options I rejected. (O6)

Instructor notes

  • Let learners choose their track. Self-selection increases engagement. If the group is mixed (students, researchers, archivists, NSO staff), encourage small groups by role.
  • Plan first. Ask to see each plan before learners write code. Ten minutes on the plan saves half an hour of rework.
  • Time management. Track A takes about 60 minutes. Tracks B and D can take 90 minutes or more, because they record two techniques each. Set expectations at the start and let faster learners help slower ones.
  • Peer review. After learners finish, pair them up to review each other's deliverables. Each reviewer should run ddi validate on the other person's files and score them with the rubric.
  • Show-and-tell. End with the presentations: 2-3 learners share their screen and follow the five parts of "Present your project". Focus on the design choices, not just what they built.
  • Common issues: Learners often forget to link variables to questions, skip the version rationale, or append a second rationale to a study that already has one (a version holds one rationale, and the file fails validation). The checklist helps catch these gaps.
  • Extension: Advanced learners can try a second track or combine elements from two tracks (for example, Track B's linkage with Track D's bash scripting).
  • Celebration. This is the final module. Acknowledge the effort learners have put in. Hand out certificates or badges if your organization supports them.

docs.title: Schema conversion benchmark
docs.text: This page outlines a baseline benchmark for converting schema definitions into ddi-l objects. Use it to validate performance changes and to keep regression testing repeatable.

docs.title: Benchmark objective
docs.text:
• Measure the time and memory required to parse, validate, and convert schema sources.
  • Capture the impact of caching, streaming, and batching options.

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
• Include a representative DDI schema bundle and a large sample XML instance.
  • Note the file sizes and any simplifications used for the benchmark run.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Warm up the environment by running a no-op command to load dependencies.
  2. Execute the conversion command against the benchmark dataset.
  3. Repeat runs at least three times and record the median.
  4. Compare results when toggling key options (e.g., caching, parallelism, schema reuse).

docs.title: Metrics to collect
docs.text:
• Wall-clock duration for the full conversion pipeline.
  • Peak memory usage and steady-state footprint.
  • Number of warnings or validation errors encountered.
